questions.question:
A 42-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. He complains of multiple joint pains, including in his hands, feet, wrists, elbows, and knees. He is unable to bend down, which is making it very difficult to continue his job as an electrician. He tells you he was unwell about ten days earlier with a diarrhoeal illness after eating under-cooked chicken. He has knee effusions more marked on the left than the right. An image of his knees is shown below:

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)137 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.4 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)243 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)144 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)118 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)78 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely cause of his arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Reactive arthritis

This man’s recent bout of diarrhoea is most likely related to Campylobacter infection. The rate of reactive arthritis is low at approximately 2.5%, although the prevalence of joint symptoms may be higher, in up to 13 percent of cases. The likelihood of developing reactive arthritis appears to be unrelated to the severity of diarrheal illness. Reactive arthritis is seen more commonly among patients with the HLA-B27 phenotype. Most cases regress spontaneously within six months of onset, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are effective in managing symptoms.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SOA-arthritis.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SOA-arthritis.jpg)

A Gout

Gout is usually characterised by mono-arthritis with redness, swelling, and limitation of movement. It does not fit with the picture seen here with multiple joint pains. NSAIDs, colchicine, or prednisolone are all potential interventions for the treatment of acute gout. Over the longer-term precipitant drugs should be withdrawn if possible, and allopurinol instituted.

B Pyrophosphate arthropathy

Pyrophosphate arthropathy, like gout, is usually characterised by mono-arthritis during an acute episode, most frequently the knee. Knee aspiration with microscopy and crystal examination can help confirm the diagnosis. Crystals have a rhomboid shape and weak positive birefringence on polarised light microscopy.

D Rheumatoid arthritis

The proximity of this patient’s symptoms to the diarrhoeal illness fits better with an episode of reactive arthritis rather than acute onset of rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with positive rheumatoid factor antibodies and/or positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (antiCCP) antibodies.

E Septic arthritis

Septic arthritis tends to affect a single joint only unless it has occurred via haematogenous spread in a condition such as gonococcal infection. In the event that septic arthritis is suspected, joint aspiration for microscopy and culture is the most important investigation. In most cases of septic arthritis, the white cell count exceeds 50 000 cells per µl.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old man presented to clinic with a 3-week history of fever, malaise and a dry cough. He was a dairy farmer who specialised in unpasteurised milk and cheeses. He had no other medical conditions and was otherwise well.

On examination his temperature was 38.4 oC. There was an ejection systolic murmur and hepatomegaly.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Bilirubin27 µmol/L1.7 - 20.5 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)89 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase 67 U/L (AST)10 - 40 U/L
Blood culturesNegative in serial samples separated by time and site
Trans-oesophageal echocardiogramVegetations visible on the aortic valve

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Coxiella endocarditis

Coxiella infection is widespread in domestic and farm animals. It usually spreads between animals by ticks, which act as reservoirs of infection. Infection may be also be spread via unpasteurised milk. It causes fever and malaise, which may progress to pneumonia, hepatitis or. in rare cases, to culture-negative endocarditis, as seen here. Coxiella is usually diagnosed via complement fixation.

B Fungal endocarditis

Fungal endocarditis is a cause of culture-negative endocarditis, but it is extremely uncommon, especially in immunocompetent individuals. In most cases it is associated with cardiac surgery or healthcare settings. This patient is more likely to have Coxiella endocarditis; Coxiella is common in domestic and farm animals and causes a culture-negative endocarditis as seen in this case.

C Libman–Sacks endocarditis

Libman–Sacks endocarditis is a non-infective vegetative endocarditis seen in systemic lupus erythematosus. Therefore although it is a cause of culture-negative endocarditis, it is an unlikely diagnosis in this case as the patient has no history of, or symptoms and signs suggestive of, systemic lupus erythematosus. This patient is most likely to have Coxiella endocarditis as a result of contact with livestock; Coxiella causes a culture-negative endocarditis.

D Staphylococcal endocarditis

It would be unusual not to identify Staphylococcus spp. in serial blood cultures in a patient with vegetative endocarditis, but this patient has culture-negative endocarditis. Coxiella causes a culture-negative endocarditis, and is common amongst farm livestock; this is the most likely diagnosis.

E Streptococcal endocarditis

If a patient had vegetative streptococcal endocarditis, it would be unusual for serial blood cultures to be negative. Instead, it is more likely that this patient has Coxiella endocarditis, which is also consistent with his prodromal illness. Coxiella is a common infection in livestock and can be carried by ticks.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of general malaise, lethargy and difficulty swallowing with some occasional regurgitation of undigested food. He had been living in Bolivia for 6 years as a relief worker.

On examination, his blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, his pulse was 95 bpm and his jugular venous pulse was elevated. He had bilateral basal inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest, and bilateral pitting leg oedema.

Barium swallow revealed a dilated oesophagus.

Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Trypanosoma cruzi

This parasite is spread via the faeces of the reduviid bug, which is left on the skin after the bug feeds and can enter the bloodstream after scratching or rubbing the skin in response to the insect bite. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas’ disease. The acute phase of Chagas’ disease manifests as constitutional symptoms and facial or generalised oedema, and there may be diarrhoea and vomiting, or ECG changes. This is followed by a latent phase and then a chronic phase; this patient has presented in the chronic phase with mega-oesophagus, which is characteristic of Chagas’ disease. Patients may also have megacolon, congestive heart failure and arrhythmias. Diagnosis is by serology, and the patient should have an ECG and echocardiogram to check for cardiac complications. Patients in the chronic phase can be treated with nitroheterocycles if they have been infected for less than 10 years, as in this case.

B Entamoeba histolytica

Entamoeba histolytica is very common in South America where it causes amoebic dysentery, and can also affect the liver. It does not cause mega-oesophagus, as seen in this patient. This patient’s travel history, combined with his signs and symptoms, would be consistent with a diagnosis of Chagas’ disease, which is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi infection.

A Borrelia burgdorferi

Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative bacterium of Lyme disease. It is not found in tropical climates, and therefore is unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s symptoms. Furthermore, Lyme disease has a variety of stages and manifestations, but it does not cause mega-oesophagus, as seen in this patient. Instead, this patient’s travel history and presentation is more consistent with Chagas’ disease, which is caused by infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by the faeces of the kissing bug, left on the skin after the insect has fed.

C Leishmania donovani

This organism causes visceral leishmaniasis and is found in India and Africa, but it is not native to South America. Furthermore, visceral leishmaniasis has a variety of manifestations but would be unlikely to cause mega-oesophagus, as seen in this patient. This patient’s presentation is consistent with Chagas’ disease, which is caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, spread by the faeces of the kissing bug which is left on the skin after feeding.

D Rickettsia rickettsi

This organism causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and is endemic in the USA and parts of South America. It is a tick-borne illness, and has a variety of manifestations but classically causes a petechial rash, beginning on the feet and hands. It does not cause mega-oesophagus, as seen here. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with Chagas’ disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. This causes mega-oesophagus and constitutional symptoms. The parasite is spread by the faeces of the kissing bug, left on the skin after feeding.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man who has recently returned from India presents with bloody diarrhoea and mucus. More recently, he has also developed some abdominal pain and vomiting which has increased over the past few days. His blood pressure 95/70 mmHg and his pulse is 100 bpm and regular.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)16.3 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)756 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Urea11.5 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)56 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)2.7 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)72 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Discharge with advice on rehydration and outpatient appointment
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D IV Fluid and electrolyte replacement

The two most likely diagnoses are infective diarrhoea and ulcerative colitis. The clinical history and laboratory results would be consistent with both. However, given his recent history of abdominal pain and vomiting, the most important diagnosis to exclude is toxic megacolon. He therefore requires fluid and electrolyte replacement, and an abdominal X-ray.

B Discharge with advice on rehydration and outpatient appointment

The extent of his abnormalities of biochemistry, especially hypokalaemia, indicates that he has had severe diarrhoea from his infection and needs inpatient electrolyte correction and fluid support.

A Oral metronidazole

Antibiotics are seldom needed for gastroenteritis. If the patient is systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or elderly. Metronidazole would be a useful treatment for protozoal gastrointestinal infection.

C IV ceftriaxone

As above, antibiotics are not indicated for this patient. Ceftriaxone is a broad-spectrum antibiotic commonly used for meningitis and can be used for typhoid and paratyphoid fever.

E Oral ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin can be used for when Salmonella, Shigella or Campylobacter infection is confirmed as the specific cause of gastroenteritis, however quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but significant risk of debilitating adverse effects. 33192

questions.question:
A 40-year-old Asian man is referred to the Neurology Clinic with a 9-month history of distal sensory loss and weakness. There is no history of headache or visual change and his co-ordination remains intact. He denies any constitutional symptoms or recent infective illnesses. He has a past medical history of diet-controlled type II diabetes and hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 5 mg once daily. On examination, he is systemically well with normal observations. He has visible wasting in the intrinsic muscles of his right foot, with a Medical Research Council (MRC) power of 4/5 for ankle dorsiflexion. There is associated loss of temperature and light touch sensation down the posterolateral aspect of his right leg. The remainder of his neurological examination shows no further motor deficits and his cranial nerves are intact. He has multiple hypopigmented patches over the extensor surfaces of his arms and legs, with associated sensory loss for all but deep pressure stimuli.

What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Skin-slit smear

This patient has leprosy. Leprosy is a granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae which affects the peripheral nerves and skin. Initial symptoms include numbness, typically with loss of temperature followed by light touch, pain and finally deep pressure. Cutaneous lesions follow later in the disease and appear as hypopigmented patches of skin with associated sensory loss. The investigation of choice is a skin-slit smear; a slit is made over a lesion of skin which is then smeared onto a glass slide. It is examined for acid-fast bacilli under microscopy. If detected, the treatment of choice is with dapsone, rifampicin and clofazimine.

D Viral DNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

This patient has leprosy, a granulomatous disease caused by M. leprae. It is detected by examining for the presence of acid-fast bacilli under microscopy. Skin biopsy and M. leprae DNA PCR are alternative methods that can be used to diagnose the disease. However, a viral DNA PCR would not diagnose leprosy, given the disease is caused by a bacterial infection.

A Nerve conduction studies

Nerve conduction studies can be useful to investigate the cause of a peripheral neuropathy and help determine if there is an underlying demyelinating or axonal cause. However, nerve conduction studies do not have a role in diagnosing leprosy.

C Lumbar puncture

A lumbar puncture would be indicated if there were reason to expect that an underlying neurological illness was responsible for this patient’s symptoms, including multiple sclerosis or a central nervous system (CNS) infection. However, it is not needed to make a diagnosis of leprosy.

E Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain

An MRI would be indicated if there were reason to expect that an underlying central neurological illness was responsible for this patient’s symptoms, including multiple sclerosis or a neurodegenerative condition. However, it is not needed to make a diagnosis of leprosy. 72446

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with severe vomiting, which began some 90 minutes after eating rice-based takeaway food that he had the night before. He complains of abdominal cramps, retrosternal pain, and has vomited ten times. He has struggled to keep water down. There is no diarrhoea. His blood pressure (BP) is 100/70 mmHg; his pulse is 98 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is a postural drop of 15 mmHg on standing. He is tender in the epigastrium.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bacillus cereus (B cereus) food poisoning

B cereus is widespread in the environment and commonly found in the soil. It is resistant to heat and desiccation and can grow if food is stored under favourable conditions, (temperature 8-55 oC), and has a pH > 4.8. It is commonly found in rice preparations and can present with either diarrhoeal or vomiting forms – although not with both. The vomiting form occurs due to ingestion of cereulide (a recognised emetic), while the diarrhoeal form occurs due to enterotoxin released in the small bowel. Most people recover without treatment within 24 hours.

E Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus) food poisoning

Staphylococcus food poisoning occurs most commonly when patients ingest bacteria from dairy products (eg fresh cream cakes) which have been left out at room temperature for a considerable period of time. It is the result of staphylococcal enterotoxin ingestion. The onset of vomiting symptoms begins 2 to 8 hours later. Symptoms rapidly resolve after a few hours.

B Norovirus infection

Norovirus infection leads to gastroenteritis with symptoms of nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. It tends to occur in outbreaks during autumn and winter, and symptoms settle without intervention in the majority of patients over a 24 to 48-hour period. Patients may excrete virus up to 48 hours after the cessation of diarrhoea, and so should not return to environments in which they will come into contact with others during this time.

C Rotavirus infection

Rotavirus is a common cause of outbreaks of diarrhoea and vomiting, particularly in children. Severe vomiting and diarrhoea are seen, and symptoms may last between 3 and 8 days in total. Outbreaks may also be seen in elderly care homes. Supportive therapy with oral rehydration/intravenous (IV) fluid replacement may be

required. The patients age, presentation and symptom timeline do not support this diagnosis.

D Salmonella typhi (S typhi) food poisoning

In salmonella infection, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps are a prominent feature, and are often accompanied by fever. Nausea and vomiting may also be seen. The diarrhoea may also be bloody. The illness usually lasts for between 4–7 days and is self-limiting. Antibiotics are not recommended for salmonella infection; they are only used in those with severe comorbidities and where there are features of significant infection with, for example, pre-renal disease.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old Sri Lankan man presented with a 4-week history of cough, intermittent fever, night sweats and malaise. Six weeks previously, he had travelled to Sri Lanka for 2 months to visit his family. He denied haemoptysis or any contacts with tuberculosis.

On examination, his temperature was 38.3 °C and pulse rate was 94 bpm. There was reduced chest expansion on the right, and the right base was dull to percussion, with bronchial breathing above. There was 2-cm, tender hepatomegaly, with an irregular border.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Bilirubin29 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase 27 IU/L (ALT)5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L (ALP)30–130 IU/L
Blood culturesNo growth
Sputum culturesNo growth
CT chest, abdomen, pelvisMulti-loculated, right-sided pleural effusion, 10 × 6 cm hepatic collection
Pleural biopsyNo acid-fast bacilli
the pleural effusion was drained.

Which is the best choice of further treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Co-amoxiclav, clarithromycin and metronidazole

This patient has signs and symptoms suggestive of amoebiasis. Entamoeba histolytica is common in South and South East Asia, and hepatic amoebiasis typically causes constitutional symptoms, as seen here. There is usually tender hepatomegaly and pleural effusions. Empyemas are a common complication. It is common for liver function tests to be normal, or there may be an obstructive picture with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin levels (mildly raised here, but the alanine aminotransferase level is normal). The patient should be

treated with metronidazole, and this can be given as a monotherapy. However, until the diagnosis is confirmed by serology or aspirate polymerase chain reaction (PCR), it would be appropriate to prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy by adding co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin.

D Peginterferon alpha

Peginterferon alpha is the first-line therapy for patients with hepatitis B. Although hepatitis B is endemic in large parts of Asia, its prevalence is low in Sri Lanka. Hepatitis B could certainly present with constitutional symptoms. However, it is highly unlikely that the patient would have a normal alanine aminotransferase level in the context of untreated hepatitis B infection. Hepatitis B increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma but would not cause a collection in the liver, and it does not explain the unilateral pleural effusion. This patient’s presentation is much better explained by an amoebic liver abscess with associated empyema and should be treated with metronidazole (though additional broad-spectrum antibiotics should be continued until the diagnosis is confirmed).

A Co-amoxiclav

This patient has recently returned from Sri Lanka with constitutional symptoms and a swinging fever. He has a collection in the liver and an associated pleural effusion; together with his symptoms, this is suggestive of amoebiasis, and therefore metronidazole should be added to his treatment. It would be appropriate to continue broad-spectrum antibiotics alongside this (ideally co-amoxiclav and a macrolide), until the diagnosis of amoebiasis is confirmed, at which point these can be stopped and metronidazole can be continued as a monotherapy.

B Co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin

This is appropriate therapy for an atypical pneumonia. However, this patient has recently returned from Sri Lanka with constitutional symptoms and a swinging fever. He has a collection in the liver and an associated pleural effusion; together with his symptoms, this is suggestive of amoebiasis, and therefore metronidazole should be added to his treatment. It would be appropriate to prescribe co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin, in addition to metronidazole, until the diagnosis of amoebiasis is confirmed, at which point metronidazole can be continued as monotherapy.

E Rifampicin, isoniazid and ethambutol

These are treatments for tuberculosis. This patient’s malaise and night sweats could be explained by tuberculosis, but tuberculosis does not normally cause a swinging fever (this is more associated with abscesses). Tuberculosis can seed into the liver, but it is uncommon. You would also expect to see acid-fast bacilli on pleural biopsy if this were tuberculosis. A more likely explanation for this patient’s symptoms and investigation findings would be amoebiasis, which is common in Sri Lanka. Amoebiasis explains the liver abscess, and pleural effusions are a common complication. The correct treatment would be metronidazole (though it is reasonable to continue additional broad-spectrum antibiotics until the diagnosis is confirmed).2354

questions.question:
A 33-year-old white man was admitted with a 1-week history of rash, pyrexia, generalised weakness and decreased urine output.

On examination, he was obese, with a temperature of 38.5 °C, BP 156/70 mmHg. He had nail-fold vasculitic skin lesions. On auscultation, he had a soft systolic murmur. Abdominal examination was limited given his size, but unremarkable.

Initial investigations reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)90 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)18.5 × 10 9/4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils16.4 × 10 9/1.5 - 7.0 × 10 9/
Platelets (PLT)80 × 10 9/150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Creatinine (Cr)336 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Urine microscopyRed cell casts
Hepatitis Bnegative
Hepatitis Cnegative
ANCA/GBMnegative
Cryoglobulinspositive
ASOTnegative
Protein electrophoresisnegative
Ultrasound renal scan of the abdomen showed an 11-cm spleen. Renal biopsy was not performed, as it was not technically possible.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Infective endocarditis

The history and investigations are consistent with infective endocarditis. One third of patients with bacterial endocarditis develop AKI. The glomerulonephritis is associated with deposition of immune complexes containing bacterial antigens in glomeruli. Cryoglobulins (polyclonal or type III) are present in 50% of subjects.

A Microscopic polyangiitis

Microscopic polyangiitis may present with nail-fold vasculitic lesions but these patients are commonly ANCA- positive.

C Acute pyelonephritis

The heart murmur, negative urinary sediment and positive cryoglobulins make this unlikely.

D HIV-associated nephropathy

There is no weight loss or lymphopenia. HIVAN occurs almost exclusively in black patients, and they tend to be normotensive.

E Renal tuberculosis

Renal TB is associated with an insidious onset of renal impairment with asymptomatic urinary abnormalities such as persistent sterile pyuria. It may or may not be associated with extrarenal systemic manifestations.70062

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of general malaise, fever up to 38.5 oC and night sweats. For the past 2 days he has had painful mouth ulcers. He returned to the UK 3 weeks previously from Nigeria, where he had been living for several months. On direct questioning, he reported having unprotected sexual intercourse with two local women over the past two months. On examination he had widespread lymphadenopathy. There was no rash. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable.

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)142 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes1.9 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 4.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)190 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
HIV antibodies-
Blood culturesNo growth in 48 h from 2 samples
Thick and thin blood filmNegative in 2 samples
Chest X-rayNormal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C HIV infection

This patient has a prolonged fever, night sweats and widespread lymphadenopathy after unprotected sex; the most likely diagnosis is HIV. HIV antibody can be negative during seroconversion; a p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR test would be a much better diagnostic test for this patient.

A Dengue fever

Typically dengue causes headache and fever in the returning traveller, and sometimes haemorrhagic rashes. However, it is unusual for dengue to cause night sweats, and very unusual for it to cause illness more than 2 weeks after returning from an endemic area. You might expect a higher fever than 38.5°C if this were dengue.

This patient’s symptoms and signs are better explained by HIV seroconversion; this would explain the lymphadenopathy and night sweats. HIV antibody can be negative in seroconversion: p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR would be a better test for this patient.

B Falciparum malaria

This patient has returned from a malaria-endemic area and does have a fever, but he has had two negative blood films for malaria which makes this diagnosis less likely. Malaria does not explain his widespread lymphadenopathy or mouth ulcers. A much more likely diagnosis is HIV seroconversion. HIV antibody can be negative in seroconversion; a much better test would be either p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR.

D Lyme disease

Lyme disease is not endemic in Nigeria. Widespread lymphadenopathy is uncommon in Lyme disease, and this patient does not have any rash. A much better explanation for his symptoms and signs is HIV seroconversion, especially given that he has recently had unprotected sex. HIV antibody can be negative in seroconversion; a much better test would be p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR.

E Typhoid infection

Typhoid results in prolonged high fever in the returning traveller and is caused by Salmonella infection. Classically patients have headache, constipation, high fever and a salmon-pink maculopapular rash. Typhoid would not explain this patient’s widespread lymphadenopathy or mouth ulcers. You might expect a higher fever than 38.5°C if this were typhoid. This patient’s presentation is much better explained by HIV seroconversion. HIV antibody can be negative during seroconversion; a much better test would be p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old student is referred by her general practitioner to the Emergency Department, suffering from pharyngitis, shortness of breath with wheeze and a morbilliform skin rash.

Examination reveals generalised lymphadenopathy; wheeze in the lower zones is confirmed, and some skeletal muscle tenderness to palpation is noted.

Investigations reveal a slightly elevated white blood cell count, with normal urea and electrolytes. The presence of cold agglutinins is noted.

A chest X-ray is shown below.

Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following would be the appropriate antibiotic choice in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Clarithromycin

The answer is Clarithromycin (Option A).

This patient has Mycoplasma pneumonia, which is primarily said to affect school-aged children and young adults. Symptoms include non-exudative pharyngitis, bullous myringitis, skin rashes and wheeze on respiratory examination. Other symptoms and signs may include muscle tenderness, nerve palsies, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and conjunctivitis. Hints as to the diagnosis come from the fact that the chest X-ray, showing extensive left lower lobe pneumonia, appears much worse than the clinical findings and that cold agglutinins are positive. For patients with microbiologically confirmed M. pneumoniae pneumonia, first-line treatment options include macrolides (eg, azithromycin), tetracyclines (eg, doxycycline), and respiratory fluoroquinolones (eg, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). Mycoplasma pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams due to its lack of a cell wall.

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is managed empirically generally, based on severity and suspicion of the cause, before an organism can be cultured. Mild and previously untreated CAP is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, and typical treatment could be oral amoxicillin. Moderate CAP is caused by the above organisms, as well as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and can be managed with oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin. Severe CAP should usually be treated in higher care areas with broad-spectrum antibiotics such as intravenous co-amoxiclav and oral clarithromycin. Clarithromycin has very good oral bioavailability and causes thrombophlebitis if given intravenously and therefore should be given orally, even in severe infections. Atypical CAP can be caused by Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydophilaspecies and Pneumocystis jiroveci. Local guidelines may differ in the progression of antimicrobial choices, due to differences in the prevalence of different infectious organisms. Also, if culture results become available, then these should be used to guide further antibiotic choice.

Image source: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/left-lower-lobe-pneumonia-1?lang=gb (https://radiopaedia.org/cases/left-lower-lobe-pneumonia-1?lang=gb)

C Amoxicillin

Amoxicillin (Option C) is incorrect.

Amoxicillin may be given to this patient with CAP, depending on the severity, as described above. It provides good antimicrobial effect against the main Gram-positive pathogens.

B Penicillin V

Penicillin V (Option B) is incorrect.

Penicillin V is more commonly used for oral infections, including tonsillitis, otitis media, erysipelas and cellulitis. It can also be used prophylactically in the prevention of recurrence of rheumatic fever, prevention of secondary group A streptococcal infection and prevention in asplenism and sickle-cell disease.

D Co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav (Option D) is incorrect.

Co-amoxiclav may be given to this patient with CAP, depending on the severity, as described above. It provides good antimicrobial effect against the main Gram-positive pathogens. Co-amoxiclav is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. Clavulanic acid prevents the breakdown of amoxicillin in some resistant

organisms.

E Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin (Option E) is incorrect.

Ciprofloxacin provides good antimicrobial activity against Pseudomonas species – important pathogens in exacerbations of bronchiectasis and in the immunosuppressed patient – but has little value in treating chest infections without evidence of an underlying chronic lung disease such as bronchiectasis or a previous Pseudomonas infection. Quinolone treatment is also no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but significant risk of debilitating adverse effects. 33184

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man was referred with a four-day history of gradual-onset headache, abdominal pain, constipation and high fevers. He had returned from a holiday in Thailand 10 days previously. He had not gone swimming in any freshwater while he was away. He had sexual intercourse and used barrier methods.

On examination, his temperature is 39.7 °C, pulse 76 bpm and regular and blood pressure 98/60 mmHg. He appeared flushed and lethargic. There was no rash, or axillary or neck lymphadenopathy. His abdomen was mildly tender in the left iliac fossa.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)107 g/L115 - 165 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)83.2 fL80 - 96 fL
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)83 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin34 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)154 U/L5 - 35 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)221 U/L45 - 105 U/L
g-glutamyl transferase264 U/L4 - 35 U/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)298 µg/L< 10 µg/L
Sodium (Na)138 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K)4.4 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.9 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)64 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Typhoid fever

This is an uncommon bacterial infection (Salmonella typhii) and typically causes high fevers, abdominal pain, constipation and headache, as seen in this patient. Classically, patients demonstrate Faget’s sign – a relative bradycardia. Note that despite a temperature of 39.7 °C, this patient has a pulse of 76 bpm, perhaps lower than expected, given the high temperature. Treatment is with ceftriaxone or azithromycin in milder cases.

B Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

Although this patient did have sexual intercourse during his trip, he used barrier protection, which dramatically reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections. HIV seroconversion can cause malaise, low-grade fever, diarrhoea and rash; however, instead this patient has constipation and a high fever, which would not be typically for seroconversion. This patient’s symptoms and signs would be more consistent with typhoid fever.

A Escherichia coli gastroenteritis

E. coli is the most common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller; however, instead, this patient has constipation. This is not a feature of E. coli infection. Although E. coli can cause diarrhoea, leading to dehydration and subsequently headache, you would not expect headache to be an early symptom. It is uncommon for E. coli gastroenteritis to cause such a high fever and high CRP. Instead, this patient’s symptoms and signs would be more consistent with typhoid fever.

C Influenza

The patient does not complain of any coryzal symptoms, and abdominal pain would be atypical for influenza infection. As influenza is a viral infection, you would not expect such a high CRP, as seen in this case, unless there was a secondary pneumonia (of which there is no suggestion in the clinical stem). A high CRP such as this is typical of typhoid fever.

D Schistosomiasis

Schistosomiasis is a flatworm, or fluke, and is typically contracted by swimming in fresh water; this patient has not swum in any lakes or rivers and therefore is unlikely to be exposed to the organism. Schistosoma mekongi is the most common species found in Thailand, and it usually causes intestinal disease, leading to abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea; this patient has constipation. It would not usually cause a headache. Instead this patient’s symptoms and signs would be more consistent with typhoid fever.

questions.question:
A 61-year-old man is admitted to the Respiratory Ward following a 10-day history of high fevers, myalgia and nausea and vomiting. Over the last four days, he has deteriorated with worsening shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. He has a background of alcohol dependence and hypercholesterolaemia and regularly takes atorvastatin 20 mg once daily, vitamin B complex two tablets daily and thiamine 100 mg daily. On examination, he has a temperature of 39.2 °C. His heart rate is 126 bpm and regular and his BP is 155/93 mmHg. He has coarse crackles at the left base of his lungs and is saturating at 94% on 6 litres of oxygen by Venturi mask. His heart sounds are normal, and his abdomen is soft, with no palpable masses.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)136 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)17.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils15.1 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.5 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes0.7 ×10⁹/L0.8–5.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)365 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)146 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea11.3 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)141 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)5060+
C-reactive protein (CRP)194 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely causative organism for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Staphylococcus aureus

This patient has staphylococcal pneumonia. Clues to the diagnosis are the onset of his pneumonia following a period of flu-like symptoms and lymphopenia on the blood results. The most likely cause of pneumonia after infection with the influenza virus is S. aureus.

A Chlamydia psittaci

C. psittaci, an obligate intracellular bacterium can rersult in pneumonia (psittacosis) in approximately 1% of all cases. Most cases occur following contact with birds (turkeys, chickens, cockatiels and various migratory birds) with an incubation period between 5-14 days. Extra pulmonary symptoms are common, such as headache, pharyngitis and diarrhoea. Given the preceding flu like illness, lack of contact with birds and a lack of extra pulmonary features described, C. psittaci is less likely here.

C Klebsiella pneumoniae

K. pneumoniae is a Gram-negative rod that causes pneumonia more commonly in those with a history of diabetes, alcohol excess, poor dental hygiene and other co-morbidities. It is associated with serious complications, including the development of lung abscesses and is associated with high mortality. While this patient has a background of alcohol dependence, the preceding flu-like symptoms and lymphopenia suggest an underlying viral illness, making S. aureus the most likely answer.

D Legionella pneumophila

Legionnaires’ disease is an atypical pneumonia commonly spread via a contaminated water supply. Not only does a patient present with pneumonia, but extrapulmonary symptoms are also seen, including hyponatraemia, deranged liver function tests and neurological symptoms, including confusion and ataxia. These are not seen in this patient’s presentation.

E Mycoplasma pneumoniae

M. pneumoniae is another cause of an atypical pneumonia. Flu-like symptoms are seen in Mycoplasma pneumonia, similarly to this patient’s case presentation. However, Mycoplasma pneumonia can also cause extrapulmonary symptoms such as haemolytic anaemia and erythema multiforme, which are not seen here making it less likely.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of a firm, painless ulcer on the glans penis. He had recently returned from a 3-month trip to Thailand, China, Hong Kong and Australia. He was otherwise well.

Examination revealed an ulcer as described by the patient, with no associated lymphadenopathy.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Syphilis

Painless ulcers, developing 10–90 days after exposure, are typical of syphilis. However, it is worth noting that syphilitic ulcers can be painful and herpetic ulcers can be painless, and therefore this ulcer should be swabbed, and bloods should be taken for an immunoassay to confirm the diagnosis. This patient has presented with primary syphilis; secondary syphilis, which can develop roughly 6 weeks after the skin lesions have appeared, typically consists of constitutional flu-like symptoms and a non-pruritic rash which classically affects the face, palms and soles. This patient should be treated with benzathine penicillin as a single intramuscular dose. Oral azithromycin as a single dose is an acceptable second-line treatment. Fifty per cent of patients with primary syphilis will develop the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction after treatment: flu-like symptoms and rigors which typically self-resolve within 24 h.

D Non-gonococcal urethritis

Non-specific urethritis does not cause genital ulceration, but instead presents with dysuria. Commonly it is caused by chlamydia, though it can be caused by other bacteria or viruses. This patient’s presentation with a painless ulcer is more consistent with syphilis: to confirm the diagnosis the ulcer should be swabbed and bloods should be taken, but he should be treated for syphilis.

A Chancroid

Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a Gram-negative bacterium, Haemophilus ducreyi. It does cause penile ulceration, but you would expect the ulcer to be painful and to have associated lymphadenopathy. There is also typically a purulent exudate. The ulcer described in this patient is much more consistent with a diagnosis of syphilis: classically syphilitic ulcers are shallow and painless. They may or may not be associated with lymphadenopathy. These ulcers should be swabbed, as it is unreliable to make a clinical diagnosis in cases of penile ulcer. However, the patient should be treated for syphilis.

B Genital herpes

Herpetic genital ulcers are typically painful, may be associated with a prodromal mild, flu-like illness and may have associated lymphadenopathy. This painless ulcer is more consistent with syphilis. The ulcer should still be swabbed, and blood should be taken, in order to make a formal diagnosis: clinical diagnosis is unreliable in cases of genital ulcers. However, this patient should be treated for syphilis.

C Gonorrhoea

Gonorrhoea can occasionally cause penile ulcers, but this is a very uncommon presentation. Typically gonorrhoea is either asymptomatic or presents with urethritis (dysuria) and/or purulent penile discharge. This patient’s symptoms and signs are more consistent with syphilis, which typically causes painless ulceration. Making a clinical diagnosis in penile ulceration is difficult, and therefore these ulcers should be swabbed and blood tests should be taken, but this patient should be treated for syphilis. 71042

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), who is poorly compliant with his medication, comes to the Emergency Department. He has been feeling increasingly unwell over the past two to three weeks with fever, shortness of breath, weight loss and diarrhoea up to five times a day. Examination reveals a temperature of 37.9 °C, a pulse of 90 bpm and regular and a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. There is generalised lymphadenopathy, and his body mass index is 21 kg/m². There is tender hepatosplenomegaly. Bilateral basal crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest.

Investigations;

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)98 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
CD4 count4/mm³500–1500 mm³
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)185 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin38 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)182 IU/L30–130 IU/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Mycobacterium avium infection

The constellation of symptoms, including respiratory symptoms, weight loss, diarrhoea, generalised lymphadenopathy and abnormal liver function tests, fit best with a diagnosis of Mycobacterium avium (MAI). Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is now available as an option for confirming the underlying diagnosis. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) should be recommenced, assuming the patient has not been compliant with his medication. Triple therapy with a macrolide, ethambutol and rifabutin is the optimal choice for management of the underlying MAI.

D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

This is an important differential in a patient who has a low CD4 count. It would be important to send this patient for computed tomography (CT) of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis to exclude this as a diagnosis.

A Cryptococcosis

Cryptococcosis is often associated with central nervous system (CNS) infection in HIV and is more rarely associated with diarrhoea, compared to the other options given. Treatment is with intravenous fluconazole.

B Cryptosporidium infection

Cryptosporidium is associated with more profuse watery diarrhoea than that reported here and an increased risk for gall bladder infection. Diagnosis is confirmed using acid staining testing. Treatment is usually supportive, but in patients with HIV, it is imperative that they maintain good compliance with their antiretroviral therapy. Nitazoxanide can be used if persistent and severe.

E Pneumocystis jirovecii infection

Pneumocystis is not usually associated with diarrhoea. It is more readily associated with significant breathlessness on exertion, weight loss and night sweats. Diagnosis is confirmed by identification of the organism by sputum staining or PCR. A presumptive diagnosis or ‘treat as’ can be made with a typical history and chest X-ray findings and elevated serum levels of beta-D-glucan. Treatment is with co-trimoxazole. 38206

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with malaise, fatigue, and night sweats. She denies any past medical history but admits to drinking excessively and having no fixed abode.

On examination, she has a temperature of 37.7 °C and tiny black streaks on her nails. A small cutaneous lesion, consisting of a central red mark with surrounding erythema, is seen in the cubital fossa.

What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Infective endocarditis

Infective endocarditis is a well known association in patients who inject heroin as in this case. Common symptoms include: fever, malaise, heart murmurs, and septic emboli (splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions).

E Meningococcal sepsis

Meningococcal sepsis causes generic signs of infection (fever, malaise, haemodynamic instability) in addition to focal signs depending on the organ that has been affected (i.e. photosensitivity in meningitis or cough in pneumonia).

A Cerebral vasculitis

Cerebral vasculitis leads to a wide range of symptoms, such as headaches, skin rashes, tiredness, joint pains, weakness, and alterations in behaviour. In addition, in 10% it can lead to intracranial haemorrhage.

C Toxic shock syndrome

Toxic shock syndrome is a potentially fatal illness caused by bacterial toxins. Patients are pyrexic with signs of haemodynamic compromise (tachypnoea, hypotension, and tachycardia).

D Heroin overdose

The skin lesions represent needle marks from intravenous (iv) injections (track marks) that indicate intravenous drug use. However, the patient doesn’t have any more signs of opiate overdose such as miosis or drowsiness. Non-fatal overdose is common among heroin injectors and is strongly related to the misuse of multiple other substances such as methadone, benzodiazepines, and alcohol.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents to the Gynaecologist with complaints of bilateral lower abdominal pain and a thick, yellowish vaginal discharge that has a foul odour for the past week. She reports unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. Her menstrual cycles are regular and her last menstrual period was five days ago. Physical examination revealed bilateral lower abdominal tenderness and cervical motion tenderness on bimanual vaginal examination. Her blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 96 bpm and temperature 37.8 °C.

Which of the following is the best line of management in this patient?
options: Intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous doxycycline for 14 days
Intramuscular ceftriaxone single dose, oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
Oral ofloxacin with oral metronidazole for 14 days
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Intramuscular ceftriaxone single dose, oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days

Ceftriaxone provides microbiological cover for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and doxycycline is combined with this to prevent/slow down the development of resistance to ceftriaxone by N. gonorrhoeae. Metronidazole is included to improve coverage of anaerobic bacteria.

D Oral moxifloxacin for 14 days

Oral moxifloxacin alone is not recommended for treatment of PID.

A Intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous doxycycline for 14 days

Inpatient admission and treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and doxycycline has been recommended in patients with severe pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) (fever > 38 °C), hypotension, features of tubo-ovarian abscess, pelvic peritonitis or lack of response to oral therapy. Since these features are not present in this patient, outpatient treatment is appropriate.

C Oral ofloxacin with oral metronidazole for 14 days

Oral ofloxacin, in combination with metronidazole, is only a second-line therapy in the treatment of PID.

E Oral azithromycin single dose

Combination drug therapy, rather than monotherapy with azithromycin, is the preferred treatment for PID.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old immigrant is transferred to the hospital from the local Detention Centre. He complained to the medical staff there of a cough and weight loss. Sputum testing and a chest X-ray have confirmed tuberculosis (TB) with multidrug resistance (MDR).

Which of the following is the most appropriate step with respect to protecting from spread of infection?
options: Negative pressure room and personal protective equipment
Single room no personal protective equipment needed
Single room and personal respiratory protection
Ward nursing and surgical mask for patient
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Negative pressure room and personal protective equipment

Guidance on MDR TB is clear that patients should be isolated in a negative pressure room, and those treating the patient should utilise full personal protective equipment. These measures should be continued until a two- week period has passed and some clinical improvement in the patient’s condition has been observed.

E Ward nursing and surgical mask for patient

Even a patient without MDR TB should not be nursed on an open ward because of the risk of infection spread between patients or between the patient and nursing staff.

B Single room no personal protective equipment needed

This patient has active MDR TB and must be placed under maximal protective measures to reduce spread of infection.

C Single room and surgical mask

Patients in the first few days of treatment for non-MDR TB are asked to wear a surgical mask whenever they are outside their room (eg to undergo radiological investigations).

D Single room and personal respiratory protection

A negative pressure environment is also required to reduce accidental spread of TB bacteria outside the room.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department from the airport, having just returned on a flight from Bangladesh. Around 1 h before landing he collapsed after severe vomiting and diarrhoea on the plane.

His travelling partner reports that he became ill one day before leaving Bangladesh, with high-volume, painless, watery diarrhoea. Blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg and his pulse is 100/min and regular. Dark-field microscopy of a fresh stool specimen reveals Gram-negative bacilli.

Given the likeliest diagnosis, which one of the following antibiotic choices would be most appropriate in the treatment of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Erythromycin

This patient has cholera, a comma-shaped Gram-negative bacillus. It causes clinical disease by releasing an enterotoxin that affects the small bowel, leading to secretion of huge amounts of fluid and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Diagnosis is via dark-ground microscopy of a fresh stool specimen. While rehydration is the primary therapy for cholera, use of antibiotics is proven to shorten the duration and severity of the illness. Antibiotic choices may include quinolones such as ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines, erythromycin and co-trimoxazole, but there are problems with resistance to tetracyclines emerging in patients from the Indian subcontinent in particular. Quinolone treatment is also no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but significant risk of debilitating adverse effects. For these reasons, erythromycin is the most appropriate answer in this scenario. With appropriate rehydration and antibiotic therapy where required, patients usually show signs of recovery over a few days.

C Amoxicillin

Amoxicillin is a good antimicrobial choice for chest infections and can be useful in the treatment of urine and skin infections, but is of limited used in gastrointestinal problems.

B Metronidazole

Metronidazole would be a good antibiotic choice if anaerobes such as Gardnerella, Entamoeba, Giardia or Clostridium were suspected. This might be suspected with bloody diarrhoea or, for C. difficile, recent antibiotic use.

D Co-trimoxazole

Co-trimoxazole is not widely used now due to associated risks of blood dyscrasias. It is still primarily utilised for the treatment and prophylaxis of pneumocystis pneumonia.

E Penicillin V

Penicillin V is more commonly used for pharyngeal infections than gastrointestinal infections. 33195

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman presents to the clinic with symptoms of indigestion and heart burn that have worsened over the past 18 months. She is most concerned as her uncle died of oesophageal carcinoma. You arrange an upper GI endoscopy on the routine list.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin131 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.3 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets175 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
EndoscopyHelicobacter gastritis

She is treated with eradication therapy, which is thought to be successful.

How would you advise her with respect to the future risk of cancers / re-treatment of her helicobacter?
options: Her future risk of oesophageal carcinoma is likely to be increased
She can be reassured that she no longer has a clinically significant increased risk of gastric cancer
She is at increased risk of gastric lymphoma
She should be re-treated with eradication therapy every 3 years
Consumption of 5 units of alcohol per week will significantly increase her risk of stomach cancer
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B She can be reassured that she no longer has a clinically significant increased risk of gastric cancer

Eradication of H.pylori can prevent the progression to atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia (a premalignant condition). Even in patients with established intestinal metaplasia, eradication of H.pylori in patients has been shown to prevent the progression to gastric cancer.

For more information see “Management of Helicobacter pylori – the Maastricht IV/Florence consensus report”. Gut. 2012.

D She should be re-treated with eradication therapy every 3 years

Recurrence of infection in developed countries is rare. H.pylori breath or stool testing should be performed where recurrence is suspected; there is no evidence to support empirical regular eradication.

A Her future risk of oesophageal carcinoma is likely to be increased

Eradication of H.pylori has no effect on symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease or its sequelae, in particular the development of Barrett’s or oesophageal carcinoma.

C She is at increased risk of gastric lymphoma

Eradication of H.pylori is the first line treatment of low grade gastric marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, curing 60-80% of cases.

E Consumption of 5 units of alcohol per week will significantly increase her risk of stomach cancer

Alcohol is one of the environmental factors that has been shown to significantly increase the risk of gastric cancer. However, 5 units (40g of alcohol) has not been shown to be statistically significant in increasing this risk. 21455

questions.question:
A 36-year-old farmer was referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 1-month history of flu-like symptoms and nausea and vomiting. He is frequently feeling bloated with intermittent abdominal pain and has lost his appetite, having lost 3 kg in weight over the last month. He has no past medical history and no known drug allergies. On examination, he appears lethargic and slightly jaundiced. He has a temperature of 37.8 °C. His heart rate is 97 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 118/77 mmHg. On auscultation, his chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. He is saturating well on room air, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. His abdomen is distended and there is right upper quadrant tenderness. Bowel sounds are present.

A computerised tomography (CT) abdomen is requested:

What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Albendazole

This patient has hydatid liver disease, a helminthic disease caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. It is a zoonotic illness found throughout the world and is more common in those who handle animals. Contact with contaminated faeces carrying the eggs of the tapeworm infects the host where the eggs later hatch and migrate to the liver, lungs, brain or other organs, forming a hydatid cyst. The disease has an insidious onset and often symptoms arise after cyst formation. The liver is the most commonly affected organ, and symptoms and signs include abdominal pain, jaundice and hepatomegaly. A CT abdomen classically shows a parent cyst with numerous daughter cysts. Treatment is with albendazole.

Image source: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/hepatic-hydatid-cyst-21 (https://radiopaedia.org/cases/hepatic- hydatid-cyst-21)

C Ivermectin

Ivermectin is used to treat parasitic infections, including Strongyloides. However, it is not indicated for the treatment of hydatid disease.

A Broad-spectrum antibiotics

This would be true if the patient was suffering from a pyogenic liver abscess. Most are secondary to an ongoing intra-abdominal infection and they are more common in the immunocompromised. Symptoms are more acute in onset and include a swinging fever, nausea and vomiting, night sweats and right upper quadrant tenderness. They often have a polymicrobial origin, needing broad-spectrum antibiotic cover and surgical drainage.

D Metronidazole

Metronidazole is the treatment of choice for amoebic liver abscess. Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan responsible for the disease amoebiasis. It is common in South and Central America, South East Asia and West Africa. The majority of infections are asymptomatic. However, in some patients, amoebiasis can lead to dysentery or invasive disease, including amoebic liver abscess formation. Abscesses in amoebiasis tend to be singular.

E Liver transplantation

Liver transplantation is a treatment option for hydatid liver disease that fails to respond to initial therapy, including pharmacological therapy and surgical removal of cysts. It is not a first-line treatment and albendazole should be trialled first.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man presents to Accident and Emergency Department. He is known to be HIV positive. His last outpatient appointment was several months ago and at that time his CD4 cell count was 210 ×10⁶/L.

He did not attend his most recent scheduled appointment. He is on no regular medication and has no other medical problems. He presents with a 3-week history of increasing shortness of breath and dry cough.

On examination: T38.5, RR30/min, Sats 89% on air, heart rate 110 bpm. His chest is clear to auscultation. A chest X-ray reveals diffusely increased shadowing bilaterally. Arterial blood gas on air reveals a p a(O₂) 8.8 kPa, p a(CO₂) 3.5 kPa, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, Sats 88%.

His chest X-ray shown below.

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Co-trimoxazole IV and methylprednisolone IV

The chest x-ray reveals diffusely increased shadowing bilaterally.The diagnosis is Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP) pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii (previously called carinii). BHIVA guidelines recommend addition of methylprednisolone to IV co-trimoxazole when p a(O₂) <9.3 kPa (or <70 mmHg) or SpO2 <92%, as this is an indicator of severe disease. The BHIVA guidelines have provided criteria for further clarification of severity of PCP.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:X- ray_of_ground_glass_opacities_of_pneumocystis_pneumonia.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:X- ray_of_ground_glass_opacities_of_pneumocystis_pneumonia.jpg)

D Clindamycin and primaquine

This combination is an option as second line treatment when co-trimoxazole fails.

A Co-trimoxazole IV

This would be the correct answer if the patient did not have hypoxia as steroids are needed to acutely help relieve breathlessness. In mild disease oral treatment can be considered.

B Co-trimoxazole IV and antiretroviral therapy

Antiretroviral treatment will be needed and should be offered soon after treatment for the PCP is commenced.

E Low molecular weight heparin

PEs occur with a much higher incidence within the HIV-positive population and should always be considered in the differential diagnosis. However, in view of the high fever and chest X-ray changes, this is less likely. 8516

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of skin lesions. The lesions had increased in number and size over preceding months. He did not have any medical conditions or take any medications.

On examination, he had a number of purple-red scaly patches, predominantly on both lower limbs. He also had oral candidiasis and widespread low-volume lymphadenopathy.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin119 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes0.9 ×10⁹/L1.5–3.5 x 10 9/l

What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B HIV testing

This rash is consistent with Kaposi’s sarcoma, an AIDS-defining illness: in the context of oral candidiasis (in the absence of a background of inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression), lymphopenia and widespread lymphadenopathy, this is highly suggestive of undiagnosed HIV infection.

D Lymph node biopsy

This patient has Kaposi’s sarcoma, and combined with his oral candidiasis without a background of inhaled steroids, this is strongly suggestive of underlying immunosuppression, particularly of HIV. HIV would explain his lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia, and hence the most appropriate next investigation would be an HIV test.

A HHV-6 testing

Human herpes virus 6 causes roseola infantum, and can also reactivate in the immunosuppressed or transplant recipient, causing bone marrow suppression or pneumonitis. This patient has a lymphopenia, widespread lymphadenopathy and oral candidiasis without any background of inhaled steroids or other

immunosuppression. In the context of his rash, which would be consistent with Kaposi’s sarcoma, this patient is likely to have undiagnosed HIV infection, not HHV-6, and so he should be tested for HIV positivity. Human herpes virus 8 (HHV-8) is the herpesvirus associated with Kaposi’s sarcoma.

C HPV testing

Human papilloma virus causes warts, and is associated with various malignancies including cervical carcinoma. This patient has a rash consistent with Kaposi’s sarcoma, which is not associated with HPV infection. Kaposi’s sarcoma is an AIDS-defining illness, and this patient should be tested for HIV, especially given that he has widespread lymphadenopathy, a lymphopenia and oral candidiasis without any history of inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression.

E Skin prick allergy testing

This patient’s rash is not consistent with allergy; the description is suggestive of Kaposi’s sarcoma. He has no history of allergy symptoms (itch, wheeze, swelling), but instead has oral candidiasis which cannot be explained by inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression. When combined with his widespread lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia, this patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of undiagnosed HIV, and he should be HIV tested.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of vague tingling over the upper right side of his face.

On waking up that morning, a vesicular rash had developed over his upper right face, including the tip of his nose, and he noticed that his right eye was watering. He had a history of lichen planus, and for the past 3 years, he had used topical tacrolimus to treat it.

What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Urgent ophthalmology opinion

This patient has herpes zoster ophthalmicus; he had a prodrome of tingling in a dermatomal distribution and subsequently developed a vesicular rash. However, the key point in this case is that he has signs of impending corneal involvement – the rash involves the tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) and he has watering of the eye. Hutchinson’s sign occurs as the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve innervates the cornea and the lateral dorsum of the nose and tip. You would start oral high-dose aciclovir immediately, but it is vital to refer him urgently to ophthalmology for assessment the same day, as herpes zoster ophthalmicus can be sight- threatening.

D Stop tacrolimus ointment

This patient has been using tacrolimus ointment for several years, and therefore this is unlikely to be a reaction to the drug. Furthermore, vesicular drug rashes are unusual. This rash is typical of herpes zoster (dermatomal, vesicular and with preceding tingling in the affected area), and in this case there are symptoms and signs to suggest corneal involvement (the rash affects the tip of the nose and there is eye watering). This case should be referred urgently to ophthalmology, as herpes zoster ophthalmicus can be sight-threatening. You would also immediately start high-dose oral aciclovir.

A Prescribe artificial tear solution

This patient has a vesicular rash involving his upper face and the tip of his nose; this is consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. The watering of his eye and the involvement of the tip of the nose are suggestive of corneal involvement. It is important to urgently refer this patient to ophthalmology, as herpes zoster can be sight-threatening. You would start high-dose oral aciclovir immediately. Artificial tear solution may reduce this patient’s symptoms, but it will not treat the underlying condition and therefore does not address the risk of sight impairment.

B Start chloramphenicol eye drops

Chloramphenicol eye drops are an antibiotic eye drop used for bacterial conjunctivitis. This patient has a rash consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus; it is vesicular and dermatomal. Consequently, antibiotic eye drops have no role in the management of this viral infection. The watering of his eye and the involvement of the tip of the nose are suggestive of corneal involvement. You must urgently refer this patient to ophthalmology for assessment to reduce the risk of visual impairment. You should also start high-dose oral aciclovir immediately.

C Start topical aciclovir

This patient’s rash is vesicular and dermatomal, and is therefore consistent with herpes zoster. Although aciclovir is the correct therapy for this condition, the patient has symptoms and signs that suggest corneal involvement (the rash affects the tip of the nose and there is eye watering). This means that high-dose oral aciclovir should be given, not topical aciclovir. You also must refer this patient urgently to ophthalmology for assessment, as ophthalmic herpes zoster can be sight-threatening.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 2-week history of general malaise, fever and myalgia after returning from a backpacking holiday in Brazil. He also complains of occasional nausea and vomiting. He has no past medical history and has otherwise been fit and well.

On examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.1 °C. His heart rate is 106 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 121/75 mmHg. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. His abdomen is soft, with a palpable 2-cm liver edge. There are prominent palpable cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph nodes. He has significant unilateral conjunctivitis and periorbital oedema affecting his left eye. His visual acuity remains intact.

Electrocardiogram (ECG): sinus tachycardia, PR interval 210 ms.

Which of the following vectors has a role in transmission of the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Triatomine bugs

This patient has Chagas’ disease, a parasitic disease spread by triatomine or ‘kissing’ bugs. The disease is prevalent in Latin America and consists of an initial acute phase and a chronic phase. In the earlier stages of the disease, symptoms include generalised malaise, fever, headaches and myalgia, along with anorexia, nausea and vomiting. Generalised lymphadenopathy is common. Unilateral conjunctivitis and periorbital cellulitis (known as Romaña’s sign) is seen in up to 50% of cases and represents the point of transmission of infection. In others, if the infection is transmitted through a bite in the skin, a chagoma (an indurated, oedematous skin lesion) may be seen. ECG findings include sinus tachycardia and a prolonged PR interval. Treatment in the acute phase includes bed rest and expert consultation regarding the prescription of antiparasitic agents such as benznidazole.

D Ticks

Ticks are well known to spread Lyme disease, a bacterial infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. They are not involved in the transmission of Chagas’ disease.

A Aedes mosquito

The Aedes mosquito is responsible for the transmission of dengue fever. Although there is an overlap of symptoms with Chagas’ disease, dengue fever tends to have a shorter duration of illness and does not cause unilateral eye signs.

B Anopheles mosquito

The Anopheles mosquito is the vector for malaria. There are multiple subtypes, of which malaria falciparum is the most common. The disease is generally transmitted in Africa, South East Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Western Pacific. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgia, headache and nausea and vomiting. Hepatosplenomegaly may appear.

C Sandfly

Sandflies spread the parasitic disease leishmaniasis. There are different species of Leishmania that are responsible for different manifestations of the disease, with cutaneous leishmaniasis being the most common. Initially, a small red papule appears at the site of the sandfly bite which gradually enlarges to up to 2 cm in diameter. It later ulcerates in the centre before spontaneously resolving. The time to resolution varies between two months and one year.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old woman has attended the GU Clinic for multiple (>7) episodes of painful genital ulceration in the last year. One such episode two years before caused acute urinary retention, and was treated with IV aciclovir.

According to the case notes from that admission, at that time she was noted to have ‘multiple small ulcers affecting the labial and vulval area with erythema of the surrounding skin, and marked tender inguinal lymphadenopathy’. However, on examination today at the Outpatient Clinic she has no ulcers.

What treatment should you offer her?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B 1 year aciclovir

This patient has frequently recurring herpes simplex virus (HSV) episodes. Usually if a patient has more than six episodes yearly they are offered prophylactic treatment, which consists of 1 year oral aciclovir (400 mg BD) with the aim of suppressing the HSV.

E 3 months’ ganciclovir

Ganciclovir is not usually used for HSV infections but can be used for cytomegalovirus (CMV).

A 5 days’ aciclovir

This would be the correct option for treating acute HSV sores but none are present at this time.

C 3 months’ valaciclovir

Valaciclovir is a pro-drug of aciclovir and has the advantage of needing to be taken only twice daily. This would be a treatment option, but it is generally not offered as it is considerably more expensive.

D 5 days’ valaciclovir

This would be an option for treating an acute course of HSV sores.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man attends because of a painful mouth. He has a past history of asthma for which he takes a fluticasone/salmeterol combination inhaler This was recently changed from using a beclomethasone inhaler alone.

On examination, he looks well but has evidence of extensive oral candidiasis.

Which is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Steroid-related candida infection

Given the history of use of inhaled corticosteroids for asthma, this is the most likely cause of this man’s candida infection. Steroids cause immunosuppression by glucocorticoid action, and inhaled steroids can lead to localised immunosuppression and opportunistic infection with poor inhaler technique. Patients should be advised on good inhaler technique, with the use of a spacer device when they are prescribed a metered dose inhaler for steroid delivery, rinsing of the mouth with water after use of the inhaler or teeth cleaning, and adequate oral hygiene when taking their night-time dose.

E Hodgkin’s lymphoma

Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a malignant disease of lymphatic system with multinucleated giant (Reed–Sternberg) cells. Presentation usually occurs in early adulthood, and again is insidious with asymptomatic lymph node enlargement, weight loss, night sweats and unexplained fever. Some patients have chest symptoms and alcohol-induced pain.

B HIV infection

HIV with a low CD4+ count could be an explanation for oral candidiasis, but in the absence of any mentioned risk factors and without evidence of systemic features and other opportunistic disease this is a less likely diagnosis.

C Chronic myeloid leukaemia

Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder affecting one or all cell lines. Progression is characterised into a chronic phase, an accelerated phase and finally blast crisis. Most patients present in the chronic phase with insidious symptoms of fatigue, weight loss and night sweats. Examination can reveal

features of cell line disruption such as anaemia and bruising, but while lymphadenopathy can occur it is not a major feature. It is not associated with immunodeficiency and would therefore not explain this patient’s oral candidiasis, and the age of presentation of CML is usually around 65 years old.

D Chronic lymphoblastic leukaemia

Chronic lymphoblastic leukaemia (CLL) is a malignant monoclonal expansion of B lymphocytes. CLL occurs at a median age of 72 years and presents insidiously with susceptibility of infection, symmetrically enlarged lymph nodes, abdominal pain from splenomegaly, bleeding from thrombocytopenia and fatigue from anaemia. Signs include lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. The absence of systemic features and organomegaly makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman attends the hepatology clinic for review. She is 14 weeks’ pregnant and was found to have abnormal hepatitis serology at her booking visit. She has no past medical history of note, although admits to intermittent IV drug abuse during her teenage years.

On examination, her blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, with pulse 65/min and regular. Her BMI is 22 and there are no signs of chronic liver disease.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)125 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)85 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)32 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Bilirubin12 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)182 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Hep B surface antibodyPositive
Hep B core antibodyPositive
Hep Be antigenNegative
Hep Bs antigenNegative

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Cleared hepatitis B

The presence of core and surface antibodies, in the absence of Hep B antigen, suggests that this patient has now cleared hepatitis B infection. It is likely she was exposed as a result of previous IV drug abuse. The elevated alkaline phosphatase will be related to the pregnancy rather than to underlying liver disease.

B Chronic hepatitis B

The absence of hepatitis B antigens and normal liver function tests makes this unlikely.

A Autoimmune hepatitis

Autoimmune hepatitis is an idiopathic cause of hepatitis and cirrhosis. There is association with autoimmune diseases and with anti-smooth muscle (ASMA) and anti-LKM-1 antibodies, as well as ASMA. Presentation is variable and can range from asymptomatic to fulminant, with associated features of liver disease on examination. This patient’s liver function tests are normal for her, given that the ALP is likely raised from pregnancy.

D Non-A non-B hepatitis

Hepatitis C is another viral infection transmitted via blood and is relatively common in IV drug users.

E Vaccination for hepatitis B

Vaccination for hepatitis B is associated with the presence of surface antibodies but not core antibodies. 39045

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man, who spent 3 months on a school building project in Nepal, visits the clinic for review. He suffered a severe episode of diarrhoea with associated blood while in the country, and now complains of intermittent sweats and pain in his right lower chest.

On examination, his temperature is 37.7 °C, and he has hepatic tenderness.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)102 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)145 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)142 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin45 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)72 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)342 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Computed tomography (CT) thorax and upper abdomenSingle homogenous abscess in the right liver lobe, measuring 5 cm in diameter

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical treatment for him?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Metronidazole

This patient has a history suggestive of amoebic liver abscess. The initial illness was colitis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. This invasive amoeba travels via the portal circulation to the liver. Diagnosis can be made based on imaging and positive serology. Unlike bacterial abscess management, this condition does not

require drainage. Metronidazole is the treatment of choice for liver trophozoites, followed by a luminal amoebacide such as paramomycin.

C Chloroquine

Chloroquine is an antimalarial drug used in the treatment of non-falciparum malaria. Its use in malaria prophylaxis and the treatment of falciparum malaria has ceased due to widespread resistance. Chloroquine can be used second line to treat amoebic liver abscess (as suggested in this case), but there is a better option.

B Doxycycline
