Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity. It is used to treat Gram-positive and atypical bacterial infections, as well as malaria. The case described is highly suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess, and therefore doxycycline would not be appropriate treatment for this.

D Cefotaxime

Cefotaxime is a third-generation cephalosporin with a broad spectrum of activity against both Gram-positive and -negative bacteria. The history and findings in this case are more suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess than a pyogenic abscess. In practice it would be appropriate to cover for both pyogenic infection and amoeba until the diagnosis is serologically confirmed.

E Quinine

Quinine is an antimalarial drug used in the treatment of falciparum malaria, though its use has been superseded by artesunate/artermisinine combination therapy where available. It is not a treatment for amoebic infection.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old builder presents with a 5-hour history of increasingly severe headaches and myalgia. Two weeks ago, he was seen in the Emergency Department following a fall from the scaffolding of a building on which he was working. At that time, he had a skull X-ray that was reported as being normal. As he had no specific symptoms or signs at that time, he was not admitted. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks 21 units of alcohol a week. He has no other past medical history.

On examination, he looks unwell. He is wearing his sunglasses. His temperature is 38 °C. His blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, oxygen saturation (Sp(0 2)) is 98% on air. He appears to have mild neck stiffness on examination. He is orientated in time, place and person but seems alternately sleepy and slightly aggressive towards staff. GCS is graded as 14/15 by the examining doctor. Blood cultures have been taken and a CT and lumbar puncture are arranged.

Which other step should be taken in the immediate management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A IV ceftriaxone

This patient has a history of a head injury and presents with what sounds like meningitis. In this particular case the fact that the patient has sustained a head injury means that CT is mandatory. That the previous skull X-ray was reported as normal is not 100% reliable as some fractures may be missed, particularly those of the temporal bones.

In general, CSF examination allowing confirmation of the diagnosis and identification of the organism is preferable prior to starting antibiotics. In most cases it is preferable to perform CT first, and this is absolutely required in the context of reduced conscious level, history of head injury or presence of focal neurological signs. However, in a very unwell patient with a typical clinical picture of bacterial meningitis, for whom waiting for such investigations would risk undue delay in starting treatment, antibiotics may be commenced simply after blood cultures and CT/LP performed afterwards. Starting antibiotics, however, usually alters the CSF obtained and the likelihood of identifying an organism becomes less the longer the delay after the first dose of antibiotics. Starting IV dexamethasone at the same time as, or just prior to, antibiotics and continued until S. pneumoniae is ruled out as the causative organism is now recommended.

D Antituberculous therapy

TB can cause meningitis which can be identified from CSF results. However, this patient has no described exposure to anyone with TB nor is there any mention of travel to TB endemic countries. Also, the acute onset makes this less likely.

B IV tazocin

Penetration of beta lactam agents across the blood-brain barrier is poor. Although it is recognised that the inflammation involved in meningitis may well improve this penetration the first line therapy remains ceftriaxone or cefotaxime.

C IV mannitol

It is a treatment option for cerebral oedema. However, the high temperature suggests an infective aetiology to this patient’s confusion.

E IV aciclovir

Aciclovir is treatment for viral meningitis and encephalitis. Viral infection is possible but would be unrelated to trauma, making a bacterial infection more likely. 33173

questions.question:
A 28-year-old nurse who was working in the Gastroenterology department presented to the Emergency Room one hour after receiving a needlestick injury whilst at work. Her needlestick injury had been received from a hepatitis C-positive patient, who was taking ribavirin and pegylated alpha interferon. At the time of the needlestick injury nurse had been wearing gloves and had punctured the pad of her left index finger. She had washed the wound with running water afterwards.

Donor virology investigations:

Hepatitis C RNALow levels detected
HBsAgNegative
Anti-HBcNegative
Anti-HBsNegative
HIV RNA PCRNegative

What should be the next step?
options: Take blood from the nurse for virology
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Take blood from the nurse for virology

It is important to take baseline samples from the nurse to determine whether she was a carrier or was infected with a blood-borne virus before her exposure to this patient (as this would have different implications for treatment). If these are negative, her blood will continue to be monitored to check whether she has contracted hepatitis C from this patient. If she has, treatment for the virus will begin at that point. Post-exposure prophylaxis is not recommended for hepatitis C.

C Reassure and discharge home

Although it is not appropriate to give this nurse post-exposure prophylaxis (this is not recommended for hepatitis C), it is important to take the nurse’s blood for virology. This is to check whether, at baseline, she was a carrier or was infected with a blood-borne virus (i.e. before her exposure to this patient). Her virology will then be monitored to determine whether she has contracted hepatitis C from this patient.

A Arrange hepatitis B vaccination

This nurse is likely to have already had the hepatitis B vaccination, as this is a requirement for healthcare workers. Furthermore, vaccinating the patient against hepatitis B will not influence her risk of contracting hepatitis C from the donor patient. The most important step is to take virology bloods from the nurse. These bloods are used to tell whether the nurse is already a carrier or infected with a blood-borne virus, before her exposure to the patient. Her virology bloods will then be monitored to decide whether she has contracted hepatitis C from the patient.

B Give anti-hepatitis C immunoglobulin

This is not a treatment option for hepatitis C, and there is no evidence that it is effective as a vaccine or post- exposure prophylaxis. Furthermore, at this stage, it is unclear whether the nurse has contracted hepatitis C from the patient. Guidance is that treatment for hepatitis C should not be started unless the patient has contracted the condition, i.e. post-exposure prophylaxis therapies are not recommended. The most important action here is to take the nurse’s blood for virology; this acts as a baseline to decide whether she was already a carrier or infected with a blood-borne virus before her exposure to the patient. Her virology will then be monitored to decide whether she has contracted hepatitis C from the patient.

D Start post-exposure prophylaxis

Post-exposure prophylaxis has not been shown to be effective in the prevention of contracting hepatitis C, and therefore is not recommended. Instead, the nurse’s blood should be taken for virology; this is in order to have a baseline sample to check whether she was carrying or was infected with a blood-borne virus before her exposure to this patient. Her blood will then be monitored to determine whether she has contracted hepatitis C from this patient.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2 hour history of sudden loss of vision in his left eye. He had a past history of hypertension but was otherwise well. A sexual history reveals that he had has unprotected intercourse with multiple partners over the preceding 2 years. He had not been screened for sexually transmitted infections for 5 years. The fundoscopic appearance of his eye is shown below.

A rapid HIV test is positive.

What would be the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ganciclovir

There is evidence of haemorrhages and exudates. This patient is likely to have HIV (the diagnosis would need to be confirmed with laboratory testing) and consequent cytomegalovirus retinitis, an AIDs-defining illness. It is the most common cause of eye disease and blindness in HIV patients. CMV retinitis is a slowly progressive disorder; visual loss may occur suddenly as a result of haemorrhage or retinal detachment, or more slowly due to progressive involvement of the macula and optic nerve. He would need treatment with intravenous ganciclovir.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fundus_photograph-CMV_retinitis_EDA07.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fundus_photograph-CMV_retinitis_EDA07.JPG)

E Warfarin

You may have considered central retinal vein occlusion as a differential diagnosis in this patient, but central retinal vein occlusion would not explain why the patient had exudates on fundoscopy. In addition, warfarin and other anticoagulants are not recommended as treatment for central retinal vein occlusion, as they can cause complications such as vitreous haemorrhage. Instead, this patient probably has cytomegalovirus retinitis as a result of untreated HIV infection, for which the most appropriate treatment is intravenous ganciclovir.

A Aciclovir

This patient likely has a diagnosis of HIV (this would need to be confirmed with full laboratory testing) and has had a sudden loss of vision. Combined with the fundoscopy findings, his presentation is suggestive of cytomegalovirus retinitis. Aciclovir is simply not potent enough to treat this; ganciclovir is the appropriate choice and is administered intravenously.

B Aspirin

You may have thought that this patient had a central retinal vein occlusion; however, this would not explain the exudates seen on fundoscopy. Furthermore, aspirin is not an appropriate treatment for retinal vein occlusion. In combination with the positive HIV test, this patient is more likely to have cytomegalovirus retinitis, for which the appropriate treatment is intravenous ganciclovir.

D Low-molecular weight heparin

You may have thought that this patient had central retinal vein occlusion; however, central retinal vein occlusion does not explain why he has exudates on fundoscopy. Furthermore, heparin and other anticoagulants are not appropriate therapy for central retinal vein occlusion due to the risk of haemorrhagic complications in the eye. This patient is more likely to have cytomegalovirus retinitis as a result of untreated HIV, and he should be treated with intravenous ganciclovir.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old veterinarian is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 2-month history of general malaise and weight loss. He describes initially having flu-like symptoms with intermittent fevers and headaches before the onset of severe lethargy and loss of appetite. He is usually well with a past medical history of mild asthma only. His regular medications include salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers. There are no allergies. On examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.1 °C. His heart rate is 117 bpm and his blood pressure is 109/68 mmHg. His capillary refill time is < 2 seconds. He has a dry cough, but his chest is clear, with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute and saturations of 94% on room air. There is a pansystolic murmur radiating towards the apex and the apex beat is palpable in the fifth intercostal space in the mid-axillary line. His abdomen is soft, with no palpable masses.

Investigations:

Haemoglobin (Hb)102 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils10.1 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.5 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.4 ×10⁹/L0.8–5.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)338 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea7.3 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)125 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)5960+
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate62 mm/hour Chest X-ray: clear lung fields with no evidence of focal consolidation or effusion Blood cultures: negative< 15 mm/hour

What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Coxiella burnetii

This patient has infective endocarditis. The history of general malaise and flu-like symptoms, together with fever and a new murmur, is suggestive of the diagnosis. This patient’s pansystolic murmur points towards mitral regurgitation, with the mitral valve being the most commonly affected valve in infective endocarditis. Blood cultures form part of the modified Duke criteria needed to confirm the diagnosis. C. burnetii causes blood culture-negative endocarditis. It is a zoonotic disease and those at higher risk of infection include those who work with animals such as farmers and veterinarians. Treatment is with a course of doxycycline.

A Brucella melitensis

Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease secondary to close contact with infected animals or from ingestion of unpasteurised milk or undercooked meat. Those who work with livestock have an increased risk of the disease. However, it is a very rare, albeit fatal, cause of infective endocarditis.

C Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis. It is particularly more common in patients with a history of intravenous drug use. However, it typically produces positive blood cultures.

D Streptococcus bovis

S. bovis is a rare cause of infective endocarditis. It is most commonly associated with colorectal cancer.

E Streptococcus viridans

S. viridans is a common cause of subacute infective endocarditis. It forms part of the normal flora of the mouth, therefore increasing the risk of infection following a dental procedure. However, like S. aureus, it generally causes a positive culture.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department some 18 h after eating tinned salmon. She complains of nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, diplopia and an extreme thirst that is unquenchable.

Over the few hours in the Observation Ward, she develops worsening double vision and ptosis. Mini-mental State Examination is normal. She has complex restriction with eye movements, with restriction of abduction and adduction bilaterally. She is also dysarthric.

Although progressive incoordination and diminished reflexes are noted, there is no sensory loss. Her blood pressure is 110/72 mmHg, with a pulse of 85/min and temperature is 37.2 °C.

Which one of the following interventions would be most appropriate given this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Urgent review by Intensivist

This clinical picture is highly suggestive of botulism, infection having occurred due to defective canning of the fish. Sporadic outbreaks of the disease, although rare, do still occur. Laboratory tests and imaging studies are not generally helpful in the diagnosis of the condition. The neurotoxin produced leads to CNS and autonomic nervous system paralysis, and later respiratory muscle weakness and hypoventilation can occur. For this reason the patient should be managed in an ITU setting. Supportive therapy with intubation and ventilation, respiratory physiotherapy, nasogastric tube placement and catheterisation is the treatment of choice for severe disease. Recovery occurs on average between 30 and 100 days after infection; severe cases may require ventilation for many months.

E Computed tomography (CT) of the brain

The likely clinical diagnosis is botulism, and a CT brain is likely to delay reaching definitive airway management before respiratory paralysis occurs.

B IV immunoglobulin

IV immunoglobulin in the form of botulinum antitoxin can be useful, but only if given very early in presentation and in those who have ingested toxin but are as yet asymptomatic. This patient has presented with severe symptoms following several hours of illness, and it is too late to be of value.

C IV Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin is not useful for botulism, which is the most likely clinical diagnosis.

D IV Metronidazole

The antibiotics which can potentially be used in botulism against Clostridium botulinum include benzylpenicillin and metronidazole. However, whilst metronidazole can be used as treatment, the most important management is to stabilise the patient’s airway as the paralysis can lead to respiratory arrest and she may need ventilation.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman presented with a 12-hour history of fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and severe myalgia. Three days ago, she had completed a 3-day course of oral trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. She took the oral contraceptive pill, and her last menstrual period had ended the previous day.

On examination, her temperature was 39.5 °C, heart rate 130 bpm and BP 72/40 mmHg. There was no nuchal rigidity or photophobia. There was a diffuse macular erythrodermic rash on the trunk and lower limbs, and marked tenderness of the thigh muscles. She had diffuse abdominal tenderness. Neurological examination was normal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResult
Blood culturesNo growth in two samples after 48 hours
Urine culturesNo growth

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Toxic shock syndrome

This is a typical presentation of toxic shock syndrome, in this case, most probably caused by a retained tampon. The patient is in shock, with a high fever, myalgia and erythroderma. The profound hypotension is due to direct inhibition of myocardial contractility by the exotoxin. It is common for blood cultures to be negative in toxic shock syndrome; high vaginal swabs may be positive for Staphylococcus.

A Bacterial meningitis

The patient does not have any signs of meningism, does not complain of headache, and meningitis could not explain this rash. Instead, this patient’s presentation is more suggestive of toxic shock syndrome, caused by a retained tampon, leading to release of staphylococcal exotoxin (TSST-1). This would explain the high fever, myalgia and rash in the presence of sterile blood and urine cultures.

B Gastroenteritis

This patient is in shock, with a high fever, myalgia and a rash; this picture does not fit with gastroenteritis. This would be more typical for toxic shock syndrome caused by TSST-1, as a result of a retained tampon.

C Renal abscess

You might expect specific flank tenderness, and a ballotable kidney, if there was a renal abscess. Instead, this patient has diffuse abdominal tenderness, erythroderma, high fever and myalgia. This is more fitting with toxic shock syndrome, caused by the release of TSST-1 as a result of a retained tampon.

E Ulcerative colitis

This patient does have diarrhoea, but otherwise her presentation is not typical for a flare of ulcerative colitis; it cannot explain the erythroderma or myalgia. This presentation of shock (with profound hypotension), erythroderma, myalgia and high fever is typical of toxic shock syndrome caused by the release of TSST-1. In this case, it is likely related to a retained tampon.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of general malaise, anorexia and fever. He has lost 6 kg in weight. He had a sore throat a week before and his General Practitioner had told him that it was a viral infection.

On examination, he has a temperature of 37.6 °C and three splinter haemorrhages on his right index finger. On cardiac auscultation, he has a pansystolic murmur, loudest at the apex and radiating to the axilla.

Blood cultures are taken from three peripheral sites which grow Staphylococcus aureus and the patient is started on intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrates a 0.5 × 0.9 cm vegetation attached to the posterior surface of the mitral valve.

Which of the following is the most likely complication of this condition in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Embolic stroke

Infective endocarditis results from microbial infection of the endothelial surface of the heart. Blood cultures are positive in > 95% of cases of infective endocarditis. Three sets of cultures should be taken with 10 ml of blood in each bottle. These should be incubated for up to three weeks to grow fastidious organisms. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is specific in 91–98% of cases at detecting vegetations, although the sensitivity is only 45–60%. Suboptimal views are seen with prosthetic valves and transoesophageal echocardiography should be undertaken if vegetations are not seen on TTE.

There are several complications associated with infective endocarditis, including acute heart failure, systemic embolisation (including stroke), acute kidney injury, valvular dehiscence (most commonly in the presence of a prosthetic valve), splenic abscess and mycotic aneurysms.

Systemic embolisation occurs in 22–50% of patients with infective endocarditis and the risk increases if the vegetation is > 10 mm in size. Other risk factors include S. aureus infection, intravenous drug use and mitral valve vegetation. Up to 65% of emboli involve the central nervous system. Other affected areas are the lungs, spleen and joints.

C Splenic abscess

Splenic abscess is a rare complication of infective endocarditis. It occurs due to bacterial seeding or direct embolism to the splenic arteries. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are the best diagnostic tools. Splenectomy is often the treatment of choice in patients who are amenable to surgery.

B Mitral valve abscess

Mitral valve abscess occurs in around 15% of patients with mitral valve involvement. It typically affects the annular portions of the valve, involving the posterior leaflet, mitral annulus and underlying myocardium. If surgical intervention is required for mitral valve abscess, this typically involves valve replacement and the use of a bovine patch to reconstruct the posterior annulus. This complication occurs less frequently than embolic stroke, making this complication unlikely.

D Valvular dehiscence

Valvular dehiscence occurs most commonly in patients with prosthetic valve involvement, particularly with S. aureus infection. As such, S. aureus infection is an indication for surgery if it has invaded a prosthetic valve. However, as this patient has a native valve, this is unlikely to be a complication in this patient.

E Valvular fistula

Valvular fistulation is most common in S. aureus infection in a prosthetic valve, making this complication unlikely as this patient has a native valve.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an 8-day history of progressive breathlessness that is worse on exertion, fevers and dry cough. He has a past medical history of HIV infection, for which he is partially compliant with his antiretroviral therapy.

His temperature is 38.5 °C, heart rate 100 bpm and BP 120/75 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 90% on room air.

On examination, scattered crackles are heard on auscultation of both lung fields. His cardiovascular and abdominal examinations are unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
CD4 count80 cells/mm³500–1500 cells/mm³
HIV viral load90 000 copies/ml< 75 copies/ml

What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Co-trimoxazole

This patient has a likely diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), given the history of fever, dry cough and progressive shortness of breath against a background of uncontrolled HIV. Immunocompromised patients are at higher risk of developing the condition, including HIV patients who are non-compliant with antiretroviral therapy. Co-trimoxazole is the preferred treatment for PCP in HIV-infected individuals.

B Empirical treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics

Empirical treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics is not appropriate for the management of PCP, as PCP is caused by a fungal pathogen and requires specific antimicrobial treatment. Clinically broad-spectrum antibiotics may be started alongside co-trimoxazole while tests are performed to confirm a diagnosis of PCP. However, the presentation here, along with the duration of symptoms, make PCP a more likely diagnosis than a bacterial pneumonia. Therefore, co-trimoxazole is the most appropriate initial management.

C Pentamidine

IV pentamidine may be used as an alternative treatment for PCP in patients who are intolerant of, or allergic to, co-trimoxazole. However, it is not the preferred first-line therapy due to its higher risk of adverse effects and lower efficacy.

D Recommence antiretroviral therapy

It is very important to ensure that this patient is compliant with his antiretroviral therapy, and reinitiation of antiretroviral therapy is an essential component of long-term management for this patient. However, it should not be used alone, as this patient also has a likely diagnosis of PCP. Initial management should be treatment with antimicrobial agents targeting the causative pathogen (eg co-trimoxazole).

E Sputum cultures for tuberculosis

While tests should be performed to confirm the underlying cause for this patient's presentation, the most likely infection is PCP. Therefore, appropriate antimicrobial therapy with co-trimoxazole should be initiated as the initial management. While patients who are immunocompromised are at higher risk of infections such as tuberculosis, the rapid onset of symptoms make this diagnosis unlikely in this case.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman is admitted with a 4-day history of profuse bloody diarrhoea, vomiting and lower abdominal pain. She had a past medical history of well-controlled hypertension and mild asthma, but her health had been good until the onset of the presenting illness. She had no recent foreign travel and did not smoke or drink. On examination, she was drowsy, but oriented when roused. Her temperature was 39 °C, pulse 110 bpm and regular, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, and she was clinically dehydrated.

Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. Her abdomen was soft and diffusely tender with scanty bowel sounds and no palpable masses. There were no focal neurological signs or rashes.

Investigation results are below:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin80 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)26.0 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets48 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)84 fL76–98 fL
Sodium (Na⁺)147 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea25 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine780 mmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin32 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)34 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase80 IU/L30–130 IU/L
GGT54 IU/L5–30 IU/L
UrinalysisProtein ++ blood ++
Abdominal X-rayNo dilated bowel loops
Chest X-rayClear lung fields, no subdiaphragmatic air

What of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B E. coli infection

The diagnosis is haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), which causes a microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia. HUS is similar to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), but there are a number of differences between the two conditions. HUS usually presents in childhood or old age, with acute kidney disease following a diarrhoeal illness, whereas TTP is more common in young adults with predominantly neurological features, such as fits and confusion. There is a strong association with verotoxin-producing E. coli 0157 and this organism should be looked for specifically in the stool culture. A normal coagulation screen will exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation which can present similarly. The blood film will show fragmented and deformed red cells. The mortality of HUS with good supportive care is less than 10%. Treatment includes fresh frozen plasma and plasma exchange, but antibiotics are not seen to positively affect prognosis.

A Campylobacter infection

Campylobacter is a Gram-negative bacterium that is typically comma- or s-shaped and it is mobile. The infection comes from contaminated food or coming in contact with infected animals. The organism produces diffuse, bloody, oedematous and exudative enteritis. Although rarely the infection been considered a cause of HUS and TTP, no unequivocal case reports exist. In some cases, a Campylobacter infection can be the underlying cause of Guillain–Barré syndrome and gastrointestinal perforation is a rare complication of ileal infection.

C Norovirus infection

Norovirus is sometimes referred to as winter vomiting bug, and it is a common cause of viral gastroenteritis. It can affect patients of all ages and is transmitted by food or water. Norovirus infection is characterised by nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhoea and abdominal pain. A person usually develops symptoms of gastroenteritis 12–48 hours after being exposed to norovirus. General lethargy, weakness, muscle aches, headaches and low- grade fevers may occur. The disease is usually self-limiting, and severe illness is rare.

D Salmonellosis

Salmonellosis presents with diarrhoea, fever, vomiting and abdominal cramps 12–72 hours after the infection. In the majority of cases, the illness lasts 4–7 days and most people recover without treatment. In some cases the diarrhoea may be so severe as to lead to dehydration and the need for hospitalisation for fluid replacement. There is no association with HUS.

E Staphylococcus aureus gastroenteritis

Staph. aureus gastroenteritis occurs as a result of eating or drinking substances that are contaminated with the staphylococcal enterotoxin. The toxin then settles in the small intestine and causes inflammation and swelling. This in turn can cause abdominal pain, cramping, dehydration, diarrhoea and fever. It is not associated with HUS.

questions.question:
A 61-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with increasing shortness of breath over the past two months. He also complains of increased lethargy, night sweats and 3-kg weight loss. He has no past medical history of note and no allergies.

Examination reveals a blood pressure of 134/72 mmHg and a heart rate of 84 bpm and regular. His temperature is 37.9 °C. There is a diastolic murmur in the aortic area on auscultation. His chest is clear and there are no signs of cardiac failure.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)103 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)171 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine122 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)85 mm/ first hour0–10 mm/first hour

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Amoxicillin and gentamicin

This patient has symptoms and signs of infective endocarditis. Management of native valve endocarditis in a patient with no drug allergies includes amoxicillin and gentamicin as the initial empirical approach. There is no evidence to suggest a route of entry for staphylococcal infection such as drug abuse, surgery or penetrating injury.

C Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is usually used when Staphylococcus aureus is considered a risk such as in cases where patients who are injecting drug abusers present with endocarditis or where there is a history of recent orthopaedic surgery or injury.

B Benzylpenicillin

Benzylpenicillin is used in the management of infective endocarditis secondary to streptococci (eg Streptococcus viridans). It is not used as the initial antibiotic in the blind treatment of infective endocarditis.

D Cefuroxime and gentamicin

Cephalosporins are considered in the treatment of endocarditis related to HACEK organisms, HACEK being an acronym based on the first letter of each organism: Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter (previously Actinobacillus), Cardiobacterium, Eikenella corrodens and Kingella.

E Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin

This is a typical regimen considered for prosthetic valve endocarditis, ensuring robust antistaphylococcal coverage. 38385

questions.question:
A 59-year-old fisherman has been referred to the Ophthalmology Department with a 6-month history of deteriorating vision. For a long time, he has been feeling generally more fatigued with myalgia and has lost approximately 6 kg in weight in the last two months since he moved from Nigeria to the United Kingdom. He has a background of type II diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, for which he takes metformin, aspirin, bisoprolol and atorvastatin.

On examination, he has multiple excoriations over his entire body and there are some patches of skin depigmentation. Using a slit lamp, multiple corneal opacities and keratoconjunctival lesions are seen bilaterally. His visual acuity is 6/36 in both eyes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Onchocerciasis

Onchocerciasis, otherwise known as African river blindness, is a filarial infection secondary to the nematode Onchocerca volvulus and is the second most common cause of infective blindness in the world. It is spread by the blackfly, which breeds in nearby fast-flowing rivers and is endemic in East, West and Central Africa, along with South America and the Middle East. The disease can initially begin with dermatological signs, such as subcutaneous papules, lymphadenitis and skin depigmentation, before the onset of eye disease. O. volvulus will affect all ocular tissues, including the eyelid and conjunctiva and as the disease progresses, the cornea and sclera. Multiple ocular findings can be seen on examination, depending on the stage of disease, including chronic conjunctivitis, chemosis and corneal opacities. Occasionally, the nematode can be visualised in the anterior chamber using a slit lamp. Treatment is with ivermectin.

E African trypanosomiasis

African trypanosomiasis, otherwise known as African sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease caused by the parasite Trypanosoma brucei, which is transmitted to humans by bites of infected tsetse flies. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa. Initial symptoms are non-specific and include general malaise, fever, myalgia and occasionally pruritus. A painless chancre appears at the site of the bite. As the disease progresses into its later stages, the central nervous system begins to become impaired with continuous headaches, daytime somnolence and behavioural changes before stupor and coma.

B Blackwater fever

Blackwater fever is the term given to intravascular haemolysis in a malarial infection causing symptoms, such as jaundice and acute kidney injury. It does not cause ocular symptoms as seen in this patient.

C Schistosomiasis

Schistosomiasis is a parasitic disease caused by flukes. The disease is contracted when a host comes into contact with contaminated water and the larval form of the parasite infects the host through direct invasion of intact skin. The larvae are then able to mature inside the host and lay eggs. It is the host’s reaction to this process that causes the initial symptoms, including abdominal pain, diarrhoea and liver enlargement. In urogenital schistosomiasis, haematuria can be seen, followed by urogenital fibrosis, with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. While it is a common disease, it does not cause blindness.

D Mansonellosis

Mansonellosis is a filarial disease that is commonly asymptomatic. The larvae are introduced into the host through different vectors, including an infected midge. They reside in the skin, subcutaneous tissues and body cavities, including the peritoneal and pleural cavities and occasionally the pericardium. If symptoms do appear, they are generally non-specific and include fever, fatigue and pruritus, although abdominal pain, pericarditis and pleuritis can occur. The microfilariae are capable of entering the eye and causing ocular symptoms. However, this is less common than onchocerciasis.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man attends the Sexually Transmitted Diseases Clinic after a recent trip to visit his grandparents in Barbados. He admits to having had unprotected sex during his 2-week holiday.

On examination, he has an extremely painful, deep ulcer with soft, ragged margins on the coronal sulcus of his penis. He has painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Which one of the following treatments would be the most appropriate choice in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Azithromycin

This clinical picture is suggestive of chancroid infection, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Chancroid is endemic in parts of the Caribbean basin, Africa and south-west Asia and is commoner in non-white, uncircumcised populations. Patients may present with single or multiple genital ulcers, and painful lymphadenopathy occurs in 30–60% of patients. Gram-staining of ulcer exudates may demonstrate a ‘school of fish’ collection of short, thick Gram-negative rods. Definitive diagnosis is based on culture using enriched chocolate agar. Patients should be screened for other sexually transmitted diseases to rule out co-infection with other organisms. Suitable antibiotic treatments for H. ducreyi include macrolides and quinolones.

D Aciclovir

This is another antiviral treatment option for herpes simplex and, as described above, this is not the most likely diagnosis.

A Metronidazole

Metronidazole could have been used for a painful oral ulcer associated with gingivitis or with bacterial vaginosis. It can also be used for some protozoal infections, but this patient is unlikely to have any of the above.

C Valiciclovir

This is an antiviral option for herpes simplex infection. Herpes causes painful genital ulcers following sexual transmission, but the ragged margin and inguinal lymphadenopathy make chancroid a more likely diagnosis.

E Oxytetracycline

This is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that can be used for treatment for Chlamydia. The presentation of genital ulceration makes Chlamydia an unlikely cause, and therefore oxytetracycline an inappropriate treatment. Chlamydia normally presents in men with dysuria or discharge. 33180

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man presented with warts around the anal margin and on the shaft and subpreputial space on the penis. He was distressed by their appearance.

Examination confirmed the presence of multiple soft, non-keratinised papillomas.

What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Podophyllotoxin ointment

This patient is distressed by the genital warts, and therefore it is appropriate to treat him. First-line therapy for non-keratinised warts is podophyllotoxin ointment, applied directly to the warts twice a day for three days. This is followed by four rest days, and can be repeated weekly until the lesions resolve. If this is ineffective, cryotherapy is an appropriate second line treatment.

A Aciclovir ointment

Although genital warts are caused by a virus (human papilloma virus), antiviral therapies are ineffective, especially if given topically. Instead, topical podophyllotoxin can be applied directly to the warts by the patient. If the warts are particularly refractory, cryotherapy can be used.

B Cryotherapy

Cryotherapy can be used to treat genital warts, but it is usually reserved for extensive or refractory cases. First- line treatment would be podophyllotoxin ointment. The patient should also be advised to use condoms, or if the warts are not covered by a condom, refrain from sexual activity until the lesions have resolved.

C No treatment

This patient is distressed by the warts and therefore should have treatment to remove them. It can be acceptable not to treat warts, as up to one third will regress spontaneously within 6 months. If warts are treated, first-line treatment for non-keratinised warts is podophyllotoxin ointment, administered by the patient.

D Oral doxycycline

This patient has genital warts, caused by the human papilloma virus. An antibiotic will be ineffective against genital warts. The most appropriate treatment in this case would be podophyllotoxin ointment, applied by the patient.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presents to the Sexual Health Clinic with a papular rash over her lower abdomen, inner thighs, and genital area. She denies unprotected sexual intercourse but admits to sharing sportswear and a towel at a hockey match a few weeks earlier.

A picture of the lesions is shown below:

https://commons.wikimedia.org

Which of the following is the most likely cause of her rash?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Molluscum contagiosum virus-1 (MCV1)

The umbilicated rash seen here is consistent with molluscum contagiosum, caused in the majority of cases by MCV1. MCV2 is seen more frequently in patients with immunocompromise who have molluscum infection. It is likely that the sharing of a towel and sports clothing is responsible for the infection seen here. Most cases of molluscum resolve spontaneously over a period of up to 18 months. A Cochrane review has revealed little evidence to support the use of agents such as imiquimod or benzoyl peroxide in healthy individuals. Cryotherapy and podophyllotoxin have some evidence of effectiveness.

D Human papilloma virus-18 (HPV18)

HPV18 is a human papillomavirus which is strongly implicated in the development of cervical carcinoma. HPV16 and HPV18 are responsible for 70% or more of cases of cervical cancer and pre-cancerous cervical lesions. Vaccination with one of the two available HPV vaccines protects against serotypes 6,11,16 and 18.

A Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV1)

HSV1 is the oral herpes simplex virus and is responsible for the development of cold sores. Infection may also transfer to the genitalia in patients who have active infection and engage in oral sexual intercourse with a partner. Topical acyclovir is the usual first-line intervention.

B Human herpes virus-4 (HHV4)

HHV4 is the Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever, where pharyngitis is the most frequent presentation. Individuals also often have evidence of viral hepatitis. Patients may complain of left upper- quadrant pain related to splenic oedema. They should be advised to avoid contact sports because of the risk of splenic rupture.

C Human herpes virus-6 (HHV6)

HHV6 is the cause of roseola infantum, also known as exanthem subitum, in children. It is readily passed between children in the group childcare setting and is therefore rarely seen in adults. Reactivation is seen in patients post-transplantation.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old man presented with intermittent sore throat, fever, joint pain and general malaise for 3 months. He also complained of decreasing exercise tolerance.

Over the past 6 weeks, he had developed raised, red, tender lesions on his shins. He was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) 8 years ago but had had a number of problems with medications because of their side-effects.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
White cell count (WCC)4 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils0.2 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin131 g/L130 - 180 g/L
Platelets120 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
CD4+ count100 ×10⁶/L430 - 1690 ×10⁶/L
Chest X-rayTwo cavitating lesions in the right lung field

Which organism is the most likely culprit?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Histoplasma capsulatum

This patient has a low CD4+ count, but importantly he is also neutropenic. Any neutropenic patient is at significant risk of opportunistic infections, including fungal infections such as Histoplasma capsulatum. In this case, the patient has a cavitating pneumonia; the only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia are Staphylococcus aureus and H. capsulatum. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, not as an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis; it is associated with erythema nodosum, as seen in this patient. Other infectious causes of erythema nodosum which can affect the respiratory system are Streptococcus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis and blastomycosis.

D Pneumocystis jiroveci

Although Pneumocystis jiroveci is an important cause of pneumonia in the immunocompromised, and particularly HIV-positive patients with low CD4+ counts, it causes an indolent, dry cough, with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray. It does not cause cavitating lung lesions. The only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia are S. aureus and H. capsulatum. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, as not an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis; it is associated with erythema nodosum, as seen in this patient.

B Legionella species

This patient is immunocompromised with neutropenia and a low CD4+ count; this makes him vulnerable to any infection, including Legionella species. However, Legionella species do not cause cavitating pneumonia, as seen here; typically, they cause consolidation. S. aureus and H. capsulatum are the only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, not as an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis.

C Mycoplasma pneumoniae

This patient is immunocompromised with neutropenia and a low CD4+ count, which makes him vulnerable to any infection, including Mycoplasma. Furthermore, Mycoplasma does cause subacute illness, with prominent malaise, headache and dry cough, and can be associated with erythema nodosum, as described in this patient. However, Mycoplasma does not typically cause cavitating pneumonia, as seen in this patient; the only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia are S. aureus and H. capsulatum. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, not as an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis; it is associated with erythema nodosum, as seen in this patient.

E Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus does cause cavitating pneumonia, as seen on this patient’s chest X-ray, but it would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, typically following a viral infection. This patient has a subacute course of illness. Any immunocompromised patient is vulnerable to fungal infection; this patient not only has a low CD4+ count but is also neutropenic. H. capsulatum is a fungal infection that can cause cavitating lung lesions and is the correct answer in this case.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old student who has been travelling in Thailand presents for review after commencing with symptoms of severe influenza in the last 36 hours. He has made a point of visiting street markets and staying in small local Thai hostels during his visit. You understand that a father and son who work in the poultry market near to where he has been staying recently died of H5N1 influenza. Both were treated with oseltamivir. On examination, his blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, pulse is 100 bpmn. He is pyrexial at 38.5 °C. He has severe shortness of breath and there are scattered crackles throughout both lung fields.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 x 10 9/l
Platelets (PLT)295 ×10⁹/L150–400 x 10 9/l
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Patchy consolidation through both lung fields

Which of the following represents the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Inhaled zanamivir

Zanamavir is a neuraminidase inhibitor shown to reduce the associated morbidity in severe influenza. It can be delivered by inhalation or intravenously. In this case the patient is at high risk of avian influenza (H5N1) and we have been told that two other patients died despite treatment with oseltamivir. There is less known resistance to zanamavir and therefore this should be the treatment of choice.

C Oral amantadine

Amantadine is a drug used both as an antiviral and for the treatment of Parkinson’s disease. Its use against influenza has been superceded by the neuraminidase inhibitors in recent years due to concerns regarding resistance and efficacy. Additionally influenza B is intrinsically resistant to amantadine.

A IV Cefotaxime

Cefotaxime is a broad spectrum third- generation cephalosporin with activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Although in this scenario it would be prudent to cover for potential bacterial pneumonia, this patient is at very high risk of avian influenza and the blood picture would be more typical of a viral infection; therefore the definitive treatment of choice should be an antiviral with activity against influenza.

D Oral co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin-based antibiotic which is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulinic acid; it has a broad-spectrum of activity against Gram-negative, Gram-positive and anaerobic bacteria. In this case the history is suggestive of a viral rather than a bacterial infection and therefore the definitive treatment would be an antiviral.

E Oral oseltamivir

Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor shown to reduce the morbidity associated with severe influenza. However there is recognised resistance to oseltamivir and we are told that two patients have died despite its use. Zanamivir would therefore be a more appropriate choice as resistance is less likely.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man is readmitted to the hospital some 14 days after his renal transplant. He has begun feeling very unwell with flu-like symptoms, a headache and sore throat. He has been checking his temperature at home and is now spiking fevers of 38.5 °C.

On examination, he looks poorly, with pyrexia of 38.2 °C in the Emergency room and evidence of pharyngitis. On reviewing his notes, you see that he was CMV-, Hep B- and Hep C- negative before his transplant.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)119 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)235 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)49 mm/hour< 10 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)105 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Intravenous (iv) ganciclovir

The most likely diagnosis here is one of CMV infection post-renal transplant, for which IV ganciclovir is the default treatment choice. It is very likely that the kidney has come from a CMV-positive donor. Symptoms of CMV infection post-transplant can appear any time from 6-60 days after surgery and are characterised by pyrexia, flu-like symptoms or an infectious mononucleosis-type picture as seen here. Indeed, transplant surgeons now consider the option of prophylactic ganciclovir in patients who are CMV- but their transplanted kidney comes from a CMV+ donor. The concern is that active CMV infection is associated with accelerated failure of the transplanted kidney.

D iv benzylpenicillin and gentamycin

This would be a reasonable option for the treatment of bacterial endocarditis.

B iv Foscarnet

Ganciclovir is preferred to foscarnet as a treatment option because of adverse events associated with foscarnet therapy, including marrow suppression.

C iv Vancomcin and teicoplanin

This would be an option for bacterial sepsis as a result of the transplant. The modest increase in ESR and normal white blood count make a viral infection more likely.

E iv aciclovir

Although acyclovir was previously used for CMV prophylaxis, valgancyclovir is now preferred.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man, whose main hobby is fishing in local freshwater lakes, comes to the Emergency Room feeling extremely unwell. Over the past few days, he has suffered from a flu-like illness but, during the past 24 h, has deteriorated further with a cough productive of blood-stained sputum, a severe headache, fevers and jaundice. On examination, he is pyrexial (37.9 °C). His BP is 100/60 mmHg, his pulse is 95 bpm and regular. He has a non-specific skin rash and tenderness in the right upper quadrant on abdominal examination.

Investigations:

InvestigationResult
Hb111 g/L
WCC13.2 ×10⁹/L
PLT95 ×10⁹/L
Na⁺138 mmol/L
K+4.9 mmol/L
Creatinine201 µmol/L
CK980 U/L
ALT152 U/L
Bilirubin280 µmol/L

Given the likeliest diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy for him?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Benzylpenicillin

This man has symptoms consistent with severe leptospirosis, or Weil’s disease. It is likely he acquired it through exposure to rats’ urine associated with his fishing trips. Erythromycin and doxycycline may be considered in patients who are unsuitable for penicillin therapy, or in those with very mild symptoms of infection, but IV penicillin is the primary treatment for severe disease. The peak in incidence of cases of leptospirosis appears to be in the late summer/early autumn in temperate climates, where it may be that moist, humid conditions allow the bacteria to persist for longer.

C Erythromycin

Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic with activity against Gram-positive and atypical organisms. This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of leptospirosis, and although erythromycin has some activity, there is a better option available.

A Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic with a wide spectrum of activity against Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria. The patient’s presentation is suggestive of leptospirosis, and so ciprofloxacin would not be an effective treatment. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects.

B Doxycycline

Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with activity against Gram-positive and atypical organisms. The patient’s presentation is consistent with severe leptospirosis, and although doxycycline is the treatment of choice for milder forms of the disease, this patient warrants admission and parenteral therapy.

D Chloramphenicol

Chloramphenicol is a long-established antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity against Gram-positive, - negative and atypical organisms. Its use has been limited due to severe potential adverse effects. The presentation described is highly suspicious for leptospirosis, and thus chloramphenicol is not an appropriate treatment for this condition.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department complaining of a severe sore throat. He was brought to the Emergency Department having returned from a holiday in the Caribbean. He has a temperature of 38.2 oC, his pulse is 58 beats per minute (bpm) and regular, and his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg.

Examination of the pharynx is shown below:

https://commons.wikimedia.org

Which of the following is the most likely cause of his infection?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Corynebacterium diphtheriae (C diphtheriae)

The clues to this patient suffering from diphtheria include the fact that he has recently returned from the Caribbean, and that he has the typical adherent grey/white membrane associated with pharyngitis seen in the condition. Sporadic outbreaks are still seen around the world, although it is extremely rare. The most recent occurred in Haiti in 2019. This patient’s relatively low pulse rate may be as a result of myocarditis related to diphtheria toxin. Diphtheria antitoxin combined with erythromycin is the preferred intervention.

E Streptococcus pyogenes (S pyogenes)

S pyogenes is a common cause of pharyngitis. It is usually sensitive to penicillin and presents with erythema where there is often adherent pus over the tonsillar bed. It does not present with the grey-white pseudomembrane seen here.

B Haemophilus influenzae (H influenzae)

The main concern with respect to H influenzae infection is acute epiglottitis which is seen in children. It is not associated with the grey/white adherent membrane seen here. Vaccination against H influenzae type B has significantly reduced the incidence of acute epiglottitis. Ceftriaxone, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and azithromycin are all potential treatment options.

C Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P aeruginosa)

Pseudomonas pharyngitis is more rarely reported. It is usually associated with erythema, but frank pus is unusual, and a membrane is not seen. Antibiotic therapy is chosen according to sensitivities, but for example, it may include ciprofloxacin, gentamycin or piperacillin, and tazobactam.

D Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus)

S aureus is recognised as a cause of recurrent tonsillitis. Patients with staphylococcal tonsillitis have erythema on examination and often frank pus, although the grey-white membrane seen here is absent. Most staphylococcal isolates seen in tonsillitis are resistant to penicillin. 72140

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of severe, watery diarrhoea. He was originally from Namibia, but had not left the UK for 45 years. He had had a similar episode of diarrhoea 15 years ago, but was otherwise well. He admits to losing around 10 kg in weight over the past year.

On examination, he was afebrile, and he appeared thin. There was non-specific abdominal tenderness. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin132 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets192 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine159 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Eosinophils0.7 ×10⁹/L0.04–0.4 ×10⁹/L

Which of the following is the most likely cause for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Strongyloides stercoralis

This patient’s presentation with non-bloody, watery diarrhoea and no significant systemic upset would be typical, especially when combined with a chronic disease course (suggested by the previous episode of diarrhoea and the weight loss) and a mild eosinophilia. Strongyloidiosis is endemic to Namibia and chronic infection can last for many years with only the mildest of symptoms. It can be diagnosed through microscopic examination of the stool for larvae. Despite only minor symptoms, all strongyloidiosis should be treated in order to avoid a hyper-infection syndrome: treatment is with ivermectin for two days.

A Campylobacter jejuni

Campylobacter is the most common cause of infectious gastroenteritis in the UK, typically transmitted through food. It classically causes a short-lived severe bloody diarrhoea accompanied by significant systemic upset, with high fevers. This patient does not have bloody diarrhoea and appears generally well. Furthermore, this patient has an eosinophilia, which would not be consistent with Campylobacter. Instead, the eosinophilia, lack of systemic upset and the patient’s Namibian background would suggest a parasite – specifically, Strongyloides spp. This parasite is endemic in Namibia and in its chronic form can cause non-specific abdominal pain and profuse diarrhoea after many years without symptoms, as seen here.

B Cryptosporidium spp.

Cryptosporidium spp. are parasites causing diarrhoea that typically affect young children and the immunocompromised. Typically the diarrhoea is green, offensive smelling and watery. Patients generally have mild malaise and a low-grade fever; high fevers are not seen in cryptosporidiosis. If this was an acute presentation of cryptosporidiosis, you would not expect to see weight loss. This patient is afebrile and systemically well. He has a background of a previous episode of diarrhoea and is thin, suggesting a long-term cause of malabsorption that could not be explained by a single episode of cryptosporidiosis. Instead, given this patient’s presentation, history and Namibian background, infection with Strongyloides spp. is the most likely cause. Strongyloidosis is endemic in Namibia. This would also explain the patient’s eosinophilia.

C Escherichia coli

E. coli is the most common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller and a common cause of infectious diarrhoea in the UK, especially in young children. E. coli would not explain the eosinophilia seen in this patient, and also could not explain his chronic weight loss. These features point towards a parasitic intestinal infection, causing a low-grade inflammatory response and prolonged malabsorption. In this case, with the patient’s presentation and Namibian background, Strongyloides spp. is the most likely cause. This parasitic infection is endemic in Namibia and chronic infection can persist for many years with the most minor of symptoms.

E Vibrio parahaemolyticus

This is a bacterial cause of infectious gastroenteritis, causing severe watery diarrhoea. It is typically contracted through eating raw or undercooked seafood. Although this patient has severe watery diarrhoea, he also has weight loss and has had a previous similar episode, which suggests a chronic disease course with malabsorption. More importantly, he has an eosinophilia which cannot be explained by a bacterial gastroenteritis. This, combined with his Namibian background, makes Strongyloides stercoralis the most likely cause of his symptoms. This is a parasitic intestinal infection endemic to Namibia, which can cause a chronic disease with episodes of mild abdominal pain and severe watery diarrhoea, and malabsorption leading to weight loss.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 9-day history of lower abdominal pain which worsened during intercourse. She also reported two episodes of post-coital per vaginam bleeding. Her sexual history included unprotected intercourse with two male partners in the preceding 2 weeks.

On examination, she was pyrexial at 37.6 °C, and there was bilateral pain on bimanual palpation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)126 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Cervical smearNeutrophils +

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Chlamydia

Chlamydia is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the UK, with a prevalence of around 8% in the under 20s and 5% in those aged 20–24. This patient’s symptoms of bilateral pelvic pain and intermittent fever, and deep dyspareunia, are suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease, of which chlamydia is the most common cause. The neutrophils on microscopy without any visible bacterial is typical of chlamydia: however, the preferred method of diagnosis now is nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) from a high vulvo-vaginal swab, rather than endocervical swabs. Men can be tested via first-catch urine samples or urethral swabs. First-line antibiotics would be either doxycycline or a single dose of azithromycin, and contact tracing should be undertaken.

D Gonorrhoea

Gonorrhoea can be asymptomatic, or cause pelvic pain as seen here. However, classically it presents with mucopurulent discharge. Furthermore, you would expect to see Gram-negative diplococci on microscopy, not simply neutrophils as seen in this case. This patient’s symptoms, signs and investigations are consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease, the most common cause of which is chlamydia.

A Bacterial vaginosis

Bacterial vaginosis does not cause dyspareunia, pelvic pain or fever. Instead, patients typically complain of a change in vaginal discharge: an increased amount of thin, whitish malodourous discharge. A cervical smear would typically show ‘clue cells’ – these are vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria. Instead, this patient’s dyspareunia, pelvic pain and intermittent fever, combined with a history of unprotected sex, are more suggestive of chlamydia, causing pelvic inflammatory disease.

B Candidiasis

Candidiasis, or thrush, causes soreness, itching, erythema and a thick, white, curd-like discharge: none of these symptoms are described here. Vaginal thrush does not cause deep dyspareunia (though if severe, it may cause superficial dyspareunia), pelvic pain or intermittent fever. Microscopy would not show polymorphs, as in this case. Instead, this patient’s symptoms and investigations are more consistent with a diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease caused by chlamydia.

E Trichomonas

Trichomonas is a very common sexually transmitted infection, typically causing cervicitis and increased frothy, yellow malodorous discharge. It can cause lower abdominal pain but would be unlikely to cause sustained pain, fevers or dyspareunia. This patient’s symptoms are more in keeping with pelvic inflammatory disease caused by chlamydia.

questions.question:
A 51-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-week history of intermittent fever and flu- like symptoms. He complains of general malaise and myalgia. There is no past medical history of note and he has otherwise been well, having recently returned from a hiking trip. He has no allergies.

On examination, he appears lethargic. He has a tachycardia of 102 bpm and blood pressure of 123/81 mmHg. The remainder of his observations are within the normal range. On his left lower leg, there is a target-shaped lesion. There is no evidence of crusting or bleeding and the rest of his skin and mucosa are spared.

He is given a prescription for an antimicrobial.

What is the mechanism of action of his antimicrobial prescription?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Inhibits 30S subunit of ribosomes

This patient has Lyme disease, an illness spread by tick bites. A recent hiking trip gives a hint to the likely diagnosis, along with the target-shaped lesion on his leg. The treatment of choice is doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic that works by binding to the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Aminoglycosides also have a similar mechanism of action.

E Inhibits deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) synthesis

This patient has Lyme disease, for which the treatment is with doxycycline, which works by blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit. Quinolones, such as ciprofloxacin work by inhibiting DNA synthesis. They bind to the enzyme DNA gyrase and, therefore, inhibit the replication of bacterial DNA.

A Damages bacterial DNA

Metronidazole is an antibiotic with a good affinity against anaerobic organisms. It works by damaging bacterial DNA through the production of toxic metabolites. It is not used in the treatment of Lyme disease.

B Disrupts cell membrane function

Penicillin antibiotics work by disrupting cell membrane function by binding to and inhibiting, proteins in the bacterial cell wall. They are not used in the first-line treatment for Lyme disease.

D Inhibits 50S subunit of ribosomes

This patient has Lyme disease, for which the treatment is with doxycycline that works by blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit. Macrolides, such as erythromycin and different classes of antibiotics, including clindamycin and linezolid, work in a similar way to tetracyclines. However, rather than blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit, they block the 50S subunit. 72475

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of fever, chills and headache. Her symptoms started shortly after returning from a trip to Ghana to see her family. She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medication.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L120–160 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)90 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)150 µmol/L50–90 µmol/L
Thick blood filmParasite level 4%
Thin blood filmMalaria falciparum species

What is the recommended management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Artesunate

This patient has a significant malarial infection, particularly given the raised parasite level (more than 2%). Other signs of severe infection include anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. The most appropriate management is parenteral artesunate, which is typically given IV. It should be continued until the parasite level drops to less than 1%, at which point the patient can be stepped down to PO treatment.

C Chloroquine monotherapy

Chloroquine is a commonly used antimalarial drug, provided that there is unlikely to be chloroquine resistance. However, it is not given to patients with symptoms of severe malarial infection, as seen in this patient’s presentation.

B Atovaquone–proguanil combination therapy

Atovaquone-proguanil is an artemisinin-based combination therapy that is recommended for the treatment of falciparum malaria. However, these drugs are usually indicated following initial treatment with artesunate and when the patient's drug regimen can be changed to PO medication. It is effective against chloroquine-resistant strains.

D Doxycycline monotherapy

Doxycycline can be used as both prophylaxis and treatment for malaria. However, it is not indicated in patients with severe malaria. Rather, IV drugs, such as artesunate, are recommended.

E Quinine plus clindamycin combination therapy

Quinine plus clindamycin combination therapy is an alternative treatment option for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. It can be considered for this patient as a PO switch after completion of IV artesunate. However, it is not indicated in the initial management, given the patient's presentation with severe disease.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Unit with groin pain that has come on over the past few hours, which is severe in intensity and leaves him unable to walk. He denies dysuria, haematuria or penile discharge. There is no history of trauma.

On examination, he has a fever of 38.3 °C, with severe tenderness on palpation of the left testis, which is also warm and swollen. A firm, tender mass is noted at the posterior aspect of the testes. The cremasteric reflex is present. There is a change in the pain noticed when the scrotum is elevated. Urine dipstick showed leukocytes. Radionucleotide scan shows increased blood flow to the left testicle.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Epididymitis

This is a case of acute epididymitis, which is commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The increased blood flow is secondary to the inflammation process.

E Testicular torsion

In testicular torsion, the pain is usually worse with elevation of scrotum, and the cremasteric reflex is usually absent. It would also not explain the leukocytes in the urine dip or the increased rather than decreased blood flow. Colour flow Doppler, in the hands of a skilled scanning technician, will demonstrate reduced blood flow in testicular torsion, and may be more available than radionucleotide scanning in the acute setting.

A Mumps orchitis

Mumps orchitis can occur 4 or 5 days following parotitis but does not occur in vaccinated patients.

B Testicular malignancy

It would not explain the acute onset, high temperature, leukocytes in the urine or tenderness.

D Urinary tract infection

This would present with dysuria and not with testicular tenderness.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is seen in the Ambulatory Care Clinic with a 6-month history of general malaise and intermittent fevers. He complains of recurrent respiratory tract infections and has recently been treated for oral candida. He has a past medical history of hypertension which is treated with ramipril 5 mg once daily.

A number of investigations are ordered and his human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antigen testing returns as positive. He is started on a combination of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) comprising lamivudine, abacavir and ritonavir.

Which of the following is the most common side-effect of lamivudine?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bone marrow suppression

Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). A common side-effect of all NRTIs is bone marrow suppression, causing anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia.

D Renal calculi

Renal calculi are a side-effect seen in patients taking HAART. However, it is a side-effect of the protease inhibitor indinavir due to its poor solubility and renal excretion, rather than a side-effect of NRTIs.

B Peripheral neuropathy

Peripheral neuropathy is a very rare side-effect of lamivudine. Paraesthesiae is another very rare side-effect of lamivudine.

C Pancreatitis

Pancreatitis is a side-effect of NRTIs but is much rarer than bone marrow suppression.

E Insulin resistance

Insulin resistance is not very common side-effect of protease inhibitors and NRTI.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old, HIV-positive man is brought to the Emergency Department by his partner, who has noticed increasing confusion over the past four weeks. The patient has been non-compliant with his antiretroviral therapy and has not attended outpatient clinic for over six months. The patient denies any headache or neurological symptoms but scores 0/10 on the Mental Test Score. Neurological examination reveals some past pointing and dysdiadochokinesis on the left but nil else. The patient is afebrile. Computed tomography (CT) of the head with contrast demonstrates no focal lesions.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Protein0.8 g/L< 0.45 g/L
Glucose (plasma)4.8 (5.2) mmol/L2.5–3.9 mmol/L
Cryptococcal antigen (CRAG)Negative
White cell count (WCC)2 cell/mm³< 5/mm³
Red blood cells (RBC)4 cell/mm³< 5/mm³
MicroscopyNo organisms seen

Which treatment is most likely to improve the symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART)

The most likely diagnosis is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is a unique demyelinating disease which usually occurs in a person with abnormal immune responses resulting from serious disease, treatment with cytotoxic drugs or irradiation, or long-term immunosuppression. The pathology of PML is distinctive and consists of multiple foci of demyelination of varying size from pinpoint lesions to areas of several centimetres. The lesions may occur anywhere but are usually in the cerebral hemispheres, less often in the cerebellum and brainstem and rarely in the spinal cord. Typically, PML evolves gradually, with impairment of mental function and disturbance of speech and vision. Movement may also be affected. The disease then progresses rapidly and the patient is severely disabled, eventually becoming demented, blind and paralysed, and finally there is coma and death. Almost any neurological sign can be part of the clinical spectrum, motor sensory or cerebellar signs depending on the white matter areas affected. Often nothing is seen on CT, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a much more useful modality in this condition.

PML generally occurs only at low CD4 counts and there is no specific therapy. PCR for JC virus, a polyomavirus and the causative organism, should be performed. Commencing HAART can improve symptoms in some patients, although some can deteriorate. It is inevitably progressive. Another possibility is HIV-associated encephalopathy, where the HIV virus itself is responsible for the pathology. HAART is also the treatment of choice for this. The clinical details do not suggest neurological toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV) or cryptococcal meningitis, so the other answers are incorrect.

E High-dose fluconazole

This is an alternative to amphotericin B in cryptococcal infection in HIV-positive individuals. Cryptococcal infection usually presents with high fever and headache, and patients may also have evidence of raised intracranial pressure. The negative antigen testing makes this a less likely diagnosis.

A Sulphadiazine and pyrimethamine

This is the treatment for toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasma gondii is a common cause of cerebral abcesses in patients with a low CD4 count. The presentation is with focal neurological signs, confusion and evidence of raised intracranial pressure. Imaging in these patients shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions which can be associated with mass effect. The absence of major neurological signs and headache makes this diagnosis less likely, as does the normal CT scan.

C IV ganciclovir

It is the first-line treatment for CMV infection. CMV infection in the HIV immunocompromised brain normally presents with worsening confusion and mental withdrawal. On examination there can be cranial nerve palsy and nystagmus. CT findings in these patients can demonstrate diffuse white matter hypodensities with ependymal enhancement, ventricular enlargement, meningeal enhancement and focal or ring-enhancing lesions. The absence of any relevant examination findings and the absence of CT findings makes this an incorrect answer.

D IV aciclovir

It is not used against any causes of confusion in HIV-positive individuals. It would be an appropriate treatment against herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated encephalitis, for example.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old intravenous (IV) drug abuser is admitted with lethargy, night sweats, and a new systolic murmur noted by the doctor at the Drug Rehabilitation Clinic. Examination reveals a temperature of 38.0 oC; blood pressure is 105/82 mmHg. His pulse is 85 beats per minute (bpm) and regular, and there is a pansystolic murmur. There is wheeze on auscultation of the chest. His body mass index is 21 kg/m². You note multiple marks consistent with self-injection of heroin.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)97 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.9 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)103 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.7 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)139 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)241 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Transthoracic echocardiogramMitral regurgitation with valve vegitations
Blood culturesBacillus cereus identified

What is the most appropriate antibiotic intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Vancomycin

Glycopeptides, such as vancomycin, are highly effective in the treatment of invasive Bacillus cereus (B cereus) infection, with little or no evidence of resistance to their use. Out of the options given, this makes intravenous (IV) vancomycin the most appropriate intervention. B cereus rarely causes serious infections but is a rare cause of both native and prosthetic valve endocarditis. In this scenario, vancomycin is the best option, but it would also depend on drug susceptibilities and response to treatment.

D Penicillin G

Most B. cereus isolates produce beta-lactamases and are resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins. For this reason, penicillins and cephalosporins should not be used for empiric treatment of Bacillus spp infection.

A Ampicillin
