Ampicillin is the intervention of choice for listeria infection. For listeria meningitis it is given in combination with gentamicin. Meropenem and linezolid are potential alternatives for the treatment of listeria meningitis.

B Ceftriaxone

B cereus isolates have significant levels of resistance to cephalosporins which precludes their use as a first-line agent here. Vancomycin is preferred where significant resistance is yet to be identified.

C Ciprofloxacin

Although quinolone resistance is not as prevalent as resistance to cephalosporins among B cereus isolates, around 10% of patients in one case series were found to have an intermediate or quinolone-resistant strain of the bacterium.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe pain in his left lower leg that began 24 hours ago. The pain has rapidly worsened, out of proportion to the physical findings, and he now has swelling and erythema extending from the knee to the ankle. He has a history of type II diabetes and hypertension. On examination, the leg is swollen with erythematous, tender skin and patches of discoloration, but there are no clear signs of fluctuance or abscess formation. His temperature is 39°C his BP is 90/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 110 bpm.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)129 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)25 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)250 mg/L< 5 mg/L
Sodium (Na⁺)129 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Creatine kinase (CK)820 U/L30–200 U/L

What is the most appropriate next step in investigating this patient’s condition?
options: Doppler ultrasound of the affected leg
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Surgical exploration

Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement to halt the spread of infection. Prompt surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic, as it allows direct visualisation of tissue necrosis and removal of infected tissue.

D MRI of the affected leg

MRI can show soft tissue involvement and may aid in diagnosis when the clinical presentation is uncertain. However, MRI may delay definitive treatment, and in cases with high clinical suspicion, immediate surgical exploration is preferred.

A Urgent tissue biopsy

While a tissue biopsy can confirm the diagnosis microscopically, surgical exploration is prioritised to establish the diagnosis and to allow for immediate debridement, which is lifesaving in necrotising fasciitis.

B Blood cultures

Blood cultures are indicated in patients with suspected severe infections, especially in the presence of systemic signs such as hypotension and fever. However, they are not diagnostic for necrotising fasciitis, which requires urgent exploration and debridement. Blood cultures are often taken alongside immediate surgical intervention.

E Doppler ultrasound of the affected leg

Doppler ultrasound may be useful in evaluating vascular compromise, but is not diagnostic for necrotising fasciitis and is not indicated in this emergency. Rapid surgical intervention is necessary to prevent mortality.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant attends the Emergency Department. She is very worried as her 3-year-old son has been sent home from nursery with ‘slapped cheek’ disease.

Which of the following is the most likely complication associated with fetal slapped cheek infection?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Hydrops fetalis

Slapped cheek disease is caused by parvovirus B19 infection. It is known to cause fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis in 1–3% (2nd trimester), and intrauterine fetal death. Infections peak in spring and autumn. Incubation period is usually around 12–14 days, meaning that this lady is likely to have been already exposed via contact with her son. In total, B19 infection may account for up to 20% of non-immune cases of hydrops. Autopsy studies indicate that highest viral concentrations are found in bone marrow and myocardium. Infection can be confirmed either with IgM serology or PCR where it is available. IV immunoglobulin may be of value in some patients.

E Congenital blindness

This can be caused by several pathologies, including antenatal rubella, antenatal varicella and antenatal cytomegalovirus. Other diseases can cause other eye problems which can lead to blindness if not treated.

A Congenital deafness

This could be caused by antenatal rubella. Rubella is a viral infection causing a pink rash and lymphadenopathy behind the ears. Infection in the first 11 weeks of pregnancy can cause fetal rubella syndrome if the mother is not vaccinated. Fetal rubella syndrome causes deafness, cataracts, learning disability, growth restriction and heart defects. Diagnosis during pregnancy is via serology. Other causes include antenatal cytomegalovirus.

C Fetal clotting disorder

This could be caused be antenatal toxoplasmosis through cat exposure. Systemic neonatal infection can include thrombocytopenic pupura, hepatosplenomegaly, pneumonia, rash and jaundice. There can also be significant neurological disease.

D Fetal polycythaemia

This can be caused by increased fetal erythropoiesis related to hypoxia which can be secondary due to placental insufficiency, endocrine disorders, delayed cord clamping, twin–twin transfusion and intrapartum asphyxia.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe sore throat. He arrived a few days earlier from Central America to visit a relative. He is extremely lethargic, with a fever, and is finding it increasingly difficult to swallow. His temperature is 38.1 oC, his blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, and his pulse is 72 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Investigation reveals a grey pseudomembrane forming on the posterior pharynx.

Which of the following is the most important initial investigation for this patient?
options: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for anthrax spores
PCR for diphtheria toxin A subunit
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E PCR for diphtheria toxin A subunit

This patient has diphtheria, with the typical grey/white pseudomembrane forming on the posterior pharynx. It is important to confirm the diagnosis as rapidly as possible, with PCR for the A-subunit of diphtheria toxin proving an early pointer to the diagnosis. This should be followed by formal culture and Elek testing. Treatment is with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics, usually erythromycin.

A Crystal Vibrio Cholera (VC) testing

Crystal VC testing is a rapid stool dipstick test for cholera that can provide rapid diagnosis for individuals out in the field who suspect an outbreak of cholera. Where a positive result is found, confirmation is recommended with formal stool culture.

B Elek testing

This is an in-vitro test of virulence performed on specimens of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, the cause of diphtheria. It is used to test for toxigenicity of strains of the bacterium. PCR is preferred to confirm the diagnosis of toxin-producing diphtheria infection because of the speed in confirming the diagnosis and potential for then isolating the patient.

C Monospot testing

Monospot testing is used to confirm the diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis. Although infectious mononucleosis does present with pharyngitis, the membrane formation here is a much stronger pointer towards diphtheria as the underlying diagnosis.

D Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for anthrax spores

Anthrax infection does cause respiratory tract symptoms, but it does not cause the pharyngitis with membrane formation seen here. Respiratory anthrax infection is extremely rare, and outside use as a bioweapon it is seen in individuals who work in poorly regulated abattoirs or in tanneries in the developing world. It is diagnosed by PCR. 72141

questions.question:
A 64-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is treated with doxycycline for an exacerbation.

Which of the following represents the mode of action of doxycycline?
options: Inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30s ribosomal subunit
Inhibits protein synthesis by blocking the action of peptidyltransferase
Inhibits bacterial DNA synthesis by inhibiting bacterial dihydrofolate reductase
Inhibit bacterial DNA replication by inhibiting the action of bacterial DNA gyrase
Inhibits bacterial wall synthesis by stopping the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30s ribosomal subunit

Tetracyclines inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30s ribosomal subunit. This prevents the binding of transfer RNA to messenger RNA at the ribosomal subunit. Amino acids then cannot be added to polypeptide chains, and new proteins cannot be made. The class are bacteriostatic and have a wide range of activity against gram-positive, gram-negative bacteria, and Plasmodium falciparum.

E Inhibits bacterial wall synthesis by stopping the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links

Penicillin inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking in bacterial cell walls. By doing this they block bacterial cell division. There is also synergy with aminoglycosides, with penicillin destroying the integrity of bacterial cell walls and facilitating their entry to interfere with protein synthesis.

B Inhibits protein synthesis by blocking the action of peptidyltransferase

Macrolides such as clarithromycin inhibit the action of bacterial peptidyltransferase, preventing the enzyme from adding the growing peptide attached to tRNA to the next amino acid. They also inhibit ribosomal translocation. They are mainly used to treat gram-positive infections and a limited range of gram-negative infections such as Bordetella pertussis and Haemophilus influenzae.

C Inhibits bacterial DNA synthesis by inhibiting bacterial dihydrofolate reductase

Trimethoprim is an inhibitor of bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. It is primarily used in the treatment of urinary tract infection. Because it may reduce folic acid levels, its use is not recommended in early pregnancy. By inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, it blocks the production of bacterial DNA.

D Inhibit bacterial DNA replication by inhibiting the action of bacterial DNA gyrase

Quinolones interfere with DNA replication, and they do this by blocking the action of DNA gyrase. They also interfere with the topoisomerase IV enzyme, another enzyme involved in DNA replication. Quinolones have fallen out of favour because of associations with adverse events, including tendon rupture, joint pains, and neuropathies. 72156

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of blurred vision and a 3- hour history of increasing shortness of breath. She was a user of intravenous heroin and had previously been admitted with groin abscesses.

On examination, her temperature was 36.7 °C, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and saturations 95% on air. There was no rash or neck stiffness. Her chest was clear. She had dysarthria and an ataxic gait. Her pupils were normal in diameter but were fixed and did not accommodate. There was bilateral ptosis and facial weakness.

Investigations:

Chest X-rayNormal
pH7.217.35 - 7.45
p(O₂)8.7 kPa11.3 - 12.6 kPa
p(CO₂)6.0 kPa4.7 - 6.0 kPa
HCO₃20 mmol/L21 - 29 mmol/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Botulism

This is a rare condition, but the patient’s presentation is typical. This patient is an intravenous drug user, which is the most common route of exposure to botulinum toxin. Initially (within 1–8 days of contact with the toxin), the patient develops bilateral cranial nerve signs; here the patient has developed the typical blurred vision resulting from diplopia, and slurred speech from bulbar involvement. She has no impairment of consciousness, and the pupils are fixed but of normal diameter – again, this is a classical presentation of botulism. The patient is afebrile – fever is unusual in botulism. Her type I respiratory failure is due to paralysis of the respiratory muscles; she is likely to progress to type II respiratory failure rapidly without appropriate treatment.

D Meningococcal sepsis

Although a raised respiratory rate is common in sepsis, meningococcal sepsis without pulmonary disease (her chest X-ray is normal) cannot explain the type I respiratory failure seen in her blood gas. If this were meningococcal meningitis, you would expect the patient to report a headache or you would expect to find fever, photophobia or neck stiffness on examination. None of these features are present. Cerebellar and bulbar signs (as seen here) have been reported in meningococcal meningitis, but it is an extremely uncommon presentation. Therefore, although the patient has neurological signs, these are unlikely to be explained by meningococcal meningitis. In fact, bilateral involvement of multiple cranial nerves and fixed pupils are typical of botulism; botulism can also explain her rapid-onset respiratory failure caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles (hence type I respiratory failure on the blood gas).

B Heroin overdose

Patients with a heroin overdose would not present with blurred vision and shortness of breath; instead patients are usually brought to the Emergency Department with severely impaired consciousness. In milder cases, patients have drowsiness, nausea and vomiting and constipation. You would also expect the patient to have pinpoint pupils in opiate overdose, which are not seen here. Finally, opiates are respiratory depressants and therefore in overdose can cause hypoxaemia (as in this patient’s case), but through a reduced respiratory rate; here the patient’s respiratory rate is raised. This patient’s presentation is classic of botulism.

C Guillain–Barré syndrome

Typically, Guillain–Barré syndrome presents with ascending weakness and sensory disturbance (ie beginning in the legs and progressing towards the arms and finally the face). It does not cause a truly ataxic gait, and ocular involvement is exceedingly uncommon. Therefore, although Guillain–Barré syndrome could explain her respiratory failure, it would not explain her presentation with blurred vision without any leg weakness or sensory disturbance. It also could not explain her fixed pupils. Instead, this constellation of symptoms and signs is typical of botulism.

E Myasthenia gravis

There are many features of this patient’s presentation that are compatible with myasthenia gravis, specifically diplopia, ptosis and facial weakness and respiratory failure due to neuromuscular weakness. However, there are two features that are not compatible: fixed pupils and ataxia. These are not features of myasthenia gravis, and therefore an alternative diagnosis should be sought. In this case, the constellation of symptoms is typical of botulism. 71445

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of fatigue, intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats and weight loss. He has a history of a prosthetic aortic valve replacement five years ago. On examination, he is afebrile, with no peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. Blood cultures are persistently negative, and ECHO reveals vegetations on the prosthetic aortic valve. Laboratory investigations show elevated inflammatory marker levels and mild normocytic anaemia.

Which test is most appropriate to confirm a diagnosis of Coxiella burnetii endocarditis?
options: Serological testing for phase I and II antibodies
Repeat blood cultures by using specialised media
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Serological testing for phase I and II antibodies

This is the gold standard for diagnosing C. burnetii endocarditis. High titres of phase I immunoglobulin G antibodies (more than 1: 800) are diagnostic in the appropriate clinical context. C. burnetii is an obligate intracellular pathogen that cannot be routinely cultured, making serological tests essential for diagnosis.

E Histopathology of the valve tissue

Valve histopathology may demonstrate inflammatory changes consistent with infective endocarditis, but it is invasive and not typically used for primary diagnosis. PCR or immunohistochemistry on excised valve tissue could confirm the organism if surgery is performed.

A 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing

This method can detect bacterial DNA and identify uncommon pathogens, but it is typically used in culture- negative endocarditis when a specific organism is not suspected. Serology remains more accessible and specific for C. burnetii.

C PCR on blood samples

PCR may detect C. burnetii DNA and can be useful in acute infections, but it is less sensitive for chronic infections such as endocarditis. PCR is usually complementary to serology.

D Repeat blood cultures by using specialised media

C. burnetii does not grow in standard or specialised blood culture media, and repeated cultures would not yield results.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with bloody diarrhoea and lower abdominal cramps. She works as a volunteer at the local petting farm. Apparently three other workers from the same farm have presented with symptoms over the past week. She is otherwise well with a history of asthma, for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, a temperature of 37.8 °C and a pulse of 88 bpm and regular. There is dull left-sided abdominal pain on palpation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)119 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.5 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)123 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Prothrombin time (PT)17.2 s10.6–14.9 s
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)33 s20–41 s
Stool sample: E. coli 0157

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Supportive therapy only

The majority of patients with E. coli 157 infection recover spontaneously within one to two weeks. Recently, application of a monoclonal antibody that specifically binds to C5, eculizumab, became available to treat patients with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, replacing plasma exchange or infusion as primary therapy.

B Naproxen

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may actually exacerbate renal impairment in patients with HUS and should be avoided here. Should pain relief be required, then paracetamol is a more appropriate option.

A Ciprofloxacin

Evidence from case series suggests that use of antibiotics may increase the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and so they are avoided in the majority of cases.

C Prednisolone

Small case series suggest a potential positive impact for immune intervention in HUS, including with prednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin, although the evidence is not strong enough to recommend routine use of prednisolone here.

D Probiotic supplements

The main evidence for benefit of probiotic supplements comes from treatment of Clostridium difficile where they may reduce the risks of infection in the elderly population.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman who has received a renal transplant for chronic renal failure related to type 1 diabetes comes to the Emergency Department with a dry cough and increasing shortness of breath. This has now limited her exercise tolerance to approximately 50 m before she gets short of breath. She is taking multiple immunosuppressive agents and received her transplant approximately eight weeks ago. She says the cough and shortness of breath began some five days earlier. She has a temperature of 38.2 °C; her blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg, and pulse 82 bpm and regular. Her renal transplant scar looks well healed. There are scattered crackles and wheezes heard across both lung fields on auscultation. Her oxygen saturation measured on pulse oximetry is 94% at rest and drops to 91%, as you ask her to walk back and forth ten times across the consulting room.

Investigations;

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine142 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)189 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)672 U/L 100–190 IU/L
Chest X-ray (CXR): Perihilar fluffy opacities.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C IV Co-trimoxazole

The underlying diagnosis is P. jirovecii (PCJ) pneumonia, to which this patient has increased susceptibility because of her immunosuppression. Out of the options given, co-trimoxazole is more effective than pentamidine, although it is not always tolerated. Duration is usually from 14 to 21 days. Prognosis is poor, and in patients without an underlying human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, mortality may be 30% or higher.

B IV Co-amoxiclav

This would be an appropriate intervention for a community-acquired pneumonia. However, the X-ray findings, history of immunosuppression and low ambulatory oxygen saturations suggest a diagnosis of P. jirovecii pneumonia.

A Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone

Ceftriaxone would be potential choices for treating bacterial community-acquired pneumonia. However, the X- ray findings, history of immunosuppression and low ambulatory oxygen saturations suggest a diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

D IV Pentamidine

This is used as prophylaxis against PCJ infection in patients undergoing stem cell transplantation. It is not commonly used as treatment due to the risk for toxicity.

E Nebulised Pentamidine

Nebulised pentamidine does offer some benefit in the treatment of PCJ pneumonia, but it is less effective than iv co-trimoxazole. It should be considered for use if iv co-trimoxazole is not tolerated. It should be noted that it is highly teratogenic, so it should be administered in a well-ventilated room away from staff members who are of childbearing age.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department after returning from a backpacking trip around South America. She has a 2-day history of abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. There is a small amount of fresh blood mixed in with her vomit. Her symptoms have followed from a 4-day period of intermittent fevers, myalgia and headaches. Prior to this, she has been well, with no other past medical history. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8 °C. Her heart rate is 113 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 117/65 mmHg. She has a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, with saturations of 95% on room air. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. She has generalised abdominal tenderness and voluntary guarding in the epigastrium. Bowel sounds are present. There is a widespread maculopapular rash over her face, trunk and limbs. Examination of the ear, nose and throat system was unremarkable, other than some mild gum irritation and bleeding.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Dengue fever

This patient has dengue fever. It is spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito and is common in many areas of the world, including Asia and South America. The presence of fever, headache, myalgia and a maculopapular rash early on in the illness is common, along with facial flushing. In some, the disease can progress to a viral haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome in severe cases. Treatment is mostly supportive with intravenous fluids and transfusion as required.

E Typhoid fever

Typhoid fever is a bacterial illness secondary to Salmonella typhi. It is an enteric fever with symptoms comprising abdominal pain and distension, along with either constipation or diarrhoea. Characteristic features that point to a diagnosis of typhoid fever include pale pink macules, otherwise known as rose spots on the trunk of infected patients. It does not explain this patient’s symptoms, making it an incorrect answer.

A Yellow fever

Yellow fever is a viral haemorrhagic illness spread by the Aedes mosquito. It presents as a mild flu-like illness followed by a brief remission period before the onset of haematemesis, jaundice and oliguria. It is common in Central and South America, as well as Africa. The presenting symptoms in the question are milder than those of yellow fever, with no mention of jaundice or oliguria and only a small amount of fresh blood mixed in with the

patient’s vomitus. While yellow fever should still be considered as a differential diagnosis, alternative diagnoses should also be considered. The presence of a maculopapular rash, for example, hints towards the diagnosis of dengue fever, the correct answer in this case.

B Zika virus

Zika virus is spread by the A. aegypti mosquito. It is common in Africa, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific. It is a short-lived illness with symptoms including fever, rash, arthralgia and conjunctivitis. Haemorrhagic symptoms are not seen in the Zika virus, making it a less likely diagnosis.

D Malaria

Malaria is a parasitic disease spread by the Anopheles mosquito. There are multiple subtypes, of which malaria falciparum is the most common. The disease is generally transmitted in Africa, South East Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean and Western Pacific countries. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgia, headache and nausea and vomiting. Hepatosplenomegaly may appear. Complications of malaria include cerebral malaria and blackwater fever which is an intravascular haemolysis causing acute kidney injury and jaundice. This patient has travelled back from South America, where malaria is less prevalent. The maculopapular rash and minor bleeding also suggest an alternative diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department following a seizure witnessed by her daughter. The daughter reports that her mother is normally fit and well but the latter has been complaining of headaches recently. The patient is on no known medications and is a non-smoker. She has recently returned from a trip to China. Physical examination findings are normal, although the patient is in a post-ictal state. An urgent computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is arranged, which shows a periventricular cystic lesion in the parietal lobe, with surrounding oedema. The Radiologist says that the appearance is compatible with neurocysticercosis.

Which of the following investigations would be most specific for neurocysticercosis?
options: Fundoscopic examination to directly visualise subretinal parasites
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detection of cysticercal antigens
Resolution of intracranial cystic lesions after therapy with albendazole
Serum anticysticercal antibodies demonstrated by immunoblot assay
Single stool examination for ova and parasites of Taenia solium
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Fundoscopic examination to directly visualise subretinal parasites

The pork tapeworm (T. solium) is the causative organism in cysticercosis, which can affect either the intestine, causing an intestinal tapeworm infection, or the central nervous system, causing neurocysticercosis. The infection is acquired through ingestion of undercooked pork containing cysticerci of T. solium. It is important to elicit a history of exposure to an area where the parasite is endemic. Since signs and symptoms can be non- specific, certain criteria are required to diagnose the infection. Diagnosis can be difficult as radiological signs and immunological tests are often non-specific. However, direct visualisation of parasites has a very high diagnostic yield and is considered an absolute criterion. The mainstay of treatment is symptomatic relief, eg anticonvulsants for seizures, and corticosteroids for cerebral oedema. Antiparasitic drugs (albendazole) are used if viable cysticerci are suspected and they should be given under expert supervision.

E Single stool examination for ova and parasites of Taenia solium

It is worth noting that since the eggs are shed intermittently, a single stool examination looking for ova and parasites may not be enough to identify the tapeworm carriers. While a positive result would be very specific, the sensitivity of the test is low.

B Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detection of cysticercal antigens

This is because while neurocysticercosis often involves high parasite counts within the ventricles and basal cisterns, there is not always evidence of antibodies within the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). If positive, it is considered a major, rather than an absolute, criterion. The CSF could also show an elevated eosinophil count and the presence of parasite antigens.

C Resolution of intracranial cystic lesions after therapy with albendazole

Albendazole is not always necessary for lesion resolution, as has been documented in many cases.

D Serum anticysticercal antibodies demonstrated by immunoblot assay

Antibody studies are frustratingly non-specific for neurocysticercosis. Antibody results are still considered a major criterion, although not as specific as direct parasite visualisation.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man presents to the clinic with headache, neck stiffness, malaise and photophobia which has been worsening over the past few days. He came to the UK 2 years ago and since then has been at university.

Over the past few months, his partner tells you that he has lost weight and seems to suffer from night sweats.

On examination, he is pyrexial 37.8 °C, has neck stiffness and photophobia. There is axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. He appears to have isolated 6 th nerve palsy.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)120 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Lumbar punctureTurbid appearance, 22 cm water opening pressure, elevated CSF protein, lymphocytes ++, neutrophils +
India ink testPositive

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Cryptococcal meningitis

Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast (fungus) which can cause a meningitis in the immunocompromised. The India ink test is used to diagnose cryptococcal meningitis, and the raised opening pressure, turbid appearance to the CSF, raised protein and mixed lymphocytic/neutrophil picture are relatively typical of the diagnosis. From his history there is a strong suspicion that he may be HIV positive, accounting for the underlying cryptococcal infection. Management of the condition involves the use of amphotericin B, which is typically given as IV combination therapy with flucytosine for a period of 2 weeks. Raised CSF opening pressure is associated with a poor prognosis in this condition.

D Meningococcal meningitis

Meningococcal meningitis is the most common bacterial meningitis in the UK and is caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Presentation is with acute-onset fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting. Prompt treatment with IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) is essential as the disease is rapidly fatal. CSF typically shows a neutrophilia, low glucose, raised protein and Gram-negative diplococci on the Gram stain.

A Herpes simplex encephalitis

Herpes simplex encephalitis is most commonly caused by HSV-1. Presentation is typically with fever and altered mentation, there may also be a recent history of cold sores. Onset is typical over a few hours to days and immunocompetent patients may be affected. In this case the tempo of presentation, as well as the CSF finding, excludes herpes simplex encephalitis.

B Cytomegalovirus (CMV) meningoencephalitis

CMV meningoencephalitis is rare but possible in the immunocompetent host. In the immunocompromised (eg HIV positive, transplant recipient) the risk is increased. Presentation would typically be with acute-onset fever, meningism and altered mentation. In this case the tempo of presentation, as well as the CSF findings, exclude CMV meningoencephalitis.

E Tuberculous meningitis

Tuberculous meningitis may result from primary infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis or reactivation of latent infection. It is more common in the immunocompromised. Presentation is often subacute with fever, neck stiffness, headache and altered mentation. Typical MRI changes are of a basal meningitis. CSF findings are typically a lymphocytosis with low glucose and raised protein. In this case we are told that the India ink stain is positive which points to an alternative explanation for the patient’s symptoms. 20978

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man returns from a trip across the Mediterranean, North and sub-Saharan Africa. He reports feeling generally unwell for the past few days with a fever.

On examination, you notice a tick bite eschar and a surrounding rash on the left mid-thigh.

Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Rickettsia conorii

This patient has infection with R. conorii, the hallmark of which is the tick bite eschar. Common presenting features include fever, rash, malaise, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and joint and muscle pain. Diagnosis is usually made on clinical history and serological testing.

The most appropriate choice for antibiotic therapy is doxycycline. Other choices include ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, however these should be avoided wherever possible, as fluoroquinolone use is associated with an increased risk of severe potentially irreversible side effects such as peripheral neuropathy and tendonitis.

Although fatalities can occur due to infection, they are rare. Complications may include neuropathy, Guillain– Barré syndrome, acute kidney disease, hepatomegaly and thrombocytopenia.

E Orientia tsutsugamushi

This organism is most common in South East Asia and is therefore unlikely. It presents with eschar, hepatomegaly, cough and lymphoadenopathy.

A Rhiphicephalus sanguineus

The vector for infection with R. conorii is commonly R. sanguineus or dog tick and is not an infectious organism of humans.

B Rickettsia rickettsii

This is the pathogen which causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF). RMSF is endemic throughout the Americas and following one to two weeks after a tick bite there is general malaise, fever and a rash. The rash starts as a centripetal macular rash progressing to a petechial rash by day six. The absence of such a rash makes this diagnosis unlikely, and RMSF usually has a target rash around the bite lesion rather than an eschar.

D Rickettsia prowzekii

Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, which is transmitted by the body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis).This causes headaches, fever, muscle and joint pain as well as nausea and vomiting, with a discrete rash six days after onset. The absence of this constellation makes this diagnosis unlikely. 33194

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman attends the Genito-urinary Medicine (GUM) Clinic. She is concerned about vaginal discharge with an unpleasant smell. She has noticed these symptoms for the past 3 weeks and has been washing her genitals regularly with soap and shower gel. She sometimes puts Dettol in her bath. She is married and has had no other sexual partners for 5 years. On examination, she has a normal vulva, vagina and cervix. There is a thin, white discharge with a fishy smell.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Bacterial vaginosis

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is caused by replacement of the usual vaginal lactobacilli with anaerobic bacteria, genital mycoplasmas and others. Douching, washing with scented soaps and gels have been implicated and the patient should be advised to stop these practices. Treatment is with metronidazole. BV is not sexually transmitted. BV is the commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age. It is twice as common as vaginal candidiasis. The prevalence of BV has varied from 5% in asymptomatic college students, 12% in pregnant women and 30% in women undergoing termination of pregnancy.

E HIV +ve

This is very unlikely given the lack of exposure and HIV does not cause vaginal discharge.

A Candida

Candida causes a severe itch and white lumpy discharge, which would commonly be seen on examination. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is the second most common cause of vaginitis and vaginal discharge after BV: the lifetime incidence of vulvovaginal candidiasis is estimated at 50–75%. The prevalence of vulvovaginal candidiasis is not known, but the disease is diagnosed in 5–15% of women who attend sexually transmitted disease and family planning clinics

C Trichomonas

Trichomonas gives an itch, offensive green discharge and is sexually transmitted. In 1997, GUM clinics in the UK reported over 5600 cases of trichomoniasis in women and 250 cases in men.

D Chlamydia

Women present with dysuria, abdominal pain, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and vaginal discharge. Men can have urethritis with dysuria and discharge and sometimes epididymo-orchitis. 8517

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department after being found collapsed at home by her partner. She is two weeks postpartum and had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. There is no past medical history of note and her only regular medication includes vitamin supplements.

On examination, she is drowsy and disoriented with a GCS of 13. Her temperature is 39.5 °C with a heart rate of 140 bpm and a BP of 88/45 mmHg. Her mucous membranes and skin are diffusely erythematous with desquamation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationResultsNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)118 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)28.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)290 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)145 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea12.1 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)180 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)229 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Toxic shock syndrome

This patient has a diagnosis of toxic shock syndrome (TSS), given the features of acute systemic upset with fever, hypotension and a desquamating erythematous rash. TSS is an exotoxin-mediated illness secondary to bacterial infection with Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and group A streptococcal species such as Streptococcus pyogenes. On the first presentation, the signs and symptoms of TSS may generally be non-specific, with signs of systemic upset and no clear source. However, if left untreated, the TSS can cause multiorgan failure and death. TSS secondary to group A streptococcus is most commonly associated with an infected cutaneous site (eg necrotising fasciitis). In contrast, TSS secondary to staphylococcus is associated with prolonged tampon use and postpartum infections. The recent history of a

vaginal delivery points toward S. aureus as the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation. Treatment of TSS involves early broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment, intravenous fluid resuscitation and likely admission to the Intensive Care Unit.

D Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a severe skin reaction associated with skin and mucocutaneous sheet loss. It is usually secondary to medication use, including anticonvulsants, antibiotics and non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drugs. Although this patient has evidence of desquamation, the only medication use given is vitamin supplements that are unlikely to cause SJS.

A Amniotic fluid embolus

Amniotic fluid embolism is a very important differential diagnosis to consider, given that this patient has recently given birth. It can also give rise to the presentation of collapse, tachycardia and hypotension. However, it is not associated with an erythematous desquamating rash, making this diagnosis less likely.

B Erythroderma

Erythroderma is a rare dermatological condition characterised by diffuse reddening of the skin, usually secondary to an underlying skin disease (eg eczema), although up to 30% of cases are idiopathic. However, the presence of systemic upset in a postpartum woman with significantly elevated inflammatory markers and evidence of an acute kidney injury is more suggestive of a more serious underlying condition.

C Gram-negative septic shock

Gram-negative septic shock is a reasonable differential diagnosis given the systemic features of sepsis. However, it is uncommon for Gram-negative organisms to give rise to a desquamating rash, as seen in this patient. The diffuse erythematous skin involvement is the key distinguishing factor that points toward toxic shock syndrome (TSS) as the likely diagnosis.

questions.question:
A schoolgirl returns from trip to France with 4-day history of headache, vomiting and fever.

On examination, she is alert with neck stiffness and no focal neurology signs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain demonstrates no obvious lesions.

Investigations of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Opening pressure24 cm water (5–18cm)6–20 cmH₂O
Protein0.8 g/L< 0.45 g/L
White cell count (WCC)110/mm³ (99% lymphocytes)< 5/mm³
Glucose3.2 mmol/L (serum glucose 4.0 mmol/L)2.5–3.9 mmol/L (two-thirds plasma value)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Viral meningitis

A clinical meningitis with an elevated CSF pressure, slightly elevated protein and lymphocytosis is likely to be of viral aetiology, particularly in young previously fit individual.

E TB meningitis

TB meningitis would result in lymphocytes in the CSF, but it is unlikely given the lack of immunosuppression and travel to a TB-prevalent country. It is also less likely given the absence of meningeal enhancement on the MRI and the short presentation.

B Cryptococcal meningitis

Cryptococcal and mycoplasma meningitis both give rise to lymphocytic CSF but the cell counts are usually lower (<80/ml) and the glucose reduced. Also, cryptococcal infection is significantly associated with severe T- dysfunction such as immunosuppression from HIV or iatrogenic immunosuppression following organ transplant. The normal MRI also makes this a less likely diagnosis.

C Pneumococcal meningitis

This diagnosis is associated with polymorphic cells in the CSF and relatively low glucose, with severe systemic upset and a shorter presentation.

D Meningococcal meningitis

This diagnosis is associated with polymorphic cells in the CSF and relatively low glucose, with severe systemic upset and a shorter presentation.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old HIV-positive patient presents to the clinic complaining of increasing shortness of breath, dry cough and wheezing.

On examination, you can hear a left-sided monophonic wheeze. You notice several lesions on his exposed skin, including on his nose, as below. He is a lifelong non-smoker.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)103 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.6 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)130 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
CD4 count92 cells/mm³500–1500 cells/mm³
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Limited left lower zone collapse

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Endobronchial Kaposi’s sarcoma

This patient has violaceous plaques on his nose characteristic of Kaposi’s sarcoma.Pulmonary Kaposi’s sarcoma is found in between 6% and 30% of patients with HIV, and is the most common tumour seen. In patients who have cutaneous Kaposi’s, up to 75% have demonstrable pulmonary tumours on endobronchial biopsy. Unfortunately use of HAART does not significantly appear to affect the prognosis in patients with pulmonary Kaposi’s, with a mean prognosis of only 1.6 years from the point of diagnosis.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=15759466 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=15759466)

D Bacterial pneumonia

Bacterial pneumonia typically presents with a history of fevers and a productive cough. Blood tests would classically show a neutrophilia. However in practice it may be difficult to exclude infection in this case and further imaging and possible bronchoscopy would be indicated.

A Bronchial carcinoma

Bronchial carcinoma would be on the differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with these symptoms and lobar collapse. However we are told he is a non-smoker and in the context of his profound immunosuppression and cutaneous Kaposi’s, an alternative diagnosis is more probable.

B Bronchial carcinoid

Carcinoid is a paraneoplastic syndrome characterised by facial flushing, diarrhoea and bronchial constriction. Pulmonary carcinoid syndrome occurs when the primary neuroendocrine tumour occurs in the lung. In our patient with profound immunosuppression and cutaneous Kaposi’s, an alternative diagnosis is more likely.

E Tuberculosis

Pulmonary tuberculosis most commonly causes upper-lobe consolidation and cavitation. Presentation would be with fever, a productive cough and weight loss. However clinically it may be difficult to exclude tuberculosis in this case and further investigation such as a bronchoscopy would be indicated.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department for review. He returned from a holiday in Spain a few days ago, during which he had unprotected sexual intercourse with a number of women. He had an onset of multiple vesicles which has now formed into multiple ulcers and he has developed burning and tingling over his penis. On examination he is pyrexial 37.8Â°C, his BP is 115/85 mmHg; pulse is 72/min and regular. There are multiple small, shallow, painful ulcers over the glans penis and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. The ulcers are swabbed and he is referred to the GUM clinic.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Oral Aciclovir

The answer is Oral Aciclovir -

Standard treatment for genital herpes is oral Aciclovir, administered at a dose of 200 mg five times daily OR 400 mg three times daily for five days. A more prolonged course of aciclovir may be required in patients who have a history of HIV. Anti-viral therapy reduces the severity and duration of herpes episodes, but does not impact on the overall course of the disease.

Chancroid is a differential diagnosis of genital herpes, but this usually presents with a single deep purulent ulcer, although in less common cases multiple can be present. Lymphadenopathy occurs usually 1 week after the onset of the initial ulcer in such cases.

E Topical Aciclovir

Topical Aciclovir, is incorrect because it is ineffective for the treatment of primary genital herpes versus oral options.

A IM Penicillin

IM Penicillin, is incorrect because 2.4 mega units of Penicillin IM is the standard treatment for syphilis, not for Herpes Simplex.

B Oral Azithromycin

Oral Azithromycin, is incorrect because Azithromycin is an alternative therapy for primary syphilis.

D Oral Famciclovir

Oral Famciclovir is incorrect, it is an option for recurrent herpes, but is not usually considered as an initial therapy. 40447

questions.question:
A 26-year-old man with HIV infection presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 2-week history of general malaise, nausea and abdominal pain. He is generally eating less than usual but is opening his bowels and passing urine normally. He is known to have gallstones. On examination, he appears cachectic and has a temperature of 38.2 °C, with a heart rate of 90 bpm and a BP of 110/63 mmHg. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant but no guarding or palpable organomegaly. Bowel sounds are present.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L135 – 175 g/L
White blood count (WCC)4.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 – 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)151 ×10⁹/L150 – 400 ×10⁹/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.0< 1.1
Bilirubin20 µmol/L1.71 – 20.5 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)37 U/L4 – 36 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)380 U/L44 – 147 U/L
Gamma GT (GGT)189 U/L9 - 48 U/L
Albumin35 g/L35 - 55 g/L
CD4 count185 cells/mm³500–1500 cells/mm³

What is the most appropriate step for a definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography

Biliary involvement in HIV infection is commonly known as acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) cholangiopathy and is a syndrome of biliary obstruction resulting from infection-related strictures of the biliary tract. There is a spectrum of involvement, including acute acalculous cholecystitis, papillary stenosis and sclerosing cholangitis. Cholangiopathy is mostly associated with Cryptosporidium parvum, but other pathogens have also been identified, including cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Microsporidium. The definitive diagnosis of cholangiopathy is made by direct visualisation by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), which can reveal several patterns of biliary abnormality; the combination of

papillary stenosis and sclerosing cholangitis is the most unique to AIDS cholangiopathy. Also, ERCP allows both confirmation of the diagnosis and the performance of therapeutic procedures, if indicated. Biliary brushings and biopsy, biliary aspiration and small bowel biopsy can also be performed to aid in diagnosis, including detection of the aetiologic agent using appropriate stains. However, other studies (particularly ultrasound and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) can be helpful in early evaluation and in selecting patients for ERCP.

Symptomatic patients with papillary stenosis have responded symptomatically to endoscopic sphincterotomy. Antibiotics have not been shown to be useful. Some clinicians use ursodeoxycholic acid in patients with intrahepatic disease, with an observed improvement in liver enzymes.

A Blood culture

Although this patient has a fever, there are no other markers of sepsis and cultures are therefore unlikely to contribute to making a diagnosis. Imaging of the biliary tree is required to explore this patient’s symptoms and pattern of liver enzyme derangement.

B CT abdomen

CT is more useful than ultrasound in identifying intrahepatic strictures and can be effective in identifying intrahepatic masses, abdominal adenopathy and pancreatic disease in jaundiced patients. However, CT is inferior to ERCP in its ability to display the necessarily precise biliary anatomical details for the definitive diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy.

C Liver biopsy

Liver biopsy has little value in the diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy. Diagnosis is informed by imaging of the biliary tree.

E Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography

This is a cost-effective and sensitive initial screening investigation. However, ERCP is considered the definitive modality, given the patient is known to have gallstones, as it carries further diagnostic and therapeutic options. MRCP pre ERCP in patients at high risk of choledocholithiasis is known to result in poorer outcomes than moving straight to ERCP.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a 1-week history of headache and 2-day history of confusion. Three days ago, he had returned from a 6-month trip to rural Kenya.

On examination, his temperature was 39 °C, his blood pressure 125/85 mmHg and his pulse 88 beats per minute (bpm) and regulation. Saturation on air is normal. A physical examination of all systems is unremarkable except for bilateral upgoing plantars.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cellcount (WCC)9 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils3.1 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)110 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Glucose4.0 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
Thick and thin blood filmNo malarial parasites in one sample
Chest X-ray (CXR)Normal
Computed Tomography (CT) headNormal
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)ResultReference Range
WCC3/µL—
Protein0.5 g/dL0.15–0.45 g/dL
Glucose3.8 mmol/L3.3–4.4 mmol/L

Which drug is most appropriate in his immediate management?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Intravenous quinine

This patient’s travel history, anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia and lower limit of blood, and their symptoms, fit with malaria. Typically, three films are required to rule out malaria, this patient had just one negative film. Intravenous quinine or artesunate would be the most appropriate treatment.

C Intravenous methylprednisolone

There is debate over the use of steroids in bacterial meningitis, and even in malaria. Steroids would certainly not be the one most appropriate medication in this case. Although steroids can be useful in reducing cerebral oedema, their administration can also suppress host immune response and therefore risk overwhelming sepsis. In this case, the most likely diagnosis is malaria, given the patient’s travel history, mild anaemia, thrombocytopenia and mild hypoglycaemia. Blood films can be negative, and three or more negative films would be required before a diagnosis of malaria could be excluded. The most appropriate treatment would therefore be intravenous quinine.

A Intravenous aciclovir

Intravenous aciclovir is used in the treatment of herpes simplex encephalitis. Although this patient could have herpes simplex encephalitis, it is not the most likely diagnosis in this case. The travel history, combined with anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia and mild hypoglycaemia, is suggestive of malaria, which is the most likely diagnosis here. If there is a strong clinical suspicion of malaria, blood films should be repeated; three or more negative blood films are needed to completely rule out malaria. Therefore the most appropriate treatment is intravenous quinine, to treat malaria.

B Intravenous cefotaxime

Intravenous cefotaxime would be an appropriate treatment for bacterial meningitis; however, this patient does not have any signs of meningism. Given his travel history, anaemia, mild hypoglycaemia and mild thrombocytopenia, malaria would be a much more likely explanation. Films can be false negatives, and three or more negative films are required to rule out a diagnosis of malaria. To treat malaria, intravenous quinine would be the most appropriate option.

E Oral antiretroviral therapy

Oral antiretroviral therapy would be a treatment for HIV; this patient does not have a history, examination or investigations consistent with HIV. The most likely diagnosis in this case is malaria; it fits with his travel history, and would explain his anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia and hypoglycaemia.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man was referred by his general practitioner after investigation for his 6-month history of lower limb peripheral neuropathy.

On examination, he had a mixed sensory–motor peripheral neuropathy affecting his feet. Romberg’s test was positive. He had some scarring over his lower legs from sores in childhood, when he lived in Jamaica. He had been living in the UK for 40 years.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Fasting plasma glucose9.1 mmol/L3.0 - 6.0 mmol/L
HbA1c78 mmol/mol29.0 - 53.0 mmol/mol (3 - 7 %)
Folate9.6 µg/L2.0 - 11.0 µg/L
Vitamin B₁₂426 ng/L160 - 760 ng/L
Treponemal EIA+
Treponema pallidum particle agglutination+
Rapid plasma reagin (RPR)-

What is the most likely explanation for his syphilis serology?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Yaws

This is a disease caused by a bacterium related to that causing syphilis – Treponema pallidum pertenue. Consequently it can cause some cross-reactivity with syphilis tests, as seen here. Yaws is not usually spread through sexual contact, but instead direct contact. It causes skin lesions which eventually can scar in the primary or secondary stage. A small number of patients will go on to a tertiary stage where there is widespread bone and joint destruction. It can be diagnosed clinically, or through dark field microscopy of lesion fluid during the primary or secondary stages. It can be treated with a single intramuscular injection of penicillin. This patient’s peripheral neuropathy is most likely caused by his poorly controlled diabetes: however, it would be impossible to completely rule out neurosyphilis and therefore this patient should have a lumbar puncture to check RPR on the CSF.

D Systemic lupus erythematosus

This patient has no clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus, and there is no reason why SLE would cause cross-reactivity with syphilis investigations. Instead this patient’s serology, Jamaican background and childhood history of leg sores are suggestive of previous yaws. This is a disease caused by a bacterium related to that causing syphilis, and hence can cause cross-reactivity in syphilis investigations. This patient’s peripheral neuropathy is likely caused by his poorly controlled diabetes.

A False positive

Two results are positive here, making false positives less likely. Furthermore, this patient gives a history of sores across his lower limbs; given that he lived in Jamaica, the most likely explanation for the lower limb sores and syphilis serology is yaws. It is caused by Treponema pallidum pertenue, a bacterium related to the syphilis bacterium and hence causing cross-reaction and positive results in syphilis serology screening. It causes ulceration of the skin, which can lead to scarring. This patient’s peripheral neuropathy is most likely caused by his poorly controlled diabetes.

B Fully treated prior syphilis infection

Although TPPA would remain positive in patients with fully treated prior syphilis infection, the clinical history here is not suggestive of prior syphilis infection.

Instead, this serology, combined with the patient’s Jamaican background and childhood history of lower limb sores, is suggestive of yaws. This is an infection caused by a bacterium related to the syphilitic bacterium, Treponema pallidium pertenue. It causes skin sores which can eventually scar.

It is likely that this patient’s peripheral neuropathy is caused by his poorly controlled diabetes.

C Primary syphilis

If this were primary syphilis, you would expect the RPR to be positive, in addition to the EIA and TPPA. However, in this case it is negative. These results, in combination with the patient’s Jamaican background and childhood history of leg sores, are suggestive of yaws. This is caused by a bacterium related to that causing syphilis, and hence there can be cross-reactivity with syphilis investigations. This patient’s peripheral neuropathy is likely caused by his poorly controlled diabetes.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old who is taking long-term oral prednisolone (10 mg/day) therapy comes to the Emergency Department because he is worried, as his brother has been admitted to the hospital with acute chicken pox infection and he had seen him two days earlier. He is certain that he has never suffered from chicken pox.

What is the most appropriate course of action?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Check varicella antibody status

Steroid use within 3 months of chicken pox exposure increases the risk of severe infection in patients who are non-immune. Guidance supports the use of varicella zoster virus (VZV) immunoglobulin within 3 days of exposure if possible, and not later than 10 days after exposure. Given that IV immunoglobulin is not without risk, antibody status should of course be assessed first. Confirmed chicken pox infection should be managed aggressively with anti-viral therapy, and specialist opinion from an infectious disease consultant is advised. Complications of infection in this population include pneumonitis, hepatitis, encephalitis and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

D Observe for signs of infection

This patient has had a significant chicken pox exposure and is known to be immunosuppressed, and as such is at risk of severe disease. In this setting, if he has no immunity to varicella it would be necessary to give varicella immunoglobulin.

B Start prophylactic acyclovir

This patient has had a significant chicken pox exposure and is immunocompromised. It is important to determine immune status to plan further management. All cases should be discussed with an infectious diseases specialist. There is no role for prophylactic acyclovir in this setting.

C Start prophylactic valacyclovir

This patient has had a significant chicken pox exposure and is immunocompromised. It is important to determine immune status to plan further management. All cases should be discussed with an infectious diseases specialist. There is no role for prophylactic valacyclovir in this setting.

E Give varicella immunoglobulin

This patient has had a significant chicken pox exposure and is known to be immunosuppressed, and as such is at risk of severe disease. However, giving varicella immunoglobulin is not without risk and is unnecessary if he is already immune (either through previous exposure or vaccination). There is sufficient time to test varicella antibody status, and therefore this should be done prior to giving immunoglobulin. 21200

questions.question:
A 44-year-old woman attends the Respiratory Clinic with a 5-week history of a dry cough. She had a mild sore throat and fever initially but says this has now resolved. Her cough is worse in the evenings and is triggered by cold air. She has mild chest pain on repeated bouts of coughing, but she denies shortness of breath and is still able to carry out normal daily activities. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, her temperature is 36.3 °C. Her heart rate is 74 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 121/79 mmHg. Her capillary refill time is < 2 seconds. She has a clear chest, with no audible crackles or wheeze and good air entry bilaterally. Heart sounds are normal and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Ear, nose and throat examination shows a mildly erythematous throat and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. She has bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhages.

What is the most likely causative organism responsible for this patient’s diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bordetella pertussis

This patient has whooping cough caused by the Gram-negative bacteria B. pertussis. A prolonged history of a dry cough that is triggered by cold air and that is worse in the evenings is a symptom of the illness. A mild fever and sore throat may be seen initially. Classically, the increased pressure from prolonged coughing can cause subconjunctival haemorrhages.

E Streptococcus pneumoniae

S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. However, symptoms of pneumonia typically include fever, shortness of breath and productive cough of purulent sputum. Secondly, the symptoms usually have a shorter duration, making it less likely to be the correct diagnosis.

B Group A Streptococcus

Group A Streptococcus is a common cause of sore throat and tonsillitis. On examination, classical findings are an erythematous throat with inflamed tonsils. Palpable cervical lymphadenopathy is also seen. As these are not the symptoms and signs present in this patient, group A Streptococcus is an incorrect answer.

C Mycobacterium tuberculosis

M. tuberculosis is the organism responsible for the respiratory illness tuberculosis. Symptoms of tuberculosis have a more insidious onset, with constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fever and night sweats also being common. This is not present in this patient, making it an incorrect answer.

D Parainfluenza virus

Parainfluenza virus is the cause of croup or laryngotracheobronchitis. It is characterised by the classical barking cough, which is often at its worst at night. The virus is typically seen in younger children and its duration is not typically much longer than one week.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of lower abdominal pain. This had not limited her activities, but the pain was persistent and on occasion she had felt feverish. She did not have dysuria or an abnormal discharge. She had had multiple urinary tract infections in her twenties.

On examination, the temperature was 37.3 °C. There was mild lower abdominal tenderness, and bowel sounds were present and normal. Urine dipstick was normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)132 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.6 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)255 ×10⁹/L400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K)4.4 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)72 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Urea4.9 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)45 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Chlamydial infection

This is a classic description of pelvic inflammatory disease. This patient complains of subacute or long-term pelvic pain; patients may also experience mucopurulent discharge, dyspareunia or abnormal vaginal bleeding. The ‘urinary tract infections’ this patient reports may have included sexually transmitted chlamydial infections causing dysuria. Typically, patients have lower abdominal pain on examination and may have cervical motion or adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination. Fever and raised inflammatory markers are common findings. As this patient is clinically stable, oral treatment, as opposed to admission for intravenous treatment, is appropriate. Current British Association for Sexual Health and HIV guidelines recommend a combination of oral doxycycline plus oral metronidazole plus IM ceftriaxone.

D Renal stones

You would expect a patient with renal stones to complain of severe, colicky unilateral loin-to-groin pain, which is not what this patient describes; instead, she has persistent bilateral pelvic pain. Although a low-grade fever (as seen here) is common with renal stones, you might expect to see some blood in the urine dipstick; instead, this patient’s urine dipstick is normal. This patient’s presentation is classic for pelvic inflammatory disease – long-standing, non-specific bilateral pelvic pain with intermittent fevers and mildly raised inflammatory markers. The background of recurrent dysuria suggests there may have been a previous sexually transmitted infection. The most common cause of pelvic inflammatory disease in the UK is chlamydial infection, and therefore this is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms.

B Gonococcal sepsis

This patient is not septic; although she has raised inflammatory markers, she is not systemically unwell. If this were acute gonococcal infection, you would expect purulent vaginal discharge, which this patient does not have. This patient has pelvic inflammatory disease – long-standing non-specific pelvic pain with mildly raised inflammatory markers on a background of recurrent episodes of dysuria. Pelvic inflammatory disease can be caused by gonococcal infection; however, Chlamydia is the most common cause in the United Kingdom and therefore is the most likely cause in this case.

C Pyelonephritis

If this were pyelonephritis, you would expect a history of dysuria and a positive urine dipstick; you would also expect the patient to be more systemically unwell with a higher temperature. This patient has pelvic inflammatory disease, with long-standing non-specific pelvic pain and mildly raised inflammatory markers on a background of recurrent episodes of dysuria. The most common cause of pelvic inflammatory disease in the UK is Chlamydia, and therefore this is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms.

E Urinary tract infection

You would not expect such a long history for a patient with a urinary tract infection. If this were a urinary tract infection, you would expect the patient to complain of dysuria and the urine dipstick to be positive. Instead, this patient has a history typical of pelvic inflammatory disease – subacute non-specific bilateral pelvic pain, with intermittent fevers and mildly raised inflammatory markers. The background of recurrent dysuria may, in fact, have included sexually transmitted infections, not simply urinary tract infections. The most common cause of pelvic inflammatory disease in the UK is chlamydial infection; therefore, this is the correct answer. 71448

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man from Nigeria presents to the Emergency Department with fevers, night sweats and 10 kg weight loss over the past 2 months. There is no cough or shortness of breath. He says that he was diagnosed HIV positive 6 months previously in Africa but does not know any further details.

On examination, he is febrile at 38 °C and cachectic. He has a 4 cm lymph node in his left axilla, and his chest is clear. On examination, he has 2 cm hepatomegaly. Chest X-ray is unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)86 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)2.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)311 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Urea and electrolytes (U&Es)Within normal range
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)330 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)75 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin9 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Albumin25 g/L35–55 g/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)1500 U/L100–190 IU/L

An ultrasound of the liver reveals diffuse hepatomegaly with no duct dilatation. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Lymph node biopsy

This is a young, HIV-positive patient with fevers, night sweats, weight loss and enlarged.The most likely diagnoses are tuberculosis and lymphoma; histoplasmosis and atypical mycobacteria are also a possibility. A tissue sample is needed to differentiate between these diagnoses and a lymph node biopsy is the least invasive method of obtain histology. Further microscopy and staining will be able to provide a definitive diagnosis.

A Sputum culture

There are two main differential diagnoses: tuberculosis and lymphoma. Sputum culture is unlikely to show any bacilli as the patient is not coughing, and even if they were the sensitivity would be low.

B Bone marrow trephine

This is a very invasive investigation to obtain a tissue sample and would be a secondary investigation following established diagnosis of lymphoma.

D CT of the abdomen

A computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen will add little; a tissue sample is needed to look for lymphoma, granulomas or acid-fast bacilli.

E Liver biopsy

The patient does have hepatomegaly, but investigating for underlying causes would be more appropriate. 7647

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man who is known to be an IV heroin abuser presents to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe muscle spasms and abdominal pain. He admits that he has had increasing problems sourcing both clean needles and sites to inject himself over the past few weeks. On examination there is an injecting abscess in the right groin. There is bilateral increased tone and hyperreflexia. He suffers from muscle spasms when you test reflexes in the arms, and has a tense, rigid abdomen. You ask him to swallow a glass of water and he begins to choke.

Investigations;

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin109 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets189 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-Reactive protein (CRP)205 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)85 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline Phosphatase185 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin22 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C IM Anti-tetanus immunoglobulin

The answer is IM Anti-tetanus immunoglobulin -

The increased tone and muscle spasms seen here, coupled with the history of IV drug abuse suggests injection related tetanus. The signs of infection with raised white count and CRP fit with this picture. The abnormal LFTs may be related to viral hepatitis. There is significant risk of this patient deteriorating very rapidly, requiring intubation and ventilation as a prophylactic measure in many cases.

A Debridement of groin abscess

Debridement of groin abscess, id incorrect, it is appropriate but not until anti-tetanus immunoglobulin has been administered, because of the risks of increasing the load of tetanus toxin in the peripheral circulation.

B IV immunoglobulin

IV immunoglobulin, in incorrect, it is an appropriate intervention for Guillain Barré (GBS), associated with flaccid paralysis not seen here.

D IV Methylprednisolone

IV Methylprednisolone, is incorrect given the underlying probable tetanus infection. In addition, corticosteroids are ineffective in managing GBS.

E IV Metronidazole

IV Metronidazole, in incorrect, it may reduce the duration of tetanus symptoms, although it is additive to use of tetanus immunoglobulin and debridement of any abscess.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man presents to the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic complaining of dysuria for the past week. He is systemically well. In his sexual history, he has had unprotected sexual intercourse with three partners in the past 6 months. The patient is allergic to tetracycline based antibiotics.

On examination, there is no penile discharge, testicular masses or tenderness. The abdomen is soft and non- tender. Urethral swab reveals 33 neutrophils per high-power field, no organisms are seen.

What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Azithromycin

The patient has non-specific or non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) as there were no gonococci seen on microscopy but presence of neutrophils on the penile swab. NGU is caused by chlamydia in 60% of cases. It can be caused by other bacteria such as Ureaplasma urealyticum and Mycoplasma genitalium. These organisms are rarely detected but are well covered by azithromycin and doxycycline which are both commonly used for NGU: doxycycline b.d is recommended as first-line treatment by the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH), with first alternative being Azithromycin and less commonly used alternative treatments include ofloxacin.

E Metronidazole

This is the correct treatment for bacterial vaginosis.

A No treatment needed

The patient most likely has a significant infection as is evidenced by the neutrophils on the penile swab and will need treatment. If the swab is negative then no treatment should be offered.

B Nitrofurantoin

This would be a possible treatment for urinary tract infection but this is unlikely to be the correct diagnosis as dysuria is a common presentation for NGU as well as UTI, especially in a male patient with a history of unprotected sexual encounters.

C Ceftriaxone

This would be the treatment for gonorrhoea. For this diagnosis microscopy would reveal Gram-negative diploccoci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old intravenous drug user comes to the Accident and Emergency Unit with a purplish rash on his arms and feet. He states that the rash has been present for nearly 2 weeks and is progressively worsening. It is not pruritic or painful.

On examination, he is not in any acute distress. There is mild jaundice present. Heart and lung examination is within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows right upper quadrant tenderness with liver edge palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin. Skin examination reveals palpable purpura on both arms and his left foot. His right lower limb shows some erythematous nodules as well as livedo reticularis. CNS examination shows decreased strength in plantar flexion as well as decreased sensation of the left foot.

Some laboratory results are shown below:

InvestigationResult
HIV testNegative
Hepatitis B surface antigenPositive
InvestigationResult
Red blood cells (RBCs)+++
Protein++
White blood cells (WBCs)Negative

What is the most likely cause of his rash?
options: Impaired coagulation secondary to liver cirrhosis
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)

The findings such as erythematous nodules, livedo reticularis, mononeuritis multiplex and kidney involvement are all suggestive of PAN, which also occurs in patients with hepatitis B. The presence of hepatitis B surface antigen demonstrates hepatitis B infection.

E Impaired coagulation secondary to liver cirrhosis

The absence of features of chronic liver disease makes this an unlikely diagnosis and it also would not explain neurological features.

A Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura

This diagnosis most often presents with bruising, petechiae and epistaxis and is usually seen in children. It would not explain the proteinuria as well.

B Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP)

The purpuric rash of Henoch–Schönlein is usually present in lower extremities and buttocks. Renal involvement can be seen in HSP, but not the signs of mononeuritis multiplex.

D Kaposi’s sarcoma

This diagnosis is extremely unlikely without HIV and would not explain the neurological features.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old patient presented with a 2-day history of progressive deterioration in his visual acuity and loss of colour vision. He had no ocular pain. Six weeks previously, he was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and HIV. He was taking quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy and antiretroviral therapy.

On examination, bilateral fundoscopy was unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
CD4 count at diagnosis146 ×10⁶/L430 - 1690 ×10⁶/L
CD4 count at presentation302 ×10⁶/L430 - 1690 ×10⁶/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Ethambutol toxicity

This patient will be receiving ethambutol as standard first-line treatment for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect of this medication. It should be stopped immediately, and the patient should be referred to ophthalmology as an emergency. It is common for fundoscopy to be normal in the early stages of neuropathy.

D Rifampicin toxicity

This patient will probably be taking rifampicin for tuberculosis, but his signs and symptoms are consistent with an optic neuropathy, which is not a side effect of rifampicin (major side effects of rifampicin are turning secretions orange and acting as an enzyme inducer). Instead ethambutol is the likely culprit: he will be taking this as part of first-line therapy for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect.

A Cytomegalovirus retinitis

Although this can present with loss of visual acuity, it would be unusual for it to affect colour vision so early in its presentation. Furthermore, you might expect to see signs of retinal inflammation on fundoscopy, which is normal here. Lastly, this patient’s CD4 count is improving and he is on effective retroviral treatment, and therefore opportunistic infection with cytomegalovirus is less likely. Instead, this patient’s symptoms are much more likely to be caused by optic nerve toxicity, a known side effect of ethambutol: ethambutol is standard first- line therapy for tuberculosis.

C Retinal vein thrombosis

This typically presents with unilateral blurred vision, but loss of colour vision would be unusual: this implies optic nerve pathology.
