Furthermore, if this were retinal vein occlusion, you would expect to see signs on fundoscopy, which is normal here. Instead, this patient is likely to be suffering from ethambutol toxicity. Ethambutol is standard first-line therapy for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect.

E Toxoplasmosis

Ocular toxoplasmosis typically presents as a blurring of the vision; however, it would be unusual for it to cause loss of colour vision as this implies involvement of the optic nerve. Furthermore, you might expect to see retinal scarring if this were toxoplasmosis. This patient may be immunosuppressed, but not significantly so: his CD4 count has improved and he is on effective antiretroviral medication. Instead, this patient’s optic neuropathy is much more likely to be caused by ethambutol toxicity. He will be taking ethambutol as a first-line therapy for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman with a history of intravenous (IV) drug use is admitted feeling generally unwell. She has a fever, arthralgia and a rash, and has been deteriorating with increasing tiredness over the past six weeks. She admits to having run out of injection sites and is currently using areas around her groin and in her feet.

Her blood pressure (BP) is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular, her temperature is 37.8 °C.

On examination, she has a soft systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.

Investigations reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
ElectrocardiogramSinus tachycardia
Haemoglobin (Hb)102 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 – 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelet (PLT)474 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)132 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.6 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea15.2 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)145 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Urine microscopyRed cell casts
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate32 mm/h1- 20 mm/h
C-reactive protein64 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Complement C320 mg/dl65 - 190 mg/dl
Complement C43 mg/dl15 - 50 mg/dl
Renal biopsyFocal segmental proliferative glomerulonephritis

Which one of the following is an appropriate next investigation?
options: Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax and abdomen
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Serial blood cultures

This patient has hypocomplementaemia and glomerulonephritis with features in the history and examination suggesting infective endocarditis as the aetiology. The blood results suggest an underlying infection with the raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate, an indicator for inflammation, is also raised. Serial blood cultures from different sites and an echocardiogram are the next investigations of choice. She should be managed with intravenous (iv) flucloxacillin and gentamicin and there is no need to wait for investigations before commencing therapy.

B Anticardiolipin antibodies

Anticardiolipin antibodies are antibodies often directed against cardiolipin and found in syphilis, antiphospholipid syndrome, livedoid vasculitis, Behçet syndrome, idiopathic spontaneous abortion and SLE. This patient does not have systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) given the clinical scenario and anti-double- stranded DNA antibody (anti-dsDNA) is negative.

A Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies

The anti-double-stranded DNA antibody (anti-dsDNA) is a specific type of ANA antibody found in about 30% of people with systemic lupus. Less than 1% of healthy individuals have this antibody, making it helpful in confirming a diagnosis of systemic lupus. SLE is associated with complement activation, and the low complement levels would fit with the diagnosis, although bacterial endocarditis should be ruled out first.

C Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax and abdomen

A CT may identify any malignancy or abnormal masses but it is not useful in infective endocarditis.

D Rheumatoid factor

Rheumatoid factor is the autoantibody that was first found in rheumatoid arthritis. It is defined as an antibody against the Fc portion of IgG and different rheumatoid factors can recognise different parts of the IgG-Fc. Although it is found in rheumatoid arthritis, it is not present in every patient. This test would not be useful in infective endocarditis. 71281

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man presented to clinic for review. He had been diagnosed with HIV 2 weeks previously and was due to be started on antiretroviral therapy at this clinic visit. He complained of some fatigue and severe headache. He had no past medical history.

On examination he had a low-grade fever at 37.7°C. He had some purpuric lesions on his lower limbs. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)95 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.6 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils3.0 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)11 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L

What is the most important test to do next?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Renal function

This patient’s anaemia and thrombocytopenia could be caused by thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which is associated with HIV. However, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is also associated with HIV: this tends to improve either over time or with treatment of the HIV. In contrast, TTP requires immediate management and can be life-threatening. In order to decide whether this is HIV-associated ITP or TTP, evidence of clinical features of TTP must be sought: there is a pentad of associated features. This pentad includes thrombocytopenia, fever, neurological symptoms, haemolytic anaemia and renal impairment. Thus renal function would be the most appropriate test in this case. If this were TTP, treatment would be by plasmapheresis and steroids.

E Ultrasound abdomen

This patient has an anaemia and thrombocytopenia; an ultrasound of the abdomen will not help to diagnose the cause or decide management. The concern is whether this could be HIV-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). TTP is characterised by a pentad of fever, haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms and renal impairment: hence renal function would be the most appropriate test in this case.

A Bone marrow aspiration

A bone marrow aspirate can sometimes be appropriate in the context of pancytopenia; however, this patient has a normal white cell count and therefore is not pancytopenic. This patient is anaemic, but also severely thrombocytopenic in the context of a new diagnosis of HIV. HIV can be associated with both thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP): ITP typically improves as the disease progresses and with treatment, whereas TTP needs specific intervention. TTP is characterised by a pentad of fever, thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms, haemolytic anaemia and reduced renal function: therefore the most appropriate investigation would be renal function.

B CD4 count

The CD4 count can be useful as a marker of the level of disease control in HIV, but the problem here is that the patient has an anaemia and thrombocytopenia: the CD4 count will not help to determine the cause or management of this. In fact, HIV can be associated with both thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). TTP is a serious condition requiring immediate treatment, whereas the ITP associated with HIV tends to improve with treatment of HIV. TTP is associated with a pentad of symptoms which includes impaired renal function: hence renal function would be the most appropriate investigation in this case.

C Liver function

This patient has an anaemia and thrombocytopenia: liver function tests cannot aid in diagnosing the cause or deciding management. HIV is associated with both thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Whilst TTP requires immediate definitive management, ITP in HIV tends to improve over time and with treatment of the HIV. To distinguish between the two, one must look for evidence of clinical features of TTP. One of these is renal impairment, and hence renal function would be the most appropriate investigation in this case. 71047

questions.question:
A 19-year-old Thai woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of malaise and shortness of breath.

On examination, she has multiple enlarged cervical and axillary nodes and mild hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)61 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.9 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.58 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)31 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Urea and electrolytes (U&Es)NAD
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)205 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)80 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Bilirubin6 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Albumin21 g/L35–55 g/L

She is admitted and transfused three units of blood. As part of her investigation, an HIV test is done, which is positive. After the transfusion, her breathlessness is much improved and she remains stable. A bone marrow trephine and lymph node biopsy are requested. On the ward round, she mentions in passing that the vision in her right eye has been steadily deteriorating for the past 3 weeks. You perform dilated fundoscopy. Whilst the left fundus shows just exudates the below changes are found on the right.

What is the best treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C IV ganciclovir

The optic disc appears swollen with evidence of exudates and haemorrhages covering the macula. The cause of these changes and of her impaired vision is cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. CMV retinitis is a common cause of blurred vision in immunodeficiency which can lead to blindness. It can be asymptomatic as well. Fundoscopy can show haemorrhagic necrosis, granular lesions or frosted branch angiitis around retinal vessels.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fundus_photograph-CMV_retinitis_EDA07.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fundus_photograph-CMV_retinitis_EDA07.JPG)

B IV foscarnet

IV foscarnet is incorrect. Either IV ganciclovir or foscarnet could be used and although trial evidence suggests marginally more rapid clearance with foscarnet versus ganciclovir, ganciclovir is still preferred under UK Guidelines as the first treatment of choice. Foscarnet is generally the second-line therapy of choice in patients who fail to gain an adequate response to ganciclovir.

A IV aciclovir

IV aciclovir is incorrect. Aciclovir would not be effective against CMV but could be used against herpes simplex virus infection.

D IV cidofovir

IV cidofovir is incorrect. Cidofovir can be used if both ganciclovir and foscarnet are contraindicated or there is a failure to respond to one of these therapies. It is, however, the drug of choice for varicella zoster retinitis. There are very limited data comparing cidofovir with ganciclovir and foscarnet, but ganciclovir efficacy is well established. Cidofovir may have a greater role in future treatment as it can be dosed less frequently with its longer half-life.

E IV ribavirin

IV ribavirin is incorrect. Ribavirin is an antiviral agent used to treat respiratory syncytial virus, hepatitis C virus and viral haemorrhagic fever.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old man is brought in with fever, rash and headache. He returned from a riding trip to Utah one week ago and admits that he had probably been bitten by many different bugs when he was out there, despite using repellent. He noticed feeling hot and cold the day before leaving Utah, but put it down to a flu-like illness as he had a headache, rhinorrhoea, dry cough and intermittent severe muscle pain in his lower back and legs. His fever and headache had, however, persisted and he was now concerned as he had developed a rash on his wrists and ankles which had now started to spread up his body.

On examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.1 °C and appears slightly agitated. He has a maculopapular eruption over his arms and legs, including a rash over the palms of his hands and soles of his feet. His pulse is 60/min and heart sounds are normal. His chest is clear but he is tender in the right upper quadrant. There is no meningism and neurology is normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.4 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)75 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)131 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)105 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin34 g/L35–55 g/L
Urea5.6 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)101 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin34 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Rocky Mountain spotted fever

This is a tick-borne disease caused by the organism Rickettsia rickettsii. RMSF can be lethal. Physicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for RMSF in patients who are febrile, as it is essentially a clinical diagnosis. Key aspects include history of potential tick exposure, travel to an endemic area and presentation in the spring or autumn.

Patients with unexplained febrile illness, even if they have no history of a tick bite or travel to an endemic area but have rash and myalgia, should be suspected to have RMSF. Rash is a major diagnostic sign. The maculopapular rash usually appears 2–6 days after the onset of fever and progresses through stages and distribution that are never pathognomonic. The rash begins as a maculopapular eruption on the wrists and ankles, and spreads centripetally to involve the trunk and extremities. The rash involves the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Later in the illness, the rash becomes petechial in 50% of patients.

For adults, the preferred drug of choice is doxycycline. Chloramphenicol is an alternative.

A Dengue fever

Dengue is caused by an arbovirus transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. The incubation period is one to two weeks and the typical symptoms are fever, frontal headache, musculoskeletal pains and a widespread maculopapular rash. Laboratory findings commonly show a rising haematocrit, falling platelets and transamenitis. The clue here is the travel; cases of dengue arising in the United States are sporadic and usually associated with travel to Central and South America. An outbreak has been seen in Florida, but to date dengue is not endemic in northern Texas.

B Ehrlichiosis

Ehrlichiosis is an uncommon tick-borne infection caused by obligate intracellular bacteria of the genera Anaplasma and Ehrlichia. Incubation is one to two weeks and the most common symptoms are fever, headache, fatigue and myalgia. A rash may be present but is uncommon. Ehrlichiosis is clinically difficult to differentiate from other febrile illnesses such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, but is much less common in the states to the Western side of the US and therefore is not the most likely diagnosis.

C Lyme disease

Lyme disease is an infectious illness caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi. It is transmitted through tick bites. It initially presents with a slowly expanding skin lesion around the tick bite, erythema migrans, malaise and joint aches. If not treated, neurological, cardiac and joint involvement can occur. The rash described is not consistent with acute Lyme disease.

E Syphilis

Syphilis is an infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, and it is most commonly acquired through sexual intercourse. Primary syphilis presents as a local painless ulcer (chancre) at the inoculation site. Secondary syphilis occurs weeks to months after the primary chancre and is typified by a widespread rash, fever, lethargy and lymphadenopathy. You might expect a question to describe risk factors for syphilis and an antecedent chancre, but in practice it may be prudent to check syphilis serology in this patient.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman presents with an infected human bite on her left arm. She says that she was involved in a fight three days ago while drunk.

On examination, there is a bite affecting the left upper arm which is discharging pus, and there is a 3 cm radius of erythema around the wound. She is pyrexial (37.8 °C).

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for antibiotic therapy?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav is the antibiotic therapy of choice for human bite wounds. It is crucial that beta-lactamase- producing Staphylococci are covered, and clavulanic acid makes sure of this. A standard course is the 625 mg TDS dose for a period of 5–7 days. It is also crucially important to make sure that the patient is covered for tetanus infection. Commonly isolated organisms include Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Haemophilus, Bacteroides and Eikenella corrodens.

E Metronidazole

Metronidazole alone does not provide adequate coverage, and should be used in combination with either a tetracycline or clarithromycin.

A Amoxicillin

Amoxicillin fails to cover against beta-lactamase-producing organisms and therefore cannot be used here.

B Pencillin V

Penicillin V only covers a limited range of mouth commensals, and doesn’t have activity against a range of anaerobes that may cause significant wound infection.

D Oxytetracycline

Tetracyclines may be used as a treatment for human bites, but only in combination with metronidazole.

Metronidazole and doxycycline, or metronidazole and clarithromycin, may be reasonable alternatives in penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.question:
A 79-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department by her carers after becoming drowsy and less responsive over the past 24 hours. On waking, she complains of a headache and refuses to open her eyes. Her past medical history includes type II diabetes and severe osteoarthritis that has left her wheelchair-bound.

On examination, her blood pressure is 124/77 mmHg, she has a heart rate of 95 bpm and her temperature is 38.5 °C. She is neglecting her left side, with a 3/5 power weakness.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)18.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)120 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Lumbar punctureGram-positive rods, low cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Listeria monocytogenes

L. monocytogenes is a motile, non-spore-forming Gram-positive bacillus. A central nervous system (CNS) infection can manifest as meningitis and meningoencephalitis or even with symptoms of hemiparesis, mimicking a stroke. Amoxicillin is the treatment of choice for Listeria CNS infection. It is worth noting that cephalosporins, such as ceftriaxone, commonly used empirically to treat meningitis have no activity against Listeria. Therefore, if the diagnosis is suspected (eg in the elderly), amoxicillin should be included in the treatment regime.

C Neisseria meningitidis

N. meningitidis (meningococcus) is a Gram-negative diplococcus which is one of the most common causes of bacterial meningitis in the United Kingdom. Symptoms are typically fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting, with or without a non-blanching rash. Treatment is with intravenous ceftriaxone. In this case, the

risk factors, presentation and CSF findings point to an alternative diagnosis.

A Klebsiella pneumoniae

Klebsiella is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria. It is a commensal of the human gut and most commonly causes intra-abdominal or urinary tract infections. A CNS infection is very uncommon outside of neonates and neurosurgery patients.

D Pseudomonas aeruginosa

P. aeruginosa is a Gram-negative bacterium that is intrinsically quite antibiotic-resistant. A CNS infection is very uncommon.

E Streptococcus pneumoniae

S. pneumoniae is another very common cause of meningitis in the United Kingdom. However, this bacterium is a Gram-positive diplococcus, making it an unlikely organism for this patient.

questions.question:
A 39-year-old sheep farmer presents to the Emergency Department with jaundice, fevers and right upper quadrant pain, which has developed over the past 24 hours. He also has diarrhoea and feels that he is passing much smaller amounts of dark urine compared to his normal toilet habits. He tells you that he has been clearing dead wood out of some flooded hedges over the past few days. Examination reveals a temperature of 38.9 °C and his blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg; pulse is 95 bpm. He is jaundiced. Abdominal palpation reveals marked right upper quadrant tenderness.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)95 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)201 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
International normalised ratio (INR)< 1.1 1.8
Glucose5.1 mmol/L2.2–2.6 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)450 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)320 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin88 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
UrineBlood ++, Protein ++

Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Intravenous (IV) benzylpenicillin

The diagnosis here is that of leptospirosis, as evidenced by the patient’s occupation presumably putting him at risk of infection from animal urine, fever, jaundice and renal impairment (Weil’s disease). Amoxicillin, doxycycline and macrolides are appropriate treatments for mild to moderate leptospirosis; however, the patient is clinically on the severe end of the condition and therefore IV antibiotics are the appropriate choice. Other supportive measures should be considered, including correction of clotting abnormalities. The role of steroids has not been fully established in leptospirosis; however, they may reduce the risk of vasculitic complications such as pulmonary haemorrhage and acute renal failure.

B IV ciprofloxacin

Although this patient is on the severe end of the condition and requires IV antibiotics, IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are the appropriate first choices for severe leptospirosis treatment. Another supportive measure should be to consider including correction of clotting abnormalities. The role of steroids has not been fully established in leptospirosis; however, they may reduce the risk of vasculitic complications like pulmonary haemorrhage and acute renal failure.

C Oral amoxicillin

This patient is on the severe end of the spectrum of leptospirosis and therefore requires intravenous antibiotics. IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are first choice for treatment. Mild to moderate forms of the condition can be treated with oral amoxicillin or doxycycline.

D Oral clarithromycin

Oral Clarithromycin is the incorrect answer. Macrolides, such as clarithromycin or azithromycin, can be used in mild to moderate disease. This patient has severe disease and should be treated with IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins.

E Oral doxycycline

Although doxycycline is sensitive to leptospirosis, it is only indicated in mild to moderate forms of the infection. This patient is systemically unwell with features of sepsis and therefore requires IV antibiotics. IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are first choice for treatment.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presented to clinic with a 2-week history of fever, myalgia and lethargy. He also complained of mouth ulcers. Two months ago he had visited friends and relatives in South Africa. He had no medical conditions. He admits to unprotected sexual intercourse during his holiday. He has no medical conditions.

On examination, his temperature was 37.6ºC. He had cervical lymphadenopathy but no hepatosplenomegaly. There were aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)136 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.2 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes0.9 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 4.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)96 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin26 mmol/L1.7 - 20.5 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)72 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Blood filmAtypical reactive lymphocytes
HIV antibodies-

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D HIV infection

This patient has recently returned from travelling in an area with a high HIV prevalence, and has a flu-like illness with lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes on a blood film, a mild transaminitis and fever. HIV antibodies can be negative if the patient is currently seroconverting; a better diagnostic test would be either HIV RNA PCR or p24 antigen.

C Hepatitis C

Hepatitis C may cause malaise, fever and liver dysfunction. However, liver function tests would likely be more markedly abnormal in symptomatic hepatitis C, and hepatitis C would not explain the lymphadenopathy or atypical lymphocytes seen in this patient. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion. HIV antibodies can be negative during seroconversion, and therefore a better diagnostic test would be either p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR.

A Cytomegalovirus infection

In the immunocompetent, cytomegalovirus infection is typically asymptomatic or may cause a mild, flu-like illness. In the immunosuppressed, cytomegalovirus can cause pneumonia, retinitis or, most commonly, diarrhoea or colitis. This patient’s fever, lymphadenopathy and liver dysfunction are best explained by HIV seroconversion. HIV antibodies may be negative during seroconversion: a p24 antigen test or HIV RNA PCR would be better suited to diagnosis.

B Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B could cause malaise and liver dysfunction, but you might expect liver function tests to be more markedly abnormal if this were hepatitis B. Furthermore, hepatitis B would not explain the lymphadenopathy or atypical lymphocytes seen here. This patient’s presentation would fit with HIV seroconversion; HIV antibodies may be negative during seroconversion. A better diagnostic test would be either a p24 antigen test or HIV RNA PCR.

E Malaria

Malaria is an important cause of fever in the returning traveller and should always be a differential diagnosis; however, malaria does not explain the lymphadenopathy or atypical lymphocytes seen in this case. This picture of malaise, a relative lymphopenia, transaminitis and lymphadenopathy is more suggestive of HIV. As the patient is seroconverting, HIV antibodies can be negative. A better test would have been either p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR. 71140

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 10-day history of fevers. He had returned from a 1-month holiday in Peru 1 week previously.

Before travelling to Peru, he had received hepatitis A and typhoid vaccinations. He took malaria prophylaxis regularly while on holiday but had stopped it 5 days before returning, as he lost his tablets.

On examination, his temperature was 39 °C, with a pulse of 56 bpm. His chest is shown below and there was also cervical lymphadenopathy. Urine dipstick was positive for leukocytes.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)124 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.4 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)340 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K)4.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)440 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Creatinine (Cr)97 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urea6.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Blood culturesGram-negative rods in two out of three bottles
Thin malaria filmsThree separate samples are negative
Chest X-ray (CXR)Normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Salmonella typhi infection

A high fever in a returning traveller should prompt you to think of two conditions: malaria and typhoid. S. typhi causes typhoid fever, which is a major differential diagnosis in a returning traveller with high fever. Typically, S. typhi has an incubation period of 10–14 days, followed by a prodrome of flu-like symptoms. In the first week, patients have a high fever, with a relative bradycardia (as seen here). Next, they develop small salmon-pink maculopapules, termed rose spots, as here. In conjunction with these changes lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly occur. Following this, complications may develop (pneumonia, endocarditis, haemolytic anaemia, meningitis, acute cholecystitis, osteomyelitis). Although the patient had been vaccinated, vaccines are unfortunately only between 30% and 70% effective. Empirical treatment of hospitalised patients is with ceftriaxone. Relapse is common, and the organism can persist in the gall bladder.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Salmonella_typhi_typhoid_fever_PHIL_2215_lores.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Salmonella_typhi_typhoid_fever_PHIL_2215_lores.jpg)

A Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection

In immunocompetent individuals, CMV infection is usually asymptomatic. It can cause a flu-like illness, which may be complicated by Guillain–Barré syndrome or Bell’s palsy. By the age of 60, around 80% of patients have been exposed to CMV, and it can be problematic if a patient later becomes immunosuppressed, for example, after transplantation or in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected patients. In such patients, it can cause colitis, severe retinitis, oesophagitis and central nervous system (CNS) disease. Treatment would be with ganciclovir. As this patient is not immunocompromised, the presentation does not fit with CMV, since it does not cause prolonged fevers or rashes in the immunocompetent.

B Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection

Primary EBV causes glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) in around 50% of infected illness. This primary infection does cause a maculopapular rash (though not typically a salmon-pink rash), but it would be unusual for EBV infection to cause such a high fever, as seen in this patient. The positive blood cultures also count against EBV infection being the diagnosis. EBV is associated with Burkitt’s lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and oral hair leukoplakia.

C Plasmodium falciparum malaria

Malaria is among the top important differential diagnoses in the returning traveller with prolonged fever; however, this patient has had three negative films, which rules out malaria. The incubation period of malaria does vary between species but tends to be at least 12 days, which would make it highly unlikely, given her prophylaxis covered this period.

E Schistosomiasis

Schistosomiasis is a trematode infection, particularly associated with freshwater lakes in Africa and the Middle East. Acute infection is usually with cercarial dermatitis (swimmer’s itch), which causes a self-limiting, itchy papular rash within 24 hours of exposure. Katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis) is less common and develops 4–8 weeks post-exposure and presents with fever, urticaria, eosinophilia and wheeze. This patient’s presentation does not fit with the incubation period of swimmer’s itch and does not have the features of acute schistosomiasis. Treatment of acute schistosomiasis would be with praziquantel and steroids.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents to the GP some 6 weeks after returning from a holiday to Thailand with a maculopapular rash. He denies sexual intercourse during the course of his holiday.

During his holiday, he went trekking through the jungle. The only thing he remembers is a very odd single lesion that looked like a large, warty lump on his arm which formed during his holiday and then healed up.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)234 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
P24Negative
TPHAPositive

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Yaws infection

Yaws is endemic in tropical areas of America, Asia, Africa and Oceania and is caused by Treponema pertenue. Early lesions may almost look papillomatous, and as well as direct skin to skin contact, the organism may be carried by biting insects. The TPHA is positive for both yaws and syphilis. Penicillin is the drug of choice for treatment.

D Tungiasis

Tungiasis is a skin condition caused by Tunga penetrans, also called sand flea. It is endemic in Africa, India, and South and Central America. It causes a black dot at the site of infection with a swollen red lesions surrounded by a white halo. It is very painful and itchy. It is always associated with desquamation. The absence of this and the fact that the patient has not travelled to an endemic area makes this diagnosis unlikely.

A HIV infection

This patient does not have any direct history of possible exposure nor does he have any evidence of multiple opportunistic infection. The negative P24 test excludes HIV infection as well.

B Syphillis infection

The warty lesion described does not correspond to a syphilitic lesion. There is also no history corresponding to primary syphilis with non-painful ulcerating genital or anal lesions. The TPHA is positive in any Treponema species, meaning that it lacks specificity for syphilis. In addition, TPHA remains positive for life following infection at any point.

E Leishmaniasis

Leishmania are protozoa spread by sandflies in Africa, Asia, India, Middle East, the Mediterranean and Latin America causing granulomata. Cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions develop at the site of the bite starting as an itchy papule which crusts to form an ulcer healing over 2-15 months. Visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, has an incubation period of months to years. It spreads to the lymphatic system and multiply in macrophages, presenting with dry, warty, hyperpigmented lesiosn whilst the patient complains of fever, burning feet, arthralgia, cough, epistaxis. Splenomegaly occurs in 96% and hepatomegaly in 63%. Diagnosis with microscopy of lymph nodes, spleen or bone marrow, or antibody detection. Treatment is with amphotericin. This patient does have a warty lesions but the fact that it healed rather than forming an ulcer makes cutaneous leishmanisasis unlikely and the absence of systemic features makes visceral leishmaniasis unlikely as well.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman comes to the Sexual Health Clinic for review. She is five months’ pregnant and has had dysuria and vague lower abdominal pain for the past few days. There has been a recent split with her partner after he admitted to an affair.

On examination, her temperature is 37.8 °C, her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, and her abdomen is consistent with a 20-week pregnancy. Chlamydia testing is positive and urine growth is negative for pathogens known to cause urinary tract infection.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Azithromycin PO

Azithromycin has the twin advantages of being a safe option in pregnancy and being a single 1 g dose. It is recommended as the pragmatic option in pregnancy for chlamydia by the SIGN guidelines. Latency and reactivation are rarely seen in pregnancy; therefore, a test of cure is usual, some six weeks after azithromycin treatment.

D Doxycycline PO

While a 7-day course of doxycycline would be a reasonable first-line option in uncomplicated chlamydia infection, this patient is pregnant. It is therefore contraindicated due to the risk of suppression of fetal bone growth and teeth staining.

A Amoxicillin PO

While amoxycillin is safe in pregnancy and is a recommended treatment when given for seven days, it has the potential to induce latency and re-emergence of infection. Therefore, azithromycin is the first-line agent here.

C Benzylpenicillin IM

Benzylpenicillin IM would be a treatment of syphilis, which is not suggested by the presenting symptoms, rather than chlamydia.

E Ofloxacin PO

Ofloxacin is a second-line option in chlamydia infection. While it is not strictly contraindicated in pregnancy, like doxycycline, it should be avoided due to the risk of arthropathy in animal models. As there is a first-line agent, azithromycin, which is able to be given here, ofloxacin is not indicated.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant is admitted to the Emergency Department with flu-like symptoms, diarrhoea and an increasingly severe headache over the last 48 hours. Apparently she has been careful with her diet but attended a wedding where a number of canapés were served approximately four days earlier. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, she is pyrexial at 38.2 °C; blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, and pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft, although there is some left-sided abdominal tenderness. She is drowsy with clear signs of meningism, although there is no focal neurological deficit.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)145 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Glucose6.1 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
CSF glucose2.9 mmol/L2.5–3.9 mmol/L / two-thirds plasma value
CSF protein1.8 g/L<0.45 g/L
CSF microscopyGram-positive bacilli; mixed neutrophils and lymphocytes seen—

Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Amoxicillin

Gram-positive bacilli associated with symptoms of meningism in a pregnant woman are suggestive of Listeria infection. It is likely that infection occurred at the wedding party and is consistent with the incubation period for Listeria which may be anything from three to 70 days in duration. The drug of choice is amoxicillin, which is used in combination with gentamicin, except in pregnant women where it is used as monotherapy. In those who are penicillin-allergic, erythromycin is the drug of choice. At least three weeks of therapy are usually indicated for meningitis.

C Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin, like all quinolones, is contraindicated in pregnancy. Resistance to quinolones is increasing, with the large plasmid pLM80 thought to be responsible for conferring more rapid emergence of resistant strains.

B Cefuroxime

Unfortunately Listeria are naturally resistant to a range of modern cephalosporins, including cefuroxime. This is therefore an inappropriate option.

D Co-trimoxazole

Co-trimoxazole may be effective in some strains of Listeria, but minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing suggests that it is at least four times less effective than amoxicillin/ampicillin at treating the infection.

E Erythromycin

Erythromycin is the intervention of choice in patients who are allergic to penicillin. There is no documented penicillin allergy here.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old teacher presents to the Respiratory Clinic following abnormal screening results found during a work up for immunotherapy for multiple sclerosis. The health provider asks him about contacts, and the patient mentions his girlfriend, a teacher, with whom he split up three months earlier.

He is reviewed in the clinic, looks well, is apyrexial and has no symptoms of infection. His blood results are described below.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin121 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.7 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets209 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)8.0 mm/hr0–10 mm in the 1 sthour
Quantiferon test+
HIV test-

His CXR is shown below.

Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage the patient?
options: Rifampicin and isoniazid for three months
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Rifampicin and isoniazid for three months

This patient has latent tuberculosis as exemplified by the positive quantiferon test against a background of definite TB exposure, with no signs of pulmonary TB and a normal chest X-ray. Dual therapy is recommended for three months, or isoniazid alone can be given for six months.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Normal_posteroanterior_(PA)_chest_radiograph_(X- ray).jpg

C Repeat CXR in four weeks

The diagnosis of latent TB can already be made, so there is no need to repeat a chest film at this point.

A Full anti-tuberculous therapy

This would be considered for a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis.

D Recheck Quantiferon

The quantiferon gold test has a sensitivity of 92% and a specificity of >99%. It is highly unlikely therefore that this patient's result is a false negative.

E Rifampicin for one month

Only isoniazid should be considered as monotherapy treatment for latent TB.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old Russian foreign exchange student presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of sore throat and bloodstained nasal discharge. He feels lethargic and complains of intermittent fevers and myalgia. He has otherwise been well and there is no past medical history of note.

On examination, he has a temperature of 39.2 °C. His heart rate is 119 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 102/55 mmHg. He is saturating at 94% on room air, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min. On auscultation, his chest is clear, with normal heart sounds. Ear, nose and throat examination shows a thin grey membrane over his tonsils and tender cervical lymphadenopathy.

What is the most likely complication associated with this patient’s diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Myocarditis

This patient has diphtheria caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive rod. It is more common in Eastern Europe and symptoms include a watery nasal discharge that turns purulent and bloodstained. A sore throat with cervical lymphadenopathy and a classical grey membrane over the tonsils leads to the diagnosis. The diphtheria toxin can damage cardiac muscle, causing cardiac complications. They initially arise within the first 10–14 days of the illness and include tachycardia, heart block and myocarditis.

Myocarditis is a potentially fatal complication of diphtheria. It is, in fact, the most important cause of mortality in patients with diphtheria. In a study by Meera et al., all deaths except one was attributed to myocarditis.

Myocarditis has been reported in 19–68% of cases with diphtheria. However, a significant proportion of these individuals will just present with ECG changes without any symptoms of failure or shock. Besides sinus tachycardia and bradycardia, atrioventricular blocks, bundle branch blocks (BBB), ST-T changes, T wave inversion and ventricular/atrial ectopics are seen in varying frequencies in patients with myocarditis.

E Encephalopathy

Neurological symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy can be seen following infection with C. diphtheriae. However, encephalopathy is not a frequently seen complication.

B Pancreatitis

This patient has diphtheria. The disease has several complications, including peripheral neuropathy, renal impairment and myocarditis. However, pancreatitis is not a complication of diphtheria and is incorrect.

C Peritonsillar abscess

A peritonsillar abscess usually arises following acute tonsillitis. Common causative organisms include Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. The clinical history of a sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy may suggest a diagnosis of tonsillitis. However, the bloodstained nasal discharge and grey tonsillar pseudomembrane should point towards diphtheria. A peritonsillar abscess is not a complication of diphtheria, making it incorrect.

D Pneumonia

Pneumonia is a complication occasionally seen following streptococcal and staphylococcal throat infections such as tonsillitis. However, it is not commonly seen following infection with C. diphtheriae.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old Burmese man presents to Gastroenterology Clinic. He has lived in the UK for 8 months and works in a nightclub. He is complaining of severe persistent diarrhoea for the past month, ever since he took a trip back home to Burma where his family live in a small village. He has lost 15 kg; he denies fever or night sweats. The diarrhoea is watery with no blood or mucus. There is some associated abdominal discomfort and he feels nauseated but has not vomited. He has noticed a rash over his trunk which seems to be more obvious at some times more than others.

On examination, he is slim but looks well, pulse 90 bpm; BP 135/72 mmHg; afebrile. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no organomegaly; the rest of the clinical examination is unremarkable.

The GP has performed some tests:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)122 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)75 fL80 - 100 fL
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils2.5 ×10⁹/L0.04 - 0.4 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes1.0 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 4.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.6 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
InvestigationResultNormal values
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea4.1 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)80 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
InvestigationResultNormal values
Bilirubin22 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)32 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)101 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Albumin30 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Amylase95 U/L23 - 85 U/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)35 mg/L< 10 mg/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for strongyloides?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ivermectin

Strongyloides is a nematode endemic in the sub-tropics. Transmission occurs via direct skin exposure followed by cutaneous larva currens seen as migrating urticarial on the legs and trunk. It can cause enteritis, malabsorption and pneumonitis. In the wake of the nematodes, bacteria infection can follow, which can cause septicaemia and meningitis. Treatment is usually with ivermectin for 48 hours.

A Mebendazole

Mebendazole would be the correct threadworm or whipworm but these infections do not cause this level of infection.

B Albendazole

This antiprotozoal can be considered in patients with AIDS and strongyloides hyperinfestation. Whilst there is positive HIV serology, there is no CD4 count or AIDS-defining illnesses at this point and therefore there is no clear diagnosis of AIDS. It is the standard second line agent in the UK.

D Thiabendazole

Thiabendazole is an older anthelminthic therapy. Side effects have limited its use, although a topical suspension of thiabendazole can be used for cutaneous larva migrans.

E IV gentamicin

This treatment is not used in the treatment of nematodes and is more suited to bacterial infections.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman, who is 4 weeks post-partum, comes to the Emergency Department. She had an uneventful pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery requiring episiotomy. She presents now feeling extremely ill, with a purpuric rash and a fever.

On examination, she has a pyrexia of 38.5 °C, a BP of 95/60 mmHg, and a pulse of 105 bpm regular. She has lower abdominal tenderness on palpation and you notice erythema around her episiotomy site. She is wearing a pad and you notice some foul-smelling, blood stained, yellow discharge on the pad.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)111 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)132 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C High vaginal swab

The patient likely has endometritis. Symptoms of endometritis include fever, foul smelling vaginal discharge, and erythema or discharge around a wound site if present. A late presentation is not unusual, given that patients may assume their feeling unwell is just a slow recovery from labour. Studies suggest that empirical treatment covering penicillin resistant anaerobes appears most effective at treating endometritis. According to Cochrane reviews, a regime containing gentamicin and clindamycin appears to be the most efficient combination. Unfortunately over the longer term, adhesions and scarring post infection may lead to problems with future fertility. A high vaginal swab would be particularly useful on this occasion in targeting appropriate antibiotic therapy.

D Urine culture

This is unlikely to be a urine infection as there is a clear gynaecological source of infection and urine testing may be misleading as samples can easily be contaminated.

A Ultrasound scan abdomen

Whilst an ultrasound may be helpful, it is not the most important investigation in the acute setting. If the patient does not improve with treatment or there are concerns about abscess formation or deeper infection, then an ultrasound can be helpful.

B Blood cultures

Whilst blood cultures should be taken as the patient is septic, they are not the most important investigation as blood cultures are unlikely have as high a diagnostic sensitivity as direct swabbing.

E Wound swab

The site of episiotomy is likely to be contaminated with dermal flora and therefore may not be as useful as a high vaginal swab.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man presents to the Dermatologist with complaints of a rash over his face, neck and upper back for the past three weeks. He also complains of intense pruritus, further adding that he is unable to sleep at night because of the pruritus. There is a history of intravenous (IV) drug abuse.

On examination, his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 74 bpm. He appears emaciated and there are multiple needle-track marks present near the cubital fossa. There are multiple papulopustular lesions present over the face, neck and upper back. Oral examination reveals the presence of a whitish membrane suggestive of oral candidiasis.

Which of the following will cause regression of this patient’s skin lesions?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART)

This patient’s rash is typical of eosinophilic folliculitis. In this patient with multiple risk factors for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, the diagnosis is eosinophilic folliculitis secondary to HIV infection. It occurs in patients with a CD4 cell count < 250/mm³. With highly active antiretroviral therapy, the lesions resolve when CD4 cell counts improve to > 250/mm³.

E Topical retinoid and oral doxycycline

This would be appropriate in a patient with acne, which is a differential diagnosis for eosinophilic folliculitis due to the similar distribution of skin lesions. However, the presence of intense pruritus and the absence of comedones are features that differentiate eosinophilic folliculitis from acne vulgaris.

B Indomethacin

Idiopathic eosinophilic folliculitis (Ofuji’s disease) usually responds to indomethacin. However, in this patient, HIV infection is likely.

C Oral fluconazole

Oral fluconazole may be helpful in the management of oral candidiasis which occurs commonly in patients with HIV infection. However, it will not cause regression of the skin lesions.

D Permethrin cream

Permethrin cream may be used in the treatment of scabies which involves the interdigital regions. It is not recommended for the treatment of eosinophilic folliculitis.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man presents with diarrhoea, which also contains blood and pus. He admits to unprotected anal sex some 2–3 weeks earlier.

On examination, he is apyrexial, and there are no abnormal findings apart from tenderness on rectal examination.

Investigations:

InvestigationResult
Hb131 g/L
WCC8.9 ×10⁹/L
PLT210 ×10⁹/L
Na⁺139 mmol/L
K+4.5 mmol/L
Creatinine130 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most important next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) swab

The suspicion here is that this patient has developed rectal gonococcus infection due to his unprotected anal sex. The investigation of choice when collecting rectal specimens is a NAAT swab, which is useful if gonococcus or chlamydia is suspected. Prior to treatment he should be screened for other sexually transmitted infections including HIV, and if he knows the partner with whom he had anal intercourse, that individual should also be screened.

A Rectal biopsy

This patient presents with a short history of bloody diarrhoea. Given his risk factors, it is likely that a less invasive test will yield the diagnosis. Of course should his symptoms persist without explanation, a rectal biopsy may be warranted at a later stage.

B Colonoscopy

This patient presents with a short history of bloody diarrhoea. Given his risk factors, it is likely that a less invasive test will yield the diagnosis. Of course should his symptoms persist without explanation, a colonoscopy may be warranted at a later stage.

D Stool culture

The patient presents with a short history of diarrhoea with blood. Given his risk factors, there is a high suspicion of gonococcal proctitis. Gonococcus is notoriously difficult to culture in the laboratory, requiring specific set-up, and therefore would not be identified on standard culture.

E Trial of antibiotics

In this patient it would not be appropriate to give empirical antibiotics, as treatment choices are dependent on the underlying diagnosis. 21240

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of watery diarrhoea. He had returned from France the previous day.

On examination his temperature was 37.3°C, blood pressure 134/76 mmHg and pulse rate 88 bpm. His abdomen was soft, with epigastric tenderness. He did not have any rashes.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)142 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.6 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)108 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Urea9.1 mmol/L (2.5–7.0)2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Bilirubin9.0 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)27 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)72 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Gamma glutamyl-transferase (GGT)31 U/L< 50 U/L

What is the most likely cause of his diarrhoea?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Escherichia coli

This is by far the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea and typically causes a watery diarrhoea that is self-limiting, with little systemic upset, as seen here.

C Giardiasis

Giardia is a parasite and is a very common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller. However, it typically causes steatorrhoea, not watery diarrhoea, and it also causes belching and flatulence, which are not reported here. The most common cause of watery diarrhoea in the returning traveller is E. coli, which is the answer in this case.

A Amoebiasis

Amoebiasis typically causes dysentery, not watery diarrhoea (although in early amoebiasis, diarrhoea may be watery. Amoebiasis can cause liver dysfunction and abscesses, but this patient has normal liver enzymes. However, most importantly, amoebiasis is very uncommon. E. coli is the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea, and therefore is the correct answer here.

D Salmonella typhi

Salmonella typhi causes bloody diarrhoea, which is not seen in this case, and it is the organism responsible for typhoid fever. Patients with typhoid fever have very high fevers, headache and often constipation. They are systemically unwell and may have a salmon-pink maculopapular rash. These features are not present in this patient, who is much more likely to have E. coli, the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea.

E Shigella spp.

Shigella spp. typically cause a bloody diarrhoea, rather than the watery diarrhoea that this patient reports. Furthermore, E. coli is the most common cause of diarrhoea in returning travellers, and therefore this is the correct answer in this case.

questions.question:
An HIV-positive man has a CD4 count of 220 ×10⁶/L. He is generally asymptomatic but has noticed white patches in his mouth. They are quite unsightly and he is keen for treatment.

On examination, you observe irregular white patches, with a corrugated appearance along the side of his tongue. On probing with a swab, they cannot be dislodged.

What is the best way to eradicate these patches?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Antiretroviral therapy

The diagnosis is oral hairy leukoplakia, which is an AIDs-defining illness but can occur in other cases or immunosuppression. The clinical picture is described above and it is often mistaken for oral candida, the only difference being that plaques of leucoplakia cannot be dislodged. The condition is caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and it only needs to be treated if it is causing symptoms such as pain or dysphagia. The best treatment is to commence antiretroviral therapy, as the CD4 count rises, it will resolve. Other treatment options are high- dose aciclovir (3 g/day) and it may respond to other antivirals. Surgery is also an option.

E Improve oral hygiene

This would be the correct treatment for gingivitis. Gingivitis is inflammation of the gum and usually presents with gums that bleed easily.

A Oral fluconazole

It would be a treatment option if the history and examination suggested oral candida. The clinical picture would be very similar except that oral candida can be rubbed off while leukoplakia cannot.

B Nystatin lozenges

This is another treatment option for oral candida, which is not the most likely diagnosis.

D Aciclovir 200 mg 5× daily

This would be the correct treatment for herpes simplex viral sores. Oral lesions can appear as ulcers filled with yellow slough or cold sores. These are typically painful as well. As the clinical description does not match, this is not the right treatment option.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She complains of paroxysms of coughing that are so severe that she is exhausted afterwards and sometimes vomits as a reaction to the coughing. She has little contact with medical facilities and spends most of her time helping look after younger siblings. Her symptoms have been continuing for around the past four weeks, and right at the beginning of her illness, around six weeks ago, she had what she thought was a heavy cold. Physical examination in the clinic is unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)123 g/L115 - 160 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)274 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.6 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)37 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What would be the most useful test to perform for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Serology testing

Key features which drive us towards a diagnosis of Whooping Cough related to Bordetella pertussis (B pertussis) infection include: the typical history of cold symptoms which last for approximately two weeks followed by paroxysms of coughing, she is also less likely to have engaged with vaccination services. Given her age and stage of infection, serology is the most appropriate next step in confirming the likely diagnosis. At this stage of her disease antibiotics have no value in shortening the duration of symptoms. Her coughing symptoms will improve over the course of a few weeks.

D Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

There is no indication for PCR testing here. PCR testing is used to test for B pertussis infection in severely ill, hospitalised infants. A nasopharyngeal swab would be used to collect material for PCR testing in these cases.

A Induced sputum culture

Induced sputum culture is primarily used in the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis, where patients struggle to produce sputum themselves. The patient inhales hypertonic saline which liquefies secretions and promotes coughing so a specimen can be collected. The symptoms here are much more consistent with a diagnosis of B pertussis (Whooping Cough), which at this stage in an adult is best confirmed by serology testing.

B Nasopharyngeal swab culture

Nasopharyngeal swab testing is most sensitive for the diagnosis of Whooping Cough when performed in the first two weeks of symptoms. It is also more sensitive for detecting infection in younger individuals. In this patient (who is 18 years old) serology testing is likely to be most useful.

C Oral fluid testing

Oral fluid testing is recommended in people aged 5-16 who have had a cough with features of whooping cough for more than two weeks. They should not have received a vaccine in the preceding year. This test for anti- pertussis toxin immunoglobulin G (IgG) is conducted when a blood sample cannot be collected. In adults, serological testing via a blood test would be more appropriate.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is admitted to the Respiratory Ward with a 1-week history of persistent fever, dry cough and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a past medical history of acute myeloid leukaemia, for which he is currently receiving chemotherapy.

His temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate 110 bpm and BP 120/65 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 93% on room air.

A CT scan is requested, which shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and a 3-cm nodule in the left upper lobe, with a halo sign.

What is the next most appropriate investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: CT-guided needle aspiration for tissue biopsy
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen

This patient has a likely diagnosis of aspergillosis, given the history of fever, pleuritic chest pain and dry cough in an immunocompromised patient. The CT findings of bilateral infiltrates and a pulmonary nodule, with a positive halo sign, are also indicative of the condition. Serum galactomannan antigen testing is a non-invasive diagnostic test with high sensitivity and specificity for invasive aspergillosis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Therefore, it is the most appropriate investigation to consider in the next step of the management of this patient.

E Sputum smear

Although a sputum smear can be used in the diagnosis of aspergillosis, with a positive sample showing hyphae, sputum production is uncommon with the condition, making it a less useful investigation than serum galactomannan antigen testing.

A Bronchoalveolar lavage for fungal cultures

A bronchoscopy can be performed with BAL for respiratory fluid, which can be used for fungal testing. In patients with aspergillosis, the BAL fluid may be positive for hyphae. However, the yield of BAL fluid is low, and the procedure itself is invasive and carries risks, particularly in more unwell patients.

B CT-guided needle aspiration for tissue biopsy

The most definitive investigation is tissue biopsy. However, this procedure is invasive and carries risks such as bleeding and post-procedure pneumothorax. Instead, alternative investigations, such as serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen testing, which are non-invasive should be utilised.

C PCR for Aspergillus DNA

PCR testing of respiratory specimens for Aspergillus DNA may be used as an adjunctive diagnostic test. However, it is not the primary diagnostic test for invasive aspergillosis.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman is seen in the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic with a 1-week history of lower abdominal pain and deep dyspareunia. She denies lower urinary tract symptoms but has noticed an occasional creamy vaginal discharge. There is no past medical history of note. She had the Mirena ® coil intrauterine system (IUS) inserted three months ago and takes no regular medications. She has no allergies. On examination, her temperature is 37.8 °C. Her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 131/83 mmHg. Chest sounds are clear, with saturations of 98% on room air and heart sounds are normal. She has lower abdominal tenderness and is guarding in the left iliac fossa. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Bimanual examination elicits bilateral adnexal tenderness. Swabs are taken.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)16.3 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils12.1 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.5 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.4 ×10⁹/L0.8–5.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)233 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)142 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.2 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)115 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)6060+
C-reactive protein (CRP)299 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Beta human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG)3 mIU/ml< 5 mIU/ml
Progesterone5 ng/ml5–20 ng/ml

What is the most likely causative organism contributing to this patient’s diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Chlamydia trachomatis

This patient has pelvic inflammatory disease. The symptoms of deep dyspareunia, along with her lower abdominal and adnexal tenderness, point towards the diagnosis. C. trachomatis is the most common cause of pelvic inflammatory disease and is responsible for up to 35% of cases.

A Chlamydia psittaci

C. psittaci causes a type of respiratory pneumonia called psittacosis. It is an organism that infects birds and is, therefore, more common in those who keep birds as pets. However, it is not a cause of pelvic inflammatory disease.

C Neisseria gonorrhoeae

N. gonorrhoeae is a causative organism of pelvic inflammatory disease. However, it is less common than C. trachomatis, making it an incorrect answer.

D Escherichia coli

E. coli is a common cause of upper and lower urinary tract infections. Raised inflammatory markers, lower abdominal tenderness and leucocytes in the urine can raise suspicion of the diagnosis. However, it does not explain this patient's vaginal discharge or adnexal tenderness.

E Mycoplasma genitalium

M. genitalium is a causative organism of pelvic inflammatory disease. However, it is less common than C. trachomatis, making it an incorrect answer.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old man with known HIV is admitted with increasing shortness of breath. He is on antiretroviral medications.

On examination, he has raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), bilateral lower limb oedema and crackles on both bases. BP is 105/60 mmHg, pulse 95/min.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)114 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.4 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)156 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)140 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
CD4 count235 cells/mm³500–1500 cells/mm³
Echocardiography (ECHO)Severe dilated cardiomyopathy
Ejection fraction24%

His chest X-ray is shown below

What is the most likely cause of his problem?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Zidovudine

Zidovudine (AZT) is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor and was the first drug licensed for treatment of HIV. It has significant mitochondrial toxicity and is known to be associated with dilated cardiomyopathy. The CXR shows evidence of left ventricular overload with pleural effusions, bilateral interstitial changes and prominent upper lobe diversion. In patients such as this, myocardial biopsy usually reveals mitochondria full of myelin, a sign of mitochondrial dysfunction. Withdrawal of zidovudine and substitution with an agent associated with less mitochondrial toxicity, coupled with appropriate treatment for heart failure with diuretics and ACE inhibition, usually resolves the problem, although HIV itself is decreasingly recognised as a cause of cardiomyopathy.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kardiale_Dekompensation_und_Rekompensation_73W_-_CR_pa_- _001.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kardiale_Dekompensation_und_Rekompensation_73W_- _CR_pa_-_001.jpg)

E Ritonavir

Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor now used at low dose in combination with other protease inhibitors to boost their potency. Serious side effects include hepatitis, pancreatitis and arrhythmia. Its use is not associated with myocarditis.

A Cytomegalovirus

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a member of the herpes virus family (HHV 5). It typically causes a glandular fever syndrome, but presentation is varied and in the immunocompromised host disease can be severe. CMV can cause a cardiomyopathy, but this is rare and an alternative explanation is more probable in our patient.

B Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. Acute infection may result in a flu-like illness, but is more commonly asymptomatic. In the immunocompromised it may cause an encephalitis. The presentation described does not fit with toxoplasmosis.

C Influenza

Influenza is a virus responsible for flu. Infection is characterised by upper respiratory symptoms, as well as fever and muscle aches. Myocarditis is a possible but uncommon sequalae of influenza infection. In the patient described above, an alternative diagnosis is more likely.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fevers, myalgia and a sore throat. She also complains of nausea and reduced oral intake. Her 2-year-old daughter has been off sick from nursery with similar symptoms. There is no past medical history and she only takes over-the-counter vitamin supplementation. She has no allergies. On examination, she is febrile with a temperature of 40.2 °C. Her heart rate is 131 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 101/65 mmHg. She is coryzal with a dry cough. Chest sounds are clear, with no audible crackles or wheeze and her saturations are 99% on room air. She has a red throat and palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of her ear, nose and throat examination is unremarkable.

Throat swab: influenza A positive

She is discharged home with advice to take regular analgesia and encourage fluid intake. An outpatient prescription of oseltamivir is given.

What is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Neuraminidase inhibitor

Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor. Neuraminidase inhibitors block the action of the neuraminidase enzyme, an enzyme found on the surface of the influenza virus, which enables movement of the virus into and out of host cells.

D Integrase inhibitor

Integrase inhibitors are designed to inhibit the action of the enzyme integrase; a viral enzyme used to incorporate the genome of the virus into the host cell’s DNA. It is an important step in the viral replication process and preventing this step helps to reduce further spread of the virus. One example of an integrase inhibitor includes raltegravir, an inhibitor of HIV integrase.

B Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)

Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), such as efavirenz, are used in the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and are one of the components of highly active antiretroviral treatment (HAART). They are non-competitive inhibitors of the reverse transcriptase enzyme, therefore stopping viral deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) synthesis.

C Protease inhibitor

Protease inhibitors are used in the treatment of HIV. An example is ritonavir. Protease inhibitors work by inhibiting the protease enzyme, which prevents the virus from packaging and releasing new virions.

E Nucleoside analogue

Nucleoside analogues incorporate into viral DNA or ribonucleic acid (RNA), causing chain termination. One example is ribavirin, used in the treatment of chronic hepatitis C infection in adults or of life-threatening respiratory syncytial virus infection in children.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe shortness of breath, and lethargy such that he is only able to walk a few yards. He admits feeling generally unwell with fevers, weight loss and a dry cough over the past few months. He is a former IV drug abuser who moved to the UK from southern Italy a few years earlier. Examination reveals blood pressure of 105/80 mmHg, with pulse is 86/min and regular. He looks pale. There is generalised lymphadenopathy and his BMI is 20.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)76 g/L (reticulocyte count not elevated)135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)197 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.4 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)65 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
Bone marrow aspiratePure red cell aplasia

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Parvovirus infection

The general deterioration over the past few months, coupled with a previous history of intravenous drug abuse, raises the possibility of underlying HIV. Parvovirus B19-related red cell aplasia is associated with HIV infection and accounts for the picture seen here: anaemia without reticulocytosis and red cell aplasia on bone marrow aspiration. B19 DNA can be identified by PCR to confirm the underlying cause. IV immunoglobulin is the intervention of choice.

D Myelofibrosis

Myelofibrosis is clonal haemopoietic stem cell proliferation with histological evidence on bone marrow biopsy. Presentation is variable and can be with features of changes in haemaglobin, white cell counts or platelet numbers, as well as constitutional symptoms and massive splenomegaly. This is unlikely based on the absence of clinical findings, and peripheral blood film should show leuko-erythoblastosis with teardrop poikilocytosis and there may be megakaryocyte fragments. Bone marrow aspiration is usually dry and biopsy is needed.

A Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is destruction of red blood cells through an antibody-mediated process. There are multiple causes split into three categories: warm antibody types (e.g. SLE, Evans syndrome, CLL), cold antibody type (viral infection, Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection) or drug related. The history may that of anaemia with the suggestion of an underlying cause, and there may also be evidence of increased bilirubin such as gallstones or jaundice. The lack of evidence of raised bilirubin does not exclude autoimmune haemolytic anaemia in this patient, but the evidence of aplasia of red blood cells does, as does the normal reticulocyte count, of which the latter should be raised during haemolysis.

B Cytomegalovirus infection

Cytomegalovirus is a common herpesvirus which can cause gastrointestinal disease, pneumonia, retinitis and encephalitis during immunosuppression. In the immunosuppressed patient complications include haemolytic anaemia via an antibody-mediated process. As with the above explanation, the absence of a raised reticulocyte count and the presence of aplasia make this a less likely diagnosis.

C Myelodysplasia

Myelodysplasias are haematopoietic disorders characterised by dysplastic changes in cell linages of the bone marrow. The marrow itself becomes hyper- or hypocellular due to clonal proliferation of abnormal cells leading to peripheral blood cytopenias. This usually occurs in the elderly, but can be due to previous chemotherapy, environmental toxins or some rare disorders. The absence of such risk factors makes this a very unlikely diagnosis, and the bone marrow results exclude this diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old man presents to the general practitioner (GP). He is from Southern India and is visiting the UK to see his son. His family has brought him to the doctor as he is unable to extend his wrist and has clawing of his fingers.

On examination, there is a dry scaling rash above the elbow on the affected side. The skin rash itself is painless and non-itchy, and there is evidence of sensory loss distal to the lesion.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Tuberculoid leprosy

This man comes from a region where leprosy infection is endemic and this clinical picture is highly suggestive of a tuberculoid leprosy picture. Serological testing can be employed to confirm the diagnosis and a number of PCR-based techniques are growing in popularity. Nerve conduction studies may show segmental slowing at the site of nerve entrapment. Skin biopsy may also be useful in confirming the diagnosis. Combination treatment with dapsone and rifampicin is usually employed for 6 months for paucibacillary leprosy; in the UK a 2-year course is recommended for multibacillary disease. While further nerve damage may be arrested by treatment, recovery of nerve function already lost is very unlikely.

Clinical leprosy lies between two extremes: tuberculoid (TT) and lepromatous (LL). Between the two ends of the spectrum lies a broad group designated as borderline, and subclassified as borderline tuberculoid (BT), midborderline (BB) and borderline lepromatous (BL). The disease does not remain static but evolves spontaneously or in response to therapy. Transition toward the TT pole is referred to as upgrading (and may lead to a reversal or type I reaction) and transition toward the LL pole as downgrading (leading to type II reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum [ENL]). The reactions reflect abrupt changes in the host–parasite immunological balance and are associated with acute clinical exacerbations.

E Syphillis infection

While secondary syphilis can have a painless and asymptomatic limb rash, and tertiary syphilis can be associated with focal neurological lesions, the absence of any other features makes this an unlikely diagnosis. Primary syphilis causes a single painless ulcer at the site of infection with lymphoadenopathy. Secondary syphilis can occur 6 weeks later in 25% of untreated patients; it features a polymorphic rash of the palms and soles, but other organs can be affected. Over time, tertiary syphilis can develop with neurological syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis.

A Herpes zoster infection

Herpes zoster virus causes varicella (chickenpox) in childhood and shingles during immunosuppression or old age. Shingles is characterised first by a pre-eruptive phase causing burning, itching or paraesthesia in one dermatome, leading to an eruptive phase with erythematous swollen plaques with clusters of small vesicles which are limited by dermatomal distribution. The absence of pain and the presence of weakness make this diagnosis unlikely.

B Rickettsial infection

Rickettsia organisms are Gram-negative coccobacilli which are obligate intracellular parasites found primarily in rats and mice. They cause several diseases, including typhus which is characterised by fever, myalgia, headache and diarrhoea with a rash on the chest which can spread to the extremities.
