The absence of systemic features and rash on the chest make this diagnosis far less likely, and it would not explain the neurological features.

C Lepromatous leprosy

This form of leprosy is systemic with symmetrical distribution and associated symptoms and signs. It is far more severe with reddish or hypopigmented patches with reduced sensation. There is also ocular involvement and systemic disease affecting the respiratory tract, kidneys and lymph nodes.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old woman was brought by ambulance after as a ‘red alert’. Her brother accompanied her and reported that she was very lethargic the previous evening and had complained of a sore throat and muscle aches. The following morning, he subsequently found her vomiting and complaining of a headache.

On examination, her blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, temperature 38.7 °C and pulse rate 110 bpm. There was a purpuric skin rash and evidence of subconjunctival haemorrhage. With the thigh flexed at the hip and the knee at 90 degrees, the patient found further extension of the leg painful.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
White cell count (WCC)14.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils11.4 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)51 s25 - 35 s
Urea10.1 mmol/L (2.5–7.0)2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine148 mmol/L (60–11050 - 120 µmol/L
Random plasma glucose4.1 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L

What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Ceftriaxone

The answer is Ceftriaxone (Option A).

This patient has signs, including a positive Kernig’s sign, and symptoms consistent with meningitis, probably meningococcal meningitis, given the evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. The most appropriate treatment is intravenous ceftriaxone, which should be given immediately. This patient will need to be transferred to intensive care. A computerised tomography (CT) scan is required before progressing to lumbar puncture, to rule out cerebral oedema and therefore the risk of coning on lumbar puncture. Cerebral herniation occurs in about 5% of patients with acute bacterial meningitis, accounting for about 30% of mortality. Bacterial meningitis would give a typically turbid or purulent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), 200–300 polymorphs/mm³, 0.5– 2.0 g/L of protein and CSF glucose levels of < 50% of the blood value. It is important to treat contacts of patients with meningococcal disease with prophylaxis against infection with oral ciprofloxacin. A single dose of ceftriaxone is appropriate for prophylaxis in pregnant women.

B Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin (Option B) is incorrect.

This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with bacterial meningitis, likely meningococcal. She is extremely unwell, with signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation. The appropriate antibiotic here is intravenous ceftriaxone. Ciprofloxacin is not a first-line agent for bacterial meningitis, though oral ciprofloxacin may be used for prophylaxis for exposed contacts.

C Glucose

Glucose (Option C) is incorrect.

This patient is not significantly hypoglycaemic and therefore does not require glucose replacement. The hypoglycaemia is likely to be a feature of sepsis, rather than a cause of her current symptoms. Hypoglycaemia as an underlying problem should be considered in patients with a low glucose on hypoglycaemic agents, who can present with reduced consciousness, hunger, irritability or confusion. In such cases, oral glucose treatment, intramuscular glucagon and intravenous dextrose can be used. Had the hypoglycaemia been more severe, then correction would have been warranted, but the highest priority should be ceftriaxone to treat the underlying cause.

D Hydrocortisone

Hydrocortisone (Option D) is incorrect.

This patient has bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal, and will require transfer to intensive care. Steroids have been shown to reduce the risk of hearing loss in bacterial meningitis, but there is no evidence that they reduce overall mortality. If steroids were given, dexamethasone would be the agent used, rather than hydrocortisone. Hydrocortisone would have been the correct answer to the management of an Addisonian crisis, which can present with vomiting and hypotension, but the fever, rash and headache make that a less likely diagnosis.

E Naloxone

Naloxone (Option E) is incorrect.

Naloxone is an opioid antagonist, used in overdose situations. There is no evidence that this patient has overdosed on opioids; instead, she has a purpuric rash, neurological signs and fever. This should be treated as bacterial meningitis, until proven otherwise. Evidence of an opiate overdose would be a low respiratory rate, pinpoint pupils and evidence of intravenous drug abuse such as track-marks. 33150

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant presents to the Emergency Department. She returned ten days ago from a visit to Bangladesh for a family funeral. She has been feeling unwell with nausea, flu-like symptoms and diarrhoea over the past few days and has become jaundiced. On examination, her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, temperature 37.8 °C and pulse 95 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination reveals a uterus consistent with her stage of pregnancy and she is tender in the right upper quadrant.

Investigations;

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)209 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine108 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)2015 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)321 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin122 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.21.1

She has been vaccinated against hepatitis A and B

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Hepatitis E

Given the acute nature of this patient’s symptoms, coupled with a lack of exposure to potential viruses borne by blood/other body fluids, hepatitis E is the most likely underlying diagnosis. It is spread by the faecal/oral route and genotypes 3 and 4, in particular, are responsible for disease in humans. While mortality is 1–4% when the

general population is considered, it may be as high as 20% in pregnant women. Treatment is supportive and immunoglobulin ineffective, and no vaccine exists.

C Hepatitis D

Hepatitis D infection always coexists with hepatitis B. As this patient has no history of contact with bodily fluids or contaminated blood products and she has been vaccinated against hepatitis B, there is no chance of her having hepatitis D.

A Epstein Barr virus

Epstein–Barr virus is associated with pharyngitis, which is not seen here. It can cause abnormal liver function tests. However, the large increase in ALT that is present in this case is not classically seen with Epstein–Barr virus infection.

B Hepatitis C

There is no history of contact with bodily fluids or contaminated blood products in this case, which makes this diagnosis unlikely.

E Typhoid fever

Typhoid fever is associated with intermittent diarrhoea, followed by headaches, high fever, a non-productive cough and eventually a tendency to constipation. Mild elevations in liver function tests can be seen, and not the very large rise in transaminases seen here. 38200

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. Her brother tells you that she has been having fevers, tiredness, a sore throat and lower body muscle ache for a week, but in the last three days has felt better. She has a regular boyfriend and only drinks at the weekends. He tells you that two weeks ago they were out clubbing and she was so drunk she fell in the city river when two of her friends had to jump in and get her out. She was seen in hospital after this and was given the all-clear.

On examination, she exhibits meningism and photophobia. She is jaundiced and is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.7 °C. She has no rash but has bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhage and has pharyngeal injection and enlarged tonsillar lymph nodes. Her heart rate is 120/min, blood pressure 90/62 mmHg. She has hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal examination. Computerised tomography (CT) of the head is normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results reveals the following:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis is caused by pathogenic spiral bacteria belonging to the genus Leptospira. The disease is more prevalent in tropical climates and those with a heavy rainfall. In the developed world it has become associated with recreational watersports and those exposed to raw sewage.

The disease incubates for 7–12 days and many patients never present with clinical features. The first phase is known as the septicaemic or leptospiraemic phase, as the bacteria can be cultured in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). In this phase, patients often have flu-like symptoms. The patient usually then feels better for three days before developing the immune or leptospiruric stage because circulating antibodies may be detected or the organism may be isolated from urine. However, it may not be cultured from blood or CSF. In this phase, patients often present with aseptic meningitis, haemorrhagic shock or kidney disease.

Treatment includes supportive management. Doxycycline and penicillin are both reasonable choices for antimicrobial therapy.

A Meningococcal septicaemia

Meningococcal septicaemia is an infection caused by the Gram-negative coccus Neisseria meningitides. Patients present with sepsis and typically a non-blanching petechial rash. Meningitis can occur, but typical CSF findings would be of a much higher white cell count (>100/microlitre) with neutrophil predominance, and a reduced glucose (<0.5 × serum level).

B Mollaret’s meningitis

This is a recurrent benign meningitis, most commonly associated with HSV-2. Patients present with recurrent episodes of meningism lasting several days which are then self-resolving. CSF analysis shows a lymphocytic CSF as seen in the question, but the rest of the clinical history is not consistent.

C Streptococcal meningitis

This is meningitis caused by the Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, a commensal of the human oropharynx. Presentation is usually with a rapid-onset meningism and sepsis. Typical CSF findings would be of a much higher white cell count (>100/µl) with neutrophil predominance, and a reduced glucose (<0.5 × serum level).

E Meliodosis

Meliodosis is an infection caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei. Most patients have subclinical disease, but infection can present with pneumonia, skin abscess formation and sepsis. While sporadic cases have been reported worldwide, the disease is endemic to South and South East Asia.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man returned 2 weeks ago from an 8-month business trip with colleagues to Peru. He noticed a few papules on his trunk and legs. One of these has changed, as shown below.

He feels well in himself and denies fever, diarrhoea or headaches. He does remember having a flu-like illness while he was in Peru.

Routine bloods, including full blood count and white cell differential, are normal.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Cutaneous leishmaniasis

The image shows a superficial ulcer which, in combination with the history of travel and flu-like illness is most likely due to cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL). The incubation time is 7 days to several months. In cutaneous larva migrans, worm-like lesions have an incubation period 1–4 days and are found mainly after holidays to Caribbean beaches. Treatment of CL is determined by species type and by the potential to develop into mucosal disease.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cutaneous_Leishmaniasis.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cutaneous_Leishmaniasis.jpg)

C Tick typhus eschar

The eschar of tick typhus is a papule, which evolves to a black scab. This condition is also found in southern Africa, and has an incubation period of fewer than 7 days.

B Cutaneous larva migrans

Cutaneous larva migrans occurs as a result of hookworm infection caused by walking barefoot. The trails caused by the larvae are usually seen on the feet and ankles.

D Dengue fever

Dengue fever occurs in tropical countries, with an incubation period of under two weeks and is associated with systemic features and a morbilliform rash.

E Cutaneous tuberculosis

Cutaneous lesions are relatively uncommon in TB infection, occurring in only 1-2% of infected patients. The clinical findings vary: inflammatory papules, verrucous plaques, suppurative nodules, chronic ulcers or other lesions may be seen. Superficial ulcers on the trunk are not a usual manifestation of TB.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old woman attends the Genitourinary Clinic with a 6-day history of vulval itching. She denies fever or lower urinary tract symptoms and there is no history of vaginal discharge. She had unprotected sex with a new partner two weeks ago. There is no past medical history of note. She is ten weeks pregnant and other than regular folic acid, she takes no other medication. She has no allergies. On examination, she has a temperature of 36.3 °C; her heart rate is 75 bpm and her blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. There are multiple flesh-coloured papules around the vulva, with the largest measuring 5 mm in diameter. Some of the papules have an irregular border with evidence of mild bleeding.

What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Cryotherapy

This woman has a diagnosis of anogenital warts secondary to human papillomavirus (HPV). The virus is spread via skin-to-skin contact and results in the appearance of itchy, flesh-coloured papules which have a tendency to bleed. Treatment is not always indicated. However, it is important to minimise the number of lesions in pregnancy to prevent neonatal exposure to HPV. Cryotherapy is a treatment for anogenital warts. It often needs to be repeated every 1–3 weeks until the warts resolve. Cryotherapy tends to be reserved for a small number of warts with a small volume in size. In pregnancy, cryotherapy is the recommended choice of treatment, as per British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) guidelines.

A Oral aciclovir

Oral aciclovir is an antiviral medication used in the treatment of the herpes virus. Herpes simplex virus (predominantly type II) causes genital ulcers – a very painful and itchy eruption of vesicles and ulcers with associated surrounding erythema. Dysuria is a common symptom with genital herpes and as the disease progresses, tender lymphadenopathy can appear. This scenario describes a young woman with fleshy protuberances, rather than painful vesicles, making genital warts the most likely diagnosis.

B Topical clotrimazole

Topical clotrimazole is a treatment of Candida albicans, otherwise known as thrush. Thrush presents with severe itch and a thick, white, curd-like discharge. Dysuria is also common, as is the eruption of dermatitis over the surrounding vulva.

C Topical podophyllotoxin

Topical podophyllotoxin is the first-line treatment for anogenital warts. However, podophyllotoxin is teratogenic, making it unsuitable to be prescribed during pregnancy.

D Topical imiquimod

Topical imiquimod, along with topical podophyllotoxin, is one of the recommended treatments for human papillomavirus (HPV). Usually, topical podophyllotoxin is used initially. There are little data to support the safety of imiquimod to treat anogenital warts in pregnancy. Therefore, the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) guidelines currently recommend that the treatment of anogenital warts in pregnant patients should be with cryotherapy.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with rapidly worsening infection of his left lower limb. He is obese and has poor mobility, and says the infection began with only a small area of erythema around 24 hours earlier. Since that time, the area of erythema has extended significantly, with large areas of necrotic tissue and the skin is boggy to touch. He is requiring large amounts of morphine for pain relief. A photograph of the affected area is shown below:

Which of the following is thought to contribute to the rapid progression of his disease?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E M protein

The diagnosis here with rapidly progressive cellulitis and large areas of necrotic tissue is consistent with a diagnosis of necrotising fasciitis. Group A streptococci are well recognised as a cause of type II necrotising fasciitis, and M proteins are a key virulence factor in the development of the disease, particularly the 1 and 3 subtypes. As well as extensive surgical debridement, a typical empirical antibiotic regimen includes piperacillin- tazobactam combined with vancomycin.

D Enterotoxin-A

Enterotoxin A is a leading cause of staphylococcal food poisoning. This is seen as a result of ingesting dairy products which have been kept at room temperature for a significant period of time. It leads to profuse vomiting, and symptoms settle spontaneously after a few hours.

A Alpha toxin

Alpha toxin is a key virulence factor in Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene. It is not linked to the progression of necrotising fasciitis, which is often related to Streptococcus group A infection. It is thought that alpha toxin in the context of gas gangrene drives inflammation and oedema and accelerates tissue necrosis.

Type III necrotizing fasciitis is usually caused by Clostridium perfringens. When type III necrotizing fasciitis occurs spontaneously, C septicum is more likely to be the etiologic agent; these cases usually occur in association with colon cancer or leukemia.

B Cereulide

Cereulide is the toxin which causes vomiting in Bacillus cereus (B cereus) food poisoning. It does not have a role in pathogenesis of necrotising fasciitis. B cereus food poisoning is most often related to under-cooked rice, symptoms of food poisoning occur 4-6 hours after ingestion, and usually resolve within 24 hours.

C Choleragen

Choleragen is the enterotoxin produced by cholera, which drives the profuse watery diarrhoea seen with Vibrio cholerae infection. It leads to constant overstimulation of chloride, water, sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate into the lumen of the small intestine.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of fever, pain and swelling over bilateral knees, wrist and hands for the past five days. She has no significant past medical history.

On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and her heart rate is 94 bpm. There is a generalised purplish rash noted. She has swelling and tenderness on palpation of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, but no deformities.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Parvovirus B19 infection

Acute infection with parvovirus B19 in young women more often causes acute symmetric polyarticular arthritis than infection in men or children. Polyarticular arthritis often involves the hands and joints of the lower limbs. It is usually associated with a vasculitic rash in up to 18% of cases. In immunocompetent adults with no haemoglobinopathies or primary red cell disorders, there is only mild anaemia that is self-limiting. The disease is usually self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals and resolves with symptomatic management.

D Rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis presents with joint pain for at least six weeks, unlike this patient who has an acute presentation and no deformities.

A Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with features of asthma, mononeuritis multiplex and renal involvement, which are not present in this patient. Other features include arthritis and arthralgia, as well as peripheral eosinophilia.

C Polyarteritis nodosa

Polyarteritis nodosa may present with a rash and arthralgia. However, it is necrotising vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries, resulting in glomerulonephritis, stroke, bowel ischaemia, etc. These features are not present in this patient.

E Systemic lupus erythematosus

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause polyarticular symmetrical arthritis but the distribution and description of this patients rash make this a less likely diagnosis. Common skin involvement in SLE involves rash over the malar distribution (termed a 'butterfly rash') and less commonly, inflammatory discoid lesions. 72826

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man presented with extensive burns over the forearms after attending a blaze as part of his work as a firefighter. Three days later the burns on his forearms deteriorated.

On examination, his temperature was 38.1 °C. The burns had developed a violaceous/black discolouration, bullae and sweet-smelling green pus.

Wound culture and microscopy revealed Gram-positive rods. The wounds were surgically debrided.

What is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin

This patient has signs consistent with gas gangrene, which is caused by Clostridium perfringens. This is further supported by microscopy, as Cl. perfringens is a Gram-positive rod. Benzylpenicillin has good activity against Cl. perfringens and should be used in combination with clindamycin.

E Vancomycin

Vancomycin gives excellent coverage of Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negative cocci. It is often used in addition to other antibiotics in the treatment of resistant Gram-positive cocci – for example, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. This patient, however, has a super-infection with Gram-positive rods. Having presented with sweet-smelling pus and multiple bullae, this is consistent with gas gangrene, caused by Clostridium perfringens. Vancomycin is not bactericidal for Cl. perfringens, and therefore would not be an appropriate choice here. A better choice would be benzylpenicillin, which can be used alone or with clindamycin.

B Chloramphenicol

The sweet-smelling pus and multiple bullae seen in this patient are suggestive of superinfection with Clostridium perfringens, which causes gas gangrene. Cl. perfringens is a Gram-positive rod, as seen on microscopy here. Chloramphenicol covers some Gram-positive rods, including Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) and Listeria monocytogenes, but it does not give adequate coverage of Cl. perfringens to treat this infection. A better choice would be benzylpenicillin, which is either used alone or in combination with clindamycin.

C Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is a good empirical choice for the treatment of cellulitis as it gives excellent coverage of Staphylococcus, a common cause of cellulitis and wound super-infection. However, microscopy has revealed Gram-positive rods in this patient (Staphylococcus would appear as Gram-positive cocci). This, combined with the sweet-smelling pus and multiple bullae, is suggestive of gas gangrene, caused by Clostridium perfringens. This organism is not covered by flucloxacillin. A more appropriate antibiotic would be benzylpenicillin, which is either used alone or with clindamycin.

D Gentamicin

Gentamicin provides excellent cover for Gram-negative organisms, and can work synergistically to treat some Gram-positive infections. This patient has an infection with a Gram-positive rod: combined with his presentation (sweet-smelling pus, multiple bullae), this is suggestive of gas gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens. Gentamicin would not cover Cl. perfringens. A better choice would be benzylpenicillin, either alone or in combination with clindamycin.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department with worsening vision affecting her left eye. She says she woke that morning with progressively worsening visual acuity and can now only detect light and dark on the left-hand side. There is a crusted papular lesion on the dorsum of her left hand, which she says was caused by a scratch from some kittens at a local farm a few days earlier. Left axillary lymphadenopathy is also observed. Fundoscopy of the left retina reveals cotton wool spots and haemorrhages. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg.

What is the most likely cause of her visual loss?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bartonella henselae (B henselae) neuroretinitis

This patient has cat scratch disease (CSD), related to B henselae infection which is often carried by young cats, and cats that live a less domesticated existence (such as those on a farm). Around 1-2% of patients with cat scratch disease develop neuroretinitis, which is characterised by a rapid deterioration in visual acuity. Retinal findings may include haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and evidence of deep retinal scarring/inflammation. Most patients have a good chance of recovery from CSD related neuroretinitis, although some have residual loss of colour vision and diminished contrast sensitivity. Azithromycin is the intervention of choice for CSD.

D Central retinal artery occlusion

Central retinal artery occlusion is associated with retinal pallor and a “cherry red” spot because the macula receives its blood supply from the posterior ciliary arteries. Retinal artery occlusion is also not associated with Bartonella infection.

B Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis

CMV retinitis has a similar appearance to that seen here, with cotton wool spots and haemorrhages, although it is more likely to be seen in patients with immunosuppressive disorders. The other symptoms seen here, including evidence of a cat scratch and lymphadenopathy, are more consistent with Bartonella infection.

C Hypertensive retinopathy

Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy is associated with multiple flame-shaped haemorrhages. The rapid deterioration seen here in visual acuity would, however, be unexpected in hypertensive retinopathy. The other features of cat scratch disease also do not fit with hypertensive retinopathy as the cause of visual acuity loss.

E Central retinal vein occlusion

Central retinal vein occlusion is associated with multiple flame-shaped haemorrhages on fundoscopy. It occurs more commonly in patients with thrombophilic disorders such as anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, protein C, protein S deficiency, and anti-thrombin III deficiency. It is not associated with Bartonella infection. 72136

questions.question:
A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department, complaining of pain when passing urine over the past few days. In addition, she has flitting arthritis affecting the small joints of her hands and feet and a generalised maculopapular rash. In particular, her left knee is causing considerable pain. On examination, you notice that there is a medium-sized effusion; the joint is hot, and flexion is limited by pain. On further questioning, she admits to having unprotected sexual intercourse with two different partners during a recent holiday to Spain.

Investigations;

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine95 µmol/L 50–120 µmol/L
Knee aspirate: Gram-negative intracellular cocci.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Ceftriaxone and azithromycin

The patient is suffering from gonococcal arthritis. Gonococcus remains sensitive to ceftriaxone. As such, it is the intervention of choice here. Intravenous (iv) therapy should be continued preferably for up to 48 hours post- initial improvement, after which treatment with an oral cephalosporin should be continued for at least a week. Chlamydia trachomatis is a frequent copathogen with N. gonorrhoeae and should be empirically treated with azithromycin if not specifically excluded with microbiologic testing.

A Benzylpenicillin

Benzylpenicillin is not routinely used in the treatment of gonococcal infection.

C Ciprofloxacin

Significant resistance to quinolones exists, and they are therefore no longer recommended for the treatment of gonorrhoea.

D Doxycycline

Increasing resistance to tetracyclines has been found in Gonococcus infection, which precludes the use of doxycycline here.

E Erythromycin

Macrolides are generally used as second-line therapy in the treatment of gonococcal arthritis where patients cannot tolerate a cephalosporin.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old sheep farmer comes to the Hepatology Clinic complaining of dull right upper quadrant pain and intermittent shortness of breath which has steadily worsened over the past 3-6 months. He has no past medical history of note, takes no regular medication, and is usually well.

On examination, his blood pressure is 125/82 mmHg, with pulse 67/min and regular. Breath sounds are slightly reduced at the right lung base on auscultation. Abdomen is soft, and he is mildly tender in the right upper quadrant with two finger-breadth hepatomegaly.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.9 x 10 9/l (elevated eosinophils)4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)212 x 10 9/l150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/h (ESR)1 - 20 mm/h
