Maraviroc is a CCR5 inhibitor (entry inhibitor). It is only effective in people infected with CCR5 trophic HIV (ie not CXCR4) and therefore testing is required prior to its use. Insulin resistance and lipoatrophy are not commonly associated with maraviroc use.

E Abacavir

Abacavir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). It is recommended by the British HIV Association (BHIVA) in association with lamivudine as an alternative to Truvada as part of a HAART regime. Abacavir cannot be used in patients who are HLA-B5701 positive due to a high risk of hypersensitivity. Abacavir may be associated with insulin resistance and lipodystrophy, but to a lesser extent that zidovudine. 20626

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a fever, shortness of breath, muscle aches, and vague right upper quadrant tenderness. He just returned from a family holiday to a farm in Switzerland. He is normally well and takes no regular medications. His temperature is 39.6 oC, his blood pressure (BP) is 118/80 mmHg, and his pulse is 106 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is occasional wheeze on auscultation of the chest.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)149 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)243 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.4 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)112 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)145 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)1231 U/L29 - 33 U/L

Which of the following best describes the likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gram-negative intracellular coccobacilli

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii (C burnetii). C burnetii is a strictly intracellular, gram-negative coccobacilli. Many species of mammals, birds, and ticks are reservoirs of C. burnetii, and as a consequence outbreaks are seen on farms and areas where animals are processed. A most recent outbreak was seen on farms in Switzerland and France. Outbreaks in Europe often manifest with symptoms of hepatitis, which fits with the marked elevation in transaminases seen here. Doxycycline is the initial intervention of choice.

D Gram-positive extracellular coccus

Streptococci and staphylococci are examples of gram-positive extracellular cocci. The clinical picture seen here with signs and symptoms of infective hepatitis in a person who has visited a farm is much more consistent with an atypical infection such as Q fever.

B Gram-negative extracellular rod

Escherichia coli (E coli) are an example of gram-negative extracellular rod-shaped bacteria which are a cause of gastroenteritis, particularly traveller’s diarrhoea, and a common cause of urinary tract infection.

C Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus

Neisseria is an example of gram-negative intracellular diplococci. There are a number of pathogenic Neisseria including gonorrhoea, which is responsible for gonorrhoea infection, and meningitis which is responsible for meningitis/Neisseria related septicaemia.

E Gram-positive extracellular rod

The Bacillus species are a good example of gram-positive extracellular rod-shaped bacteria. Examples include Bacillus cereus (B cereus) which causes food poisoning, particularly with respect to re-heated rice, and Bacillus anthracis, the cause of anthrax. B cereus requires supportive therapy only, with symptoms usually settling within 24 hours.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old man presents complaining of a 4-week history of joint pain since returning from his holiday in Spain with a group of male friends. He has noticed stiffness and pain in his fingers and hands, and pain in his lower back. A couple of weeks previously he had also noticed stinging when passing urine, although this has now improved a lot. His mother has commented on how red his eyes look. He has no past medical history but is concerned as his uncle has ankylosing spondylitis.

On examination, there is no swelling of the joints of the hand but there is some clear discomfort on movement. Flexion and extension of the spine is also limited by pain and there is tenderness over the sacroiliac joint. There are no skin rashes but he his eyes are shown below.

Which test will be most useful in making the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Urethral swab for microscopy

The symptoms (arthralgia, urethritis and conjunctivitis) are classical of sexually acquired reactive arthritis (SARA) with symptoms developing within 30 days of unprotected sexual intercourse and a mean lag of 14 days between the symptoms of urethritis and the joint symptoms. If the patient is found to have >5 polymorphonuclear cells/high-powered field then that will give the diagnosis. Associated conjunctivitis is a common association, more rarely, iritis can occur.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cropped_CHK0386.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cropped_CHK0386.jpg)

A Urinalysis

This would be the correct answer if urinary tract infection was the right diagnosis. However, this is very unlikely given the patient is a young man, and also would not explain joint pain and conjunctivitis.

B Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing

This option suggests a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis. Ankylosing spondylitis is a possibility but should not cause dysuria. However, even if typing reveals human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27, that will in no way prove ankylosing spondylitis as imaging of the sacroiliac joints and a close history would be far more helpful in establishing that diagnosis.

C Rheumatoid factor

It would be helpful in establishing a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. While rheumatoid arthritis can cause joint pain and eye symptoms, the absence of any joint swelling, erythema or tenderness on examination, as well as stiffness in the history, makes this unlikely. His demographics and the presence of dysuria further make this an unlikely diagnosis.

E X-ray of the sacroiliac joint

This would be the most appropriate investigation to establish ankylosing spondylitis and would have been the correct answer if the history did not have dysuria and there was stiffness of his back.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of malaise and arthralgia, and a non-itchy red rash all over his body, particularly his lower legs. Two days before he presented, his right knee became increasingly red, swollen and painful with extreme limitation of movement. He had no other past medical history.

On examination he had a temperature of 38.5 °C, and pulse rate was 105 bpm. He had an erythematous maculopapular rash formed of small (< 5 mm) lesions in the distribution mentioned above. His right knee was swollen, erythematous and exquisitely painful with a large effusion. On examination of the other joints, there was some evidence of tenosynovitis at the wrists.

His right knee joint was aspirated and a turbid yellow fluid was removed.

What is most likely to be seen on microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A High numbers of neutrophils

This patient clearly has a septic arthritis of the right knee. The history is classic for gonococcal septic arthritis, with malaise caused by disseminated gonococcal infection and a triad of tenosynovitis, arthritis and dermatitis. This is followed by a localised phase where the arthritis can either resolve spontaneously (as in 40–60% of cases) or develop into a septic arthritis. However, organisms are seen in the joint aspirate in less than 25% of cases: it is far more common simply to find turbid fluid and a large number of neutrophils. The aspirate and blood should be cultured. Clearly, intravenous antibiotics are needed for this degree of sepsis and joint involvement. There is significant resistance of gonorrhoea to penicillin and ciprofloxacin, and therefore ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice. Examination of the joint and wash-out under anaesthetic is also indicated.

D Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals

Acute gout can cause a hot, swollen joint and fever; however, given this patient’s age and lack of comorbidities, gout is an unlikely diagnosis. Furthermore, gout does not explain the prodromal rash, or the tenosynovitis evident in the patient’s wrists. Instead, this is a classical history for gonococcal septic arthritis. There is a bacteraemic phase with a triad of arthritis, tenosynovitis and dermatitis. This is followed by a localised phase where the patient can develop a septic arthritis, as seen here. Organisms are only seen in 25% of joint aspirates in gonococcal septic arthritis, and therefore the most likely finding in the aspirate is high numbers of neutrophils.

B Gram-negative diplococcic

You may have identified that this patient has a history consistent with gonococcal septic arthritis: however, organisms are seen in joint aspirates in less than 25% of cases and it is far more likely that the aspirate will be turbid and reveal neutrophils alone. The malaise and triad of tenosynovitis, arthritis and dermatitis (as seen in

this patient) is caused by a bacteraemic phase. There is then a localised phase where either the arthritis resolves spontaneously or patients develop a septic arthritis, as seen here.

C Gram-positive cocci

This patient has a septic arthritis, and his prodrome of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and arthritis is typical of disseminated gonococcal infection, with a bacteraemic and then a localised phase. Gonococcus is a Gram- negative diplococcus; however, organisms are only seen on microscopy of joint aspirates in 25% of cases. It is far more common for the aspirate to simply show high numbers of neutrophils.

E Positively birefringent rhomboidal-shaped crystals

Pseudo-gout can cause a hot and swollen joint, and sometimes a fever. However, given this patient’s age and lack of comorbidities, it is an unlikely diagnosis and the patient should be assumed to have septic arthritis until proven otherwise. In fact, this patient’s history is classic for gonococcal arthritis: a bacteraemic phase with a triad of arthritis, tenosynovitis and dermatitis, and then a localised phase in which patients can develop a septic arthritis. Organisms are seen in the joint aspirate in only 25% of cases, and therefore the most likely finding on microscopy is high numbers of neutrophils.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with some crusted vesicles on the back of his left hand and enlarged lymph nodes in the left axilla. He says he has had a fever and felt off-colour over the past few days. A cat scratched his hand the weekend prior.

What is the most likely causative agent responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bartonella henselae (B henselae)

This patient has cat scratch fever. Lesions occur 3-12 days after an initial scratch from a cat (often one infested with fleas or a kitten) and are accompanied by a non-specific illness and axillary lymphadenopathy. B henselae is an intracellular bacterium that infects red blood cells and is the cause of cat scratch fever. No treatment is usually required, although azithromycin can be used for patients with marked lymphadenopathy.

E Streptococcus gallolyticus (S gallolyticus)

S gallolyticus (formerly known as Streptococcus bovis) is a cause of bacterial endocarditis and is often associated with either a colonic malignancy or with abnormalities of the biliary tree. When it is identified as a cause of endocarditis it should prompt imaging of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract to rule out malignancy.

B Clostridium perfringens (C perfringens)

C perfringens is the cause of gas gangrene, where bacterial infection leads to subcutaneous emphysema and rapidly spreading infection. It is a surgical emergency which requires debridement of necrotic tissue as well as antibiotic therapy. Clindamycin, metronidazole, and rifampicin are potential interventions.

C Pasteurella multocida (P multocida)

P multocida is a cause of cellulitis at the sites of injury in patients with both dog and cat bites. It contrasts to the picture here, where there are very limited local lesions and distant lymphadenopathy. Animal bites are usually managed with co-amoxiclav specifically to cover against Pasteurella infection.

D Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus)

Staphylococcal infection is associated with marked local cellulitis in contrast to the relatively minor local symptoms seen here. Flucloxacillin is the intervention of choice for staphylococcal cellulitis, with a macrolide such as clarithromycin the alternative option in patients with penicillin allergy.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of productive cough, weight loss and night sweats. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is on long-term corticosteroid therapy for autoimmune disease. On examination, he is febrile and has coarse crackles in the right upper lung field. A CXR reveals a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. Sputum Gram staining shows filamentous, branching and Gram-positive rods.

What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis of nocardiosis?
options: Sputum culture on standard bacterial media
Blood culture for aerobic and anaerobic organisms
Biopsy of the affected lung tissue
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Acid-fast staining of sputum samples

Nocardia species are partially acid-fast due to the mycolic acids in their cell walls. Acid-fast staining (using a modified Ziehl–Neelsen method) is a critical diagnostic test. Positive results, along with branching Gram- positive rods on Gram staining, strongly suggest Nocardia infection.

D Biopsy of the affected lung tissue

Lung biopsy may be considered in cases where sputum samples fail to provide a diagnosis. However, it is invasive and not the first-line investigation when sputum samples can provide the necessary information.

B Sputum culture on standard bacterial media

While Nocardia can grow on standard bacterial media, prolonged incubation (up to two weeks) is required for colonies to become visible. Culture is an important diagnostic tool, but acid-fast staining provides more rapid results.

C Blood culture for aerobic and anaerobic organisms

Blood cultures are less sensitive for diagnosing nocardiosis, as it is primarily a localised infection in the lungs, brain or skin, with haematogenous spread occurring only in severe cases.

E Fungal culture of sputum samples

Fungal culture is not appropriate for diagnosing Nocardia, which is a bacterial organism. Fungal cultures target organisms such as Aspergillus or Histoplasma, and would not detect Nocardia.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man returns from a significant period abroad working abroad for a bank in Barbados. He complains of chronic diarrhoea over the past few months with associated weight loss, fatigue, and now lower limb oedema.

Examination reveals pallor, stomatitis and glossitis. His BMI is only 20 and he admits to having lost 6 kg in weight in 2 months.

Investigations reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Blood count and filmMegaloblastic anaemia
Albumin24 g/L35 - 55 g/L
D-xylose malabsorption testPositive
Faecal fat excretion8.5 g / 24 h< 7 g / 24h
Anti-endomysial antibodiesNegative

Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Tropical sprue

First described by William Hillary in an account of medical observations of Barbados, this disease is most common in the Caribbean and the Far East. It is characterised by a picture of small intestinal malabsorption and the cause is thought to be infectious in origin. Jejunal biopsy reveals mild villous atrophy, increased villous crypts and mononuclear cellular infiltrates, enlarged epithelial cells, and large nuclei caused by folate and/or vitamin B12 deficiency. Tetracyclines or ampicillin are treatments of choice; prolonged therapy for 6 months or more may be required. Folate and B12 deficiencies should also be corrected: folic acid with oral replacement and B12 with intramuscular injection. Complete recovery is possible with appropriate therapy.

D Giardiasis

Giardiasis can result in a malabsorption type picture, but the symptom picture is similar to intermittent irritable bowel syndrome after an acute diarrhoeal illness, rather than the marked faecal fat loss seen here.

A Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is the alternative possible diagnosis, although negative anti-endomysial antibodies are possible in coeliac patients with selective IgA deficiency, given the history of travel to Barbados, tropical sprue is more likely.

B Helicobacter pylori infection

Helicobacter pylori infection is a cause of peptic ulcer disease rather than small bowel malabsorption syndromes.

E HIV enteropathy

HIV enteropathy may present with the symptoms of malabsorption seen here and could be considered a differential, although we are not provided with any pointers in the scenario towards possible HIV infection.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-week history of malaise, fever, abdominal pain and reduced appetite, with associated weight loss. She also reported nausea and vomiting. Although she suffered from diarrhoea at the beginning of the illness, this seems to have settled now. She did not have any respiratory symptoms. One month previously, she had noticed a rash on the front of her shins associated with lumps in her groin area, which had settled but which had been followed by the onset of her current symptoms. She took a picture of her shin at the time, which is shown below.

On examination, her temperature was 37.1 °C. Her abdomen was generally tender, especially in the right lower quadrant. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. There were several small ulcers on her pharynx. There were no rashes, and she had a BCG scar on her upper arm.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)202 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.6 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Bilirubin9.0 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)19 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)61 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Yersinia enterocolitica infection

The patient has mesenteric adenitis, characterised by fever, abdominal pain and tenderness of the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. In association, the patient may also experience nausea, vomiting and aphthous ulcers of the mouth, all of which are present in this case. The symptoms may be preceded by the appearance of erythema nodosum – painful, raised red/purple lesion on the front of the shin – which is the fleeting rash described by the patient in this case. Yersinia enterocolitica can also cause a reactive asymmetrical polyarthritis, enteritis, uveitis, appendicitis, and glomerulonephritis amongst other complications.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Erythema_Nodosum.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Erythema_Nodosum.jpg)

C Salmonella infection

This patient does not have diarrhoea, which would be unusual in Salmonella infection; furthermore, she has had symptoms for several weeks, whereas Salmonella typically causes acute symptoms. This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with mesenteric adenitis, and also erythema nodosum and mouth ulcers. This history would be consistent with Yersinia enterocolitica infection, which can also cause polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications.

A Campylobacter infection

Campylobacter typically causes a bloody diarrhoea; it would be unusual to have an infection without diarrhoea. It is also usually an acute illness, whereas this patient has three weeks of symptoms. This patient’s fever, abdominal pain (particularly in the right lower quadrant) and lack of diarrhoea, combined with the preceding rash of erythema nodosum, and then mouth ulcers, are suggestive of Yersinia enterocolitica infection. It causes a mesenteric adenitis, which accounts for her abdominal symptoms, and can also cause mouth ulcers, polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications.

B Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection

This patient has had BCG vaccination (which does not rule out tuberculosis, but does reduce her risk). She also has a normal chest X-ray, which would be unusual in the context of tuberculosis. She does have a history and signs consistent with mesenteric adenitis and erythema nodosum (both of which can be caused by tuberculosis) – the right lower quadrant tenderness, vague history of malaise, abdominal pain and nausea without diarrhoea – and she also has mouth ulcers. This history would fit with Yersinia enterocolitica infection, which can also cause polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications.

D Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis does cause erythema nodosum, as described here. However, typically sarcoidosis would cause breathless and a dry cough, with an abnormal chest X-ray, but this patient has no respiratory symptoms or signs. In addition, she has a history and examination consistent with mesenteric adenitis; sarcoidosis would be very unlikely to cause this. A more likely diagnosis would be Yersinia enterocolitica infection, which would explain the mesenteric adenitis, the mouth ulcers and the erythema nodosum; it can also cause polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea since returning from a holiday to India one week ago. He reports > 10 bowel motions a day. Before this, he has been well, with no past medical history.

On examination, he is afebrile. His eyes are sunken and he has reduced skin turgor. He has a heart rate of 130 bpm and blood pressure of 98/52 mmHg. On auscultation, his chest is clear and his heart sounds are normal. He is saturating well on room air. There is generalised discomfort on palpation of his abdomen, but no guarding or masses.

Which of the following is the most common complication, given the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Acute tubular necrosis

This patient has a history of profuse diarrhoea following a trip to India. Clinical examination findings indicate severe dehydration with sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor and hypotension. The history and examination together suggest a diagnosis of cholera caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Cholera is associated with poor sanitation and drinking contaminated water. The mainstay of treatment is aggressive fluid resuscitation to prevent circulatory collapse, along with antibiotic treatment. Tetracyclines, such as doxycycline and ciprofloxacin, are both antibiotics of choice. There are a number of complications of the disease, including circulatory collapse, acute renal failure, sepsis, severe hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Acute tubular necrosis due to V. cholerae infection leads to acute renal failure and may require treatment with dialysis, although this frequently occurs where facilities are not available.

A Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS)

Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is a complication of Campylobacter jejuni infection, which leads to ascending paralysis that often requires Intensive Care support. Campylobacter infection is the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the United Kingdom. For V. cholerae infection, GBS is not a common complication.

B Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)

Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a complication associated with Escherichia coli infection. It consists of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and kidney failure. It is usually associated with infection with the E. coli strain O157:H7. Given this man’s presentation with profuse watery diarrhoea following a holiday in India, the most likely diagnosis here is V. cholerae infection, the most common complication of which is acute renal failure.

D Small bowel perforation

Small bowel perforation is a complication of V. cholerae infection. However, this is less common than acute renal failure due to acute tubular necrosis.

E Toxic megacolon

Toxic megacolon is a complication associated with diarrhoeal diseases such as Clostridium difficile infection and amoebiasis. Although bowel complications can rarely arise due to V. cholerae infection, it is more likely to cause small bowel obstruction, ileus or perforation, rather than toxic megacolon.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman who received a cadaveric renal transplant two years ago comes to the Emergency Department complaining of watery diarrhoea that began three days ago. She has just returned from a holiday to Tunisia. Medication includes immunosuppression and ramipril for control of blood pressure.

On examination, her temperature is 38.4 °C, her BP is 120/68 mmHg with a 20 mmHg postural drop and her heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. She looks dehydrated and has a soft, diffusely tender abdomen.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)185 µmol/L 50–120 µmol/L (142 µmol/L at the last clinic visit)
Stool sampleOocysts (4-6 µm) identified, stained Red with modified ZN stain

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts only
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Supportive therapy and oral nitazoxanide

This woman almost certainly has Cryptosporidium acquired through the water supply at her Tunisian hotel. Given that she is significantly dehydrated, as evidenced by her postural drop and elevated creatinine, it is appropriate to treat her with anti-microbial therapy.

Patients with immunocompromising conditions other than HIV (eg, those who have undergone solid organ transplant) have also been reported to have refractory cryptosporidiosis. For such patients, the dose of immunosuppressive therapy should be reduced, if possible, and antimicrobial therapy should be started. Nitazoxanide (500 to1000 mg twice daily) interferes with the ability of the parasite to generate energy, by blocking the pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase reaction. Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts is of course also an essential part of therapy.

C Supportive therapy and oral loperamide

Given that this patient has significant dehydration associated with diarrhoea, supportive therapy is an important aspect of treatment. However, the history is suggestive of an underlying infectious aetiology and in this context loperamide would be contraindicated.

A Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts only

This patient’s clinical presentation and stool microscopy results are highly suggestive of Cryptosporidium. Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts is an important part of her treatment; however, in the context of immunosuppression and significant dehydration, antimicrobial treatment would also be indicated.

B Supportive therapy and oral ciprofloxacin

This patient’s presentation is suggestive of Cryptosporidium diarrhoea. Supportive therapy is important, but ciprofloxacin is not a recognised treatment. Furthermore quinolone use should be avoided wherever an effective alternative is available due to risk of debilitating side effects.

E Supportive therapy and oral metronidazole

This patient’s presentation is suggestive of Cryptosporidium diarrhoea. Supportive therapy is important, but metronidazole is not an effective treatment.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe, unremitting headache and muscle aches after recently returning from a business trip to the northern Philippines. He has been suffering from drenching fevers and sweats for five days since returning and tells you a rash started around two days into his illness. On examination, there is a maculopapular rash, conjunctival and pharyngeal injection, as well as lymphadenopathy affecting the neck lymph nodes. He has a fever of 39.5 °C.

Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Paracetamol

The most likely diagnosis is dengue fever, which is endemic throughout the Philippines. Dengue fever is caused by infection with one of four subtypes of the dengue virus and was first described in Chinese writings as early as AD 265. It typically produces severe fever, headache, rash and arthralgia, and in many cases, it is a self- limiting illness that lasts 5–7 days. The fever may only disappear for one day and then reappear, the so-called ‘saddleback’ pattern. A more severe form – dengue haemorrhagic fever – occasionally presents and requires more intensive supportive therapy, including correction of clotting abnormalities. As in this case, uncomplicated dengue should be managed with IV fluid rehydration and paracetamol for pain relief and as an antipyretic.

D Oral quinine

Oral quinine is a treatment option for malaria. The risk of malaria, except on Palawan and Mindanao Islands, is low and almost non-existent in urban areas. The description of a maculopapular rash in the setting of muscle aches is more in keeping with dengue, which is endemic in the Philippines, rather than malaria.

A A thick and thin film

The risk of malaria, except on Palawan and Mindanao Islands, is low and almost non-existent in urban areas. The description of a maculopapular rash in the setting of muscle aches is more in keeping with dengue, which is endemic in the Philippines, rather than malaria. Thick and thin films, the standard investigation that can help identify malaria and the species involved, are therefore not required.

B IV broad-spectrum antibiotics

Although this patient has a fever, there is no evidence of a source of a bacterial infection. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are therefore not indicated.

C IV quinine

IV quinine can be used as a ‘loading dose’ in severe malaria. Severe malaria is characterised by the presence of Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia, impaired consciousness, generalised weakness, seizures, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia and acute renal failure. As these features are not present, IV quinine is, therefore, not indicated.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) comes to the Emergency Department for review. He felt something ‘go’ at the base of his left ankle, and he is now unable to weight bear or to move his foot up and down. He is currently suffering from an exacerbation of his COPD and has been prescribed prednisolone and ofloxacin by an Emergency General Practitioner (EGP). His other medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, and ramipril for hypertension and ischaemic cardiovascular disease. Examination of his left lower limb reveals a ruptured Achilles tendon.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of his ruptured Achilles tendon?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ofloxacin

Ofloxacin has been recognised in rare cases to cause tendon rupture, and the case rate may be further increased when prednisolone is also prescribed. Other problems with quinolone use can include arthralgia, pain in the extremities, gait disturbance, neuropathies associated with paraesthesia, depression, fatigue, memory impairment, sleep disorders, and impaired hearing, vision, taste, and smell. For these reasons, routine use of the class is no longer recommended, and the Common Safety Method (CSM) issued a warning to this effect in 2019.

D Prednisolone

Prednisolone use doesn’t lead to tendon rupture per se and is an essential component of the armamentarium to manage acute exacerbation of COPD. It is associated with increased insulin resistance, which may precipitate worsening of glycaemic control in patients who take it. In patients taking quinolones, it may further increase the risk of tendon rupture.

A Aspirin

Aspirin may increase the chance of traumatic bruising, but it is not associated with an increased risk of tendon rupture. Specifically, quinolones are not advised to be used in the management of bacterial infections unless no other options are available.

B Atorvastatin

Atorvastatin is associated with myositis, rather than with tendon rupture. Myositis is more likely to occur with drug-drug interactions which increase systemic exposure to statins. As atorvastatin is metabolised by the Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) system, potent inhibitors of 3A4 such as macrolide antibiotics may drive

accumulation of statins. In patients taking these in combination with a background of atorvastatin or simvastatin, the dose of statin should be temporarily reduced or stopped.

E Ramipril

The major concerns associated with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor use are significant worsening of renal function in patients who have a background of renovascular disease and angioedema. It is important to note that episodes of angioedema related to ACE inhibitor use may be seen many months after starting therapy, and do not necessarily need to be seen close to therapy initiation.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old Eastern European man is identified at an asylum assessment centre as suffering from persistent cough. On questioning, he admits to fever, night sweats and weight loss which have continued for nearly a year. Occasionally, his sputum has been blood-stained.

Past medical history includes smoking unfiltered cigarettes for the past 20 years. On examination, his body mass index is noted to be 17; he is pyrexial at 37.9°C. On examination, there is non-specific wheeze and occasional crackles.

Which of the following would be the most appropriate initial investigation in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Chest X-ray

This history is highly suspicious for either pulmonary tuberculosis or underlying bronchial carcinoma. The most appropriate initial investigation therefore would be a chest X-ray to look for calcified nodules or hilar lymph node calcification in primary infection, or fibrosis and cavitation in the case of reactivation of the tubercle.

E Mycobacterium serology

Mycobacterium serology is not suggested as first-line investigation. T-spot testing can be used to help aid diagnosis.

A Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax

Chest X-ray should be able to demonstrate pathological apical findings and a CT is seldom necessary. However, if a chest X-ray is normal then a CT can be helpful in finding further lesions.

B Bronchoscopy with induced sputum

First attempts should be to use sputum samples to test for acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, with confirmation by growth. If no sputum can be obtained by coughing, then sputum should be induced.

D HIV testing

Clearly HIV positivity may increase the risk of tuberculosis, and testing should be considered later.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old woman presented with a history of an abrupt onset of high fever, headache, cough and abdominal pain. About 2 days later, she developed a maculopapular rash that began on the extremities and there was associated swelling of the hands and feet. She works as a kindergarten teacher.

She has no past medical history that she is aware of, but is unsure of her vaccination history as her parents divorced when she was young and there may have been missed vaccinations during the divorce proceedings. She denies any IV drug use and does not take any regular tablets. She a tattoo on her right ankle that she had done 3 months ago while on holiday in the USA. Apart from that trip, during which she was camping with friends, she has not had any other journeys outside of the UK.

On examination, there is a rash as described affecting the hands and feet, but no other lesions. Her chest is clear on auscultation and she has no meningisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Atypical measles syndrome

Atypical measles syndrome (AMS) occurs in persons who were incompletely immunised against measles. This may occur either because they were given the old killed-virus measles vaccine (no longer available) or they were given the attenuated (weakened) live measles vaccine which had been inactivated due to improper storage. The latter does not prevent measles but causes an alteration in its expression, resulting in AMS. The presentation of the patient above is typical of AMS: fever, headache, cough, headache and abdominal pain followed by a rash with oedema of hands and feet 1–2 days afterwards. Key to the diagnosis is also an immunisation history suggestive of incomplete immunity and contact with children, who are more likely to have measles. Virus isolation, serological studies, or both, may be necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

D Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis is caused by Leptospira interrogans and is spread via rat urine. Contact can occur with activities associated with exposure to water, such as canoeing, cycling through puddles or swimming outdoors. Following an incubation period of 20 days there is fever, myalgia, chest pain and there can be haemoptysis. There is no clear exposure within the range of the incubation period and this would not explain her rash, abdominal pain or oedema.

A Rocky Mountain spotted fever

This condition is caused by infection with Rickettsiae rickettsii, a tick-borne pathogen endemic to the Rocky Mountains and the south-eastern USA, after an incubation period of days to up to 2 weeks. There is typically headache, high fever and muscle ache with abdominal ache and vomiting. This is followed by a macular rash of the hands and feet 2–5 days later which can then spread and become haemorrhagic. While the clinical description is similar, the fact that the trip was 3 months ago to a possible endemic area makes this diagnosis very unlikely.

C Atypical pneumonia

While she has a cough, fever and systemic symptoms, her hand and foot oedema, clear chest and abdominal pain make this a less likely diagnosis. Rashes with atypical pneumonia can occur, such as erythema multiforme.

E Meningococcal meningitis

While the patient does have a headache, fever and rash, it is not in keeping with a description of meningism such as neck stiffness and photophobia and the rash is not petechial or non-blanching. Being in contact with children would increase the risk of meningitis.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man who has recently returned from a trip to Africa attends the clinic because he is feeling unwell. You understand that he had been swimming in a local river each day, while helping out on a school building project. After swimming, he noticed an itchy rash on his skin. Around a week later, he returned to the UK. Another 4 weeks passed, and symptoms of a viral illness have now developed including fever, myalgia, headache and lethargy. He is pyrexial 38.5 °C.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)119 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.0 ×10⁹/L, increased eosinophil count4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)290 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)62 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)General increase in vascular and interstitial markings—
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)46 mm/hour<10 mm/hour

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Praziquantel

This man has Katayama fever, which has developed some 4-6 weeks after infection with Schistosomes. It is usually caused by either schistosoma japonicum or mansonii infection. The high egg and worm antigen load is thought to lead to a serum sickness type syndrome. Management involves treatment with Praziquantel, an anti-

heminthic agent which leads to a cure in around 85% of patients. In those who are not cured, the egg load is normally markedly reduced.

A Quinine sulphate

This would be a possible treatment for malaria. Malaria might have been suggested as a possible diagnosis by travelling to Africa and returning with a fever and malaise, but the history of an itchy rash following swimming makes this a less likely diagnosis. Also, the absence of jaundice makes this a less likely diagnosis.

B Paracetamol

This would be part of supportive management if a diagnosis such as dengue fever was suspected. Whilst dengue could explain the myalgia, headache and fever, the incubation period is too long.

D Primaquine

This is a treatment option for malaria making it an incorrect choice.

E Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin could be used as treatment for various bacterial infections but is no longer recommended as first line if other options are available due to a small but significant risk of permanent or long lasting debilitating side effects. The history of fever in the returning traveller is unlikely to warrant ciprofloxacin as treatment.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man was admitted after a motorcycle accident in which he suffered extensive soft tissue injury to his right lower leg.

Prior to the accident, he had been fit and well. He was reviewed on the ward 5 days later and was complaining of thoracic back pain.

On examination, his temperature was 37.8 °C. He was tender over the T8 vertebra.

Investigations:

InvestigationResult
X-ray whole spineNormal
MRI whole spine (T2)High signal in disc space; high signal in adjacent endplates, signifying bone marrow oedema: likely discitis

Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible for his back pain?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Staphylococcus aureus

This patient has symptoms and signs of discitis, which is confirmed on MRI. It is common for X-rays to appear normal in the early stages of disease. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of discitis in immunocompetent patients and patients who do not use intravenous drugs. Given this patient’s extensive soft tissue injury, it is especially likely that Staph. aureus was able to enter his bloodstream and cause his discitis. He should have multiple sets of blood cultures to confirm the organism and its sensitivities. Sometimes needle aspiration of the disc space under imaging guidance is required for identification. Once the organism and sensitivities are confirmed, he should be treated with 6–8 weeks of intravenous antibiotics.

D Staphylococcus epidermidis

This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with infective discitis. It is common for X-rays to appear normal in the early stages of the disease. Staph. epidermidis is a common skin commensal and can be a cause of infective discitis, especially in a trauma setting, as seen here. However, it is not the most common cause, and therefore is not the most likely. Staphylococcus aureus would be a much more common cause of infective discitis in an immunocompetent individual, especially given the patient’s extensive soft tissue injury.

A Clostridium perfringens

Cl. perfringens causes gastroenteritis and gas gangrene, but would be a very uncommon cause of discitis. This patient has thoracic back pain and MRI findings consistent with infective discitis. It is common for the X-ray to appear normal in the early stages. The most likely causative organism, given his extensive soft tissue injury, is Staphylococcus aureus. This is the most common cause of discitis in the immunocompetent.

B Mycobacterium tuberculosis

This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with infective discitis. It is common for the X-ray to appear normal in the early stages of infection. Tuberculosis is an important cause of discitis and spinal abscesses (also known as Pott’s disease), but this patient was well before his accident with no symptoms of tuberculosis. He is not immunocompromised. The most common causative organism in discitis is Staphylococcus aureus: given his extensive soft tissue injury, this is particularly likely to be the causative organism in this case.

E Viridans streptococci

This patient has symptoms and signs of infective discitis, which is confirmed on MRI: it is common for X-rays to appear normal in the early stages of the disease. Viridans streptococci are a relatively common cause of infective discitis in intravenous drug users or the immunocompromised: however, this patient is neither. The most common cause of infective discitis in the immunocompetent is Staphylococcus aureus, and this is made more likely by the patient’s extensive soft tissue injury. 21558

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He complains of a rash on the left upper chest and has trouble with extensive papillary warts. He admits to weight loss of 2 stone over the course of the past year. He admits to having had a number of sexual partners and has regularly had unprotected sex.

On examination, he has erythematous blistering rash in a dermatomal distribution, extensive papillary warts and other lesions, pictured below. He is emaciated and there is evidence of cervical lymphadenopathy.

Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A HIV infection

With this picture of weight loss, extensive papillary warts, the pictured pink macular lesions which may be Kaposi’s sarcoma and herpes zoster infection, confirmatory HIV antibody testing is recommended, and measurement of CD4+ lymphocyte levels is useful in assessing risk of opportunistic infections. The overlying picture is that of several opportunistic infections without a known cause. Aciclovir is the treatment of choice for herpes zoster infection, and a number of topical treatments for viral warts are available. Retinoid gels may be of value in the management of Kaposi’s sarcoma.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kaposi%27s_sarcoma_lesion.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kaposi%27s_sarcoma_lesion.jpg)

C Hodgkin’s lymphoma

Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a malignant disease of lymphatic system with multinucleated giant (Reed–Sternberg) cells. Presentation usually occurs in early adulthood, and again is insidious with asymptomatic lymph node enlargement, weight loss, night sweats and unexplained fever. Some patients have chest symptoms and alcohol-induced pain. This patient does not have night sweats or fever, and Hodgkin’s lymphoma would not explain the presence of multiple opportunistic infections.

B Chronic myeloid leukaemia

Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder affecting one or all cell lines. Progression is characterised into a chronic phase, an accelerated phase, and finally blast crisis. Most patients present in the chronic phase with insidious symptoms of fatigue, weight loss and night sweats. Examination can reveal features of cell line disruption such as anaemia and bruising, but while lymphoadenopathy can occur it is not a major feature. It is not associated with immunodeficiency and would therefore not explain this patient’s infections, and the age of presentation of CML is usually around 65 years old.

D Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia

Acute lymphoblastic lymphoma (ALL) is incorrect. ALL is a malignant transformation of lymphoid progenitor cells which replace normal bone marrow and blasts, eventually spilling into circulation. It is primarily a childhood disease, mostly occurring before the age of 6 years. It is associated with fatigue and malaise leading to bone marrow failure, and can cause bone pain, recurrent and severe infections and unexplained fevers, among other symptoms. This diagnosis could explain the immunosuppression in this patient, as well as lymphadenopathy and weight loss; however, the age of the patient, as well as the absence of features of other cell line disruption, make this diagnosis less likely.

E Herpes zoster infection

Herpes zoster is an opportunistic infection in this patient, and while it is most likely present, it would not explain his general symptoms.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of severe, worsening headache, vomiting and double vision. He was HIV-positive and had refused antiretroviral treatment or prophylactic medications. He has a CD4 count of 120 ×10⁶/L (normal range 300–1400).

On examination, his temperature was 37.5°C. There was a right-sided facial nerve palsy.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
CD4 +120 ×10⁶/L430 - 1690 ×10⁶/L
CT headTwo large ring-enhancing lesions, with midline shift


Based on the likeliest diagnosis, what treatment should be started?
options: Sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine, plus folinic acid
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine, plus folinic acid

This patient has untreated HIV and, as such, is extremely vulnerable to opportunistic infection. One such infection is toxoplasmosis, which can infect the CNS causing focal neurology due to mass lesions, visible on imaging as ring-enhancing lesions. Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection contracted from infected raw meat or from handling cat faeces or soil contaminated with cat faeces. First-line therapy is with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid. The patient should also probably receive dexamethasone given the presence of midline shift.

C Ceftazidime

Because this patient has untreated HIV, he is severely immunocompromised and vulnerable to opportunistic infection. In this case he has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis: focal neurology with signs of raised intracranial pressure, and ring-enhancing lesions on brain imaging. As toxoplasmosis is caused by a parasite, antibiotics such as ceftazidime will not be an effective treatment. The correct therapy would be sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid.

A Aciclovir

This patient has untreated HIV and is severely immunocompromised. As a result he has contracted cerebral toxoplasmosis, as evidenced by the focal neurological signs and ring-enhancing lesions on CT head. An antiviral such as aciclovir will not treat cerebral toxoplasmosis, as this is caused by a parasite. The correct

treatment is sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid.

B Amphotericin

This patient has untreated HIV, and consequently he is severely immunocompromised. This renders him vulnerable to opportunistic infection: in this case, he has contracted cerebral toxoplasmosis. This causes focal neurological signs and is visible as ring-enhancing lesions on CT or MRI head. An antifungal such as amphotericin will not treat toxoplasmosis, as this is caused by a parasite. The correct therapy would be sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid.

D Chemotherapy

This patient has untreated HIV; although HIV, and especially poorly controlled disease, is associated with malignancy (particularly with primary CNS lymphoma), the presentation and appearance of this patient’s central nervous system lesions are not quite consistent with cerebral malignancy. The time course is quite rapid for metastases in the brain, and he does not have any other symptoms of primary malignancy elsewhere in the body. Ring-enhancing lesions would be an atypical appearance for primary CNS lymphoma. It is much more likely that this patient, in his immunocompromised state, has contracted cerebral toxoplasmosis. This should be treated with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid.

questions.question:
You are examining the peak and trough concentrations of gentamicin from a 32-year-old man who is treated with a once-a-day dosing regimen. You wish to minimise the nephrotoxicity from the antibiotic.

Where is the most likely site of renal damage due to gentamicin?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Proximal tubule

Aminoglycoside related renal damage occurs predominantly in the proximal tubule. Aminoglycoside molecules bind to anion phospholipids within the plasma membrane of proximal tubular cells. They are taken up and transported by lysosomes to the Golgi body where they effectively act as a mitochondrial poison.

E Vascular endothelium

Vascular endothelial cells are not subject to damage by gentamicin. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) are renoprotective because they inhibit efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Other agents such as Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors are also thought to be renoprotective because they improve microvascular function.

A Collecting duct

Aminoglycosides are not taken up in collecting duct cells. Absorption of water in the collecting duct is governed by aquaporin-2 expression, which is partially under the control of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH). Other biologically active agents which influence aquaporin-2 expression include bile salts. In patients with chronic liver disease, accumulation of bile acids may reduce water excretion and increase the risks of acute kidney injury.

B Distal tubule

Gentamicin impacts on cells in the proximal tubule. Cisplatin is an example of an agent that is toxic for distal tubular epithelial cells. Effects on renal function are generally dose-related, and both aminoaciduria and proteinuria are seen.

C Loop of Henle

The loop of Henle is not the primary site of toxicity for aminoglycosides. The function of the descending loop of Henle is to allow for reabsorption of water. The ascending loop of Henle is where sodium, potassium, and chloride ions are reabsorbed via the Na-K-Cl cotransporter.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting. She had returned from a holiday in Morocco 1 week ago. She has no significant past medical history and she was well while on holiday.

On examination, she is unwell and slightly jaundiced. There is no lymphadenopathy and abdominal examination was normal. Her temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure was 98/56 mmHg, pulse of 110 beats/min and Glasgow Coma score of 15/15.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)69 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)22 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)86 fL76–98 fL
Reticulocyte count160 ×10⁹/L25–100 ×10⁹/L
Blood filmMultiple fragmented red cells
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea21.5 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)350 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin58 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)300 IU/L100–190 IU/L
Aspartate transaminase (AST)38 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)36 IU/L5–30 IU/L

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS)

Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome is characterised by widespread deposition of loose strands of fibrin in multiple small blood vessels, which damage platelets and red blood cells (RBCs), resulting in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombocytopenia. The signs of the disease are: thrombocytopenia, fragmented RBCs on blood film (acanthocytes, shistocytes, burr cells, helmet cell, etc.), fever, kidney disease, central nervous system (CNS) manifestations (confusion, coma) and jaundice (elevated direct and indirect bilirubin). HUS often follows gastroenteritis associated with Shiga-toxin-producing bacteria such as enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7.

B Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis is caused by a thin, spiral-shaped Leptospira bacterium, especially Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae. There may be liver abnormalities with jaundice. Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia is not a usual feature.

A Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura (TTP)

TTP and HUS are part of the same spectrum of microangiopathic disease. Similar to HUS, TTP is characterised by widespread deposition of loose strands of fibrin in multiple small blood vessels, which damage platelets and red blood cells (RBCs), resulting in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombocytopenia. In TTP, manifestation of ischaemic organ damage such as neurological disturbance (confusion and coma) and myocardial damage are characteristically found. TTP is differentiated from HUS by the following points:

Children account for 90% of the cases of HUS, while adults are more frequently affected with TTP. Kidney disease and fever predominates in HUS, while in TTP neurological symptoms are more common. The prognosis is worse in TTP compared with HUS. Treatment is supportive with plasma exchange until the activity of the disease has subsided. Steroids are also beneficial.

C Familial Mediterranean fever

Familial Mediterranean fever is an inherited condition with episodes of inflammation such as peritonitis, pleurisy and arthritis.

E Acute hepatitis B infection

Although acute hepatitis B infection cause acute hepatitis, it doesn’t lead to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. It wouldn’t also account for the acute GI upset and renal impairment seen here.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man is admitted to hospital after being found by his home help in a confused state. He is usually able to care for himself, with help for cooking and cleaning, but on this occasion she found him slumped in a chair complaining of pain in his right knee, and shouting at her to get help. He has a history of gout and drinks four pints of beer per day. It is unclear whether he is compliant with medication for blood pressure. On examination, he is pyrexial (39.1 °C), his blood pressure (BP) is 95/70 mmHg and his pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. The right knee is swollen and erythematous, and he cannot flex it more than 30 degrees.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)16.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)189 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)132 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)225 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Urate8.74 mg/dl3.4 - 7.0 mg/dl (male)
Knee joint asperate-ve birefringent crystals, 350 × 10 9 neutrophils/ml

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Flucloxacillin

Given significant evidence of sepsis, with relative hypotension, tachycardia and marked pyrexia, antibiotic intervention is essential until blood culture results are known. The neutrophil count is outside the normal range and may represent septic arthritis. Although urate crystals are seen in the joint, it is possible for sepsis and gout to co-exist.

D Naproxen

In this situation with a moderate elevation in creatinine, colchicine is potentially preferred as an anti- inflammatory.

A Allopurinol

Even in proven acute gout, allopurinol can worsen symptoms initially and therefore should be avoided during the initial period of therapy.

B Colchicine

This is a first-line option for the treatment of gout, but given the degree of systemic symptoms, sepsis should be ruled out/treated first. It is associated with symptoms of diarrhoea, which means it be poorly tolerated in some patients.

E Prednisolone

This is an option for acute gout, but there are significant signs of sepsis and this should be the assumed initial diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of swelling and pain affecting his lower limbs, worse on the right than on the left. He also felt generally unwell and had had intermittent fevers. He had returned from Sri Lanka 2 days previously, where he had been working as an aid worker in rural areas surrounded by paddy fields. On examination, both legs were swollen with non-pitting oedema to the knee, unchanged by elevation of the legs. There was painful bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin121 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC) 8.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils1.2 ×10⁹/L0.04–0.4 ×10⁹/L
Chest X-rayBilateral pulmonary infiltrates
Ultrasound of the groinBilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with lymphatic obstruction

What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Ivermectin

This patient has filiariasis. He has travelled to an endemic area, surrounded by paddy fields which provide the perfect breeding ground for the parasitic vector (mosquitoes). The parasitic worms block the lymphatics, leading to limb swelling and lymphadenopathy. Filiariasis also explains his general malaise and intermittent fevers, and the marked eosinophilia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. First-line treatment is with diethylcarbamazine (DEC), but if there is any suggestion of a high parasitic load or concomitant onchocerciasis, ivermectin is an appropriate second-line treatment.

D Itraconazole

This patient has filiariasis: this explains his intermittent fevers, leg swelling, painful lymphadenopathy and the findings on chest X-ray and ultrasound. The marked eosinophilia is highly suggestive of a parasitic infection. Filiariasis is caused by tiny parasitic worms which are contracted through vector transmission, by infected

mosquitoes; paddy fields provide perfect breeding grounds for mosquitoes. The nematodes block the lymphatics, which leads to limb swelling and lymphadenopathy. Itraconazole is an antifungal medication, and therefore would not be appropriate to treat this patient. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) would be first line, but should not be used if there is any suggestion of high parasite load or concomitant onchocerciasis. The most appropriate treatment for this patient would be ivermectin.

B Chloroquine

This patient has filiariasis: this is infection with microscopic worms, causing blockage of lymphatics and hence lymphadenopathy and limb swelling. It is contracted through bites from mosquitoes carrying the parasite. This patient has been working near paddy fields: these watery environments provide perfect breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Filiariasis would explain his limb swelling and painful lymphadenopathy; the nematodes can also migrate to the lungs causing bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Finally this patient has a significant eosinophilia – an eosinophilia of this level is most likely to be caused by a significant parasitic infection. Filiariasis can be treated with diethylcarbamazine (DEC), albendazole or ivermectin. Ivermectin is the most appropriate choice if there is any risk of concomitant onchocerciasis. Chloroquine would not be appropriate as it is an antimalarial agent; this patient’s symptoms and signs are not consistent with malaria.

C Ciprofloxacin

This patient’s leg swelling, intermittent fevers, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and significant eosinophilia would be best explained by filiariasis. This is a parasitic worm infection contracted after being bitten by an infected mosquito; rural paddy fields are typical breeding grounds for mosquitos. The filarial nematodes cause blockage of lymphatics, leading to lymphadenopathy and limb swelling. Ciprofloxacin is an antibiotic and will not treat this patient’s parasitic infection. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is first line but should not be used if there is suggestion of a high filarial load or concomitant onchocerciasis. The most appropriate treatment for this patient would be ivermectin.

E Metronidazole

The intermittent fevers, malaise, limb swelling, lymphadenopathy and marked eosinophilia, against the background of this patient’s travel history, suggest filiariasis. This is a parasitic worm transmitted through mosquitoes (for which rural paddy fields provide the perfect breeding ground). The worms block the lymphatics, leading to limb swelling and lymphadenopathy. They can also cause bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. As metronidazole is an antiprotozoal and antibacterial, it is not effective against a parasite such as filarial worms. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is first-line treatment, but should not be used if there is suggestion of a high parasite load or concomitant onchocerciasis: the second-line option of ivermectin would be most appropriate in this case.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 2-week history of a new rash. The rash first appeared on his trunk and then spread to his arms and face. There is no history of itch or bleeding. He denies any recent coryzal symptoms but says he has been feeling generally more fatigued recently. His past medical history includes pneumonia, but he has otherwise been well, with no regular medications or allergies. His vaccination record is up-to-date.

On examination, he is afebrile. His heart rate is 89 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 112/65 mmHg. Chest sounds are clear, with saturations of 93% on air and heart sounds are normal. There is a widespread pale pink papular rash over his torso, with papules as shown below. The rash extends to his upper limbs and face where there are more small papules. The papules have a waxy appearance and an umbilicated centre. The surrounding skin is dry and erythematous.

What is the next most appropriate investigation to reach a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antigen test

This patient has a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum, a viral rash that is characterised by small pale pink waxy papules with an umbilicated centre which cluster. It usually presents in young children, and a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum in an adult raises suspicion of an underlying immunodeficiency, including HIV. HIV antigen testing, along with a CD4 count, should be measured in affected adults.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molscum_contagiosum_new_image.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Molscum_contagiosum_new_image.jpg)

C Viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

In rashes that produce vesicles, such as the herpes simplex virus, a viral PCR of vesicular fluid can be sent for diagnosis. Although molluscum contagiosum is a viral rash caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, viral PCR does not play a role in diagnosis.

A Full blood count

This patient has a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum, a viral rash that is often diagnosed clinically. The diagnosis is made based on the appearance of the rash characterised by clusters of small waxy papules with an umbilicated centre. While a full blood count is useful to investigate his fatigue and the extent of infection, it is not needed to make a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum and is not the next most appropriate test to request.

B Skin biopsy

Skin biopsies are also useful if a diagnosis is not certain and other differentials need to be excluded. However, molluscum contagiosum is usually a clinical diagnosis. In some circumstances, a skin biopsy can be taken for histopathology, but it is not normally required.

E Herpes zoster virus (HZV) serology

Herpes zoster virus (HZV) is responsible for shingles, a dermatomal painful vesicular rash that is caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. While it mostly has a dermatomal distribution, in immunocompromised individuals, the rash may be bilateral or diffuse. However, this question describes a patient with a non-painful, umbilicated papular rash. Furthermore, in contrast to HZV, the contents of the papules contain a thicker white material rather than clear vesicular fluid. This makes a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum more likely, making HZV serology incorrect.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old male is admitted with behavioural changes. One month before admission, he was on holiday in North Tanzania. He was exposed to multiple bites from insects and he developed an erythematous swelling on his left ankle. He then developed intermittent fever, myalgia and headache and was given quinine by a local doctor, with little effect. Over the last week, he has been sleeping most of the day and been up all night and has developed episodes of mania with rapid bursts of speech, followed by generalised apathy. He also complains of generalised headache with no blurred vision or change with posture, sneezing or coughing. He smokes 20 cigarettes/day and drinks alcohol at weekends, he has tried cannabis in the past and admits to occasional crack use, but his partner is not sure whether he has taken any recently.

On examination, he is agitated but afebrile. His pulse is 120/min and blood pressure 102/65 mmHg. His chest is clear and abdomen soft although there is generalised tenderness. On examination of his peripheral nerves there is a fine tremor in his upper limbs and increased tone throughout. He has generalised decreased power but reflexes are normal. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
White cell count (WCC)9.8 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)95 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)82.1 fL80 - 100 fL
Platelets (PLT)67 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Total protein84 g/L60 - 83 g/L
Albumin29 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)35 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)68 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Bilirubin9 µmol/L1 - 22µmol/l
Chest X-raynormal
ECGsinus tachycardia
Thick and thin films for malaria parasitesnegative

Which investigation would be most appropriate as the next step, given the suspected diagnosis?
options: Urgent computerised tomography (CT) of the brain
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Urgent computerised tomography (CT) of the brain

This patient has Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (East African or Rhodesian African trypanosomiasis) infection. A number of tourists to game parks in northern Tanzania recently acquired East African trypanosomiasis, which is transmitted through the bite of the tsetse fly. This illness manifests as an erythematous swelling or chancre at the site of the fly bite 5–15 days later, fever, headache and myalgia, before it progresses to meningoencephalitis. The second phase often occurs after a few weeks or a month in East African trypanosomiasis, but can take longer than one year in the West African disease. It is manifested by persistent headaches, daytime somnolence followed by night-time insomnia and behavioural changes, mood swings and, in some patients, depression. In late disease the patient becomes comatose (i.e. sleeping sickness) and it can be fatal.

A computerised tomography (CT) of the head is required in order for a LP (lumbar puncture) to be performed. CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain in late disease reveal cerebral oedema and white matter enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) investigations should always be performed in patients with parasitaemia or lymphadenopathy. The double centrifugation technique is the most sensitive method to detect trypanosomes. Other CSF findings include a high white cell count (WCC), elevated IgM and elevated protein levels.

The treatment of choice is suramin in stage 1 (chancre/fever/myalgia) disease and melarsoprol in stage 2 (central nervous system (CNS)/meningoencephalitic) stage.

B Blood culture

During the acute phase of the disease, trypanosomes are often detectable on smears of peripheral blood, but blood cultures would not be able to demonstrate any parasites.

C Psychiatry consultation

There is plenty of evidence for organic disease such as low platelet count, high white cell count and abnormalities on physical examination that would require a physical cause to be sought before seeking a psychiatric explanation.

D Serology

There is no current serological test for East African trypanosomiasis, but there is serological testing for T. gambiense, which occurs in West and Central Africa. There is also serological testing for T. cruzi, American trypanosomiasis.

E Serum electrophoresis

There is unlikely to be monoclonal expansion, this is unlikely to be a helpful investigation.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man is rushed into the Emergency Department by his wife. He complains of generalised weakness and blurred vision. Other than a short-lived episode of diarrhoea and vomiting two days ago, he has been well recently, with no past medical history.

His observations are recorded as being within normal limits. On examination, he has bilateral third and sixth cranial nerve palsies and failure of pupil accommodation. He has dry mucous membranes and impaired swallowing. There is flaccid paralysis of his upper limbs, with normal power and reflexes in his lower limbs. Sensation is spared throughout.

What is the most likely causative organism responsible for this patient’s symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Clostridium botulinum

This patient has botulism, a bacterial infection caused by C. botulinum. It is a common environmental organism that is often contracted from contaminated canned or bottled food. The symptoms of the disease often begin with blurred vision and occasionally diarrhoea and vomiting can be seen. They later manifest as a profound neuromuscular blockade with a classical symmetrical descending pattern of paralysis. Often cranial nerves are affected first, with bilateral cranial nerve palsies being common. This is followed by upper limb and lastly lower-limb paralysis. Death can occur from paralysis of respiratory muscles.

E Clostridium tetani

Tetanus is a bacterial illness caused by C. tetani. It is found in soil and enters the body through a contaminated wound or through a break in the skin, including from intravenous drug use. After an incubation period of between a few days to several weeks, symptoms of the disease will manifest, typically starting with general malaise and progressing to muscular spasms such as lockjaw. In more severe disease, muscular spasms can be painful and affect different organ systems. Respiration can be impaired from laryngospasm and oesophageal and urethral spasm can cause dysphagia and urinary retention, respectively. This is in contrast to the question given where the patient is suffering from paralysis rather than muscular spasm, hinting towards an alternative diagnosis of botulism.

A Campylobacter jejuni

Very rarely, following infection with C. jejuni, a neurological condition known as Guillain–Barré syndrome can develop. However, Guillain–Barré syndrome classically causes an ascending pattern of paralysis, rather than descending paralysis, which is seen in this question.

B Clostridium perfringes

C. perfringes is a common cause of gastroenteritis and is also the most common bacterial cause of gas gangrene. While this patient exhibits symptoms of vomiting and diarrhoea, C. perfringes would not explain his neurological symptoms, making it incorrect.

D Clostridium difficile

C. difficile is a severe and highly contagious gastrointestinal illness. While this patient does exhibit symptoms of vomiting and diarrhoea, C. difficile would not explain his neurological symptoms, making it incorrect.

questions.question:
You are the medical senior house officer (SHO) on call. A 40-year-old man has presented to the Emergency Department with jaundice. He gives a week-long history of worsening jaundice with associated nausea and malaise. He has had mild diarrhoea, although there is no history of abdominal pain. He has felt unwell for the past 3 weeks but initially his symptoms were more ‘flu-like’ with muscle aches and fever. He reports multiple sexual partners in the past 3 months. He often has unprotected anal intercourse. He uses ecstasy and cocaine as recreational drugs. He used to occasionally inject drugs but has not done so for over 10 years. He regularly attends the Genitourinary Clinic for sexual health screens and his last HIV test was negative 6 months ago.

On examination, he is afebrile, pulse 95 bpm. He is deeply jaundiced and his abdomen is soft with very mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. There is no organomegaly.

The Emergency Department SHO performed some blood tests, which reveals the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)132 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)360 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin154 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)872 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)300 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L
Hepatitis B S antibody (Ab)Positive
Hep B S antigen (Ag)Negative
Renal functionNormal ranges

Which test is most likely to give you the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Anti-hepatitis A Ab

This patient has symptoms suggestive of hepatitis A infection, a flu-like prodromal illness followed by an icteric illness. He is at risk as he has had unprotected anal sex with many partners; anal intercourse is a likely route for enteral transmission. Parenteral transmission can also occur.

A Liver ultrasound

A liver ultrasound may be useful if, for example, the patient does have chronic hepatitis C and has now developed a hepatoma. However, in this case, the symptoms are highly suggestive of an acute viral infection.

C Anti-hepatitis C Ab

It would be correct when hepatitis C is the most likely diagnosis. Hepatitis C is almost always asymptomatic during the acute infection; furthermore he has not been at high risk of contracting hepatitis C virus (HCV) for over 10 years – sexual transmission is rare compared with blood transmission. Chronic HCV would present as chronic liver disease which does not fit with this clinical picture.

D Anti-hepatitis D Ab

It would be correct when hepatitis D is the most likely diagnosis. Hepatitis D only causes this picture when superinfection occurs in patients who are already hepatitis B positive. His results show that he has already been vaccinated against hepatitis B, or that he has had a previous (now inactive) infection. If HBsAg was positive then it might raise suspicion of hepatitis D infection.

E HIV antibody test

The patient may well be HIV positive but the HIV antibody titre will not give you the diagnosis on this occasion.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old homeless man presents to the Emergency Department with severe headaches, behavioural changes and pyrexia. He has been admitted to the unit on two previous occasions with heroin overdoses.

On examination, he is emaciated and has a number of needle marks consistent with drug abuse, his temperature is 38.6 °C. You also notice that he has finger clubbing and nail bed haemorrhages. There is an ejection systolic murmur. Neurological examination reveals evidence of mild papilloedema.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 x 10 9/l4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)120 x 10 9/l150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)87 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)155 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
CT headFrontal lobe abscess

He is to be urgently reviewed by the neurosurgical team.

Which of the following would be the most appropriate initial antibiotic choice pending culture results?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E IV linezolid

In intravenous drug abusers (IVDAs), a methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) is the causative organism in about 60-70% of cases with haematogenous spread of the bacteria resulting in the frontal lobe abscess seen here. Linezolid is the initial empiric therapy of choice because it covers against MRSA infection and achieves good brain penetration.
