In the event that a sensitive staphylococcus is isolated, flucloxacillin can be substituted. Trans-oesophageal echocardiography is the investigation to confirm the diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis

B IV cefotaxime

This is the treatment for meningitis rather than cerebral abscess. If the picture was of a meningism and no evidence of raised intracranial pressure and a normal CT scan this would be a better treatment option.

A IV penicillin

This could be the treatment for a streptococcal cause of infection but this organism is unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s abscess.

C IV co-amoxiclav

This could be a useful broad-spectrum treatment if the patient was not known to be a IVDA.

D Oral doxycycline

Doxycycline is a potential oral option for community-acquired infection. Given the severity of infection here, it is unlikely to be sufficient to clear the underlying staphylococcal infection. 70614

questions.question:
A 45-year-old farmer presents to the hospital with a 2-week history of fever, chills, headache and muscle aches. He reports exposure to cattle and sheep on his farm. Physical examination reveals a temperature of 38.5 °C and there is mild hepatomegaly without jaundice. Laboratory tests show mildly elevated liver enzyme levels and leukocytosis. Chest X-ray reveals mild infiltrates. Serology confirms a diagnosis of Q fever caused by Coxiella burnetii.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)17.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L

What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B PO doxycycline for 14 days

Doxycycline is the first-line treatment for acute Q fever, administered over a 14-day course. It is highly effective against C. burnetii and helps to prevent chronic complications. In cases of acute Q fever, early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to reduce the risk of progression to chronic Q fever.

E PO metronidazole for seven days

Metronidazole is ineffective against C. burnetii and is not used in the treatment of Q fever, as it primarily targets anaerobic organisms.

A PO azithromycin for five days

Azithromycin is not the first-line treatment for Q fever. While macrolides are sometimes used in cases of severe allergy to tetracyclines, doxycycline remains the preferred choice due to higher efficacy against C. burnetii.

C IV amoxicillin

IV amoxicillin is not effective for Q fever, as C. burnetii is resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. These are not used in the management of Q fever.

D PO ciprofloxacin for 14 days

Ciprofloxacin is not the first-line treatment for Q fever and is generally less effective than doxycycline for this infection. Tetracyclines remain the preferred class of antibiotics. 74464

questions.question:
A 40-year-old farmer is admitted to the Cardiology Ward with a 2-month history of general malaise and weight loss. His symptoms were preceded by a flu-like illness and intermittent fevers. There is no significant past medical history, and he is normally fit and well.

His temperature is 38.7 °C, heart rate 105 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.

On examination, there are vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. There is a loud pansystolic murmur radiating towards the apex. His jugular venous pressure (JVP) is not elevated and there are no signs of peripheral oedema. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L120–160 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)350 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50–90 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation 70 mm/hour rate (ESR)< 15 mm/hour
ECHOEvidence of mitral regurgitation with visible vegetations on valve leaflets
Blood culturesNegative × 3 sets

What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Doxycycline

This patient has infective endocarditis. The history of general malaise and flu-like symptoms, together with fever and a new murmur, is highly suggestive of the diagnosis. This patient’s pansystolic murmur and ECHO findings are indicative of mitral regurgitation, with the mitral valve being the most commonly affected valve in

infective endocarditis. Blood cultures form part of the modified Duke criteria needed to confirm the diagnosis. Coxiella burnetii causes blood culture-negative endocarditis. It is a zoonotic disease and individuals at higher risk of infection include those who work with animals such as farmers and veterinarians. Treatment is with a prolonged course of doxycycline.

B Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin

Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin are used for cases of infective endocarditis caused by streptococcal species. It seems less likely to be the cause of this patient’s presentation, making benzylpenicillin an unlikely antibiotic of choice.

A Amoxicillin and gentamicin

Amoxicillin and gentamicin are usually given in the first instance for infective endocarditis when a patient has native valves and an unclear causative organism. However, this patient is a farmer with negative blood culture results, making the probability of a zoonotic infection (eg C. burnetii) more likely.

D Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is indicated for patients who are likely to be infected with Staphylococcus aureus (eg IV drug users). Given the negative blood culture results, this is very unlikely to be the causative organism in this patient, making flucloxacillin an unlikely antibiotic of choice.

E Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin

Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin are combined as blind antibiotic therapy for patients with a prosthetic heart valve or those with S. aureus infection who are allergic to penicillin. There is no past medical history to suggest that this patient has had a heart valve replacement or that he is penicillin-allergic.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old veterinarian is brought into the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of headache, deteriorating cognition and worsening confusion. His partner reports an obvious change in behaviour and no longer responds to simple questions appropriately. He has a past medical history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and reports to be incompliant with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). On examination, he has a low-grade temperature of 37.9 °C. His heart rate is 90 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 122/82 mmHg. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen, with no palpable organomegaly. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14 (E4 V4 M6) and he is clearly disorientated to time, place and person. There is mild left-sided hemiparesis, with 4/5 power on myotome testing of his left upper and lower limbs.

CD4 count: 100 cells/µl Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scan: multiple ring-enhancing lesions.

What is the most likely causative organism for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Toxoplasma gondii

This patient has neurotoxoplasmosis, an opportunistic infection caused by the parasite T. gondii. It is the most common cause of neurological brain abscesses in patients with HIV. Domestic cats are a common source of transmission. This patient is a veterinarian, making his chances of contracting toxoplasmosis much more likely. Symptoms include headache, fever and neurological changes, including seizures, hemiplegia, cerebellar signs or an acute confusional state. Toxoplasmosis can be diagnosed with a combination of clinical history, serology testing and imaging. Classically, the disease can be seen on an MRI brain scan as multiple ring-enhancing lesions.

D Streptococcus pneumoniae

S. pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common causes of a bacterial brain abscess. Bacterial intracranial abscesses commonly arise from infections in adjacent structures, including otitis media, sinusitis or mastoiditis. Other sources of infection include bloodborne spread, such as from endocarditis. A swinging fever is common, along with headache and neurological symptoms. Cerebral abscesses appear as a radiolucent space- occupying lesion with ring enhancement. However, unlike toxoplasmosis, a double rim sign is common, secondary to a hypodense outer rim and a hyperdense inner rim.

A Cryptococcus neoformans

C. neoformans causes an opportunistic fungal infection of the central nervous system (CNS) called cryptococcosis. The disease presents similarly to meningitis with headache, fevers, confusion, altered mental state and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Imaging studies, including computed tomography (CT) and MRI, show leptomeningeal enhancement, cryptococcomas, hydrocephalus or dilated perivascular spaces. It usually occurs when the CD4 count drops below 100 cells/µl and it does not cause ring-enhancing lesions, making it incorrect here.

B Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a viral infection which commonly causes illness in patients with HIV, particularly in those with a CD4 count < 50 cells/µl. The most common form of CMV is CMV retinitis and the presentation is variable due to involvement of the brain, meninges, spinal cord, retina and peripheral nerve roots. However, cognitive decline is frequently seen. On imaging, meningoencephalitis and ventriculitis are most often present.

C Mycobacterium tuberculosis

M. tuberculosis can cause central neurological involvement from direct extension into the central nervous system (CNS) or via haematogenous spread. CNS involvement with M. tuberculosis can take various forms, most commonly tuberculous meningitis and tuberculomas. Tuberculosis is particularly more common in individuals with HIV and symptoms are usually similar to those of bacterial meningitis (eg fever, headache, meningism). Tuberculous meningitis can be seen on imaging as leptomeningitis from the presence of thick exudative material in the subarachnoid space, whereas tuberculomas present as ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding vasogenic oedema. In areas of the world where tuberculosis is endemic, tuberculous meningitis and tuberculomas are much more common. However, in this patient, the clinical history of working as a veterinarian and the presence of multiple ring-enhancing lesions make the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis more likely. 72582

questions.question:
A 21-year-old hill walker presents to the Emergency Department with severe fever, left-sided lower abdominal pain and diarrhoea with blood and mucus over the past 48 hours. He has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medication. He has been staying in hikers’ huts over the past few days where cooking and toilet facilities are shared. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, with a postural drop of 30 mmHg on standing, and his pulse is 85 bpm.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)139 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.3 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)204 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine132 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urea12.2 mmol/L2.5–7.8 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)152 mg/L < 5 mg/L
Stool screen:Positive for Shigella.

He is given oral rehydration sachets and wants to continue with his holiday.

Which other intervention is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Oral azithromycin

Although quinolones were the default first-line option for the treatment of symptomatic Shigella infection, their use is now discouraged because of the risk for seizures and tendon rupture associated with this drug class. A Cochrane meta-analysis showed that a range of antibiotics had similar efficacy, including azithromycin, which drives this as the treatment of choice for Shigella infection here.

C Oral Metronidazole

Oral metronidazole is the intervention of choice for giardiasis, which is suggested by symptoms similar to irritable bowel syndrome with intermittent diarrhoea and constipation, and infection is usually acquired because of exposure to contaminated food or water. Infection is not usually seen in the United Kingdom.

B Oral Ciprofloxacin

Oral quinolones are now reserved for serious or life-threatening illness when other options for treatment are unavailable. This is because of a Committee on Safety of Medicines (CSM) warning detailing significant adverse effects associated with their use, including seizures in patients with no known epilepsy and tendon ruptures.

D Single-dose intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone

IV ceftriaxone is the preferred option for patients who are severely unwell because of Shigella infection. Although this patient does have a postural drop in his blood pressure, oral azithromycin would be considered adequate to treat his infection.

E No other intervention required

Given this patient has severe dehydration and ongoing diarrhoea and is on an activity holiday, antibiotic intervention is warranted to relieve his symptoms here.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of profuse diarrhoea. She passed watery stool flecked with blood up to 10 times per day. She also complained of cramping abdominal pain, a low-grade fever and increased lethargy. She had recently completed a course of clindamycin for a dental abscess.

On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C. Her abdomen was soft but the lower portion was generally tender.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin121 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)18.3 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Urea13.4 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Sodium (Na⁺)142 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine165 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Rigid sigmoidoscopyRaised, yellowish white plaques throughout sigmoid

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Oral vancomycin

This patient has Clostridium difficile infection, as evidenced by her profuse, offensive diarrhoea, pseudomembranous colitis on rigid sigmoidoscopy and high white cell count. This was probably caused by taking clindamycin, which increases the risk of C. difficile infection. Oral vancomycin is the first-line treatment for C. difficile; other options include oral metronidazole and oral and intravenous fidaxomycin.

C Oral ciprofloxacin

This patient’s profuse diarrhoea, pseudomembranous colitis on rigid sigmoidoscopy and high white cell count point towards Clostridium difficile infection, probably precipitated by the clindamycin she was prescribed for her dental infection. Both clindamycin and ciprofloxacin are strongly associated with increased risk of C. difficile

infection; consequently ciprofloxacin would not be a good choice of antibiotic for treatment of this patient. First- line treatments would be oral vancomycin or oral metronidazole; second-line therapies include oral fidaxomycin.

A Intravenous ciprofloxacin

This patient has developed pseudomembranous colitis on sigmoidoscopy, and her symptoms and high white cell count are consistent with C. difficile infection. Clindamycin, which this patient had received for a dental infection, is known to be associated with C. difficile infection. Unfortunately ciprofloxacin is also associated with the development of C. difficile infection, and therefore would not be an appropriate choice of treatment. Also, please note that bioavailability for intravenous and oral ciprofloxacin is virtually identical, therefore treating with intravenous ciprofloxacin provides no advantage unless the patient is unable to take oral ciprofloxacin. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. First-line treatment of C. difficile is usually oral vancomycin or oral metronidazole, but sometimes oral fidaxomycin is used.

B Intravenous vancomycin

This patient has Clostridium difficile infection, as evidenced by the profuse diarrhoea, pseudomembranous colitis on sigmoidoscopy and high white cell count. Clindamycin, which this patient has recently taken, is known to be associated with C. difficile infection. Whilst vancomycin is an appropriate choice of antibiotic, it should be given orally, not intravenously, otherwise it will not reach sufficient therapeutic levels in the gut. Other antibiotic options include metronidazole and fidaxomycin.

E Rectal budesonide

Budesonide is a steroid, and rectal budesonide is used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease and gut graft-versus-host disease in order to tackle inflammation. However, this patient has Clostridium difficile infection, as evidence by her profuse, offensive diarrhoea and high white cell count after taking a course of clindamycin, an antibiotic known to be associated with C. difficile. The rigid sigmoidoscopy confirms a pseudomembranous colitis. Treating this with steroids would be highly inappropriate; she requires antibiotic therapy with oral vancomycin. Other appropriate options would be oral metronidazole or fidaxomycin. 21441

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with right upper quadrant tenderness and bloody diarrhoea. He has been unwell since returning from a period supervising a 1-year Operation Raleigh expedition to Brazil. This was one of a number of trips to South America. While there, he took part in watersports and went fresh-water swimming. He visited the jungles and was bitten by the occasional insect. He was always careful however with what he ate and drank. He had night sweats and fever for 1 week, with headache, a non- productive cough and arthralgia. He smokes 40 cigarettes/day and drinks heavily on the weekend. He admitted to having casual unprotected sex with some of the local women.

On examination, his temperature is 38.1 °C and his pulse 110 bpm. He has cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. His chest is clear but he has a large liver, which measures 10 cm below the right costal margin, and a spleen which is 8 cm below the left costal margin.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
White cell count (WCC)15.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils9.3 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.58 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.2 ×10⁹/L1.5–3.5 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils2.1 ×10⁹/L0.0–0.4 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/L135–175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)84 fL76–98 fL
Platelets (PLT)140 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)36 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)134 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)157 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin21 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Albumin34 g/L35–55 g/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Normal
Abdominal ultrasound scan shows an enlarged liver 15 cm, enlarged spleen 10 cm, kidneys and pancreas normal, two gallstones in the gallbladder, no common bile duct (CBD) dilatation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Schistosomiasis

This patient has an exposure to fresh-water immersion and jungle activity in a country where schistosomiasis is endemic. The key findings from his history and investigation are fever, hepatosplenomegaly and bloody diarrhoea in the returning traveller. The disease is caused by one of several species of parasitic trematodes of the genus Schistosoma. Schistosomes infect particular species of susceptible freshwater snails, which release cercariae, which are fork-tailed 1-mm-long free-swimming larvae. These survive in freshwater for up to 48 hours, during which time they must attach to human skin/susceptible host mammal or die. Once attached, they migrate through intact skin to dermal veins and, over the next several days, to the pulmonary vasculature. The worms then migrate through the pulmonary capillaries to the systemic circulation, which carries them to the portal veins where they mature. In the portal circulation the males and females pair off and produce eggs.

Diagnosis is based on a good travel history with the risk of exposure clarified. Patients in the acute stage can present with an urticarial illness as they react to the antigenic eggs produced. Symptoms are those of serum sickness and hepatosplenomegaly is often present. Diagnosis can be made by observing eggs in the stool or urine depending on which species of Schistosoma has caused infection. Treatment is primarily with praziquantel and supportive therapy.

C Giardiasis

It would not explain the bloody diarrhoea or hepatosplenomegaly. The patient could be exposed to Giardia lamblia, the causative pathogen, through unprotected sex or swimming and it would cause diarrhoea, but the additional features of the history and examination makes it less likely. Giardiasis typically presents as explosive diarrhoea and malabsorption.

A HIV

It does not explain the bloody diarrhoea or hepatosplenomegaly. Acute HIV seroconversion is more likely to present with fever and general malaise. However, it would be worthwhile to test for HIV due to the potential exposure history.

B Crohn’s disease

It cannot account for the hepatosplenomegaly and does not explain the lymphoadenopathy. It would fit with the fevers, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, and could also explain the arthralgia as an extra-intestinal symptom, but the cough is difficult to explain.

E Leishmaniasis

Visceral leishmaniasis is a cause of fevers, night sweats and hepatosplenomegaly but would not present with bloody diarrhoea and does not cause arthralgia. Leishmaniasis is endemic to east Africa and India and more commonly presents in a cutaneous form, but visceral leishmaniasis is an important cause of hepatosplenomegaly as untreated it is often fatal.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old woman attended clinic with a 6-month history of breathlessness, wheeze and general fatigue. She had returned to the United Kingdom 2 weeks previously after an 8-month mission in Zanzibar, mainly spent in rural areas. She swam in the lakes and walked around barefoot. She had been well during her trip, apart from a 2-month period during which she experienced vague abdominal discomfort, which disappeared after taking a tablet prescribed by her doctor.

On examination, her pulse was 80 bpm and respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min at rest, increasing to 28 breaths/min on walking 40 m. Her body mass index (BMI) was 24, and she appeared pale. Auscultation of the chest demonstrated scattered wheeze.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)88 g/L115 - 165 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)72.1 fL80 - 96 fL
White cell count (WCC)8.4 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)460 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin21 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)45 U/L5 - 35 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)84 U/L45 - 105 U/L
Albumin32 g/L37 - 49 g/L
Chest X-rayNormal
UrineBlood negative, protein negative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Hookworm infection

The patient mentions that she has been walking around barefoot, a classic risk factor for infection by hookworm. In the early stages of the infection, the hookworms are found in the small intestine (explaining her non-specific abdominal pain). They then migrate to the lungs and can cause wheeze and a dry cough and breathlessness.

This can lead to poor exercise tolerance, as demonstrated in this case. Typically, patients present with iron deficiency anaemia from ongoing gastrointestinal blood loss, as seen here.

C Left ventricular failure

Left ventricular failure would explain her progressive breathlessness. However, there is no underlying pathology to explain the development of heart failure in this patient. She does have anaemia; however, it is unlikely that this level of anaemia could have caused left ventricular failure. It also does not explain her vague abdominal pain. Left ventricular failure does not explain why she has developed anaemia. This patient’s presentation could be better explained by hookworm infection.

A Duodenal ulcer

A duodenal ulcer would cause central abdominal pain, worse at night and relieved by eating. A duodenal ulcer could explain her abdominal pain. However, the duodenal ulcer cannot explain her wheeze or breathlessness (if a duodenal ulcer was causing her to be anaemic, you would not expect the symptoms to have resolved after receiving a medication from her doctor). These symptoms could be better explained by hookworm infection.

D Pulmonary embolism

The time course is too long for an acute pulmonary embolism, and you would expect pleuritic chest pain accompanying sudden-onset breathlessness. Chronic pulmonary thromboembolic disease can cause breathlessness, but this patient is young and of normal weight; there are no identified risk factors for venous thromboembolism. It is unlikely that she would have chronic thromboembolic disease, and it does not explain the anaemia or the history of vague abdominal pain. This patient’s presentation could be better explained by hookworm infection. Treatment is highly successful with albendazole or mebendazole.

E Schistosomiasis

Schistosomiasis typically causes urinary pathology (such as haematuria and later urinary tract malignancies) or intestinal pathology (such as abdominal pain, diarrhoea and later hepatosplenomegaly), depending on the species. Schistosomiasis can cause katayama fever which can cause pulmonary symptoms and an acute illness. However, this patient's presentation could be better explained by hookworm infection due to the more chronic exercise tolerance and microscopic anaemia.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man attends the Dermatology Clinic with a growing lesion on the back of his arm. He initially noticed it two weeks ago when it appeared as a small red raised spot. The lesion is not painful or itchy, and he is otherwise well. He has just completed a tour in Iraq in the military. On examination, his chest is clear and his heart sounds are normal. He has a soft abdomen and no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. There is a 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm round lesion on the extensor surface of his arm, as shown below. His mucous membranes are spared and there are no further lesions on his body.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Leishmaniasis

The lesion with an ulcerated centre and superficial crusting is consistent with leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease spread by sandflies. Different species of Leishmania are responsible for different manifestations of the disease, with cutaneous leishmaniasis being the most common. Initially, a small red papule appears at the site of the sandfly bite, which gradually enlarges to up to 2 cm in diameter. It later ulcerates in the centre before spontaneously resolving. The time to resolution varies between two months and one year. This patient is a soldier, and countries in the Middle East, North Africa and Asia are more common areas for contracting the disease.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cutaneous_leishmaniasis2.jpg

E Yaws

Yaws is a chronic skin infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum pertenue. It usually occurs in tropical parts of the world, including Africa, South East Asia and South America. It is spread through direct contact of infectious ulcers and the bacterium enters the skin through superficial wounds and skin trauma. Similar to syphilis, yaws has several stages of illness. Initially, a papule appears at the site of infection, which enlarges and ulcerates. In secondary yaws, more widespread papules appear over the rest of the body, after which the bacterium enters either a silent latent period or a tertiary stage which begins to affect the bones.

A Anthrax

Anthrax is a bacterial disease caused by Bacillus anthracis. Infection is associated with exposure to infected carcasses and the introduction of the organism into the body through a superficial wound. An initial pustule appears at the site of infection, which progresses to a black eschar (a necrotic-looking ulcer with a black scab). The infection usually resolves spontaneously, but in some, it can lead to death. The lesion described and shown in this question is not that of a black eschar but rather that of a crusted ulcer from a sandfly bite. This makes leishmaniasis the most likely diagnosis.

B Leprosy

Leprosy is a granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, which affects the peripheral nerves and skin. Initial symptoms include numbness, typically with loss of temperature followed by light touch and pain, and finally deep pressure. Cutaneous lesions follow later in the disease and appear as hypopigmented patches of skin, with associated sensory loss. This patient has a painless, crusted ulcer, with no other lesions or neurological features, making leprosy an unlikely diagnosis.

D Melioidosis

Melioidosis is a bacterial illness caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. It is a tropical disease seen in South East Asia, as well as in Africa, the Middle East and the South Pacific. In many, exposure to the bacterium causes asymptomatic seroconversion. In others, it can cause localised infection, with the appearance of a nodule or ulcer at the site of entry via the skin. In severe cases, it can progress to septicaemia and abscess formation. Localised infection is associated with fever and pain, which are not seen in this patient’s presentation, making melioidosis unlikely here.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman is referred to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has begun HAART for the treatment of HIV a few months earlier and has recently returned from a holiday to Pakistan.

Whilse there, she visited her uncle who has just been diagnosed with tuberculosis. She has a positive quantiferon gamma test. She did not receive the BCG vaccination as a child.

Her chest X-ray is shown below.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Isoniazid / Rifampicin for 3 months

With no symptoms of TB, a normal CXR and a positive quantiferon test, this patient fits the criteria for diagnosis of latent TB. As such, the BHIVA guidelines recommend either 6 months’ treatment with Isoniazid or 3 months’ combination therapy. For non-CNS TB, BHIVA guidelines recommend treatment with 4 drugs for 2 months, then 2 drugs for a further 4 months. Where there is CNS TB, a 9-month treatment period is recommended.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Normal_PA_chest_x-ray_(5414485536).jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Normal_PA_chest_x-ray_(5414485536).jpg)

A Four-drug anti-TB therapy for 6 months

This duration is for drugs in total. Four drugs are needed for two months, and then a further four months of two drugs.

B Four-drug anti-TB therapy for 12 months

Again, this duration is not usually needed for four-drug TB therapy.

C BCG vaccination

BCG is a live vaccination and, as such, it may be potentially harmful in this situation and is therefore not recommended.

E Observe

The positive quantiferon test means that latent TB is likely to be present, despite the absence of clinical evidence and X-ray findings. Patients with HIV have a much greater risk of progression to active TB from the latent state; for this reason, observation only is not appropriate.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman presents to clinic complaining of shortness of breath. She has a CD4 count of 120 ×10⁶/L and has recently been started on antiretroviral therapy (ART). She admits that she quite often forgets to take her medication, including her prophylactic co-trimoxazole.

She describes a 1-week history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and of retrosternal chest pain. She has a dry cough and has not produced any sputum.

On examination, she is febrile at 38.5 °C, respiratory rate is 28/min, O₂ saturations 97% on air, pulse 100 beats/min. The chest is clear on auscultation, cardiovascular examination is normal. Her chest X-ray is shown below.

Which investigation is the most useful pointer to the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Exercise oximetry

The chest x-ray shows reticular interstitial changes in all lung fields.The most likely diagnosis is obviously Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) Exercise oximetry is an extremely useful test in this setting, as patients who are oxygenated well at rest may desaturate dramatically on exercise. An arterial blood gas is also important as it will influence the treatment given. If p(O₂) <9.3 kPa, then high-dose methylprednisolone should also be prescribed in addition to IV co-trimoxazole. The main differential here is of pulmonary embolus. Being HIV-positive is an independent risk factor for thromboembolic disease. However, the history is inconsistent, with a progressive course and a dry cough and a very immunocompromised patient. Retrosternal chest pain is commonly seen in PCP. The next investigation would probably be an electrocardiogram (ECG), but exercise oximetry and an arterial blood gas are even more pressing.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PCP_CAP_CXR.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PCP_CAP_CXR.jpg)

A Electrocardiogram (ECG)

Whilst an ECG should definitively be done for this patient, the question asked is what investigation would most likely lead to a diagnosis. As the clinical history is suggestive of PCP, an ECG is unlikely to guide to that diagnosis and is therefore not the correct option.

B Lateral chest film

A lateral X-ray would give a good view of the retrosternal space and would also help demonstrate a subtle pneumothorax, but would not help diagnose PCP.

D Bedside spirometry

Bedside spirometry is helpful in the diagnosis of obstructive airway illness, such as asthma and COPD, as well as restrictive airway disease such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, but is unlikely to be useful in this patient. Had there been a history or examination findings of wheeze, diurnal variation or heavy smoking history this would have been more relevant.

E D-dimer

D-dimer is a biochemical test which can help exclude pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis and is very unlikely to lead to diagnosis even under those circumstances, due to low specificity. It should be requested in the case of a moderate suspicion of DVT or PE as determined by Wells score.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of painless lesions on his oral mucosa and sides of the tongue, as shown below. These lesions tended to change in appearance over the course of a few days. He travelled extensively in East Asia for work. He had no other medical conditions.

On examination, he appeared underweight. He had painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, and the lesions on his tongue were as described.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.9 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)167 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Oral hairy leukoplakia

The rough, white, painless patches on the oral mucosa is classic for this condition. The disease is caused by reactivation of Epstein–Barr virus, which occurs in patients who are immunosuppressed. This patient has weight loss and widespread lymphadenopathy, on a background of travel in East Asia: the implication is that he may have undiagnosed HIV. In most cases, the diagnosis of oral hairy leukoplakia is clinical, but EBV can be

demonstrated in epithelial cells with immunohistochemical staining. Specific treatment for this condition is not usually required, but he should be encouraged to have HIV testing and be managed with appropriate anti- retroviral therapy.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Leucoexo.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Leucoexo.jpg)

D Oral candidiasis

You may have correctly surmised that this patient has signs and symptoms consistent with an undiagnosed HIV infection – specifically, widespread lymphadenopathy and weight loss, on a background of travel to East Asia. Oral candidiasis is a common complication of immunosuppression, and is seen in undiagnosed HIV relatively often. However, oral candidiasis causes smooth white patches and soreness of the oral mucosa – it is not painless, and the lesions are not rough. This description is more consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia, a dermatological manifestation of Epstein–Barr virus reactivation, which can happen as a consequence of immunosuppression (as seen in undiagnosed HIV infection).

A Geographic tongue

Geographic tongue is in fact caused by the loss of areas of papillae on the tongue; hence it is characterised by smooth, red areas interspersed with normal, paler areas with papillae present. These are seen on the dorsal surface of the tongue. It does not cause rough white patches on the sides of the tongue, as described here. This description is consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia, a condition caused by Epstein–Barr virus reactivation in immunosuppressed individuals. This patient has concerning signs – in particular, widespread lymphadenopathy and weight loss on a background of travel in East Asia – and he should be tested for HIV.

B Herpes simplex infection

Herpes simplex would cause mucosal ulceration, which can include the sides of the tongue, but does not cause rough, white patches as described here. This presentation is more consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia, caused by reactivation of Epstein–Barr virus. This reactivation tends to occur in individuals who are immunosuppressed. In this case, the patient has symptoms and signs that could be compatible with undiagnosed HIV: he has a background of travel in East Asia, and has weight loss and widespread lymphadenopathy with oral hairy leukoplakia. He should be HIV tested.

C Lichen planus

Lichen planus is a dermatological condition which has several oral manifestations, including painful mucosal ulceration and Wickham’s striae. Wickham’s striae appear as a white, lacy network on the buccal mucosa; this is not raised or rough (as described in this patient), and the appearance does not change over a period of days. This patient has mouth signs consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia. This is caused by a reactivation of Epstein– Barr virus, which most often occurs in immunosuppressed individuals. Given his weight loss, travel background and widespread lymphadenopathy, he should be tested for HIV.

questions.question:
You see a patient in the HIV Outpatients Clinic. He was diagnosed HIV-positive 6 weeks ago and was found to have a CD4 count of 12 ×10⁶/L. He was commenced on prophylactic co-trimoxazole, but developed a rash and derangement of his liver function tests and it was stopped.

He feels well now. He is planning to go mountain trekking in the Himalayas for the next three weeks. You try and dissuade him on the basis that he needs to be more immunocompetent before he goes but he will not be moved, as the trip was organised months ago and is for charity.

The patient wants to reduce his risk of catching a range of infections and would like some information about vaccinations. He wants to know what vaccinations he should have, both routine and for travelling purposes.

Which of the following groups of vaccines would you recommend as being safe in HIV-positive patients?
options: Hep A, Hep B, BCG, flu jab
Hep A, Hep B, flu jab, pneumococcal vaccine
Flu jab, pneumococcal vaccine, typhoid 21a, Hep B
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Hep A, Hep B, flu jab, pneumococcal vaccine

In general, non-replicating vaccines, including whole inactivated, polysaccharide, conjugated and subunit vaccines, can be safely used in HIV infected people. Live replicating vacines have traditionally been seen as contraindicated, but with immunorestoration following antiretroviral therapy some vaccines are recommended including MMR, varicella-zoster virus and yellow fever. For the latter three, a CD4 count >200 is advised.

Most clinics will routinely vaccinate all HIV-positive patients against hepatitis A and B. Every traveller with HIV should be sure they are vaccinated against hepatitis A and B. Pneumovax and flu vaccine are recommended. Countries have different vaccination requirements for entry. If polio vaccine is required, it should be the inactivated version, not the live oral version.

E Flu jab, pneumococcal vaccine, typhoid 21a, Hep B

Typhoid is a live vaccine and is therefore contraindicated.

A Hep A, Hep B, mumps

Mumps is part of the MMR vaccine and is a live attenuated vaccine. As the patient is immunocompromised with a low CD4 count this is not recommended.

B Hep A, Hep B, BCG, flu jab

BCG is a live vaccine and is therefore contraindicated.

D BCG, Ty21a typhoid, pneumococcal vaccine

BCG is a live vaccine and is therefore contraindicated. 33165

questions.question:
A 33-year-old Botswana woman with a 2-week history of confusion was brought to the Emergency Department by her husband. Over the preceding year, she had lost weight and had had intermittent fevers and night sweats and recurrent chest infections.

In the 3 months before her presentation, she became withdrawn and irritable, then unsteady on her feet, before becoming confused and requiring help with daily activities. She had lived in the United Kingdom for 6 months.

On examination, her temperature was 36.6 °C. There was widespread lymphadenopathy and mild hepatosplenomegaly. There was no neck stiffness or photophobia. She had dysarthria and an ataxic gait. There was left-sided hypertonia and mild weakness.

Investigations and cerebrospinal fluid investigation reveals the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Blood glucose7.8 mmol/L5.0–10.0 mmol/L

Her chest X-ray is shown below:

By Mikael Häggström [CC0], from Wikimedia Commons

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

This is a progressive demyelinating condition caused by the JC virus. It is very rare in immunocompetent individuals. However, this patient has a year’s history of weight loss, fever and night sweats; combined with lymphadenopathy and recent emigration from an area of high prevalence, it is possible that she has human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The indolent history of personality change, confusion and ataxia are typical for PML. The CSF is usually unremarkable, besides a raised protein level, as in this case. CT findings of hypodense periventricular lesions are typical. This patient’s need for HIV treatment needs to be addressed rapidly, as, without it, the mean survival of a patient with PML due to untreated HIV is < 3 months.

B Cryptococcal meningitis

Cryptococcal meningitis would present acutely, not indolently as in this case. You would expect the patient to be febrile and have meningism (neck stiffness or photophobia). The CSF typically demonstrates a very low glucose level (normal in this case) and a raised WCC with predominantly lymphocytes (again, the WCC is normal in this case). The subacute course, personality changes, ataxia and CT findings in this case are typical of PML.

A Bacterial meningitis

Bacterial meningitis would not present with such an indolent course of confusion and personality change and would not explain her constitutional symptoms. You would also expect fever, neck stiffness or photophobia, which are not present in this case. Lumbar puncture would show a high WCC (polymorphs) and low glucose level, but in this case, there is a normal WCC and glucose level in the CSF. The subacute course, personality changes, ataxia and CT findings here are typical of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).

D Multiple sclerosis

There are some features of this patient’s presentation that would fit with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, namely: dissociated focal neurological signs, the CSF findings and the CT imaging (though patchy widespread lesions are more common). Personality change is sometimes seen but is a less common presenting feature of multiple sclerosis. However, multiple sclerosis could not explain her constitutional symptoms of weight loss, night sweats and fevers, or the lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Combined with her recent emigration from an area of high prevalence, it is more likely that these symptoms and signs are due to untreated HIV infection, and consequent PML.

E Tuberculosis

Tuberculous meningitis can present with an insidious course of personality change, cranial nerve signs and confusion, as seen here. It is also far more common in first-generation immigrants from countries with a high tuberculosis rate, like Botswana. However, it would be very unusual for a patient to have a normal chest X-ray in the context of tuberculosis meningitis – you would expect to see apical abnormalities consistent with active or previous infection. If this were tuberculous meningitis, you would also expect the patient to have meningism, but there is no photophobia or neck stiffness here. Typically, a lumbar puncture in tuberculous meningitis reveals CSF with a spidery blood clot (here it is clear) and a low glucose level (normal in this case). Finally, CT imaging would show tuberculomas (which do enhance on CT imaging), whereas in this case there are multiple non-enhancing periventricular lesions, typical of PML. 2306

questions.question:
A 19-year-old student is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his flat-mates called 999. They had been back at university for approximately 10 days since the summer break. He complained initially of flu like symptoms, but over the past 24 h has taken to his bed complaining of a severe headache and neck stiffness. He is now drowsy and confused. On examination, he is pyrexial (38.9 °C), his BP is 95/50 mmHg and pulse is 95/min and regular. He has cold peripheries and a purpuric rash which appears to be extending even as you examine him. By the time you finish examining him he is unresponsive to commands. The paramedics have started a normal saline IV which is running through stat. An intubation tray is prepared.

Which of the following is the most important next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C IV ceftriaxone

Early antibiotic therapy is crucial with respect to successful management of meningococcal meningitis. As such, IV ceftriaxone is the most important next step. Ceftriaxone covers meningococci, pneumococci, H. influenzae type B and streptococci, and is therefore a very prudent empirical choice. In the community, IM or IV benzylpenicillin should be given.

D IV FFP

DIC is a potential complication that can be noted on the coagulation screen, but treating the underlying cause is more appropriate.

A Further IV fluid loading

Although this patient may require further circulatory support / fluid loading, at this stage time to antibiotics is the most important factor in his survival.

B IV hydrocortisone

IV steroids may reduce neurological sequelae, and as such are an important addition to therapy, although not initially.

E IV benzylpenicillin

IV benzylpenicillin is not recommended because of the possibility of resistant meningococci.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever and malaise. She has a mild cough but denies shortness of breath or chest pain. She has noticed the onset of a new rash over her face that is spreading to her arms and chest.

Her past medical history includes hypothyroidism and congenital kidney disease for which she received a renal transplant from her younger sister ten years ago. Her regular medications include levothyroxine, tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. She has no allergies. Until three days ago, she has been fit and well and working as a nursery school teacher.

On examination, she has a temperature of 40.1 °C. Chest sounds are clear, with saturations of 97% on air. Her heart rate is 140 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 125/76 mmHg. She has normal heart sounds and capillary refill time is < 2 seconds. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender and a palpable mass is felt in the left iliac fossa. She has a widespread morbilliform macular rash over her torso, upper arms and face as shown below on her arm. Her conjunctivae are red and she has dry mucous membranes.

What is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA)

This patient is on immunosuppressive medication following a renal transplant. Immunocompromised patients are susceptible to an increased number of infections, including common childhood infections against which most are normally immunised. The history of coryza and a maculopapular rash over the face and torso, along with conjunctivitis, is suggestive of measles. Her occupation as a nursery schoolteacher further increases this risk. The investigation of choice for diagnosing acute measles is an NPA or a throat swab for viral PCR. This is particularly true in the immunocompromised, where a decreased immune response may reduce the sensitivity of serological evidence.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Measles_in_African_Child_2.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Measles_in_African_Child_2.JPG)

D Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common cause of illness in the immunocompromised, particularly post-solid organ transplant. The virus can present itself in various ways, including a mononucleosis-like syndrome similar to Epstein–Barr virus pneumonia, colitis and retinitis. While it is an important differential to consider, the presence of a morbilliform rash and conjunctivitis is more suggestive of infection with the measles virus.

B Blood culture

While a blood culture is a good investigation to rule out alternative diagnoses, it is not needed to diagnose measles.

C Measles immunoglobulin M (IgM) serology

IgM antibodies are raised in the acute phase of measles and, therefore, can be sent for to test for the disease. However, in immunocompromised patients, there may be a reduced immune response, making it a less sensitive diagnostic test.

E Monospot test

A Monospot test is used to diagnose glandular fever. The disease can present similarly with a sore throat and high fever. Other distinguishing clinical features include swollen and tender lymph nodes, along with lymphocytosis and deranged liver transaminases on blood testing. However, it has no role in diagnosing measles.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man is admitted after collapsing with a severe headache at the airport. He has a 3-day history of fever and flu-like symptoms. He has returned from Kenya the previous day after a 3-week visit, including time spent visiting the national parks. He was prescribed doxycycline before his trip but admits that he has been poorly compliant. On examination, his temperature is 38.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 105 bpm and regular and fingertip glucose level 4.5 mmol/L. The cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable. His abdomen is soft, with palpable splenomegaly.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)114 g/L130 - 180 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.6 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)44 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Blood gasesResultNormal values
pH7.217.35 - 7.45
p(O₂)12.4 kPa11.3 - 12.6 kPa
p(CO₂)2.4 kPa4.7 - 6.0 kPa
HCO₃14 mmol/L21 - 29 mmol/L

Given the likely diagnosis, what clinical feature is most indicative of severe disease?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Metabolic acidosis

According to the World Health Organization, the presence of severe metabolic acidosis (base deficit > 8 mmol/L, HCO3- level < 15 mmol/L or plasma lactate level > 5 mmol/L) qualifies as severe malaria. As this patient has a HCO3- level of 14 mmol/L, he has severe metabolic acidosis.

A Glucose 4.5 mmol/L

Hypoglycaemia is a criterion for the diagnosis of severe falciparum malaria (as per the World Health Organization’s guidelines); however, this patient is not hypoglycaemic. A glucose level of < 2.2 mmol/L would qualify as hypoglycaemia and lead to a diagnosis of severe falciparum malaria.

C Platelet count of 44 ×10⁹/L

Thrombocytopenia is almost invariable in significant malarial infection and, in itself, is not sufficient for a diagnosis of severe malaria.

D Splenomegaly

Splenomegaly is a clinical feature seen in patients with malaria. However, it is not an indicator of severe disease.

E Temperature of 38.8 °C

It is common for patients with malaria to have a high fever, regardless of whether they have severe falciparum malaria or not. A fever > 39 °C is significant for severe disease.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man is referred to the Infectious Diseases Clinic for review. His problems began around six weeks ago, when he suffered cold symptoms for a period of approximately ten days. These symptoms resolved, but he is now left with paroxysms of rapid coughing after which he sometimes vomits. He tells you these leave him exhausted. He has normal breath sounds on auscultation of the chest. He did not receive vaccinations as a child.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)141 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)281 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)112 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)28 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gram-negative coccobacillus

This patient’s symptoms, with an initial cold-like illness followed by recovery and then paroxysms of coughing, in a patient who has not received childhood vaccinations, are typical of Bordetella pertussis (B pertussis), or whooping cough. Symptoms are usually much less severe in adults, and, as a consequence, most patients present later to medical services. Although macrolides are effective in shortening the period of illness and symptoms, they only impact if used in the first 3 weeks.

E Gram-positive coccus

Staphylococcus aureus is a typical gram-positive coccus which leads to human infection. It can cause pneumonia following an influenzae illness. It is not, however, a cause of the symptoms here, where ‘paroxysms of coughing’ are consistent with B pertussis infection leading to Whooping Cough.

B Gram-positive coccobacillus

Listeria is a bacterium characterised by small gram-positive coccobacilli. It is a cause of gastroenteritis, and may cause meningitis, particularly in very old or pregnant patients. Amoxicillin is the intervention of choice.

C Gram-negative bacillus

Gram-negative bacilli are a prominent cause of bacteraemia necessitating hospital admission. Risks of gram- negative bacteraemia are significantly increased in patients with comorbidities, with the urinary tract a common source of infection. In approximately one-fifth of cases, Escherichia coli (E coli) is identified as the cause of sepsis. Where pseudomonas is not suspected to be the cause, ceftriaxone and piperacillin-tazobactam are typical empirical agents used in monotherapy for treating gram-negative sepsis. Where severe pseudomonas infection is suspected, then an aminoglycoside is used in combination.

D Gram-positive bacillus

Bacillus cereus (B cereus) and Bacillus anthracis (B anthracis) are examples of gram-positive bacteria. B cereus is a cause of gastroenteritis related to reheated rice, while B anthracis leads to the development of anthrax, which is usually fatal if the spores are inhaled.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has recently returned from a diving training trip to the Caribbean and complains of severe cellulitis and irritation affecting his right ear. He has been diving both in the sea and in a large heated training pool. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication. Examination reveals an erythematous right external auditory meatus with obvious discharging pus, which has a very strong odour. The right eardrum appears not to have perforated. There is no significant pain on palpation of the skull around the ear.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gentamicin drops

The most likely diagnosis is otitis externa, commonly caused by pseudomonas otitis externa. Pseudomonas infections are sensitive to local therapy with gentamicin drops. This can be combined with local corticosteroids to reduce local inflammation and pain due to swelling. Where the eardrum has perforated, local preparations that do not contain gentamicin are preferred to reduce the risks of ototoxicity. Should systemic therapy be indicated, such as if cellulitis spreads beyond the ear canal or has systemic signs of infection, then a 7-day course of flucloxacillin or, in the case of penicillin allergy, clarithromycin is indicated.

E Oral erythromycin

This patient does not have features of systemic illness or cellulitis extending beyond the ear canal. As such, local therapy is indicated. Should systemic therapy be indicated, then a 7-day course of flucloxacillin or, in the case of penicillin allergy, clarithromycin should be used.

B Intravenous (IV) ciprofloxacin

IV antibiotics are reserved for systemic infection and extensive local infection only. While quinolones +/- aminoglycosides are suitable IV options in severe disease, should there be an absence of suitable alternatives, quinolone use should be avoided due to orthopaedic and neurologic complications.

C Oral ciprofloxacin

The most likely diagnosis is otitis externa, commonly caused by pseudomonas otitis externa. The patient’s presentation indicates local infection and treatment should be guided based on this. Should IV treatment be required, due to severe or refractory disease, then fluoroquinolones should only be used if there are no suitable alternatives due to orthopaedic and neurological complications associated with the class of antibiotics.

D Oral co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav’s spectrum of antibiotic activity doesn’t covers pseudomonas. the first treatment of choice in systemically well patients is gentamicin drops. Should systemic therapy be indicated, then a 7-day course of flucloxacillin or, in the case of penicillin allergy, clarithromycin is indicated.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man attends the clinic complaining of diarrhoea, fatigue, fevers and right upper quadrant pain. He admits to recreational use of crystal metamphetamine.

On examination, he looks very thin and has tender hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. He attends with his partner who is very concerned about him.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)90 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.6 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)184 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)282 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Computed tomography (CT) abdomenRetroperitoneal, para-aortic lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly
Small bowel biopsyAcid-fast bacteria (AFB) seen, MTB PCR negative

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Mycobacterium avium

This patient is anaemic, with low platelets and a low white cell count giving evidence of infection, evidence of lymphadenopathy on CT scan, and non-TB AFBs identified on biopsy. The additional abnormalities seen in LFTs point towards the possibility of Mycobacterium avium as being the most likely cause of this presentation. This

patient has a history of crystal metamphetamine use, raising the possibility of HIV infection, and subsequent immunocompromise. Triple antibiotic therapy is usually required in HIV-infected patients; one possible combination suggested is clarithromycin, ethambutol and rifabutin.

D Myocbacterium tuberculosis

Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic bacterial infection caused by M. tuberculosis. Primary TB most commonly affects the lungs, however almost all organ systems may be infected. A similar syndrome to that described may be present in patients with GI or miliary (disseminated TB); however we are told in the vignette that the MTB PCR is negative, this makes Mycobacterium TB infection much less likely.

A Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection

Primary CMV infection causes a glandular fever syndrome typified by fever, lethargy and lymphadenopathy. Although CMV reactivation in the immunocompromised host can present with colitis, the small bowel biopsy results point to an alternative diagnosis.

B Cryptosporidium

Cryptosporidium parvum is a protozoan which causes a self-limiting diarrhoeal illness. In the context of immunosuppression it may cause a severe diarrhoeal illness or disseminated infection affecting multiple organ systems which may prove fatal. Treatment is primarily supportive in the immunocompetent host while treatment of the underlying immunosuppression (eg HAART in HIV-positive patients) is key in the immunocompromised. Here the small bowel biopsy results point to an alternative diagnosis.

E Tropical sprue

Tropoical sprue is a gastrointestinal condition in which inflammation and subsequent flattening of small bowel villi leads to malabsorption. The underlying aetiology is not well understood but there may be an infectious cause. The presentation is with signs and symptoms associated with malabsorption (particularly of vitamin B12 and folic acid). 20591

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of frontal headache, nausea and vomiting. Eleven months ago, he had had a left cerebellopontine angle tumour removed, and 1 week before this presentation, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt had been inserted for hydrocephalus.

On examination, the temperature is 37.9 °C. Pupils are reactive and equal to light, and fundoscopy is normal. There is a left facial nerve palsy, without sparing of the upper face. Kernig’s sign is positive.

Initial investigations are as follows:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)310 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
C-reactive protein180 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Serum glucose5.1 mmol3.9–7.1 mmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)35 mm/first hour1–10 mm/first hour

Which is the most likely causative organism to be found in the cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Staphylococcus epidermidis

This is a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species and it is the most common cause of meningitis after neurosurgical procedures; this patient has just had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed. Therefore, it is the most likely culprit in this case. The consideration of coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species is important, and these organisms are typically penicillin-resistant. Treatment would need to be given in line with local guidelines but is likely to include vancomycin.

C Neisseria meningitidis

N. meningitidis is one of the most common causes of meningitis in the United Kingdom. However, this patient has had a neurosurgical procedure; meningitis in these patients is caused by a different group of organisms. The most common cause of post-procedure meningitis is S. epidermidis, a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species, and this is the answer in this case.

A Escherichia coli

Although E. coli is one of the causes of meningitis in patients following neurosurgical procedures (such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion), it is not the most common. The most common organism implicated in these infections is the coagulase-negative Staphylococcus epidermidis, which is the correct answer in this case.

B Haemophilus influenzae type B

Before routine vaccination against Haemophilus, this was a common cause of meningitis in ‘normal’ patients. However, a different group of organisms are implicated in post-surgical meningitis, the most common of which is the coagulase-negative S. epidermidis (which is the correct answer in this case).

E Streptococcus pneumoniae

This is one of the most common causes of meningitis in adults in the UK; however, this patient has recently had a neurosurgical procedure which has a different epidemiology. The most common cause of meningitis post- procedure is coagulase-negative S. epidermidis, and therefore this is the correct answer. 71449

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man is admitted unconscious to the Emergency Department, brought in by his partner. His partner states he has has been complaining of increasingly severe headaches over the past few days and collapsed that morning, having suffered a tonic–clonic seizure. The patient has lost approximately six kg in weight over the past five months and has been suffering from multiple chest infections. On examination, he is pyrexial at 38.1 °C. His BP is 155/90 mmHg and his heart rate 90 bpm and regular. He has a GCS score of 10. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema and his pupils are poorly reactive.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.3 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
CD4 lymphocyte count82 cells/mm³430–1690 cells/mm³
Platelets (PLT)171 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)130 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine102 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Glucose5.4 mmol/L 3.5–5.5 mmol/L
On the CT head, there are multiple ring-enhancing lesions.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Toxoplasmosis

This patient has a likely diagnosis of toxoplasmosis, given the presentation with fever, headaches, altered mental status, reduced GCS score and ring-enhancing lesions on CT, imaging. In association with a history of weight loss, recurrent infections and a low CD4 count (particularly under 200 cells/mm³), toxoplasmosis should be considered as the likely diagnosis. The CT findings typically include multiple ring-enhancing lesions of variable sizes.

B Cryptococcal meningitis

Cryptococcal meningitis is a fungal infection secondary to Cryptococcus neoformans and presents similarly to bacterial meningitis with fever, headache, altered mental status and seizures. However, CT imaging does not demonstrate ring-enhancing lesions. Rather, CT imaging shows leptomeningeal enhancement, cryptococcomas and hydrocephalus.

A Cerebral lymphoma

Cerebral lymphoma is a reasonable differential diagnosis, given the presence of ring-enhancing lesions in a patient with a likely underlying diagnosis of HIV with a CD4 count of under 200 cells/mm3. On the CT, a single ring-enhancing lesion may be seen. However, given the presence of fever and multiple ring-enhancing lesions, an alternative diagnosis, such as toxoplasmosis, must be considered.

C Tuberculous meningitis

Although immunosuppression would put this patient at risk of tuberculous meningitis, CT imaging is similar to cryptococcosis, with leptomeningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus in the later stages.

E Subarachnoid haemorrhage

Subarachnoid haemorrhage classically presents with the sudden-onset occipital headache associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness and reduced GCS score. This presentation is more gradual in onset and would not explain the CT findings.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old woman presents to the Genitourinary Clinic for review. She complains of a 5-day history of mucopurulent vaginal discharge and dysuria. She confirms that she has had three regular sexual partners and uses the intrauterine system as contraception. She has no past medical history of note and no allergies.

On examination, she has a temperature of 36.7 °C. Her blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg and her heart rate is 88 bpm. There is lower abdominal tenderness on palpation.

Endocervical swab – nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT): Gram-negative diplococci.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline and oral metronidazole
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Intramuscular ceftriaxone

This patient has a likely diagnosis of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, given the positive endocervical swab for Gram-negative diplococci. The most recent guidelines from the British Association of Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) advise giving a one-off dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone for the treatment of gonorrhoea.

E Oral doxycycline

Oral Doxycycline is not indicated for gonorrhoea. Rather, it is used in the treatment of chlamydia.

B Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin

This used to be the recommended treatment for gonorrhoea, particularly if there were concerns regarding additional infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. However, this is no longer recommended by BASHH.

C Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline and oral metronidazole

This is used in the treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease. Although Neisseria gonorrhoeae is capable of causing pelvic inflammatory disease, additional features that this patient would be expected to present with would be signs of systemic upset such as fever and tachycardia.

D Oral ciprofloxacin

Traditionally, this was the treatment of choice for gonorrhoea. However, it is no longer the first-line treatment of choice because of the widespread resistance of Gonococcus to quinolones.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man presents with his partner for review. For the past few days he has had worsening diarrhoea with voluminous fluid loss.

On further questioning, he admits to weight loss over the past 6 months. Modified acid-fast staining of stool culture reveals red-stained round oocysts against a blue–green background. Investigations reveal a reduced CD4/CD8 ratio.

Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial step in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D HIV testing

This patient has diarrhoea with a stool sample that suggests oocysts consistent with Cryptosporidium infection. The reduced CD4/CD8 ratio raises the possibility of HIV infection, and screening for HIV is clearly required. In patients with a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm³ blood, chronic diarrhoea is common once Cryptosporidium infection is established. Antibiotic trials for Cryptosporidium have been disappointing, and at present there is not enough evidence to recommend any particular regime, but some patients do appear to respond to nitzoxanide. In patients who are HIV-negative, the infection tends to be self-limiting and patients recover after only a few days.

C IV cefotaxime

Cefotaxime provides good broad-spectrum cover and is useful in meningitis and pneumonia rather than for gastrointestinal infections.

A Oral ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin may be considered as a treatment option for gastrointestinal infection with Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter. The abnormal staining of acid-fast pathogens makes this unlikely. In addition, the partner is not unwell and there is no history of ingestion of contaminated food.

B Oral metronidazole

Metronidazole would be a good antibiotic choice if anaerobes such as Gardnerella, Entamoeba, Giardia or Clostridium were suspected. This might be suspected with bloody diarrhoea or, for C. difficile, recent antibiotic use.

E Oral co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav provides far better cover for respiratory and urinary infections and would be of little use for this patient. 33186

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presented with fever 1 week after returning from India. Her fevers followed a specific pattern, rising over the course of the day and then dropping by the next morning. She also had non-specific abdominal pain, malaise and a dry cough. She had noticed a rash on her trunk.

On examination, her temperature was 38.1 °C and she appeared dehydrated. She had diffuse abdominal tenderness and a pink maculopapular rash over her trunk.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin119 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
PLatelets201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Stool cultureIsolates of Salmonella paratyphi

The patient is keen not to be admitted to hospital.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Azithromycin

This patient has typhoid fever, which can be caused by Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi subtypes. Her presentation with high intermittent fever, dry cough, malaise and abdominal pain is typical. Patients classically have constipation rather than diarrhoea. Typhoid fever can be treated with fluoroquinolones; however, given that this patient has contracted typhoid fever after travelling to India, there is a high chance that the organism is fluoroquinolone resistant, and azithromycin would be a safer choice of treatment.

B Doxycycline

This patient has typhoid fever, caused by S. paratyphi and indicated by her intermittent high fevers, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and non-specific abdominal pain, in combination with the findings on stool culture. Although doxycyline provides some coverage of Salmonella, there is widespread resistance amongst typhi and paratyphi species. A better and safer choice of antibiotic in this case would be azithromycin.

A Ciprofloxacin

This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with typhoid fever: the high intermittent fever, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and non-specific abdominal pain, and stool culture has confirmed the presence of S. paratyphi. Typhoid fever can be treated with fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin; however, there is widespread resistance amongst typhoid organisms to fluoroquinolones, especially in India. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. Consequently, azithromycin would be a safer choice of treatment for this patient.

C Erythromycin

This patient has typhoid fever – hence the intermittent high fever, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and non-specific abdominal pain – confirmed by the finding of S. paratyphi in the stool culture. Salmonella paratyphi is a Gram- negative rod: erythromycin has poor Gram-negative coverage and is used for Gram-positive infections. Consequently it would be a poor choice of antibiotic to treat this patient: a better choice would be azithromycin. Ciprofloxacin can also be used to treat typhoid fever, but resistance to fluoroquinolones is rife, especially in India, and therefore azithromycin is the best choice in this case.

E Flucloxacillin

This patient’s intermittent high fever, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and diffuse abdominal pain is consistent with typhoid fever, given her travel history. This is confirmed with the finding of S. paratyphi in her stool. Salmonella paratyphi is a Gram-negative rod: flucloxacillin is typically used for Gram-positive infections and has poor activity against Salmonella. Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin would be better choices of antibiotic for this patient. Due to the prevalence of fluoroquinolone resistance, especially in India, azithromycin would be the best choice in this case.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department, having returned 24 hours earlier from a holiday to Thailand. He has been living in the remote north of the country and been eating mainly local food. He admits to a diarrhoeal illness a few days earlier but now feels constipated and is complaining of increasing abdominal pain and distension. He also has a severe headache that is non-responsive to paracetamol. On examination, his temperature is 38.9 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg and pulse 85 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination reveals mild hepatosplenomegaly with tenderness. Bowel sounds appear sluggish but normal, and the rectum is empty on rectal examination. You notice a rash with sparse pink papules over the upper body.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)189 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine95 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)189 mg/L< 5 mg/L
Glucose7.0 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L

Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Ceftriaxone

The history here fits with possible typhoid fever, given the likelihood of exposure during his holiday to Thailand and typical features, including abdominal pain and a typhoid fever-associated skin rash. In this case, with significant fever and abdominal pain, ceftriaxone is the most appropriate intervention. Use of quinolones (an alternative here) is discouraged because of adverse events associated with the class.

A Chloramphenicol

Chloramphenicol is an option for treating typhoid fever where there is evidence of multidrug resistance. We have no evidence here that treatment with ceftriaxone will be unsuccessful.

C Metronidazole

Metronidazole is the intervention of choice for giardiasis, which does not fit with the symptom picture here. Giardiasis is associated with symptoms typical of irritable bowel syndrome.

D Oral rehydration salts

Oral rehydration salts are most important in the management of severe diarrhoea where pre-renal failure may ensue. Examples where they are of value is in norovirus infection in vulnerable patients and in patients with cholera.

E Senna

Prokinetic agents, such as senna, are not advised in the treatment of typhoid fever. Bowel function recovers slowly once the underlying infection is treated.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of fever, shortness of breath and a cough with haemoptysis. He had returned from Mississippi 3 weeks previously, where he was studying bats. He had no other medical conditions.

On examination, his temperature was 37.6 °C, and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. He appeared well and comfortable at rest. There was bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin112 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets120 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)35 mm/1 st hr0–10 mm in the 1 st hour
Sputum cultureYeast forms

His chest X-ray is shown below.

What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Itraconazole

This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with a diagnosis of histoplasmosis. This would also fit with his travel history as it is endemic to areas with large bat and bird populations, such as Mississippi, Ohio and Missouri. In this relatively mild case, a prolonged course of itraconazole would be most appropriate.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HilarAdenopathyNo.png (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HilarAdenopathyNo.png)

C Doxycycline

Doxycycline is an antibiotic used in the management of community-acquired pneumonia in patients with pre- existing respiratory conditions, and in the management of rickettsial illness (e.g. Rocky Mountain spotted fever).
