It would not be appropriate for the treatment of a fungal or yeast infection, as seen here. It has no role in histoplasmosis.

B Amphotericin

This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with histoplasmosis where amphotericin would be the correct treatment in severe disease, but here in relatively mild disease, a prolonged course of itraconazole would be more appropriate.

D Ganciclovir

Ganciclovir is an antiviral therapy, which would not be appropriate for the treatment of this patient’s yeast infection.

E Prednisolone

Occasionally steroids such as methylprednisolone may be used in conjunction with antifungals in the treatment of severe disease, or complications of histoplasmosis (such as pericarditis); however, prednisolone has no role in treating mild disease.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a febrile illness one day after commencing oral doxycycline prescribed by the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic the previous day. He has a temperature of 38.0 °C; his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. There is a generalised maculopapular rash. His cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable and his neurological examination is entirely normal.

Investigation results from Genitourinary Medicine Clinic are shown below:

InvestigationResult
Treponemal enzyme immunoassay (EIA)Positive
Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) serologyPositive

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Paracetamol

This patient has a diagnosis of syphilis, given the positive treponemal enzyme immunoassay and venereal disease research laboratory serology tests. He almost certainly is experiencing a Jarisch–Herxheimer (JH) reaction, which is thought to be related to the sudden release of large amounts of endotoxin due to the death of spirochaetes after initially commencing antibiotics. In the majority of patients, it carries a benign course and no intervention is required. Initial therapy is with paracetamol. Steroids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can be considered for patients with severe symptoms, although they are not thought to influence outcomes.

D Prednisolone

Corticosteroids are usually only prescribed for patients with a severe JH reaction whose symptoms are not responsive to paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. They do not have an impact on the clearance of syphilis infection.

A Aspirin

Given the Jarisch–Herxheimer (JH) reaction is driven by endotoxin release, aspirin does not have a role in its management. Paracetamol is the initial therapy of choice, and a conventional non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen, could be added in the event that symptoms are not controlled.

B Chlorpheniramine

Although chlorphenamine is not a routine component of treatment for the JH reaction, it is recommended as part of European guidelines on syphilis as pre-treatment to prevent it from occurring.

C Diazepam

Sedatives are not usually considered in the management of the JH reaction. In cases where sedation is required, a sedating antihistamine, such as chlorphenamine, is more commonly prescribed.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 2-week history of malaise, headaches and reduced oral intake. He also has a history of dry cough for the last week and sharp right-sided chest pain on deep inspiration.

His observations show a temperature of 38.3 °C, a heart rate of 108 bpm and regular and a blood pressure of 142/91 mmHg. On examination, he has coarse crackles at the right base but no audible wheeze. His respiratory rate is 23 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturations of 90% on room air. He has dry mucous membranes with mild stomatitis.

A rash is seen over his arms and trunk and is shown below:

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)90 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)16.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils13.4 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.5 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.1 ×10⁹/L0.8–5.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)243 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)148 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.7 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea10.3 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)175 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)4960+
Bilirubin36 µmol/L1–22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)60 U/L7–55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)90 U/L30–150 U/L
Albumin40 g/L35–55 g/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)99 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Mycoplasma pneumoniae

This patient has an atypical pneumonia that is most likely secondary to the bacterium M. pneumoniae. Common presenting features include a preceding phase of flu-like symptoms before the onset of respiratory symptoms, including shortness of breath and productive cough. Extrapulmonary symptoms are also seen. This patient has erythema multiforme, as shown by the target lesion rash, and the low haemoglobin and raised bilirubin levels suggest a haemolytic process. It is likely that this patient would have a positive Coombs’ test.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bulls_eye_lesion_of_Erythema_multiforme.jpg

C Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is a common cause of pneumonia in patients following an infection with the influenza virus. Although this patient does give a history of flu-like symptoms, staphylococcal pneumonia would not cause all of this patient’s presenting symptoms.

A Mycobacterium tuberculosis

M. tuberculosis is the organism responsible for the respiratory illness tuberculosis. Symptoms of tuberculosis have a more insidious onset, with constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fever and night sweats also common. This is not seen in the patient, making it unlikely here.

B Streptococcus pneumoniae

S. pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia. However, it does not explain the erythema multiforme. These additional symptoms suggest an atypical pneumonia, with Mycoplasma pneumonia being the most likely diagnosis.

E Legionella pneumophila

Legionnaire’s disease is a bacterial pneumonia caused by the bacterium L. pneumophila. It presents with symptoms of community-acquired pneumonia. However, additional symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea are commonly seen and blood tests often show hyponatraemia and deranged liver function tests. It is commonly spread in contaminated water supply, and a careful travel history is needed as it can spread via air conditioning in hotels. It does not explain all of the findings in this patient, making M. pneumoniae more likely here.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man presents to the Sexual Health Clinic with painful lesions on his penis that have progressively worsened over the past four weeks. He reports having unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. The lesion began as small, red and raised and slowly progressed to intensely painful ulcers.

On examination, he was found to have multiple painful penile ulcers, with the largest measuring 2.5 cm. A tender, soft, fluctuant swelling is present in the right inguinal region.

Gram staining from the base of the largest penile ulcer revealed Gram-negative rods arranged in a chain-like fashion.

Which of the following is the best line of treatment in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone

This person is suffering from chancroid due to infection with Haemophilus ducreyi. Gram staining shows the presence of a school of fish appearance. Single-dose therapy with intramuscular ceftriaxone is recommended as the first line of management. Oral azithromycin has also been found to be equally effective. In addition, fluctuant lymphadenitis (as present in this patient) should be drained by needle aspiration.

E Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole

Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole is not the first line of management for chancroid. It has been used as an alternative to azithromycin in the management of granuloma inguinale caused by Klebsiella granulomatis.

A Intramuscular benzathine penicillin

Intramuscular benzathine penicillin has been used for the treatment of syphilis, which usually presents with a painless ulcer and non-fluctuant, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.

B Oral aciclovir

Genital herpes usually presents with multiple painful ulcers that start as vesicles and Gram staining is usually negative. Treatment for genital herpes is oral aciclovir.

C Oral doxycycline

Oral doxycycline is the treatment of choice for lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. LGV presents with a small, painless ulcer, which usually disappears by the time the inguinal buboes appear.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of increasing fatigue, fever and rigors. The fever appears to come on every few days. He has recently come back from Long Island, where he stayed with family. He remembers being bitten by a tick, which he subsequently removed. He has a history of hypertension and he had his spleen removed following a road traffic accident 12 years ago. He is taking aspirin, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and penicillin V. He is a non-smoker.

On examination, he is jaundiced, looks unwell, is slightly confused and has a temperature of 38.7 °C. He has no lymphadenopathy. His pulse is 120 bpm and regular and blood pressure 95/60 mmHg. His chest is clear and his abdomen is soft but non-specifically tender. He has no neurological abnormality.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)71 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.3 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)97 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)132 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)189 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)80.2 fL76–98 fL
C-reactive protein (CRP)213 µg/L< 10 mg/L
Serum electrophoresisPolyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia
Chest X-ray (CXR)Clear
UrinalysisHaemoglobinuria

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Babesiosis

This is a tick-borne malaria-like illness caused by species of the intra-erythrocytic protozoan Babesia. Patients present with similar symptoms to malaria, i.e. fever, chills and rigors. The intra-erythrocytic Babesia destroy the red blood cells, causing haemolytic anaemia and haemoglobinuria. Symptoms are greater with a higher percentage of parasitism. A B-lymphocyte response is elicited with a secondary reactive polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia Babesiosis is frequent in endemic areas of the USA, particularly Long Island, New York and Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts.

Patients without a spleen have a more fulminant and prolonged clinical course and may have an overwhelming infection and a fatal outcome.

Babesiosis is often a clinical diagnosis, and the history of a recent trip to Long Island and being bitten should differentiate this from malaria. In addition, patients with malaria often have a more pronounced headache. Lyme disease does not cause haemolytic anaemia, and nocardiosis is only fulminant in the immunocompromised.

For immunocompetent individuals with mild to moderate Babesia microti infection, treatment with oral azithromycin (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/azithromycin-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link) plus oral atovaquone (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/atovaquone-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link) is needed. For immunocompetent individuals with severe B. microti infection, treatment with intravenous (IV) azithromycin (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/azithromycin-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link) plus oral atovaquone (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/atovaquone-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link); IV clindamycin (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clindamycin-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link) plus oral quinine (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/quinine-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link) is an alternative regimen. Patients with severe B. microti infection may warrant exchange transfusion. Exchange transfusion is recommended for patients with high-grade parasitemia (>10%), severe hemolysis (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), or organ (pulmonary, renal, or liver) impairment. For immunocompromised patients with severe B. microti infection, initial treatment with IV azithromycin (https://www.uptodate.com/contents/azithromycin-drug-information? search=babesiosis+treatment&topicRef=113483&source=see_link) plus oral atovaquone is recommended. The usual duration of treatment is 7-10 days. In immunocompromised with high risk of relapse up to 6 weeks of treatment may be required.

C Lyme Disease

Lyme disease is an infectious illness caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi. It is transmitted through tick bites. It initially presents with a slowly expanding skin lesion around the tick bite, erythema migrans, malaise and joint aches. If not treated, neurological, cardiac and joint involvement can occur. The patient described here is profoundly unwell and does not have erythema migrans; this would not be typical of acute Lyme disease.

B Perforated duodenal ulcer

The history presented here is not consistent with a perforated duodenal ulcer, you would not expect a 2-week history of fatigue and rigors. In addition, examination would more usually reveal abdominal guarding with tenderness localising to the epigastrium. Jaundice and thrombocytopenia would also not be present.

D Malaria

Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by several different species of the genus Plasmodium. It is transmitted by the female anopheles mosquito. Malaria is endemic neither in the United States nor the United Kingdom, and therefore could not be the diagnosis in this patient.

E Nocardiosis

Nocardiosis is an uncommon infection caused by Gram-positive bacteria of the genus Nocardia. It may present as a localised (most commonly pulmonary or central nervous system) or systemic infection. The majority of patients affected have underlying immunodeficiency (HIV, immunosuppressive therapy, malignancy), which makes nocardiosis unlikely in our patient. 7235

questions.question:
A 33-year-old pregnant woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 6-day history of worsening shortness of breath. Since the breathlessness has worsened, she has developed pleuritic chest pain and a cough productive of purulent green sputum. She has been feeling very lethargic with generalised body aches and occasional episodes of diarrhoea. Her past medical history includes iron deficiency anaemia, for which she takes ferrous sulfate 200 mg three times a day. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination, she is tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 29 breaths/min and her saturations are 89% on room air. She has audible crackles at the base of her right lung. Her heart rate is 100 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 110/69 mmHg; her heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is soft, with a palpable uterus consistent with 20-week gestation. She has a temperature of 38.1 °C.

What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Intravenous amoxicillin

This question describes a pregnant woman who has presented with symptoms of pneumonia. She is lethargic with flu-like symptoms and is systemically unwell on examination with tachycardia, tachypnoea and hypoxia. A presentation similar to this in a pregnant woman should raise suspicion of listeriosis. Patients who are immunocompromised and pregnant women are more susceptible to listeriosis and it can lead to miscarriage or premature delivery, making prompt treatment vital. Treatment of listeriosis is with amoxicillin or ampicillin.

D Intravenous ceftriaxone

This patient has listeriosis. Listeria has shown resistance to cephalosporins, making ceftriaxone a less appropriate choice.

A Intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin

This patient has listeriosis, the treatment of which is intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin. While intravenous co- amoxiclav would be appropriate, clarithromycin is teratogenic and studies have shown higher rates of spontaneous abortion in those treated with clarithromycin in the first trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, clarithromycin should be avoided.

B Oral doxycycline

Doxycycline is not used in the treatment of listeriosis and is contraindicated in pregnant women due to the risk of teratogenic side effects, including enamel hypoplasia and teeth discolouration and should be avoided when possible.

E Oral ciprofloxacin

This patient has listeriosis, the treatment of which is intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin. Ciprofloxacin has no role in treating listeriosis. Animal studies have shown an increased risk of arthropathy during pregnancy and for that reason, ciprofloxacin is contraindicated in pregnant women.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of flu-like symptoms and fatigue. Six weeks previously he had had unprotected receptive anal sexual intercourse.

On examination, he had low-volume cervical lymphadenopathy; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
White cell count (WCC)5.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils3.9 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes0.9 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 4.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)40 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Hepatitis B surface antigen-
Hepatitis B core antibody+
HIV antibody-
Epstein–Barr virus IgM-
Epstein–Barr virus IgG+

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D HIV

This would explain the patient’s flu-like illness and lymphadenopathy, and the timing would fit with his exposure through unprotected sexual intercourse: seroconversion is typically at 6 weeks after exposure. The lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia are common features of seroconversion. It is quite common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion: a p24 antigen test should also be carried out, and testing should be repeated as suspicion is high. If investigations confirm the diagnosis, guidance suggests that the patient should be started on antiretroviral therapy straight away.

E Influenza

Influenza would explain his symptoms, and the lymphopenia (commonly seen in viral infections). However, lymphadenopathy is less typical of influenza and he does not complain of any coryzal symptoms. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion; he has had a potential exposure 6 weeks previously, which would fit with the timing of his illness. HIV seroconversion would also explain his thrombocytopenia and lymphadenopathy. It is common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion.

A Early Epstein–Barr virus

This patient has serology consistent with a previous, but not a recent, infection. After Epstein–Barr infection, IgG remains positive at a variable titre for life; IgM is only positive 4–8 weeks after an acute infection, and remains positive for up to a year. This patient has a positive IgG, indicating previous infection, but with a negative IgM it is unlikely that this is acute Epstein–Barr virus infection. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion – HIV antibody can be negative before seroconversion is complete. This would explain the flu- like illness and lymphadenopathy; the timing would also fit with a possible exposure through unprotected sexual intercourse.

B Hepatitis B

This patient has serology consistent with past infection with hepatitis B virus (i.e. he is core antibody positive), but there is no evidence that he is a carrier as he is surface antigen negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen would be positive within the first 3–5 weeks of infection. Instead, this patient has symptoms and signs consistent with acute HIV infection and seroconversion: he has a flu-like illness, lymphadenopathy and he has had unprotected sex 6 weeks previously. It is common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion.

C Herpes

Patients who contract genital herpes can have a prodromal flu-like illness and lymphadenopathy, but this would typically occur earlier than 6 weeks after exposure. There are no genital ulcers on examination, though these can occur after the flu-like illness has subsided. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion: this would explain his flu-like illness and lymphadenopathy, and the timing would fit with his exposure through unprotected sexual intercourse. It is quite common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old woman with type I diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with severe earache and discharge. She has recently returned from a holiday in the Dominican Republic where she regularly swam in the hotel pool.

She saw her GP one week early and was prescribed co-amoxiclav, but her partner thinks that the problem is getting worse and they can now see the infection around her ear.

Her ear is shown below.

Which of the following represents the most likely infectious agent?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Pseudomonas aeruginosa

The image shows severe otitis externa with surrounding erythema and tissue destruction. This woman has presented with so called “Swimmer’s Ear” due to pseudomonas infection which may have occurred via the swimming pool at the hotel where she was staying Pseudomonas is the cause of swimmer’s ear and is not responsive to co-amoxiclav therapy. Severe spreading infections occur more commonly in patients who also suffer from diabetes mellitus, as in this case. Therapy may involve a combination of systemic and locally delivered antibiotic therapy, and in this case an ENT surgical opinion should sought.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OtitisExterna10.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OtitisExterna10.JPG)

D Streptococcus pneumoniae

Streptococci are gram-positive diplococci, of which S. pneumoniae cases pneumonia, meningitis and otitis media. The clinical finding of otitis externa makes this a less likely pathogen.

A Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is a gram-positive commensal pathogen which can cause infection of skin, eyelids and wounds. In severe infections can cause pneumonia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis and septic arthritis. The toxins can cause food poisoning and toxic shock syndrome. S. aureus is unlikely to cause infection, and unlikely to be acquired by swimming in a swimming pool.

B Staphylococcus epidermidis

S. epidermidis is a coagulase negative species of Staphylococcus. These species are only pathogenic if associated with immunosuppression or insertion of foreign objects such as following hip replacements. These bacteria are likely to cause otitis externa in an immunosuppressed individual.

E Streptococcus pyogenes

S. pyogenes is s group A Streptococcus, referring to the Lancefield classification by degree of heamolysis. These species cause wound and skin infections, including impetigo and erysipelas, and are also associated with tonsillitis, scarlet fever and rheumatic fever.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. Her bowel movements were normal.

On examination, her temperature was 37.9 oC and her blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg. Her abdomen was soft but tender in both iliac fossae. There was anterior tenderness on digital rectal examination. On speculum examination there was profuse white–yellow vaginal discharge and tenderness. A urine pregnancy test was negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Acute salpingitis

Most cases are associated with sexually transmitted infection. Patients present with lower abdominal pain, a fever and vaginal discharge. The Fitz–Hughes–Curtis syndrome associated with Chlamydia infection is caused by infection tracking up the right paracolic gutter to cause a peri-hepatitis. These patients may also have right hypochondrial pain, fever and mild elevations in liver biochemistry.

D Ectopic pregnancy

This patient has a negative pregnancy test, which would make an ectopic pregnancy very unlikely. Ectopic pregnancies typically cause a unilateral lower abdominal pain, and may be accompanied by vaginal bleeding. It would not cause vaginal discharge of the type seen here. This constellation of abdominal pain, fever and vaginal discharge is more suggestive of acute salpingitis.

A Acute appendicitis

Acute appendicitis is an important differential diagnosis in any patient presenting with right iliac fossa pain; however, this patient is opening her bowels normally, does not have any signs of peritonism and has vaginal discharge. Acute salpingitis would be a better explanation of her presentation.

C Bacterial vaginosis

Bacterial vaginosis does cause vaginal discharge, but does not cause abdominal pain or fever. It is most commonly caused by Gardnerella vaginalis. This patient’s abdominal pain, fever and vaginal discharge are suggestive of acute salpingitis, which is typically caused by a sexually transmitted infection such as Chlamydia. Gardnerella is not a sexually transmitted infection.

E Ruptured ovarian cyst

A ruptured ovarian cyst can cause abdominal pain, but it could not explain the vaginal discharge seen here. The patient may have a low-grade fever. Instead, this patient’s symptoms of abdominal pain, fever and vaginal discharge are consistent with acute salpingitis. 71142

questions.question:
A 47-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with foul-smelling diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and excessive burping since returning from his annual summer holiday to Thailand.

Examination reveals a BP of 122/72 mmHg, and his heart rate is 70 bpm and regular. He is apyrexial. His abdomen is mildly distended, but soft and non-tender. There are active bowel sounds. Flagellate protozoa are identified in the stool sample.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Metronidazole

The symptoms here fit with giardiasis, and the presence of protozoa in the stool sample confirms the underlying diagnosis. Potential interventions include metronidazole and tinidazole. Some activity of mebendazole is noted against Giardia, although it is not a first-line therapeutic option. Long-term complications of giardiasis are rare. Lactose intolerance is the most commonly reported long-term consequence of infection. Very rare sequelae include cholecystitis and reactive arthritis.

A Azithromycin

Azithromycin can be used in the treatment of traveller’s diarrhoea caused by Escherichia coli, although it does not have a role in the treatment of giardiasis.

B Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin is a potential intervention for Salmonella or Campylobacter infection. These are both associated with acute presentations with gastroenteritis rather than with the chronic symptoms of Giardia colonisation seen here.

C Nitazoxanide

Cryptosporidium is a reasonable differential for giardiasis. It results in a diarrhoeal illness with lethargy, nausea, abdominal cramps and fever. It typically occurs in patients who are immunocompromised, such as patients with untreated HIV. It can be distinguished from giardiasis via stool antigen testing or microscopy, where the oocysts can be seen, unlike in the stool sample here. Where a patient has untreated HIV, the initial management is supportive and with the initiation of anti-retroviral therapy. Where symptoms are persistent, but not severe, nitazoxanide can be considered.

E Praziquantel

Praziquantel is an anthelmintic used to treat flukes and schistosomiasis. While it does have some efficacy in treating giardiasis, it is not used as it is not as effective as metronidazole or tinidazole. 38392

questions.question:
A 53-year-old woman presented to clinic with concerns about her exposure to chickenpox. She had a background of systemic lupus erythematosus and was taking high-dose prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine. She had no personal history of chickenpox. The patient had been exposed to chickenpox 2 days ago whilst looking after her 4-year-old granddaughter, who had become symptomatic with chickenpox. The patient is tested for IgG varicella antibody, which is found to be positive.

What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Reassurance

This patient is IgG positive for varicella, and therefore she has previously had chickenpox and is immune to her granddaughter’s infection. She may have been so young, or had sufficiently mild symptoms, that she has no memory of the original infection. There is no need for any treatment and the patient can be reassured.

E Varicella zoster immunoglobulin

This would be the correct treatment if this patient had never had chickenpox and had been exposed, given her background of immunosuppression. However, this patient is in fact immune to chickenpox: she is varicella IgG antibody positive. She may have had the infection at such a young age that she has no memory of it, or she may have been minimally symptomatic and therefore failed to realise that she had contracted the disease. As she is immune, she does not require any specific treatment and can be reassured.

A Aciclovir

This patient is IgG antibody positive, which suggests that she has had a previous chickenpox infection and therefore will be immune to reinfection. Even if this patient were not immune, aciclovir would not be appropriate: instead the patient should be given varicella immunoglobulin within 4 days of exposure. In this case, as the patient is already immune to chickenpox, no treatment is necessary and she can be reassured.

B Ganciclovir

As this patient is IgG antibody positive for varicella, she has previously had chickenpox. Sometimes patients are almost completely asymptomatic with only a few lesions, and she may have contracted the disease at a young age and had no memory of it. As such, she is immune and therefore reassurance is the only management necessary. If she had not been immune, varicella immunoglobulin would have been the most appropriate treatment.

D Varicella immunisation

Varicella is a live vaccine and therefore should not be given to immunosuppressed patients. In fact, this patient is already immune to varicella (as she is IgG positive). She may have had the disease at a very young age and forgotten, or had minimal symptoms. As such, she does not require any treatment and can be reassured. If she were not immune, varicella immunoglobulin would be the appropriate treatment.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old woman returns from a trip to America in May. During her stay, she became unwell with a high fever, headache and muscle pains. She consulted a local doctor who noticed a rash on the palms of her hands and soles of her feet. She was admitted to hospital where a diagnosis was made and she was commenced on antibiotics. The patient improved and was discharged and allowed to fly home with a course of oral antibiotics. She recalls the doctors in America telling her that the infection had been transmitted by a tick bite.

She currently takes medication for diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and atrial fibrillation.

What medication would you stop till the antibiotic course is finished?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Aluminium hydroxide

The patient is most likely to be taking a tetracycline antibiotic for a rickettsial infection. The diagnosis in this patient is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. It is caused by a tick bite that results in the above symptoms. The classic rash is described as occurring on the palms and soles. Treatment of choice is doxycyline, which is a tetracycline and acts on 30S ribosomes to prevent protein synthesis in the infecting organism. Aluminium hydroxide can complex with this antibiotic in the gastrointestinal tract, preventing absorption. Dairy products ingested at the same time can also cause this. Side effects of tetracyclines include discoloration of teeth in children, hepatoxicity and photosensitivity.

D Aspirin

The main concerns with respect to aspirin are pharmacodynamic ones with anti-coagulants or other anti- platelet agents.

A Metformin

There are few significant drug interaction concerns for metformin. One of the main problems is bile salt malabsorption leading to diarrhoea, which can be worsened if the dose is increased too quickly in the early stages of therapy.

C Gliclazide

Concurrent use of gliclazide and doxycycline may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia and the patient should have been warned about this at the time of commencing antibiotic therapy, although there is no need to discontinue treatment.

E Atorvastatin

The main concern with respect to atorvastatin prescription is use with CYP3A4 inhibitors, which may lead to an increase in atorvastatin exposure.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old Ghanaian woman was referred with fatigue. She has been followed for the past year with bizarre behaviour and psychotic symptoms and is treated with amisulpiride. She was diagnosed five years ago with HIV-1 infection but was lost to follow-up.

The physical examination was unremarkable. CD4 count was 16 ×10⁶/L and HIV viral load > 500 000 copies/ml. Treatment with antiretroviral medications was commenced and the patient was discharged.

One month later the patient presents to you with confusion. She is afebrile on admission. She is disorientated in time and place but not in person.

On this occasion, the CD4 count is 44 ×10⁶/L and HIV viral load 503 copies/ml.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils72%
Lymphocytes18%
Platelets (PLT)435 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)8 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain reveals multiple low-density lesions in the left hemisphere
InvestigationResultNormal values
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) White cell count (WCC)120/ml< 5 /ml
CSF glucose3.4 mmol/L3.3 - 4.4 mmol/L
CSF protein0.56 mg/dl0.15 - 0.45 mg/dl
CSF cultureNo growth in 48 h
CSF cryptococcal antigenNegative
CSF toxoplasmosis PCRNegative
India ink stainNegative
Four days later, in hospital, she develops right-sided weakness. Magnetic resonance of the brain with contrast diffusely enhances the lesions.

Which one of the following diagnoses is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

The history and investigations are consistent with cerebral lymphoma or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is characterised by hemiparesis, disturbances of speech and vision and progressive dementia. The lesions in the brain comprise multiple areas of demyelination, abnormal oligodendrocytes and later pronounced astrocytosis. Lesions may enhance with gadolinium contrast. However, they do not usually have the characteristic ring-enhancing appearance seen in the cerebral lesions of toxoplasmosis. PML is associated with the ‘JC’ virus named after the patient in whom the polyoma virus was first isolated.

A Toxoplasmosis

Typically, presentation can occur with neurological signs developing over days to weeks and then can cause seizures. In addition, raised intracranial pressure can cause headaches and vomiting. Some present with diffuse encephalitis causing confusion, seizures and reduced consciousness. Normally toxoplasmosis would show ring- enhancing lesions on a CT scan. Also, the negative PCR makes this unlikely.

C Cryptococcal meningitis

Crytococcal infection is a common cause of meningitis and meningo-encephalitis in HIV-infected patients. It can present with headache, confusion, altered mental status, seizures and can have focal neurological signs present. The absence of antigens makes this less likely.

D Cytomegalovirus encephalitis

CMV establishes latent infection which reactivates as immunosuppression in HIV progresses. CMV can affect the central nervous system, retina, GI tract, lungs and biliary tract. In CNS infection there is usually progressive disorientation, withdrawal and apathy. On examination cranial nerve palsies and nystagmus are typical signs. Typically ring-enhancing lesions are seen on CT, but MRI is the best mode of imaging and diagnosis is confirmed on CSF PCR and treatment is with ganciclovir. The imaging findings in this patient makes CMV an unlikely but ideally should be excluded on PCR.

E Tuberculous meningitis

With this condition there would likely be meningeal enhancement on imaging studies, detectable AFB in the CSF and low glucose in the CSF as well.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old Ugandan woman is seen in the HIV Clinic. She has a CD4 count of 140 ×10⁶/L and was started on prophylactic co-trimoxazole 2 weeks previously. Unfortunately, this resulted in a severe rash and deranged liver function tests and was discontinued.

She has glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency and is a type 2 diabetic. Her only current medication is metformin 500 mg bd.

What is the most appropriate Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Pentamidine nebuliser

This is a patient with a low CD4 count. If a patient has a CD4 count below 200 ×10⁶/L then they should be offered prophylaxis against PCP. First-line treatment is oral co-trimoxazole. If this cannot be tolerated then the second-line treatment is oral dapsone. However, this is inappropriate in a patient with G6PD deficiency. Third- line prophylaxis is with nebulsed pentamidine.

D Oral clindamycin

Clindamycin can be used in the treatment of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) but not the prophylaxis.

A Co-trimoxazole nebuliser

The drug cannot be administered by nebuliser and may also be associated with haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency.

B Oral dapsone

It can cause haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. Other drugs that have a definite risk include primaquine, methylthioninium chloride, nitrofurantoin, quinolones (including ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, nalidixic acid, norfloxacin and ofloxacin) and sulfonamides.

C Oral pentamidine

Pentamidine is only effective in nebulised form or delivered IV. 7645

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman has been referred to the General Medical Clinic with persisting dysuria.

Since returning from a long trip around Africa, she has continued pain on passing urine and has recently noticed haematuria towards the end of micturition. She otherwise feels well.

The general practitioner (GP) has tried a couple of antibiotics with no improvement in her symptoms.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils7 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.8 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.1 ×10⁹/L1.5–3.5 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils1.3 ×10⁹/L0.04–0.4 ×10⁹/L
Basophils0.1 ×10⁹/L0.0–0.1 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)252 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Urine sample microscopySchistosome eggs

What is the appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Praziquantel

The patient has urinary schistosomiasis, most likely caused by Schistosoma haematobium. Diagnosis is made with the raised eosinophils and the schistosome eggs in the urine. Other forms of schistosomiasis (Schistosoma mansoni, Schistosoma japonicum) affect the portal venous system, the lung and the central nervous system. It is a disease of the tropics and treated with praziquantel. With urinary schistosomiasis there is an increased risk of bladder cancer.

B Mebendazole

This is used to treat the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides; this remains asymptomatic in many cases.

A Metronidazole

It will treat amoebic dysentery and amoebic liver abscesses (Entamoeba histolytica) and is also used in the treatment of giardiasis.

D Nifurtimox

Nitrofurimox is used to treat Trypanosoma cruzi, the organism responsible for causing Chagas disease.

E Niclosamide

Niclosamide is used to treat tapeworm infections, which may be asymptomatic or present with iron deficiency anaemia ± GI disturbance.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 2-day history of headache and nausea, and a 6 h history of increasing drowsiness and confusion. She has no past medical history.

On examination, her temperature was 37.9 °C. She was drowsy and confused. There was no nuchal rigidity or photophobia.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Opening pressure160 mm H₂O50–180
Protein0.33 g/L0.15–0.45
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Glucose3.7 mmol/L
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) White cell count (WCC)16/ml (lymphocytes)< 3
Serum glucose4.9 mmol/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Normal
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) headShown below


What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Herpes simplex encephalitis

This short history of increasing confusion and drowsiness is typical, and she has the characteristic MRI findings of signal increase in the temporal lobes. Seizures and a prodrome of headache and nausea are common. Treatment with intravenous aciclovir should be started.

A Cerebral lymphoma

This is highly unlikely given the acute nature of the patient’s presentation and her fever. Cerebral lymphoma would typically present insidiously as confusion or focal neurological signs, or it could present suddenly with a stroke-like picture. Instead, this short history of fever, confusion and drowsiness is more typical of herpes simplex encephalitis.

B Cryptococcal meningitis

Cryptococcal meningitis would be extremely unlikely in an immunocompetent patient. This presentation, with a short history of increasing confusion, drowsiness and mild fever, would be more consistent with herpes simplex encephalitis.

D Pneumococcal meningitis

This presentation does not fit with bacterial meningitis – she has a low-grade fever and there are no signs of meningism. The MRI findings are typical for herpes simplex encephalitis, which would also explain her presentation.

E Tuberculous meningitis

Tuberculous meningitis typically has an insidious onset; this patient has become unwell acutely. TB meningitis can cause confusion but may also cause cranial neuropathies, as it can affect the basal skull. It would be unusual to have TB meningitis with a normal chest X-ray. This patient is more likely to have herpes simplex encephalitis; this would fit with her presentation and would also explain the MRI findings.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old farmer is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. She is very worried about him, as he has been unable to leave the house and get to work because of a fever and feeling completely washed out. He has been working particularly hard as they have some concerns about finance. They tell you that he was clearing some drainage ditches on the edge of one of his fields a week. On examination, he is pyrexial 38.2 °C and looks jaundiced. There is a bandage on his right leg from where he cut himself on some brambles. He has abdominal tenderness, particularly over his liver.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)114 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.3 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)56 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)6.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)235 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)320 U/L25–55 U/L
Bilirubin290 µmol/L1.7–20.5 µmol/L
Creatinine kinase (CK)780 U/L22–198 U/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for him?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Benzylpenicillin

This unfortunate man has the severe form of leptospirosis known as Weil’s disease, spread via rats’ urine. It is likely that the cut on his leg, and wading through his drainage ditches, provided the route for infection. Infection leads to thrombocytopenia, jaundice with only a modest rise in transaminases, kidney disease and increased CK. Benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are drugs of choice for severe infection, with doxycycline a possible alternative in patients who are penicillin allergic. Thankfully most patients with leptospirosis suffer from a relatively mild infection and recover. Mortality from Weil’s disease is particularly high, however, in patients who are elderly or in those with pre-existing pathology.

D Fresh frozen plasma

Fresh frozen plasma may be used to correct specific clotting factor deficiencies or to reverse the effect of warfarin (although its use is superseded by prothrombin complex concentrate). This patient’s presentation is suggestive of leptospirosis and therefore targeted antimicrobial therapy is the treatment of choice.

A N-acetylcysteine

N-acetylcysteine is the treatment of choice for significant paracetamol overdose. This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of leptospirosis, and as we are not given any suggestion of paracetamol exposure, targeted antimicrobial treatment is the treatment of choice.

B Erythromycin

Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic with activity against Gram-positive and atypical organisms. This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of leptospirosis, and although erythromycin has some activity there is a better option available.

E Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic with a wide spectrum of activity against Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria. Because the patient’s presentation is suggestive of leptospirosis, ciprofloxacin would not be an effective treatment. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever there is an effective alternative available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. 21201

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is reviewed in clinic six weeks after starting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). She had been feeling clinically well prior to starting therapy, but over the past fortnight has been feeling increasingly tired and weak. She is also complaining of exertional dyspnoea. She denies fever, chest pain or cough. She has no other previous medical history of note and is taking tenofovir, emtricitabine and elvitegravir/cobicistat, along with co-trimoxazole for prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
TestPre-treatmentAfter six weeks Normal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)132 g/L86 g/L 115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)95 fL102 fL 76–98 fL
CD4 count205266 500–1500
Haptoglobin830 mg/L850 mg/L 410–1650 mg/L

What is the most likely cause for the anaemia?
options: Bone marrow infiltration by Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI)
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Red cell hypoplasia

The anaemia associated with emtricitabine therapy is due to red cell hypoplasia or aplasia. This is seen more rarely than with zidovudine and lamivudine and more frequently in children than in adults. Bone marrow examination may demonstrate pure red cell aplasia, erythroid maturation arrest, erythroid hypoplasia, and megaloblastic erythropoiesis. Erythropoietin levels are normal or increased.

A Bone marrow infiltration by Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI)

Given this patient has commenced treatment and has seen an improvement in their CD4 count, infiltration by MAI is unlikely versus other causes of anaemia.

B Haemolytic anaemia with anti-erythrocyte antibodies

Overt haemolysis is rarely seen in the context of HIV infection, and is likely to be less common once HAART is initiated.

C Folic acid deficiency

Folate deficiency is usually only seen with co-trimoxazole therapy when it is given concurrently with other anti- folate drugs such as methotrexate.

E Erythropoietin suppression

Levels of erythropoietin are usually increased in patients with red cell hypoplasia.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the Gynaecologist with complaints of a thin, greyish-white vaginal discharge with a foul odour for the past five days. She notices it to be more prominent after sexual intercourse. She has multiple sexual partners and says she has been having unprotected sexual intercourse for the past few months.

A saline wet mount is shown below.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Oral metronidazole

This patient is suffering from bacterial vaginosis, which occurs due to a shift of the local microbiota away from Lactobacillus and increased growth of bacterial species such as Gardnerella, Prevotella, Bacteroides, etc. The picture shows the presence of a clue cell (vaginal epithelial cell studded with coccobacilli) in the bottom left corner and two other normal epithelial cells.

Amsel criteria include: homogenous, thin, greyish-white discharge, vaginal pH > 4.5, positive whiff amine test and clue cells on saline wet mount.

The treatment of choice is oral metronidazole for seven days. Alternatively, clindamycin intravaginally as a cream for seven days may also be used in the management of these patients.

Image Source: Mikael Häggström, CC BY 1.0 via Wikimedia Commons

A Intramuscular ceftriaxone

Intramuscular ceftriaxone is used in the management of pelvic inflammatory disease in combination with other agents. This patient has bacterial vaginosis and oral metronidazole is the treatment of choice.

B Intravaginal clotrimazole

Intravaginal clotrimazole can be used for the treatment of Candida infections, which usually present with a thick, creamy white vaginal discharge, which is not the case in this patient.

C Oral doxycycline

Oral doxycycline is used for the treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis infection in non-pregnant women. This patient has bacterial vaginosis, and not an infection with C. trachomatis.

D Oral fluconazole

Oral fluconazole can be used for the treatment of Candida infections, which usually presents with a thick, creamy white vaginal discharge, which is not the case in this patient.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with what they describe as “the worst headache he has ever had”, coupled with a severe fever with a temperature of 39.4 oC. He also has muscle and joint pains which he describes as like someone has broken his bones. He has also vomited three times. He returned from a holiday to the Queensland (Australia) rainforest some 24 hours earlier. His blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg, and his pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm). He has an extensive macular rash.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)119 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)144 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)141 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)421 IU/L0 - 37 IU/L

Which of the following insect types is most likely have transmitted his infection?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Aedes mosquito

Possible differentials for this patient’s presentation include both Dengue fever and malaria. Given Queensland is malaria-free, this means Dengue fever is the most likely diagnosis and is consistent with the symptoms of severe fever, a macular rash, and “bone-breaking” muscle and joint pains. Dengue is spread via the Aedes aegypti mosquito. Most patients recover following the febrile phase - which this patient is currently in - although some may progress to developing Dengue related coagulopathy. 90% of severe Dengue cases occur in children.

D Tokunagayusurika midge

Tokunagayusurika midges are lake flies, which were first identified in Japan. They are not associated with significant human disease apart from frequent allergic reactions to midge bites.

B Anopheles mosquito

The Anopheles mosquito is responsible for the transmission of malaria. Although there may be cross-over between symptoms of malaria and those of Dengue, malaria is not present in Australia. This makes Dengue, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, much more likely to be the diagnosis here.

C Ixodes tick

The Ixodes tick is carried on deer, and is responsible for the carriage of Borrelia, which is the causative organism responsible of Lyme disease. (In many areas of the world tick-borne encephalitis). Erythema chronicum migrans is the most prominent initial feature of Lyme disease and is often what prompts initial presentation to medical services.

E Xenopsylla flea

The Xenopsylla flea is a cause of flea-borne typhus, which is caused by the bacterium Rickettsia typhi. Signs are similar to those of Dengue and include headache, fever, muscle pains, joint pains, nausea, and vomiting. A rash is seen later, where 40–50% of patients will develop a discrete rash six days after the onset of other signs. Doxycycline is the intervention of choice.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 4-day history of general malaise and loss of appetite. Her past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis, for which she takes methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. Her childhood vaccinations were administered appropriately, as far as she is aware.

Her temperature is 39.2 °C and her BP is 125/82 mmHg. She has bilateral conjunctivitis, as well as a rash which covers her face, upper arms and trunk. The patient's rash is shown below:

What is the most likely complication of this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Otitis media

This patient has a diagnosis of measles. Clinical symptoms and signs leading to the diagnosis include a history of coryzal symptoms followed by a maculopapular rash, as shown here, spreading from the face to the torso. Conjunctivitis and Koplik spots are also common features. This patient is taking immunosuppressant medication, making it more likely for her to develop measles, even if she was vaccinated as a child. The most common complication of measles is otitis media, affecting approximately 1 in 10 people.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Morbillivirus_measles_infection.jpg

E Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is an extremely rare complication of the measles virus, characterised by progressive neurological decline, including memory loss, behavioural changes and seizures. It often develops within 2–10 years after initial infection with the measles virus and affects 1 in 25 000 patients.

A Encephalitis

Encephalitis is a rare complication of measles, affecting 1 in 1000, and results in permanent neurological sequelae in 25% of those affected, with a fatality rate of 15% of cases.

B Glomerulonephritis

Glomerulonephritis can be seen in patients diagnosed with group A Streptococcus infection. However, it is not a common side-effect seen secondary to the measles virus.

D Pneumonia

Pneumonia is the most common cause of death secondary to measles. However, it is not the most common complication. It affects 1 in 20 people.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man comes to the Immunology Clinic for review. He has a history of multiple infections including two episodes of otitis media, three episodes of pneumonia, and one episode of Campylobacter infection over the course of the past year. He admits to unprotected sexual intercourse with other men on two occasions in the past two years. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 122/82 mmHg; pulse is 70/min and regular. There is no lymphadenopathy and his BMI is 23.

Investigations;

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin121 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.7 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets181 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)12 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)14 mm/1 st hour0–10 mm in the 1 st hour
IgG4.0 g/L (low)5–16 g/L
IgA0.5 g/L (low)1.0–4.0 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)23 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase85 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin10 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Albumin35 g/L35–55 g/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Common variable immunodeficiency

The answer is Common variable immunodeficiency (CVI) -

Both the IgA and IgG are low, coupled with the range of infections this patient has suffered from, raises the possibility of CVI. It is a rare defect of B cell maturation (1 in 25,000 incidence), which produces reduced immunoglobulin production. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy reduces the risk of infection and is the primary intervention of choice.

C Protein losing enteropathy

Protein losing enteropathy is incorrect, it is ruled out by the normal albumin of 35 g/L.

B HIV infection

HIV infection is incorrect, it is less likely here given he has suffered primarily from opportunistic bacterial infections, and two episodes of unprotected intercourse represents relatively limited potential exposure to HIV.

D Selective IgA deficiency

Selective IgA deficiency is incorrect, it is ruled out by the fact that IgG deficiency is also reduced.

E Severe combined immunodeficiency

Severe combined immunodeficiency is incorrect, it presents in early childhood with massive infection.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old intravenous drug user attends the Genitourinary Clinic for an asymptomatic screen. His syphilis serology reveals positive TPHA (Treponema pallidum haemagglutination test), negative RPR (rapid plasma reagin). He denies having been previously treated for syphilis and is prescribed a course of intramuscular (IM) procaine penicillin which is administered by a nurse in clinic. Within 1 minute of receiving the injection, the patient becomes acutely agitated, leaping off the couch and throwing the trolley across the room. He is not amenable to reasoning and is crying out, apparently experiencing visual hallucinations. Eventually, he is restrained by the security staff.

What is the explanation for this behaviour?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Procaine reaction

The procaine reaction occurs when procaine penicillin is accidentally given intravenous (IV) rather than intramuscular (IM). It results in an instantaneous feeling of impending doom with delusions and hallucinations. Patients often need restraining. The process is self-limiting within 20 minutes. Occasionally the patient may have a seizure, which should be terminated with IV or PR diazepam.

D Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is a sudden-onset, severe systemic hypersensitivity reaction, associated with flushing, urticaria and rash. While the patient has a sudden reaction following a new drug, the symptoms do not match as anaphylaxis is not associated with hallucinations and there are no features of systemic hypersensitivity such as a rash or breathing problems.

A Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction

A Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction is a systemic reaction to endotoxin-like products that are released when bacteria are destroyed during antibiotic treatment. It has been documented to occur with treatment of syphilis, Lyme disease, leptospirosis and relapsing fever. It occurs 1–12 hours following the first antibiotic dose and is not seen with subsequent treatment. It causes malaise, pyrexia, flushing and tachycardia. This can be followed by hypotension due to peripheral vasodilatation. While this reaction is most commonly associated with syphilis, the timing is too early and the clinical picture does not match.

C Acute opiate withdrawal

Early symptoms of opiate withdrawal include feeling hot or cold, dehydration, muscle aches, coryzal symptoms and yawning, but can also include agitation and confusion. The rapid onset makes withdrawal unlikely, and hallucinations are not associated with this.

E Paranoid schizophrenia

The patient has no history of psychiatric problems and the rapid onset of symptoms makes a chronic psychiatric diagnosis unlikely. It would also be highly coincidental following introduction of a new drug.

questions.question:
A 76-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department some 8–12 h after eating a ready-made chicken meal. She complains of fever, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

She has recently been taking co-amoxiclav for a respiratory tract infection, but nothing else of note. Her blood pressure (BP) is 122/72 mmHg, with a post-drop of 20 mmHg on standing with corresponding increase in pulse rate.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)129 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Platelets (PLT)560 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
White cell count (WCC)4.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)148 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea18.4 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)195 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Salmonella

This patient has acute bacterial gastroenteritis. She is likely to have acquired this from the ready-made chicken meal eaten some hours previously. Given this food history and the evidence of severe dehydration due to the infection, the most likely candidates are Salmonella or Campylobacter infection. The incubation period of Campylobacter infection can sometimes be much longer, up to 7 days, but can be as short as 24 h, as is the case here. The incubation period of Salmonella gastroenteritis is 6–72 h, making it the more likely diagnosis in this case. Uncomplicated infections with these agents do not require treatment, but where there is significant dehydration as in this case, oral or intravenous rehydration therapy ± quinolone antibiotics could be considered.

D Giardiasis

It is caused by Giardia lamblia, a flagellated protozoon, which infects the jejenum and deuodenum following faecal–oral spread. Causes explosive diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and malabsorption. Diagnosis is with stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites or PCR. Treatment is with tindazole 2 g stat, with high levels of hygiene. May cause lactose intolerance as well.

A Norovirus

Norovirus causes symptoms 12–48 h after exposure. It is spread via droplets and is highly infectious. It causes outbreaks of ‘winter vomiting illness’, with projectile vomiting, diarrhoea and fever and settles quickly. Treatment is supportive but patients will need to be strictly isolated.

B Rotavirus

Rotavirus is a cause of viral gastroenteritis up to the age of five. Following 1–5 days of incubation there is malaise, diarrhoea, vomiting and fever.

C Amoebiasis

Ameobiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoon. Spread is via the faecal–oral route. Presentation is usually with gastrointestinal symptoms but in 1% there can be invasive liver disease. Subtle amoebic dysentery presents slowly but can lead to bloody diarrhoea and fever. Diagnosis is with stool microscopy demonstrating trophozoites, bleed and pus cells.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman is brought by her partner to the Emergency Department. She has been complaining of worsening headache and neck stiffness over the past few days and is now drowsy and disorientated.

On examination, she has signs of meningism, a pyrexia 39 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and pulse 105 bpm. There is a purpuric rash.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)140 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Lumbar punctureDecreased CSF glucose, increased protein, neutrophils, gram-negative diplococci
You commence IV benzylpenicillin and there is initial improvement. 72 h later, however, she spikes a new fever of 39 °C, with increased eosinophil count in the peripheral blood.

What is the most important management step?
options: Stop penicillin and substitute an alternative antibiotic
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Stop penicillin and substitute an alternative antibiotic

Penicillin is one of a number of agents which may cause an eosinophilic drug reaction. Other causes include meloxicam, l-tryptophan, dantrolene and ethambutol. Clearly this woman does have meningococcal meningitis given that she presented with fever and menigisms and found to have diplococci in her CSF. As such it is important to continue antibiotic therapy. Alternatives to penicillin include cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime at high dose. Indeed, most centres use a cephalosporin as first line therapy because of the small risk of meningococcal resistance to penicillin.

D Commence amphotericin

Amphotericin is a potent antifungal medication which can be used against systemic aspergillus which can be a cause of eosinophilia. However, there is very strong evidence for bacterial, not fungal, infection, and this is a very unlikely diagnosis given the original presentation of meningism, purpuric rash and fever.

B Commence prednisolone

This is a very tempting option as the patient likely has suffered a drug reaction. However, removing the offending drug is a far more sensible option than using prednisolone to mitigate the drug reaction.

C Commence aciclovir

This would be the correct treatment option for viral meningitis but the presence of diplococci in the blood film and purpuric rash on presentation makes this an unlikely diagnosis and therefore makes acyclovir an inappropriate treatment option.

E Commence chlorpheniramine

Chlorphenamine is an antipruritic medication which would only provide symptomatic relief against itch and therefore not address the underlying problem. Given that there is a fever and haematological evidence of eosinophilia an underlying cause should be saught and addressed.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of severe headache and neck stiffness. He also had a 4-day history of non-bloody diarrhoea.

On examination, his temperature was 37.9 °C, blood pressure was 128/72 mmHg and pulse rate was 88 beats/min. He had meningism and mild photophobia. There were no neurological signs.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Random plasma glucose6.1 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
CT headNormal
InvestigationResultNormal Values
Opening pressure22 cmHg10 - 20 cmHg
AppearanceClear fluid
AppearanceNo organisms seen
Cell count80 cells/mm³ (lymphocytes)
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein0.8 g/dL0.15 g/dL
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose4.2 mmol/L3.3 - 4.4 mmol/L

What is the most important next investigation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with meningitis (headache, fever, meningism). Investigations are suggestive of a viral cause (lymphocytic CSF, normal glucose, no organisms on CSF microscopy). It is likely that this patient’s meningitis was caused by an enterovirus, given his preceding diarrhoea. However, it is important to rule out herpes simplex meningoencephalitis, as this would require specific treatment with aciclovir. If this is simply enterovirus, he can be treated with supportive therapy only.

D CSF spectrophotometry

This is a useful investigation where subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected and CT head is normal: spectrophotometry can identify xanthochromia, caused by blood breakdown products in the CSF. However, the CSF was not bloody and this patient does not describe a sudden-onset headache. This patient’s fever, headache and meningism are more suggestive of an infective meningitis: this is most likely viral given the CSF lymphocytosis and lack of organisms on microscopy. Herpes simplex meningoencephalitis should be ruled out with CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

A Blood cultures

This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with meningitis (fever, headache, meningism) and the investigations are suggestive of a viral meningitis (lymphocytosis in CSF, normal glucose, no organisms seen). The most important investigation is CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to identify whether this is herpes simplex meningoencephalitis. Given this patient’s preceding diarrhoea, however, it is likely that this meningitis has been caused by an enterovirus. Blood cultures should be taken in addition to other investigations, as he is febrile, but it is not the most important investigation.

B CSF culture

Fluid should be sent for culture to rule out a bacterial cause for this patient’s meningitis, but investigations suggest that this is a viral meningitis (lymphocytic CSF, normal glucose, no visible organisms). Fluid culture results will take some time, and therefore are not going to be immediately useful in the management of this patient. CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR), however, would be helpful, as this could rule out herpes simplex meningoencephalitis, which would require specific treatment. If this is negative, the patient can be treated with supportive care only.

E MRI head

This patient likely has viral meningitis: he has a fever, headache and meningism, and investigations demonstrate a clear, lymphocytic CSF with no visible organisms. His preceding diarrhoea suggests enterovirus as a cause. CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) should be carried out to rule out herpes simplex meningoencephalitis: this can produce suggestive features on MRI, but MRI is not the diagnostic tool of choice.

questions.question:
A general practitioner (GP) refers a 21-year-old man, who had been previously fit and well, for a second opinion. He had presented with a 6-week history of flitting arthralgia and myalgia. Prior to the onset of this problem, he had been on holiday in the Far East where he had unprotected sexual intercourse on one occasion only. On general examination, there was no evidence of arthritis but it was noted that the patient had bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Investigations showed a white cell count at the lower end of normal, mild anaemia, normal urea and electrolytes, and abnormal liver function tests with all the liver enzymes elevated. Urethral swabs for chlamydia and gonococcus were negative.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Acute HIV infection

Acute HIV infection can affect any number of organ systems, including the lymphatics, skin, gastrointestinal system, genitourinary system, bone marrow and nervous system, with the clinical findings being related to the organ system affected. These signs include persistent generalised lymphadenopathy, oral thrush, oral hairy leukoplakia, shingles (especially in a patient under the age of 40), anaemia, thrombocytopenia and secondary opportunistic infections, eg Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The work-up of the patient varies depending on the initial presenting complaint but it is important to exclude all other treatable causes. Acute infection may be detected by the presence of P24 antigen or HIV RNA, both of which precede the development of IgM or IgG antibodies.

E Relapsing polychondritis

The clinical picture does not match relapsing polychondritis, which is characterised by nasal and auricular chondritis and usual onset is between 40 and 50 years. It can have greater systemic involvement and can even be fatal with airway involvement. It would explain the arthralgia but little else in the history.

B Brucellosis

The lack of direct exposure and travel to an endemic area makes it a less likely diagnosis. It is a zoonosis endemic in the Middle and Far East, as well as Bosnia, which is spread via the contact with animals, their exhalations or some animal products, such as unpasteurised goat’s milk. It is therefore common in veterinarians and farmers. Presentation of brucellosis is highly varied, but generally includes fever and malaise.

C Reactive arthritis

It is a triad urethritis, conjunctivitis and seronegative arthritis secondary to infection in another part of the boy. There is not enough evidence to make this diagnosis likely, and there is also no evidence of a sexually transmitted infection, the most likely cause. In addition, this diagnosis would not explain the abnormalities in the blood tests.

D Adult-onset Still’s disease

The presentation makes it unlikely. Adult-onset Still’s disease is characterised by a triad of persistent and high fevers, arthralgia and a salmon-coloured rash. There is no evidence of a rash and hence still’s disease is unlikely.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man presented to clinic with a 10-day history of malaise, headache, fever, night sweats, back pain and myalgia. He was a sheep farmer, and had no other medical conditions.

On examination, he appeared unwell. His temperature was 37.9ºC, and there was widespread lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. There was mild tenderness on palpation of the sacroiliac joints.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)138 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.4 ×10⁹/L4.0 – 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils3.4 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Basophils0.08 ×10⁹/L< 0.1 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils0.1 ×10⁹/L0.04 - 0.4 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)100 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin35 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 102 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase 51 U/L (AST)10 - 40 U/L
Blood filmLeukoerythroblastic
X-ray lumbar spineLumbar degenerative changes with osteophyte formation

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Brucellosis

It is caused by a Gram-negative bacterium that is transmitted by contact with infected livestock. The typical incubation period is 1–3 weeks with an insidious onset. This patient’s symptoms of malaise, fever, back pain and night sweats are typical. Back pain is common, occurring in around 50% of patients. The findings of a

leucoerythroblastic blood film and raised transaminases fit with the diagnosis. Diagnosis is via bone marrow culture or serum agglutination testing.

E Organophosphate poisoning

Organophosphate poisoning leads to an over-abundance of acetylcholine, and therefore causes pinpoint pupils, excess salivation and seizures. It does not cause a subacute malaise, fever and back pain as seen here. This picture, combined with the transaminitis and history of sheep farming, would fit with brucellosis.

A Acute myeloid leukaemia

Typically a patient with acute myeloid leukaemia would either have a very high white cell count or very low, but it would be unusual to have a normal white cell count. Furthermore, you might expect bone marrow failure, with bleeding and bruising, and pancytopenia. Lymphadenopathy is possible but not common. Instead, this patient’s symptoms, signs and investigations would be consistent with brucellosis through exposure to sheep.

C Chronic myeloid leukaemia

You would expect a patient with chronic myeloid leukaemia to have a raised basophil and eosinophil count, but these are normal here. You might also expect a leucocytosis and teardrop poikilocytes on the blood film. This patient’s signs and symptoms are more consistent with brucellosis through exposure to infected sheep.

D Hydatid disease

Hydatid disease can be caught from sheep. In 90% of cases it causes liver dysfunction. However, that is characteristically obstructive in nature, whereas this patient’s investigations fit with a hepatitic cause. This patient’s symptoms and signs are more consistent with brucellosis.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old HIV-positive man is on day seven of his inpatient treatment for tuberculosis (TB) on the Infectious Diseases Ward with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He has a CD4 count of 91 ×10⁶/L, and the plan is to start him on antiretroviral therapy as an inpatient.

On the ward, he has a 30-second seizure, which self-terminated. Neurological examination reveals right-sided weakness affecting the arm and leg. Urgent CT of the head is requested and performed, which reveals a solitary focal lesion in the left internal capsule, with some surrounding oedema and mild effacement of the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle.

What is the most urgent next step?
options: Add in an additional antituberculous drug
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Commence sulphadiazine and pyrimethamine

Possible causes for a solitary focal lesion in a HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count include cerebral toxoplasmosis, lymphoma and tuberculoma (although solitary lesions are only seen in about 15% of toxoplasmosis cases). In an immunocompromised patient, there should always be a low index of suspicion for multiple pathologies, and toxoplasmosis is the most common central nervous system (CNS) infection in patients with a CD4 count below 100 who are not receiving prophylaxis.

This patient is on appropriate antituberculous treatment for CNS TB (note tuberculomas can develop during treatment due to an immune response against dying Mycobacterium tuberculosis and does not necessarily indicate treatment resistance). Therefore, the most important next step is to cover for toxoplasmosis as a potential co-infection. Initial treatment with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine is provided for six weeks before lower doses are used for long-term prophylaxis. Seizures in the presence of an intracranial lesion warrant antiepileptic medication; in this case, providing the patient can be completely treated, short- to medium-term treatment (ie 6–12 months) may be all that is required.

A Add in an additional antituberculous drug

The presence of unilateral weakness following a seizure is not in keeping with CNS TB, which is more likely to present with meningitic symptoms.

B Urgent Toxoplasma serology

This would be a useful test to confirm the most likely diagnosis but takes several days to be analysed. In some cases, results can be falsely negative for 2–3 weeks after initial exposure. Treatment should not be delayed to await this confirmation.

C Lumbar puncture

The seizure and intracranial lesion with oedema and effacement of the lateral ventricle indicate an increased intracerebral pressure. A lumbar puncture undertaken in such circumstances may cause tonsillar herniation and therefore has a high risk of mortality.

E MRI of the brain

An MRI scan may help confirm the underlying diagnosis and rule out differentials such as meningitis TB. However, this will take time to be organised and reported, which could cause a significant delay in treatment for this patient. 73439

questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of fever and headache. She had returned 2 weeks previously from a 1-month safari holiday in South Africa. She took malarial prophylaxis while away and on her return, in accordance with her general practitioner (GP)’s instructions.

On examination, her temperature was 37.7 °C. She had a 1 cm-diameter black scab on her right forearm, surrounded by erythema and mild swelling. There was right axillary lymphadenopathy. She had a non- blanching petechial rash over her trunk. Her abdomen was mildly tender on examination, with no hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations:

InvestigationResult
Thin films for malariaNegative in two separate samples
Chest X-rayNormal

Which is the management of choice?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Doxycycline

This patient has classic symptoms and signs of tick typhus, or Rickettsia, which is a common condition caused by a tick bite while walking in grassland in South Africa. The black lesion on her forearm is an eschar that forms at the site of the tick bite.
