The eschar, along with regional lymphadenopathy, vasculitic rash and flu-like symptoms, are features of a typical presentation. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice, as there is a risk of complications (end-organ damage, peripheral gangrene or secondary infections) and mortality.

E Praziquantel

Praziquantel is used in the treatment of schistosomiasis and other fluke infections. Schistosomiasis presents acutely in two ways. The most common is with swimmer’s itch, which causes a self-limiting, itchy papular rash within 24 hours of exposure. Less commonly, katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis) develops 4–8 weeks post- exposure and presents with fever, urticaria, eosinophilia and wheeze. This patient’s lesion is not characteristic with either of these presentations.

A Artesunate

Artesunate is an anti-malarial treatment, but this patient does not have typical symptoms for malaria and has had two negative blood films. Although, strictly speaking, three malarial blood films are required to rule out malaria, this patient’s symptoms and signs are not typical for malaria and she took appropriate prophylaxis, making the diagnosis even less likely.

B Ciprofloxacin

This patient’s symptoms and signs are typical for tick typhus, or Rickettsia: the eschar at the site of the tick bite, with regional lymphadenopathy, a vasculitic rash and flu-like symptoms. It is a common condition contracted when walking in grassland in South Africa and other game parks. Doxycycline is the correct treatment for tick typhus; although ciprofloxacin has been used, it has been associated with treatment failures. Quinolones are also no longer recommended if there are other effective options available do to an increased risk of long term debilitating side effects.

C Conservative measures only

This patient has tick typhus, caused by infection with Rickettsia through a tick bite; this is common in travellers who have been walking through long grass whilet on safari. The black lesion on her arm is an eschar at the site of the tick bite, and regional lymphadenopathy, petechial rash, fever and flu-like symptoms are typical. This condition is easily treated with doxycycline; without treatment, the risk of complications (end-organ damage, peripheral gangrene or secondary infections) is much higher, and untreated, the condition has significant mortality.

questions.question:
A 39-year-old man presents with a history of poor urine output over the past 2 days. Other than bloody diarrhoea about a week ago, he has no other significant history. There were several other patients who had presented with bloody diarrhoea in the last 24 h and who had attended the same eatery that he had attended. He takes no regular medications. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg, with a heart rate of 110 bpm.

Which of the following tests would be useful for establishing the cause of his acute kidney disease?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Blood film

You should suspect a diagnosis of haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS) associated with diarrhoea caused by Escherichia coli. Once the bacteria colonize, diarrhoea followed by bloody diarrhoea with oliguria, haematuria and kidney disease ensues. On the blood tests there is thrombocytopenia and destruction of red blood cells – microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia – and this may be seen on blood film.

E Stool culture

Shiga-like toxin-producing bacteria such as enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC), of which E. coli O157:H7 is the most common serotype, may be the cause of HUS. However, it is the toxin rather than culture of bacteria which would be indicative of the cause.

A AXR

The bowel loops may be distended due to colitis, but it will not be diagnostic of HUS. Distended bowel loops may be present in many other forms of diarrhoea.

C Clotting screen

The clotting screen will be normal unless the patient becomes so unwell they show a disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) picture.

D Potassium measurement

The potassium concentration may well be high in cases of both acute kidney disease and haemolysis, but it will not give you the diagnosis.

questions.question:
An 85-year-old Jamaican man, who is visiting his son, is admitted to the Emergency Department with a left pneumonia. He has a number of large, painless subcutaneous nodules which he says have been developing over a number of years; these are particularly marked over his shins. Some of these have ulcerated but have a well-defined edge with granulation tissue and yellowish slough. There is hyperkeratosis of the soles of the feet and the palms of the hands.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)150 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)141 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
VDRL+
TPHA+
FTA-ABS+

He tells you he has been with the same partner for the past 65 years. Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis of his skin lesions?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Yaws

Yaws is caused by Treponema pertenue, a non-venereal treponemal disease which, similar to syphilis, may persist for many years. Serological testing is indistinguishable from that seen for syphilis, and differentiation is made on history and clinical features. Presentation is with one or multiple skin lesions which may ulcerate. Transmission is via skin-to-skin contact. Like syphilis, penicillin remains the drug of choice for treatment of yaws, with erythromycin, tetracycline or doxycycline being possible alternatives. Patients with yaws, particularly where the infection is chronic, may require re-treatment every few years. Pinta is caused by Treponema carateum and is characterised mainly by chronic pigmentary skin lesions which occur predominantly in a young adult population.

D Tertiary syphilis

Tertial syphilis occurs approximately 10–15 years after initial infection. Presentation can be divided into three forms: gummatous syphilis, neurosyphilis and cardiovascular syphilis. Gummatous syphilis is characterised by rubbery subcutaneous growths. The presentation described does not fit with tertiary syphilis and the positive syphilis serology can be explained by endemic treponematoses.

A HIV

The skin lesions described would not be typical of HIV or associated complications.

B Pinta

Pinta is one of the endemic treponeal diseases. It is endemic to central and south America. Presentation is with flat hyperkeratotic skin lesions with lymphadenopathy which resolve over time. Pinta is serologically indistinguishable from syphilis hence the positive result. In this case epidemiology makes an alternative diagnosis more likely.

C Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is a multisystem, inflammatory condition, characterised by non-caseating granuloma formation. Typical presentation (Lofgren syndrome) is with bilateral hilar adenopathy, arthritis and erythema nodosum.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fevers, severe headache, dry cough and intermittent episodes of diarrhoea. He has been teaching English in a rural school in Africa and has returned to the United Kingdom for a planned holiday.

On examination, his temperature is 38.7 °C; his heart rate is 65 bpm and regular, and his BP is 88/62 mmHg. An image of his upper chest is shown below – the lesions blanch on pressure.

Investigations:

Which of the following treatments is likely to be most effective?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ceftriaxone

The pale pink lesions are rose spots which are characteristic of typhoid fever. Options for therapy include ciprofloxacin, azithromycin and ceftriaxone. As significant resistance exists against ciprofloxacin, oral azithromycinis the recommended first-line treatment in mild cases which can be treated as an outpatient.

Where an alternative to azithromycin is needed in mild disease, then ciprofloxacin can be used after sensitivity testing. In patients with more significant symptoms (as here, where there is hypotension likely secondary to prerenal failure) or resistance, IV ceftriaxone is the preferred option. Patients are usually retested one week after completion of therapy to rule out chronic carriage or Salmonella.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Salmonella_typhi_typhoid_fever_PHIL_2215_lores.jpg

E Metronidazole

Metronidazole is primarily used for the treatment of giardiasis, where symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome with intermittent diarrhoea and abdominal bloating are seen. The picture here with the cough, gastrointestinal disturbance and characteristic rash is more consistent with typhoid fever.

A Amoxicillin

Amoxicillin was used as a treatment for typhoid fever, although extensive Salmonella resistance now exists, meaning it should only be used if sensitivity has been proven.

B Azithromycin

Oral azithromycin is the intervention of choice in patients with uncomplicated typhoid fever, which can be managed as an outpatient. Between five and seven days of treatment are recommended in such cases. Here, with hypotension at presentation, possibly being indicative of prerenal failure, IV ceftriaxone is recommended.

D Doxycycline

Like amoxicillin, doxycycline is a largely historical therapy for typhoid fever due to resistance. Other options, such as ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin, are preferred.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fever and myalgia. He has also been experiencing mild coryzal symptoms and a dry cough. His oral intake has declined over the last four days and he has lost approximately 1 kg in weight. However, he denies vomiting or diarrhoea. There is no known past medical history and he is not taking any regular medications. His family recently immigrated from Pakistan four months ago.

On examination, he appears to be clinically dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. His temperature is 39.8 °C and he is warm to touch, with a capillary refill time of < 2 seconds. His heart rate is 127 bpm and regular, and his blood pressure is 119/77 mmHg. He has normal heart sounds and a clear chest, with no audible crackles or wheeze. His abdomen is soft, with no palpable masses. There is a diffuse maculopapular rash across his face and trunk that is not bleeding or blistering. His conjunctivae are red and inflamed.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Measles

This patient has a diagnosis of measles. Clinical symptoms and signs leading to the diagnosis include a history of coryzal symptoms followed by a maculopapular rash spreading from the face to the torso. Conjunctivitis and Koplik spots are also common features. Developing countries within Africa and Asia have lower numbers of childhood vaccinations, with over 6 million children from India, Pakistan and Nigeria not receiving a single dose of the measles vaccine in 2018.

E Pityriasis rosea

Pityriasis rosea is a viral rash that characteristically develops after the appearance of a single pink/red patch called a herald patch. Viral symptoms can be seen prior to the onset of the rash, but on many occasions, patients can be asymptomatic and generally well. A pityriasis rash is uncommon on the face.

B Rubella

Rubella is a viral illness that causes coryzal symptoms followed by the onset of a maculopapular rash. However, the rash is usually more limited compared to measles. Cervical and post-auricular lymphadenopathy is very common in these patients. Conjunctivitis is not a common presenting symptom of rubella, as seen in this patient, making it incorrect.

C Steven–Johnson syndrome (SJS)

Steven–Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a very rare and serious type of skin reaction. It can arise secondary to a drug reaction or infection with mycoplasma or cytomegalovirus. It can present similarly to measles with coryza, sore throat, fever, conjunctivitis, myalgia and a diffuse macular rash. However, distinguishing symptoms include an eruption of flaccid blisters and mucosal involvement, including mouth ulcers. Given its rarity, the lack of medication use and other distinguishing symptoms, a diagnosis of measles is more likely.

D Morbilliform drug reaction

A morbilliform drug reaction is less likely in this patient as there is no history of him taking any regular medications and it does not explain his fever or coryzal symptoms.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old woman is seen in clinic with a 1-month history of malaise, tiredness, chest pain and breathlessness on walking up the stairs. You establish that she has not felt well for about 6 months since returning from Puerto Rico. She went fresh-water swimming there and often walked barefoot. She boiled her water but occasionally dined out on local delicacies. She developed an itch of both feet shortly after returning and noticed a rash, which responded to cream prescribed by her doctor. A week later, she had an episode of dyspnoea and wheeze, which her general practitioner (GP) told her was asthma and she felt better with salbutamol. About 3 months ago she had abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhoea, which settled after a few weeks.

On examination, she looks pale but there is no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. She is tachycardic at 104 bpm but her heart sounds are normal. Chest exam reveals scattered wheeze. Her abdomen is soft and her per rectum (PR) examination is normal.

Chest X-ray reveals small bilateral pleural effusions.

Blood results reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)76 g/L115–155 g/L
Platelets (PLT)532 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Albumin31 g/L35–55 g/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)6 mg/L< 10 mg/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Hookworm infection

The most common pathogens are Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. This patient has a history consistent with hookworm infection. Hookworm is endemic in the Americas, south-east Asia, India and Africa The worms often get in through the feet and cause an intense local rash. After about a week they move through the lung causing wheezing and cough and then they migrate to the intestine where they become adults and start laying eggs. With heavy infection the patient may have an episode of abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea and anorexia. This patient has experienced all of these symptoms. The examination findings are consistent with pulmonary infiltration, and the pallor and tachycardia can be explained by anaemia. Hookworms cause anaemia by attachment to the upper gastrointestinal mucosa leading to chronic bleeding and iron deficiency. After 8–12

weeks the hookworm eggs are present in the faeces and the isolation of these is the investigation of choice. Anthelminthic drugs effective against hookworms include albendazole, mebendazole and thiabendazole, as well as ivermectin.

C Colonic carcinoma

It would not explain the wheeze or pleural effusions, and her age and lack of risk factors make the diagnosis very unlikely.

A Dilated cardiomyopathy

It can present with shortness of breath and chest pain, but it does not explain many of the respiratory or abdominal aspects of the history or examination, nor the anaemia. Also, it is commonly associated with a family history of sudden death as that may the first presentation and it is inherited in an autosomal-dominant fashion.

B Polyarteritis nodosa

While polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) can start with a rash and develop into systemic features and have gastrointestinal features and also cause anaemia, one would expect a raised WCC and CRP. It is also associated with hepatitis B and twice as common in men than women.

E Schistosomiasis

It would not explain her respiratory symptoms or findings. Schistosomiasis in the Americas is caused by Schistosoma mansoni and this species causes abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting, and then progresses to hepatic symptoms and findings. African causes of schistosomiasis can have pulmonary infiltration.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old burns victim is treated with gentamicin 60 mg three times daily (tds). His gentamicin regimen needs to be reviewed as he is recovering from extensive burns and evidence of superficial skin infection is improving.

Gentamicin levels are taken:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Peak level4 µg/ml3–4 µg/ml
Trough level1.9 µg/ml2 µg/ml

Which of the following is the correct course of action?
options: Increase the gentamicin dose to 80 mg tds
Reduce the gentamicin dose to 40 mg tds
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Leave regimen unchanged

Although a ‘traditional’ three times daily (tds) approach to dosing of aminoglycosides is now rarely used, it is still employed in certain patient groups, including:

patients with burns (over 20% of total body surface area) patients with ascites pregnant women patients with creatinine clearance under 40 ml/min.

In other patients, evidence suggests daily dosing is as effective, with a reduced incidence of adverse events. In this tds dosing setting, a peak level of 3–4 µg/ml is targeted, with a trough level of above 2 µg/ml; hence, the levels are within the acceptable range, and the dose and frequency of injection should be left unchanged. In serious invasive infections, a greater peak of 6–8 µg/ml may be targeted.

D Reduce the gentamicin dose to 40 mg tds

This risks trough levels falling below the recommended therapeutic range, leading to inadequate coverage against bacterial infection, given that trough values approximate to the recommended level of 2 µg/ml on the current dose.

A Increase the gentamicin dose to 80 mg tds

The peak level of gentamicin here is 4 µg/ml. Increasing the gentamicin dose to 80 mg tds will result in possible toxicity, as the levels would be increased into the toxic range.

C Move to twice-daily dosing

Dosing at tds is preferred to bd dosing in burns patients to reduce variance in plasma levels of gentamicin as much as possible. This would ensure coverage against bacterial pathogens and reduce potential toxicity.

E Skip the next gentamicin dose

When assessing gentamicin dosing, it is essential to look at the predose (trough) level and peak level (taken approximately one hour after administration). If the trough level is raised, the interval between the first gentamicin dose and the next dose should be increased. However, if the peak concentration is raised, the gentamicin dose should be decreased. As the trough dose is within the normal limits for this patient, the dosing interval should be kept the same.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man attended the Emergency Department with haematemesis 30 min previously. He is visiting the UK from Africa, but had been well prior to presentation.

On arrival, he was shocked and pale and therefore underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy after adequate resuscitation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)66 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)65 fL80 - 100 fL
White cell count (WCC)6.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)87 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Albumin4.0 g/dL3.4 - 5.4 g/dL
Bilirubin5 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)12 U/L10 - 40 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)12 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)66 U/L30 - 150 U/L
International normalized ratio (INR)1.0< 1.1
Examination of the oesophagus revealed two large varices with stigmata of recent bleeding. No blood was seen but two red worms, about 10 mm in length, were noted adherent to the mucosa in the duodenum

Which of the following is he most likely to be infected with?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Necator americanus

Although part of the explanation for this man's anaemia may be his haemorrhage, GI haemorrhage does not typically cause haemodilution this quickly, and his very marked microcytosis also implies that another factor is contributing to this. The presence of worms is the probable explanation here; the commonest cause of iron- deficiency anaemia worldwide being hookworm infection (N. americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale), which affects 25% of the global population. Mebendazole or albendazole is the treatment of choice.

C Strongyloides stercoralis

S. stercoralis is not visible to the naked eye, and may cause malabsorption.

A Trichuris trichiura

T. trichiura infests the distal ileum and colon, and with heavy infestation may cause diarrhoea and GI bleeding.

B Schistosoma haematobium

S. haematobium affects the urinary tract rather than the liver and GI tract. Treatment is with praziquantel.

D Enterobius vermicularis

E. vermicularis lives in the colon, is more common in temperate climates and may cause pruritus ani. 70165

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV after presenting with fever, weight loss and oral candidiasis. His CD4 count is 180 cells/μl, and his viral load is 120 000 copies/ml. Genotypic resistance testing reveals no resistance mutations. He has no previous medical history and is not on any medications. The patient reports occasional recreational drug use and has a history of poor adherence to medical care. LFTs and renal function tests are normal.

What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
options: Begin a protease inhibitor-based regimen with strict monitoring
Initiate a single-tablet regimen with integrase strand transfer inhibitors
Delay therapy until the patient demonstrates better adherence
Start prophylaxis for opportunistic infections and delay highly active antiretroviral therapy
Use nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors alone
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Initiate a single-tablet regimen with integrase strand transfer inhibitors

Single-tablet regimens are the preferred first-line therapy for most patients with HIV due to their high efficacy, favourable side-effect profile and ease of adherence. Examples include bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir or dolutegravir/lamivudine.

E Use nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors alone

NRTI-only regimens are outdated and less effective due to high rates of resistance and suboptimal viral suppression. Modern regimens always include at least two drug classes.

A Begin a protease inhibitor-based regimen with strict monitoring

While protease inhibitors are effective, modern guidelines favour nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI)-based regimens due to their potency, better tolerability and simpler dosing.

C Delay therapy until the patient demonstrates better adherence

Current guidelines emphasise early initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), regardless of adherence concerns, as delayed therapy can lead to rapid progression of HIV and opportunistic infections. Supportive interventions should be used to improve adherence instead.

D Start prophylaxis for opportunistic infections and delay highly active antiretroviral therapy

Prophylaxis for opportunistic infections is crucial at low CD4 counts (eg Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis for CD4 counts of fewer than 200 cells/μl). However, it is not a substitute for initiating HAART, which remains the cornerstone of treatment.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old man presented to clinic with a 3-month history of a skin lesion on his left leg. He explained that when the lesion first appeared, it had been a small, red, painless raised lump, which had gradually enlarged. He was a sailor who worked on ships in the Middle East, India and Pakistan.

The lesion has now ulcerated and is shown below.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Cutaneous leishmaniasis

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is caused by a parasite conveyed in a sandfly bite, and ‘Old Word cutaneous leishmaniasis’ can be contracted whilst travelling in Asia and the Middle East. The description of an enlarging red, painless papule which develops central ulceration is typical. Many lesions will spontaneously resolve within a year of forming.

E Squamous cell carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma would typically cause an enlarging scaly or crusted lump; it would not progress from a red papule as seen here. Instead, this patient’s presentation combined with his travel history is more suggestive of cutaneous leishmaniasis, caused by a parasite conveyed in a sandfly bite.

A Basal cell carcinoma

Although the current appearance of the lesion could be consistent with a basal cell carcinoma, the progression of the lesion from a red papule to a lesion with central, dry ulceration is not typical. Instead, combined with the patient’s travel history, this is more likely to be cutaneous leishmaniasis. It is caused by a parasite conveyed in a sandfly bite and typically progresses from a red papule, which enlarges and develops either wet or dry central ulceration. These lesions often spontaneously resolve within a year.

B Chronic venous ulceration

Chronic venous ulceration causes background skin changes, which are not reported here, and you would expect a venous ulcer to be shallow with exudate. Furthermore, a venous ulcer would not develop as a papule and then progress to a lesion with central ulceration. This description, combined with the patient’s travel history, would be more typical of cutaneous leishmaniasis.

D Leprosy

Leprosy classically causes hypopigmented patches of anaesthetised skin; it may cause irregular red plaques, or skin thickening, but the progression of the lesion described in this case would not fit with leprosy. It is much more likely to be caused by cutaneous leishmaniasis, caused by a parasite conveyed in a sandfly bite, which would also fit with this patient’s travel history.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cutaneous_Leishmaniasis.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cutaneous_Leishmaniasis.jpg)

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man presents to the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic, requesting post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) following a high-risk encounter.

Under which of the following circumstances would PEP be recommended?
options: Following a bite which punctured the skin, but not deep tissue, from a person with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and a detectable viral load
A woman having receptive unprotected anal sex with a HIV positive man, who takes anti-viral therapy, and has a viral load of between 140-180 copies/ml one day ago
A woman performing fellatio with an HIV-positive man without ejaculation one day ago
A man having insertive anal sex with a woman from the UK one day ago
A woman receiving unprotected insertive anal sex from a man who has sex with men with an unknown HIV status
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E A woman receiving unprotected insertive anal sex from a man who has sex with men with an

unknown HIV status

Within the United Kingdom men who have sex with men are currently deemed to be high risk for transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), where the HIV status is unknown or known to be positive. In cases of unprotected receptive anal intercourse, but not vaginal intercourse, and an unknown HIV status, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended. The risk of transmission in vaginal or insertive anal intercourse is felt to be lower, and PEP is not required.

Ideally, according to guidelines, PEP should be started within 72 hours of exposure.

A Following a bite which punctured the skin, but not deep tissue, from a person with human

immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and a detectable viral load

Generally, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is not recommended following a bite as the risk of transmission is likely to be negligible unless the following three criteria are all met:

1. The person who performed the bites' saliva is visibly contaminated with blood 2. There is a known HIV viral load of over 1000 copies/ml 3. The bite has caused deep tissue injuries

These criteria are fortunately rarely met.

B A woman having receptive unprotected anal sex with a HIV positive man, who takes anti-viral

therapy, and has a viral load of between 140-180 copies/ml one day ago

Typically, PEP is not required if the if the HIV-positive partner is adherent to antiviral therapy and has sustained undetectable viral load (less than 200 copies/ml).

C A woman performing fellatio with an HIV-positive man without ejaculation one day ago

The rate of transmission is considered to be low risk, even if ejaculation occurred.

D A man having insertive anal sex with a woman from the UK one day ago

While the behaviour is considered to be high risk for HIV transmission, a woman from the UK is considered to be in the low-prevalence group and therefore, no PEP should be recommended.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man was admitted to the Emergency Unit with a headache and neck stiffness.

On examination, he was pyrexial 38.8 °C, with a BP of 95/60 mmHg and a pulse of 105/min and had a purpuric rash. There was significant neck stiffness with signs of meningism. Apparently, three other cases of meningococcal group C meningitis have been reported in the past two weeks at his university.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)140 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)157 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Lumbar punctureGram-negative diplococci identified

His girlfriend uses the oral contraceptive pill and refuses to use other forms of contraception.

Which of the following would be the most appropriate prophylaxis against infection for his girlfriend?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Single dose oral ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin as a single dose, rifampicin PO (4 doses over 2 days), and ceftriaxone (single dose IM) have been used as prophylaxis for contacts of patients with meningococcal infection. Data suggests that ciprofloxacin is the preferred first line option, and is now recommended by the HPA.

E IV Immunoglobulin

IV immunoglobulin treatment can be used in some exposure to viral pathogens such as rabies, but has no role in meningococcal meningitis.

A Rifampicin PO for 2 days

Although rifampicin is the second line option, in this case it may also act as an enzyme inducer, reducing the effectiveness of the oral contraceptive pill and risking potential pregnancy, and is therefore best avoided.

B Meningococcal group C vaccination

Whilst strategies for mass vaccination of populations where cases of meningococcus group C have proved effective in reducing new cases, antibiotic prophylaxis is the key step for close contacts.

C Penicillin V PO for 7 days

Penicillin V is the treatment for streptococcal throat infection and would not provide adequate prophylaxis against meningococcal group C species.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old Italian man presents to the gastroenterology clinic. He has a 6-month history of worsening abdominal pain. Over the past month, he has become noticeably jaundiced and has noticed dark urine and pale stools. He has also had two episodes in the past 2 weeks where he suddenly felt hot and dizzy. When this happened he noticed an itchy rash appear over all of his body, which only lasted for 24 hours. He has a past history of angina and is awaiting an angiogram. He takes aspirin, simvastatin and isosorbide dinitrate. He has no drug allergies. He moved to the UK from Italy 20 years ago and has not left the UK in the past 6 years. He has retired.

On examination, the only finding is marked tenderness in the RUQ.

His blood tests are as follows:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)127 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.9 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.6 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 4.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils3.1 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L

Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Bilirubin89 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)60 U/L10 - 40 U/L

An abdominal US reveals a large 5-cm cyst within the liver that is pressing on the common bile duct.

What is the most important investigation to arrange?
options: Aspiration of the cyst under US guidance
Stool microscopy for ova cysts and parasites
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E CT abdomen

The history is highly suggestive of hydatid cyst disease, which is due to infection with the helminth Echinococcus granulosus. The adult worm is found normally in the dog and sheep intestine and man is an accidental intermediate host. The infection is seen in Mediterranean areas, parts of East Africa, Australia and South America and the liver is the commonest organ involved. The cysts grow slowly, and a cyst is rarely diagnosed during childhood or adolescence unless the brain is affected.

In the liver, the pressure effect of the cyst can produce symptoms of obstructive jaundice and abdominal pain. Minor leaks lead to increased pain and a mild allergic reaction characterised by flushing and urticaria. Major rupture can lead to a full-blown anaphylactic reaction in some cases. WHO stage CE1 and CE3a cysts that are >5 cm may be treated with PAIR and adjunctive albendazole. In situations where albendazole treatment is not feasible, percutaneous treatment with PAIR (in the absence of adjunctive drug therapy) is an acceptable alternative approach.

CT scan has an accuracy of 98% and the sensitivity to demonstrate the daughter cysts. It is the best test for the differentiation of hydatid from amoebic and pyogenic cysts in the liver.

A Blood cultures

Blood cultures could be useful in investigation of pyogenic liver abscesses but are only positive in 30% of patients.

B Amoeba serology

Serology of amoeba is rarely available due to expenses and poor sensitivity.

C Aspiration of the cyst under US guidance

Aspiration may cause rupture of the cyst. Since the history is suggestive of hydatid disease, this could be very dangerous due to the risk of major rupture and anaphylaxis.

D Stool microscopy for ova cysts and parasites

If amoebic liver abscess was suspected; Latex agglutination assay is positive in more than 90% and stool microscopy may identify the organism (but unlikely with no symptoms of dysentery). Amoebic liver abscess is unlikely in this patient who has not been abroad in 6 years, and the history of urticaria and flushing combined with an eosinophilia are highly suggestive of hydatid disease.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of increasing breathlessness, dry cough and joint swelling. She has a painful left ear and when she breathes in she has sharp stabbing pains on the right side of her chest. She is also concerned about a rash that has started on both her arms and legs which burns her but is not itchy. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day and her mother died of lung cancer at the age of 43 years. On examination, she is febrile, with a temperature of 38.2 °C, respiration rate 20/min on exertion and her saturation is 94% on room air. She has symmetrical, mucocutaneous lesions, with concentric colour changes in most lesions. She has an erythematous left ear and occipital lymphadenopathy. She has coarse inspiratory crackles in the right lung mid-zone.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)93 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)16.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)84.6 fL76–98 fL
Sodium (Na⁺)131 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Urea6.3 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)93 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)135 IU/L5–30 IU/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Mycoplasma pneumonia

This lady has a typical history for mycoplasma pneumonia, the onset of which occurs over 1–3 weeks, often with a dry cough and fever. It is associated with bullous myringitis and erythema multiforme. She has a low haemoglobin, which points to mycoplasma pneumonia as it is associated with an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia due to the presence of anti-I antibody. The treatment of choice is a macrolide antibiotic.

B Small cell lung cancer

The rapidity of symptom onset and the associated fevers point towards an infectious aetiology for this patient’s symptoms. Typical extrapulmonary manifestations of small cell lung cancer include a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone hypersecretion (SIADH) and Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), but not erythema multiforme, myringitis or arthritis.

A Influenza A

Influenza is an RNA virus and the cause of pandemic flu. Presentation is typically with fever, myalgia, shortness of breath and a non-productive cough. The extrapulmonary symptoms described in this patient, such as erythema multiforme and myringitis, as well as the duration of illness, are not typical of influenza A.

C Tuberculosis

Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Primary TB most commonly affects the lungs and patients will present with a longer history of fever, weight loss and a productive cough, with or without haemoptysis. In addition, you might expect the question to highlight TB risk factors (such as contact with a known case or travel from an area with a high incidence).

D Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is a multi-system, inflammatory condition characterised by non-caseating granuloma formation. Typical presentation (Lofgren syndrome) is with bilateral hilar adenopathy, arthritis and erythema nodosum (the rash described in the question is erythema multiforme, which is not classically associated with sarcoidosis). In addition, patients with sarcoidosis do not usually have audible crackles on respiratory examination.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of increasing shortness of breath, cough and wheeze. He also complained of a rash, which appeared over the preceding 7 days. He had been travelling extensively in Cambodia.

On examination, he was pyrexial at 37.8 °C and had a linear erythematous rash over his groin and buttocks. He had an audible wheeze on auscultation of his chest.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)124 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils1.9 ×10⁹/L0.04 - 0.4 ×10⁹/L
Chest X-rayDiffuse pulmonary infiltrates

What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ivermectin

This patient has strongyloidiasis, a common infection in South East Asian countries such as Cambodia, and is caught by contact between bare skin and contaminated soil. Strongyloides is a parasitic roundworm that causes a linear skin rash, larva currens, which advances as the parasites move under the skin. The wheeze described here is Loeffler syndrome, caused by the migration of the filarial larvae towards the lungs. It can also cause gastrointestinal upset. Strongyloidiasis explains the significant eosinophilia seen in this patient. Diagnosis can be challenging and is usually achieved by finding larvae in the stool. Ivermectin is the appropriate treatment, and albendazole can be used as a second-line agent. All patients should be treated to avoid the risk of hyper- infection syndrome, where huge numbers of larvae cause pulmonary haemorrhage and migrate to organs that are not usually involved, such as the brain and liver.

E Prednisolone

Strongyloidiasis is caused by a parasitic worm, and therefore prednisolone will not treat this infection.

A Artesunate

Artesunate is a treatment for malaria: there is nothing in the history or investigations here to suggest this patient has malaria. His wheeze and linear rash, after travel to Cambodia, is typical for strongylodiasis. Artesunate would not treat strongylodiasis.

B Hydrocortisone

Hydrocortisone is not used in the management of strongyloidiasis: instead ivermectin is an appropriate first-line antiparasitic agent.

D Metronidazole

Metronidazole is not an appropriate treatment for a parasitic roundworm infection: the most appropriate agent would be ivermectin, or albendazole as second line.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old man from Brazil, who has been visiting his sister in England, attends the Neurology Clinic with a left-sided foot drop.

On examination, you note a number of hypopigmented lesions on his upper and lower limbs within which there is decreased sensation. The superficial nerves in his limbs are palpable and tender. He also has a non-tender ulcer on the palmar region of his hand.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)141 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most useful test to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Skin biopsy

The answer is Skin biopsy (Option B). Skin biopsy is the most specific investigation. It can reveal the presence of granuloma, neuritis and the presence of acid-alcohol-fast bacilli. Treatment is defined by the morphologic index, a measure of the number of viable bacilli per 100 bacilli seen in the lepromatous tissue.

E Culture of skin scrapings

Culture of skin scrapings (Option E) is incorrect.

This is used in the diagnosis of superficial fungal infections of the skin with both dermatophytes (such as Trichophyton and Microsporum species) and yeasts (such as Candida and Malassezia species).

A Lepromin test

Lepromin test (Option A) is incorrect.

The features above are highly suggestive of leprosy. While the lepromin test may be used to determine the type of leprosy a person has contracted, it is not used in confirming the diagnosis of leprosy.

C Heaf test

Heaf test (Option C) is incorrect.

The Heaf test used to be performed to determine whether a person has been previously exposed to infection with tuberculosis (TB).

The test required the injection of multiple areas on the forearm with tuberculin purified protein derivative. Interpretation was performed a few days later and graded on a scale ranging from negative to strongly positive. The production line of the Heaf test was discontinued in 2005, and the Mantoux test is now used instead.

D Mycobacterium leprae serology

Mycobacterium leprae serology (Option D) is incorrect.

While serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) may be useful in making the diagnosis, they are not always positive, especially in early disease.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old man presented to clinic with a 2-week history of intense itching, predominantly affecting the web spaces on his hands and his groin area.

On examination, there were excoriations and evidence of inflammatory papules.

Which of the following would be first-line treatment for this condition?
options: Topical permethrin, applied to the hands and groin area
Topical permethrin, applied to the whole body
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Topical permethrin, applied to the whole body

This patient has scabies, caused by mites which burrow into the stratum corneum to lay eggs. Standard treatment includes washing of all clothing and towels used in the 48 h before therapy, a bath and then the application of permethrin lotion to all skin areas. It should remain on the body for 8–12 h and then be repeated 1 week later.

A Oral antihistamine

This patient has scabies. Oral antihistamines can be useful for the associated pruritus, but they are not a first- line treatment for the condition. The most appropriate treatment would be topical permethrin, applied everywhere on the body below the neck.

B Oral permethrin

Permethrin is a treatment for scabies but it is not taken orally. It is applied topically everywhere including the face and scalp. Oral ivermectin can be used in cases of resistant scabies.

C Topical hydrocortisone

This patient has scabies. Although topical hydrocortisone may be somewhat useful in preventing itch, it does not treat the condition. The most appropriate first-line treatment would be topical permethrin.

D Topical permethrin, applied to the hands and groin area

This patient has scabies, and topical permethrin is the correct therapy; however, it should be applied everywhere, not simply to the affected areas.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman is referred by her General Practitioner to the Medical On-call Team with a 3-day history of frontal headaches and backache. She was seen two days previously and given a course of amoxicillin for a presumed chest infection. She has a past medical history of a right cerebellopontine angle tumour removed a year ago, with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted for hydrocephalus. On examination, her temperature is 38 °C. Fundoscopy is normal. Pupils are reactive and equally so to light. There is a right lower motor neurone cranial nerve VII palsy. Kernig’s sign is positive. She does not complain of photophobia or neck stiffness. The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable.

Which investigation is the most useful next step?
options: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E MRI of the brain

In a patient who has had a neurological procedure with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt in situ, a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis and/or an infected shunt is the most likely possibility. Obstruction of the shunt also needs to be excluded by MRI, given the headache. The histology of the original tumour is unknown, and tumour recurrence with malignant meningitis is also a differential to be considered. As the patient has had antibiotics for a few days, the likely diagnosis is partially treated meningitis. Therefore, gram staining of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is unlikely to reveal any organisms, although CSF analysis is the next logical step after imaging.

Ultimate eradication of the infection would involve the removal and replacement of the shunt.

A Blood cultures

While cultures should be taken as the patient is febrile, it is less likely to provide useful information since the patient has already been taking antibiotics, which will lower the yield.

B Chest X-ray

While a chest X-ray should be taken, given the initial concerns of a respiratory tract infection, it is not the most important investigation as the source of infection seems now to be less likely to be from the patient’s lungs.

C CT of the brain

A CT brain scan might show hydrocephalus. However, it provides much poorer views of the posterior fossa than MRI and may not reveal a blocked or partially blocked shunt, making MRI the clear preference in this case.

D Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level

While inflammatory markers will help monitor the response to antibiotic treatment, they are very non-specific and will not aid in the diagnosis. 73440

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man visits the doctor some 4-5 weeks after returning from a photography trip to mainland China. He admits to having swum in local water on particularly hot days. He has a history of fever, lethargy, myalgia, lack of appetite with vague abdominal pain.

On examination, you find evidence of an urticarial rash and he has a temperature of 38.1 °C. There is generalised lymphadenopathy and evidence of hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)118 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.2 ×10⁹/L (marked eosinophilia)4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)195 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)135 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Generalised increase in vascular / interstitial markings, lymphadenopathy

Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Katayama fever

Katayama fever occurs some 4-6 weeks after infection and is thought to coincide with initial egg release. High worm and egg stimuli are thought to lead to immune complex formation and a serum sickness type illness. Schistosomiasis may be diagnosed via a stool sample although it is not particularly sensitive, serology may be more useful but does not differentiate between acute and previous illness. Standard therapy for shistosomiasis is with praziquantel. Adjunctive corticosteroids are controversial, with some commentators recommending use in severe disease, although randomised controlled trial evidence is not easily accessible.

E Visceral leishmaniasis

Leishmaniasis is endemic to east Africa and India and more commonly presents in a cutaneous form, but visceral leismaniasis is an important cause of hepatosplenomegaly as untreated it is often fatal. Visceral leishmaniasis is a potential alternative diagnosis but the respiratory features seen here would be unusual.

A Weil’s disease

Weil’s disease is a severe form of leptospirosis. The organism are spirochaetes which are spread from rat urine into aquatic areas and then contact with abraded skin or mucosa leads to infection. Water activities, such as swimming outdoors as this patient has, can cause exposure. Following an incubation of one to three weeks, there is an abrupt onset of fever, headache, myalgia, dry cough and lethargy. This phase may resolve without treatment but can lead to an immune phase with jaundice, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, rash, meningitis and organ failure. It is unlikely to explain the hepatosplenomegaly and severe lymphoadenopathy. Weil's disease is also primarily associated with hepatic dysfunction and acute renal impairment not seen here.

B Dengue fever

Dengue fever is endemic in tropical South-East Asia, and outbreaks have also occurred in the tropical regions of Australia. The illness is a haemorrhagic fever, carried by the Aedes mosquito and is caused by the Dengue virus. It is characterised by fever, severe headache and facial flushing. In the early stages there is a lymphocytosis, with later lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and bleeding. Treatment is supportive.

D Typhoid fever

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella subspecies following typically 10-20 days. It causes a high fever, dry cough, malaise, abdominal pain following by green diarrhoea and hepatosplenomegaly and in the final stages can causes complications in multiple organs. There can be associated bradycardia as well. Diagnosis is by culture and treatment is usually with azithromycin but if severe then IV ceftriaxone. Typhoid fever is associated with neurological features including headache and confusion, accompanied by vague abdominal symptoms including constipation. The absence of diarrhoea and the presentation over the incubation period makes this a less likely diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 39-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal cramps and watery diarrhoea. His symptoms started two days ago, the morning after a family barbecue. He denies passing any blood in his stool and he has not been vomiting. He has a past medical history of borderline type II diabetes and mild gastric reflux, which is managed with omeprazole 20 mg once daily. On examination, he appears dehydrated. He is tachycardic and hypotensive with a blood pressure of 99/72 mmHg. His abdomen is soft, with generalised tenderness throughout, but no guarding or palpable masses.

Blood culture: Gram-positive rods

What is the most likely causative organism responsible for this patient’s diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Clostridium perfringes

C. perfringes is a Gram-positive rod that causes acute gastroenteritis following ingestion of contaminated food, particularly meat and poultry if it is not cooked thoroughly. The incubation period is usually between ten and 12 hours from ingestion. As this patient developed symptoms shortly after a barbecue and Gram-positive rods were identified in blood cultures, C. perfringes is most likely to be the correct answer.

E Campylobacter jejuni

C. jejuni is the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the United Kingdom. However, it is a Gram-negative rod with a 2- to 4-day incubation period, making this answer incorrect.

A Bacillus cereus

B. cereus is a Gram-positive rod that causes acute gastroenteritis. Symptom onset usually follows approximately 6–12 hours following ingestion and the most commonly associated food is contaminated rice. While this patient’s symptoms manifested in a similar time frame, they also appeared after a barbecue where undercooked meat is more likely to be the source of infection.

B Shigella dysenteriae

S. dysenteriae is a Gram-negative rod that causes shigellosis or bacillary dysentery characterised by bloody diarrhoea and passing mucus per rectum. In immunocompromised patients, it can cause systemic upset and complications include haemolytic uraemic syndrome. The bacterium isolated in this patient is a Gram-positive rod and the symptoms are less severe than those caused by S. dysenteriae, making this answer incorrect.

C Salmonella enterica

S. enterica causes acute gastroenteritis after consumption of contaminated water or food, most commonly poultry and eggs. It is a Gram-negative rod and, therefore, does not fit with the patient’s blood culture results, making it incorrect. 72458

questions.question:
A 41-year-old woman is seen in the Emergency Department with a 3-week history of increasing breathlessness. She has a non-productive cough and has been feeling hot and cold. She feels fine at rest, but after walking 10 yards she becomes dyspnoeic. She has suffered from rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years and is currently taking methotrexate, folic acid and prednisolone. She had a flare 4 months ago which required a course of etanercept. She is a non-smoker.

On examination, she is afebrile and comfortable at rest. She has candida of the tongue. Her respiratory rate is 20/min at rest, but on transferring from a chair to bed increases to 28/min. Saturations on room air are 92%. You ask her to take a few steps across the room and her saturation drops. Her heart sounds are normal and chest is clear.

Chest X-ray is shown below.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)98 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)142 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)85.6 fL76–98 fL

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Pneumocystis jirovecii

Given this patient’s recent treatment with etanercept and now the use of methotrexate and prednisolone, she is immunosuppressed. She has a classic history, and X-ray changes (perihilar intestinal mid and upper zone infiltrates) are consistent with Pneumocystis jirovecii.

Diagnosis is usually confirmed with cytological examination of broncheoalveolar lavage fluid, although this is not always necessary. First-line treatment includes high-dose co-trimoxazole.

Image source: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/pneumocystis-pneumonia-2?lang=gb (https://radiopaedia.org/cases/pneumocystis-pneumonia-2?lang=gb) Case courtesy of Dr Andrew Dixon, Radiopaedia.org, rID: 9613

B Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is a multi-system, inflammatory condition characterised by non-caseating granuloma formation. Typical presentation (Lofgren syndrome) is with bilateral hilar adenopathy, arthritis and erythema nodosum. The chest radiograph would most likely show hilar adenopathy.

A Tuberculosis

Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Primary TB most commonly affects the lungs, but almost all organ systems may be infected. A productive cough and history of previous TB exposure would be expected. Typical chest radiograph findings include apical cavitation, lobar consolidation and hilar adenopathy.

D Histoplasma capsulatum

Histoplasmosis in an infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Histoplasma capsulatum. Infection usually presents as a pneumonia, and associated changes on the chest radiograph would be expected such as hilar lymphadenopathy, lung nodules and lung cavities. Histoplasmosis is present worldwide but is most common in North America.

E Rheumatoid lung disease

Rheumatoid lung disease can take many forms, but most commonly it presents with interstitial lung disease or pleural disease. The typical presentation of rheumatoid-associated interstitial lung disease is with gradually progressive shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance and interstitial shadowing (lower zones) on chest

radiography. In this case the rapidity of symptom onset and the associated candidiasis point to an alternative diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female is referred to your Neurology Outpatients Clinic by the general practitioner (GP) as she is not able to smile. She has been generally unwell for about a month and has had malaise, a runny nose and muscle ache. She also noticed a rash on her arm about a month ago, but this has now cleared up. She is studying for her masters at Yale in Connecticut and does not drink, smoke or take drugs. On examination, her pulse is 48 bpm in sinus rhythm. She has no lymphadenopathy and her chest is clear. Heart sounds are normal. There is evidence of bilateral VIIth nerve palsy, but the remainder of the neurological examination is normal. You also notice that her right knee is swollen, but she feels she must have fallen on it.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)138 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes5.6 ×10⁹/L1.5–3.5 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)335 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Sinus bradycardia
Chest X-Ray (CXR)Normal

What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Doxycycline

This patient has early disseminated Lyme disease with evidence of peripheral nerve and musculoskeletal involvement. The treatment of choice would be a 2–3-week course of oral doxycycline (amoxicillin may be used instead in children and pregnant women for whom doxycycline is contraindicated).

E Aciclovir and prednisolone

This patient has Lyme disease. Valacyclovir and prednisolone would be the treatment of choice for Ramsay Hunt syndrome (reactivation of varicella zoster in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve). Typically patients would present with a unilateral facial nerve palsy, ear pain and a vesicular rash within the ear canal.

A Oral prednisolone

This patient has Lyme disease, and there is no evidence that steroid therapy is of benefit in treating Lyme disease. If this patient had presented with an idiopathic VIIth nerve palsy alone (Bell’s palsy), then the treatment of choice would be high-dose oral steroid.

B Intravenous hydrocortisone

This patient has Lyme disease, and there is no evidence that intravenous steroid therapy is of benefit in the treatment of this condition.

D Aspirin

This patient has Lyme disease and there is no role for aspirin in the treatment.

This patient has Lyme disease. Lyme disease is an infectious illness caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi. It is transmitted mainly through tick bites. It is very common in Connecticut, where it was given its name when it infected a large group of children in Lyme.

It initially presents with a slowly expanding skin lesion around the tick bite, erythemamigrans, malaise and joint aches. If not treated, neurological, cardiological and joint involvement can occur. The treatment of choice in those aged over 8 years and non-pregnant females is a 2–3-week course of doxycycline.

Bilateral facial weakness can occur with Lyme disease, myasthenia gravis, sarcoidosis and bilateral Bell’s palsy.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old man, who immigrated from Peru 2 months ago, comes to the Emergency Department with left- sided hip pain. He fell one week ago and claims that since then he has had difficulty walking, secondary to pain. He has had occasional headaches recently. He tells you that his appetite has been poor for three months and he has lost 4 stones in weight. He is a non-smoker and is currently a student. On examination, he is cachectic and febrile with a temperature of 37.7 °C. Pulse is 54/min, blood pressure (BP) 130/78 mmHg and you feel an enlarged spleen of 10 cm. His hip is generally tender but there is a full range of movement. He has an unsteady gait and has generalised weakness with normal tone.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)128 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Platelets (PLT)32 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
White cell count (WCC)3.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils1.4 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
X-ray of the spine and left hip AP (anteroposterior) and lateral were all normal

Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following investigations would be the gold standard to confirm the underlying pathology?
options: Ultrasound scan (U/S) of the left hip
Computerised tomography (CT) of the left hip
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Bone marrow aspiration and culture

This patient has brucellosis. Brucellosis is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by intracellular slow- growing bacteria. Transmission to humans occurs after occupational exposure or through ingestion of contaminated food products, especially unpasteurised milk products. It remains a significant health problem in many developing countries. This patient has a three-month history of weight loss, bone pain, splenomegaly and paradoxical bradycardia. Bone symptoms occur in 55% of patients with brucellosis, which often presents as pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO). Neutropenia and thrombocytopaenia are relatively common. Bone marrow aspiration and culture is the gold standard for diagnosis. Blood culture is positive in 15–70% of patients, but a high clinical suspicion is required as subculture often takes four weeks; sensitivity is less than that for bone marrow aspiration and culture and, as such, bone marrow tissue culture is preferred.

Treatment guidelines as issued by the World Health Organization (WHO) include doxycycline in combination with streptomycin or rifampicin for 6 weeks. Quinolones have also been tried.

E Oesophageo-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD) and biopsy

There are no symptoms to suggest an upper GI cause in this case apart from weight loss. If Whipple’s disease was suspected then biopsy would be helpful, but the absence of diarrhoea and the presence of hip pain make this unlikely.

A Ultrasound scan (U/S) of the left hip

If there was a suspicion of septic arthritis with acute fever, isolated joint pain and reduced range of movement, then joint ultrasound and aspiration would have been diagnostic.

B Computerised tomography (CT) of the left hip

If an underlying malignancy or abscess was suspected, then this would have been an appropriate investigation. An abscess might have been suggested by a swinging temperature and tenderness, but would not explain many features of the history such as the bradycardia and splenomegaly.

C U/S of the abdomen

Whilst the abdominal ultrasound would confirm splenomegaly it is unlikely to be helpful in this case. If renal cell cancer was suspected with more urinary symptoms as a cause for PUO, in an older patient this would be far more likely to be a diagnostic investigation.

questions.question:
A 47-year-old man, who recently emigrated from South Africa, presents to the Emergency Department with fatigue.

On further questioning, he also describes chronic productive cough and has had two negative blood films. He is found to be human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive. He takes no regular medications and has not sought medical treatment in many years.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)107 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)131 ×10⁹/L400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na)143 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.7 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)82 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
CD4 +count40 ×10⁶/L430–1690 × 10 6/
High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) chestHilar lymphadenopathy with multiple nodules and multifocal bronchiectatic changes
Blood sugar3.8 mmol/L3.9 mmol/L–5.6 mmol/L

Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Mycobacterium avium intracellulare

This patient has a productive cough, a CD4 count of < 50 and widespread lymphadenopathy within his chest. These findings are most in keeping with Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI). MAI is a non-tuberculous Mycobacterium. It is spread though inhalation and ingestion, as MAI is ubiquitous in the environment. Presentation is typically in two separate ways. In individuals with known lung disease, the presentation is

similar to that of tuberculosis, with cough, weight loss, upper lobe infiltrates and cavitations. In patients with no known lung disease, it typically presents with a persistent cough and purulent sputum, but without weight loss, fever and haemoptysis.

Radiographic changes in this presentation are as described in the case, with signs of bronchiectasis coupled with multiple nodules. This infection usually affects those with a CD4 count of < 50 cells/mm³; therefore, patients who fall into this group should receive MAI prophylaxis, usually with azithromycin. It is thought that transmission is not via person-to-person spread, but from waterborne sources. Patients are treated with a combination of antimycobacterial drugs, and in this case, antiretroviral treatment needs to be started.

E Toxoplasma gondii

T. gondii is a parasite found in poorly cooked meat and cat faeces. In immunocompetent adults, infection is usually asymptomatic, though it can cause retinal infection and scarring. In the immunocompromised, it can cause serious and life-threatening infection. Classically, Toxoplasma causes encephalitis or cerebral abscesses (shown as ring-enhancing lesions on imaging). Both of these are AIDS-defining illnesses in HIV-positive patients.

Toxoplasma can occasionally cause pneumonitis; imaging will demonstrate pulmonary infiltrates, but you would not expect toxoplasmosis to present with bronchiectatic changes, as seen here. Consequently, T. gondii is not the most likely organism in this case.

A Cryptococcus

Cryptococcus is a yeast, and although it can cause pulmonary disease (ranging from pneumonia to adult respiratory distress syndrome) in the immunocompromised, it is more commonly associated with meningitis or meningo-encephalitis. Cryptococcal meningitis is an acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)-defining illness.

Pulmonary Cryptococcus is unlikely to result in widespread lymphadenopathy nor in bronchiectatic changes, making it a less likely diagnosis. Cryptococcal chest infections typically present with an enlarging, asymptomatic nodule in the chest, with possible subacute consolidation and flu-like symptoms. The history of a chronic productive cough goes against this diagnosis.

B Cytomegalovirus

CMV is a virus and can be carried asymptomatically or may produce mild malaise and low-grade fever. However, in the immunocompromised, it can cause more serious consequences. CMV retinitis or colitis are both AIDS-defining illnesses. CMV can occasionally cause pulmonary disease in the immunocompromised, usually presenting with a dry cough, weight loss and fever.

Imaging will show diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, predominantly affecting the lower lobes, but the presence of bronchiectatic changes and lymphadenopathy is not in keeping with this diagnosis. Also, the history of productive cough would not be suggestive of CMV pneumonitis.

D Pneumocystis jiroveci

Commonly known as ‘PCP’ (referring to the former name for the organism), P. jiroveci is a yeast. In the immunocompromised, it can cause a pulmonary syndrome, and in HIV-positive patients, this is AIDS-defining. Typically, patients present with a dry cough, weight loss, low-grade fever and desaturation on exercise; it is unlikely that Pneumocystis would cause bronchiectatic changes, as seen here.

Imaging in Pneumocystis infection classically demonstrates pulmonary infiltrates; however, you would not expect to find bronchiectatic changes if this were a P. jiroveci infection on a background of a previously healthy respiratory system. Therefore, it is not the most likely causative organism. 2209

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV. He is treated with an abacavir containing HAART regimen. He attends his regular clinic appointment some 6 months later and complains of increased shortness of breath, with difficulty walking upstairs, and the fact that he wakes short of breath at night.

On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm. He has bilateral crackles on auscultation of the lungs.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)102 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)102 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)102 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Echocardiogram (ECHO)Cardiomyopathy

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor related cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor related cardiomyopathy

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) therapy is thought to reduce vascular responsiveness to acetylcholine, and hence lead to endothelial dysfunction. Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by HAART may also lead to decreased myocardial contractility. This is because cardiac myocytes can utilise energy less well, leading to decreased ejection fraction and dilative cardiomyopathy.

A Abacavir hypersensitivity

Abacavir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). It is recommended by the British HIV Association (BHIVA) in association with lamivudine as an alternative to Truvada as part of a HAART regime. Abacavir causes a hypersensitivity reaction in patients who are HLA-B5701 positive. However this would occur within 1–

2 months of starting treatment and in the UK all patients would be tested prior to initiation. It is typified by nausea, vomiting, malaise and fever, with or without a rash.

B Autoimmune cardiomyopathy

Cardiomyopathy may be associated with autoimmune disease (eg lupus, sarcoid, vasculitis). However you might expect the patient to have a history of autoimmune disease and in this case an alternative explanation is more likely.

C Viral myocarditis

Viral infection is a common cause of myocarditis and is certainly possible in this case. However you would typically expect to have a history of fever and possible recent viral symptoms (eg coryza, myalgia). In this case an alternative aetiology is more likely.

E Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

Although ischaemic heart disease is the most common cause of cardiomyopathy in the UK, our patient is young with no apparent vascular risk factors. In this context ischaemic cardiomyopathy would be uncommon. 20979

questions.question:
A 22-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a 1-day history of dark urine, 3-day history of headache, fever, feeling generally unwell and a 5-day history of diarrhoea and vomiting. He is a medical student who returned from an elective in East Africa one day ago. He had unprotected sexual intercourse with two fellow students while abroad, and just before returning to the United Kingdom, he did some freshwater swimming in Lake Malawi. He took doxycycline as malarial prophylaxis throughout the trip and had continued to do so since his return. He has no other complaints.

On examination, he has rigors, mild jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. He had tachycardia of 100 bpm and a temperature of 38.1 °C.

What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Artesunate

This patient has a malarial infection due to poor absorption of doxycycline, following a bout of diarrhoea and vomiting. His presentation with signs of possible blackwater fever (jaundice) is concerning and therefore, he needs aggressive treatment with intravenous artesunate and admission to the Intensive Care Unit.

D Praziquantel

Praziquantel is a treatment for Schistosoma haematobium, which is a fluke infection causing itchy rash, eosinophilia and Katayama fever 4–8 weeks post-exposure. Although this can be the result of swimming in freshwater, the patient’s signs and symptoms do not suggest this.

B Benzylpenicillin

Benzylpenicillin would be a treatment option for syphilis, which is not the diagnosis of this patient.

C Malarone

Malarone is a treatment for uncomplicated malarial infection. The jaundice found on examination and the presence of dark urine is suspicious of blackwater fever (intravascular haemolysis due to malarial infection), and therefore, treatment for uncomplicated infection is not appropriate.

E Stop doxycycline

Doxycycline is unlikely to be a cause of this patient’s presentation. The most common side effects are oesophagitis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and photosensitivity. Although the patient has had diarrhoea and vomiting (which may have been due to doxycycline or ingestion of pathogen during freshwater swimming), it is likely that this resulted in inadequate cover from doxycycline allowing malarial infection to occur. 72977

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of facial weakness. He also reported a 1-month history of joint pain and stiffness, particularly affecting his elbows and knees. Three months previously, he had had a flu- like illness with a red rash, fever and malaise. In the preceding 6 months he had travelled to Kenya and Massachusetts, USA for cross-country running competitions. On examination, he was afebrile, and there were no skin rashes. He had bilateral lower motor neurone facial nerve palsies. There was no evidence of active synovitis in his joints though his elbows appeared stiff and painful.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Lyme disease

Lyme disease is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted through tick bites. This patient has travelled to Massachusetts, an area known to harbour Lyme disease, and has been running in the countryside and therefore could have been bitten by a tick. The description of a rash consistent with erythema migrans, malaise and joint pain is classical. Weeks or months later the arthritis and neurological complications develop. Diagnosis is via serology for antibodies to B. burgdorferi. Treatment should be with 2–3 weeks of oral doxycycline.

E Secondary syphilis

Although syphilis can cause a rash and cranial nerve palsies, it would be extremely uncommon for it to cause bilateral facial palsies. It would also not explain the arthritis experienced by this patient. A much better explanation would be Lyme disease, contracted from a tick bite whilst running in Massachusetts. The rash could have been erythema migrans, and Lyme would also explain the myalgia, fever, malaise and arthritis. It is a known cause of bilateral facial palsies.

A Cerebral toxoplasmosis

There is no suggestion that this patient is immunocompromised, and therefore cerebral toxoplasmosis is extremely unlikely. Furthermore, cerebral toxoplasmosis would not explain his history of rash, malaise and joint pain. This presentation is more typical of Lyme disease, to which the patient was presumably exposed whilst in the countryside of Massachusetts, via a tick bite. This would explain the rash (erythema migrans), general malaise, joint pains and bilateral facial palsies.

B Leprosy

It would be very unusual for leprosy to cause facial nerve palsies without any sensory involvement, which is not reported in this case. Given the patient’s travel history and history of a rash, myalgia, malaise and joint pain, a diagnosis of Lyme disease is more likely. He is likely to have contracted this after a tick bite whilst running in Massachusetts.

D Reactive arthritis

Although this patient has arthritis and flu-like symptoms, he does not have urethritis or conjunctivitis/uveitis. Reactive arthritis would also not explain the rash, or his bilateral facial palsies. Bilateral lower motor neurone facial palsies are extremely uncommon. This patient’s constellation of symptoms and signs would be better explained by Lyme disease, caused by a tick bite. He may have contracted it whilst running in Massachusetts. The rash would be erythema migrans, and Lyme disease would explain his malaise, arthritis and bilateral facial palsies.

questions.question:
A woman who is 35 weeks pregnant presents feeling unwell with frequency and pain on urination.

On examination, she is pyrexial 37.9 °C and has suprapubic tenderness.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)111 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)145 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
UrineNitrites, blood and protein ++

Which of the following is the most likely infective organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Escherichia coli

E. coli is a Gram-negative bacterium which colonises the human gut. It is the most common cause of urinary tract infections. In the non-pregnant patient, empirical treatment for an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection is usually nitrofurantoin (contraindicated if eGFR <45 ml/min) or trimethroprim. Trimethoprim is contraindicated in the first trimester, however its use is considered safe in the second and third trimesters. Oral cephalexin is a commonly used alternative in the pregnant patient.

E Streptococcus agalactiae

S. agalactiae (group B strep) is a Gram-positive streptococcus which may colonise the human gut and genitourinary system. It is a recognised cause of urinary tract infection but is less common that the other listed organisms.

B Klebsiella

Klebsiella is a Gram-negative bacterium which colonises the human gut. Although this is a recognised cause of urinary tract infections, it is not the most common of the options presented.

C Proteus

Proteus is a Gram-negative bacterium which colonises the human gut. Although this is a recognised cause of urinary tract infections, it is not the most common of the options presented. Of note, Proteus is associated with renal calculi and is intrinsically nitrofurantoin resistant.

D Enterobacter

Enterobacter is a Gram-negative bacterium which colonises the human gut. Although it is a recognised cause of urinary tract infections, it is much less common than the alternatives. Of note Enterobacter spp. are intrinsically resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins (AmpC mechanism). 20977

questions.question:
You see a previously well 56-year-old Asian gentleman referred by his general practitioner (GP) with a 5-week history of abdominal pain, weight loss, night sweats and fever. He returned 6 weeks ago from Pakistan where he spends half the year. The pain is colicky and generalised and is not associated with meals or relieved by defecation. He has no vomiting or recent change in bowel habit, nor noticed per rectum (PR) bleeding or melaena.

On examination, he is wearing loose clothes and is afebrile. His abdomen is soft but tender in the right lower quadrant.

He has an abdominal ultrasound scan, which reports the presence of a stone in the gall bladder, but otherwise a normal scan.

Oesophageo-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD) is normal. Barium enema shows narrowing of the terminal ileum.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Tuberculosis
